archetypes.name: The Self
archetypes.oneLine: Totality of the psyche: the centre and circumference of conscious and unconscious.
body: The Self is where the map folds back on itself: the whole of the psyche, conscious and unconscious together, and the centre toward which a life is drawn. It is never met directly. It shows itself through images of wholeness, above all the circle and the quaternity.
On this globe the Self is the quiet field behind every other presence, reached through images as far apart as Upanishadic light and the alchemical stone.

definition.text: Psychologically the self is a union of conscious (masculine) and unconscious (feminine). It stands for the psychic totality. So formulated, it is a psychological concept. Empirically, however, the self appears spontaneously in the shape of specific symbols, and its totality is discernible above all in the mandala and its countless variants. Historically, these symbols are authenticated as God-images.

archetypes.name: Anima
archetypes.oneLine: The inner feminine in a man: life itself, personified as soul, muse and guide.
body: The Anima is the figure through which a man's unconscious turns toward him: siren and sophia, nymph and guide. She is watery, shifting and bipolar, and she draws the soul toward images rather than arguments.
She appears wherever a threshold is crossed by water, by song, by an unknown woman.

definition.text: Like the 'supraordinate personality,' the anima is bipolar and can therefore appear positive one moment and negative the next; now young, now old; now mother, now maiden; now a good fairy, now a witch; now a saint, now a whore.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶352

archetypes.name: Animus
archetypes.oneLine: The inner masculine in a woman: spirit, word and conviction.
body: The Animus is the masculine counterpart within a woman's psyche. It speaks as opinion and as spirit; at its best it is a bridge to the creative mind rather than a chorus of verdicts.
Its images are quicker and cooler than the anima's: the wind, the horse, the hero-lover who arrives from elsewhere.

definition.text: I have called the projection-making factor in women the animus, which means mind or spirit. The animus corresponds to the paternal Logos just as the anima corresponds to the maternal Eros.

archetypes.name: Child
archetypes.oneLine: Beginning and futurity: the newborn possibility of wholeness.
body: The Child is the archetype of what has not yet happened: the threatened newborn, the abandoned and invincible one, the little figure who turns out to hold the whole.
It is dawn-coloured in this atlas: soft, rising, unfinished.

definition.text: The child motif represents the preconscious, childhood aspect of the collective psyche.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶270

archetypes.name: Great Mother
archetypes.oneLine: Giver and devourer: earth, womb, cave and the realm of the Mothers.
body: The Great Mother holds both sides of origin: the nourishing earth and the swallowing dark. She is goddess, cave, well and tree before she is anyone's personal mother.
Her images sit at the instinct end of the spectrum: dense, warm and terrestrial.

definition.text: The “mother,” as the first incarnation of the anima archetype, personifies in fact the whole unconscious. Hence the regression leads back only apparently to the mother; in reality she is the gateway into the unconscious, into the “realm of the Mothers.”

archetypes.name: Hero
archetypes.oneLine: The struggle toward light: slayer of the dragon, bearer of renewed life.
body: The Hero is consciousness fighting its way out of the mother, the monster and the night. Solar and lucid, the hero's journey is descent and return; its dangers are inflation and identification with the light.
Its colour is the lucid white-gold of the risen sun.

definition.text: Taken purely as a psychologem the hero represents the positive, favourable action of the unconscious, while the dragon is its negative and unfavourable action—not birth, but a devouring; not a beneficial and constructive deed, but greedy retention and destruction.

archetypes.name: Kore
archetypes.oneLine: The maiden: youth before transformation, soul in bloom and in descent.
body: Kore is the maiden figure who is carried off, hidden or crowned: Persephone in spring and in Hades. She stands between the anima and the Self, both a young girl and an intimation of wholeness.
Her images are green and early, always about to change.

definition.text: The 'Kore' has her psychological counterpart in those archetypes which I have called the self or supraordinate personality on the one hand, and the anima on the other.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶306

image.title: Watercolor of Acropolis kore 679 by Émile Gilliéron (ArchEph 1887, pl 9)

archetypes.name: Mana-Personality
archetypes.oneLine: The charged, fascinating figure who holds numinous power over the ego.
body: The mana-personality is the figure who has absorbed more power than any person should carry: magician, prophet, hierophant. The ego is fascinated by such a figure and tempted to become it.
It sits between the wise old man and the hero, closer to the numinous than either.

definition.text: The hero is the protagonist of God's transformation in man; he corresponds to what I call the "mana personality." The latter has such an immense fascination for the conscious mind that the ego all too easily succumbs to the temptation to identify with the hero, thus bringing on a psychic inflation with all its consequences.

archetypes.name: Psychopomp
archetypes.oneLine: Guide of souls across thresholds: mediator between conscious and unconscious.
body: The Psychopomp leads across: Hermes with the dead, the bird that carries the soul out of the vessel, the unexpected companion on the road. It is a function more than a face, and it keeps the passage between worlds open.
Its colour is dusk, between the instinct and spirit ends.

image.title: Landscape with the crossing of the Styx label QS:Les,"El paso de la laguna Estigia" label QS:Len,"Crossing the River Styx"

archetypes.name: Shadow
archetypes.oneLine: The hidden, rejected side of the personality; everything we will not see in ourselves.
body: The Shadow gathers what a person or a culture pushes out of sight: the guilty, the primitive, the unlived. It is met first because it is nearest, and it tends to arrive as an enemy, a double, a dark beast or a stranger on the stair.
Its images are dense and low in the spectrum: dragons, apes, the blackened sun, the devil as the other half of the sacred.

definition.text: The first of these is the SHADOW, that hidden, repressed, for the most part inferior and guilt-laden personality whose ultimate ramifications reach back into the realm of our animal ancestors and so comprise the whole historical aspect of the unconscious.

archetypes.name: Syzygy
archetypes.oneLine: The divine pair: masculine and feminine joined as one image of wholeness.
body: The Syzygy is the paired opposite: king and queen, sun and moon, anima and animus held in one picture. In alchemy it is the conjunction at the centre of the work; in dreams it often arrives as a wedding.
Its images show up wherever a tradition has pictured the two as one.

definition.text: This youth is an animus-figure, the embodiment of the masculine element in a woman. Youth and young girl together form a syzygy or coniunctio which symbolizes the essence of wholeness (as also does the Platonic hermaphrodite, who later became the symbol of perfected wholeness in alchemical philosophy).
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶322

image.credit: Richard Mortel from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

archetypes.name: Trickster
archetypes.oneLine: Shape-shifter and fool: archaic, unconscious cunning that unsettles the order.
body: The Trickster is the joker and boundary-crosser: half divine, half beast, careless of rules and strangely generative. Out of his blunders something new, and sometimes something healing, gets made.
Mercurius, the quicksilver spirit of alchemy, carries the trickster into the laboratory.

definition.text: The trickster is a primitive 'cosmic' being of divine-animal nature, on the one hand superior to man because of his superhuman qualities, and on the other hand inferior to him because of his unreason and unconsciousness.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶473

archetypes.name: Wise Old Man
archetypes.oneLine: Spirit as meaning: the guide who appears when thought has run out.
body: The Wise Old Man is meaning given a face: a sage, a magician, a prophet, sometimes an animal or a gnome. He comes with knowledge the dreamer lacks, and with the reflection and resolve to use it.
He sits near the spirit end of the spectrum: fine, clear, cool.

definition.text: Mostly, therefore, it is the figure of a 'wise old man' who symbolizes the spiritual factor. Sometimes the part is played by a 'real' spirit, namely the ghost of one dead, or, more rarely, by grotesque gnome-like figures or talking animals.
definition.cite: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i) ¶397

occurrences.title: Adam as prima materia pierced by the arrow of Mercurius — Miscellanea d'alchimia (14th c.)
occurrences.label: Adam as prima materia pierced by the arrow…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Adam as prima materia, pierced by the arrow of Mercurius
body: Plate 131: "Adam as prima materia, pierced by the arrow of Mercurius. The arbor philosophica is growing out of him." It accompanies the anonymous text: "I pray you, look with the eyes of the mind at this little tree of the grain of wheat, regarding all its circumstances, that you may be able to plant the tree of the philosophers" (¶357) — which Jung reads as "active imagination as the thing that sets the process really going."

The plate fuses the anthropogony and the opus: the first man as raw matter, wounded by the Mercurial arrow, sprouting the tree of the philosophers. Its pendant (fig. 135) shows the skull of Eve with the tree growing from her head — "the mortificatio of Eve, the feminine aspect of the prima materia."

occurrences.title: Paracelsus: Adech the self, Scaiolae the four (De vita longa)
occurrences.label: Paracelsus: Adech the self, Scaiolae the four
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: one can almost speak of Adech as hostile
body: "In De vita longa, Paracelsus describes the 'four' as Scaiolae, but the self as Adech (from Adam=the first man). Both, as Paracelsus emphasizes, cause so many difficulties in the 'work' that one can almost speak of Adech as hostile" (¶150).

Jung invokes the pair while reading dream 11 (the croquet ball, "a symbol of wholeness, that is, of the self, here shown to be hostile to the intellect"): the alchemists already knew the self and its fourfold periphery as personified agents that resist and complicate the opus. Adech's Adamic etymology ties the self to the original man.

occurrences.title: Nebo hands Asurbanipal to the divine Queen of Nineveh — adoption hymn
occurrences.label: Nebo hands Asurbanipal to the divine Queen…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hymn of Nebo to Asurbanipal: 'Small wert thou, Asurbanipal, when I left thee with the divine Queen of Nineveh, Feeble wert thou... when thou didst sit in the lap of the divine Queen of Nineveh, Of the four udders that were placed in thy mouth thou didst suck from two, And in two thou didst bury thy face' (cw14 ¶384). Jung sets it in the adoption-complex of the Cantilena: the child hidden under the mother's skirt and drawn forth (an ancient rite, still practised by Bosnian Turks), Heracles 'adopted' by Hera, the 'tutelary Madonna' whose mantle adopts the believer (¶383-385). Ripley uses adoption to 'circumvent the scandal of the customary incest' (¶383): renewal through the mother without consummated incest.

occurrences.title: The Enigma of Bologna: epitaph of Aelia Laelia Crispis
occurrences.label: The Enigma of Bologna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Bologna (villa near the Porta Mascarella, 'Junonia' in Roman times)
occurrences.yearDisplay: first reported 1548 (Venice); claimed antique; probably a 16th-c. joke
occurrences.quote: Aelia Laelia Crispis, nec mulier, nec androgyna,... sed omnia.
body: The "monument" that never quite existed: "Aelia Laelia Crispis, nec mulier, nec androgyna, nec puella, nec iuvenis, nec anus, nec casta, nec meretrix, nec pudica, sed omnia... Nec coelo, nec aquis, nec terris, sed ubique iacet... Hoc est sepulchrum, intus cadaver non habens. Hoc est cadaver, sepulchrum extra non habens. Sed cadaver idem est et sepulchrum sibi" (¶51).

Jung calls it "sheer nonsense, a joke, but one that for centuries brilliantly fulfilled its function as a flypaper for every conceivable projection" (¶52). The commentary chain is the real locus: Maier and Barnaud (1597) alchemize it — uroboros "devours itself," "slays itself with its own dart, like the scorpion" (¶58); Malvasius (1683) collects 45 interpretations; Aldrovandus makes Aelia a hamadryad in the Junonian oak; Richard White reads the androgynous soul, "a girl has a masculine and a man a feminine soul" (¶92); Turrius, prima materia "conceived solely by the imagination" (¶94); Gevartius/Veranius, Eros; Schwartz (1727), the Church. Jung: "the philosopher stared at the paradoxes of the Aelia inscription, just as he stared at the retort, until the archetypal structures of the collective unconscious began to illuminate the darkness" (¶88).

occurrences.title: 'Horridas nostrae mentis purga tenebras, accende lumen sensibus!' — prayer of an alchemist-cleric from the nigredo
occurrences.label: Horridas nostrae mentis purga tenebras, accende…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Thus an old alchemist—and he a cleric!—prays: 'Horridas nostrae mentis purga tenebras, accende lumen sensibus!' (Purge the horrible darknesses of our mind, light a light for our senses!)" (cw12 ¶41).

Jung's dating of it to the work's first stage is exact: "The author of this sentence must have been undergoing the experience of the nigredo, the first stage of the work, which was felt as 'melancholia' in alchemy and corresponds to the encounter with the shadow in psychology." The prayer stands in the row of those who "seek direct experience of the eternal roots" when the Christian dominant decays.

occurrences.title: Alchemist meditating in the initial nigredo — Jamsthaler, Viatorium spagyricum
occurrences.label: Alchemist meditating in the initial nigredo
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The word meditatio is used when a man has an inner dialogue with someone unseen.
body: Plate 137: the artifex seated in meditation while the work stands in its initial blackness. Jung prints it against Ruland's Lexicon definition of meditatio as "an inner dialogue with someone unseen … with God, or with himself, or with his good angel" (¶390).

His reading: the alchemists' meditation was not cogitation but "a living relationship to the answering voice of the 'other' in ourselves, i.e., of the unconscious" — the technique Jung formalized as active imagination. Khunrath's companion injunction: "Therefore study, meditate, sweat, work, cook … so will a healthful flood be opened to you."

occurrences.title: Androgynous deity between the sun-serpent and moon-serpent — Late Babylonian gem
occurrences.label: Androgynous deity between the sun-serpent…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 183. Androgynous deity standing between male serpent with sun and female serpent with moon.—Late Babylonian gem
body: Late Babylonian gem: an androgynous god flanked by the male serpent bearing the sun and the female serpent bearing the moon.

Jung prints it at the pivot where the Gnostic myth — Nous and Physis — collapses into the single hermaphroditic natura abscondita of the prima materia: "the devourer is a sort of material earth-spirit, an hermaphrodite possessing a masculine-spiritual and feminine-corporeal aspect" (¶447). The gem shows the dual-serpent polarity carried by one androgyne — the pre-alchemical form of the rebis.

occurrences.title: Ayesha, 'She-who-must-be-obeyed' — Rider Haggard's She
occurrences.label: Ayesha, 'She-who-must-be-obeyed'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Rider Haggard's She (1887), the tale of the immortal, beautiful and deadly Ayesha, enters the Aion Conclusion through the English editors' footnote to Jung's remark on novelists' anima-figures: "[In English literature, perhaps Rider Haggard's She.—EDITORS.]" (cw09ii ¶424 fn 1). The attribution is theirs, not Jung's sentence — a distinction this vault keeps (Jung elsewhere, e.g. CW9i, uses She at length). Ayesha instantiates the anima as numinous seductress and devouring great-mother in one: the "glamorous, possessive, moody, and sentimental seductress" of ¶422, "working now for good, now for evil" as a numen (¶425).

occurrences.title: Brünnhilde as spirit-mother of Siegfried — Wagner's Ring
occurrences.label: Brünnhilde as spirit-mother of Siegfried
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Who am I If I am not your will?
body: The Valkyrie who favoured the brother-sister incest and banished for it; she sends Sieglinde east with the child — the night sea journey of the spirit-mother (¶555). Her avowal "Thine own self am I / In the bliss of thy love!" (¶606) makes her "the mother-sister-wife" (¶607); her flood-longing (¶608–609) gives the anima's water aspect, and the regeneration she offers "is a deadly embrace" (¶609). She stands to Wotan as the Kore of the Acts of Thomas, the "Mother of Wisdom" (¶560–563).

image.title: Siegfried and the Twilight of the Gods p 110

occurrences.title: Imago — Carl Spitteler's anima novel
occurrences.label: Imago — Carl Spitteler's anima novel
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Carl Spitteler's novel Imago (1906) — whose title Jung borrowed for his own 1912 word-association study of the unconscious imagos — is named by Jung as the supreme literary case of the anima: fn 1 to the Aion Conclusion reads "The outstanding example in Swiss literature is Spitteler's Imago" (cw09ii ¶424). The context is his claim that "anyone who has a little knowledge of belles-lettres will have no difficulty in forming a picture of the anima; she is a favourite subject for novelists, particularly west of the Rhine." Spitteler's Sidelike woman belongs to the glamorous, possessive seductress phenomenology of ¶422.

occurrences.title: The double salamander vision — young Benvenuto Cellini
occurrences.label: The double salamander vision
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The double vision of a salamander, of which Benvenuto Cellini tells in his autobiography, would be an anima-projection caused by the music his father was playing.
body: In the Kore essay Jung footnotes Benvenuto Cellini's autobiography: as a child, sitting by the fire while his father played lute and sang, Cellini saw in the flames a salamander — doubled. Jung's reading: "The double vision of a salamander... would be an anima-projection caused by the music his father was playing" (¶310 n5). A fire-creature seen double at music's onset: the anima as shimmering apparition in the element of passion, exactly the fishtail/nixie register of the maiden's "superhuman nature".

occurrences.title: Case Z — the 'unknown woman' dream series: eleven transformations of the anima
occurrences.label: Case Z — the 'unknown woman' dream series
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A white bird perches on a table. Suddenly it changes into a fair-haired seven-year-old girl and just as suddenly back into a bird, which now speaks with a human voice.
body: Jung's densest single anima dossier: eleven dream-fragments in which "a mysterious feminine being with qualities like those of no woman known to the dreamer" (¶370) recurs — a white bird changing into a seven-year-old girl and back; the blind dancer-daughter of a magician-prophet in an underground house; a Gothic Madonna holding "a sort of flame or a snake or a dragon"; a black-clad countess with red hair and pearls surrounded by the spirits of the dead; a female snake speaking tenderly "only 'accidentally' shaped like a snake"; a helpful bird; the unknown woman on the tip of a church-spire; an old attendant in an underground public lavatory at forty below; an over-life-size goddess clad in blue "looking like Athena"; and finally the woman standing in the church in place of the altar, veiled. Jung: "Every conceivable shade of meaning glitters in her, from the highest to the lowest" (¶370); as snake she plays the negative role, as bird the positive (¶376).

occurrences.title: Verlaine's 'Mon Rêve familier' — the unknown woman who understands (1866)
occurrences.label: Verlaine's 'Mon Rêve familier'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung closes the Miller drama with Verlaine's sonnet: "Je fais souvent ce rêve étrange et pénétrant / D'une femme inconnue, et que j'aime, et qui m'aime, / Et qui n'est, chaque fois, ni tout à fait la même / Ni tout à fait une autre, et m'aime et me comprend" — the recurring unknown woman, neither the same nor another, who alone cools the fevered brow "en pleurant."

He sets it as the poetic proof of his etymological thesis that to understand (verstehen, comprehendere, κατασυλλαμβάνειν) means "to stand round about something" — embracing — "and there is no doubt at all that nothing in the world ever embraces us so completely as the mother. When the neurotic complains that the world does not understand him, he is telling us in a word that he wants his mother" (¶682). The dream-woman who "me comprend" is therefore the anima-figure at her most maternal: the soul's understanding twin — precisely the figure Chiwantopel seeks as "she who will understand" (Ja-ni-wa-ma).
Verbatim: "et m'aime et me comprend" (¶682).

occurrences.title: Anima mundi, guide of mankind, herself guided by God — de Bry engraving for Fludd's Utriusque cosmi (1617)
occurrences.label: Anima mundi, guide of mankind, herself guided…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Engraving by J.-T. de Bry for Robert Fludd's Utriusque cosmi historia, captioned by Jung: "The anima mundi, guide of mankind, herself guided by God.". Set at the head of the dream series, it announces the guide-figure theme the dreams will develop.
Jung touches the anima mundi concept at cw12 ¶116: the alchemical vessel must be round "so that what comes out of the vessel shall be equally 'round,' i.e., simple and perfect like the anima mundi."

occurrences.title: Anima Mundi — Thurneisser zum Thurn, Quinta essentia (1574)
occurrences.label: Anima Mundi — Thurneisser zum Thurn, Quinta…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The idea of the anima mundi… coincides with that of the collective unconscious whose centre is the self
body: Plate 91: "Anima Mundi," from Thurneisser's Quinta essentia (1574). It illustrates the dream-40 commentary where the Pole is "the heart of Mercurius… Mercurius is the world-soul, and the Pole is its heart. The idea of the anima mundi (fig. 91; cf. fig. 8) coincides with that of the collective unconscious whose centre is the self" (¶265).

One of the load-bearing identifications of the whole volume: the Renaissance world-soul picture, the alchemical Mercurius, and Jung's collective unconscious with its self-centre are asserted as the same idea in three idioms.

occurrences.title: Antaeus and mother earth
occurrences.label: Antaeus and mother earth
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The giant Antaeus, invincible so long as he touched his mother earth, was strangled by Heracles holding him aloft.

Jung's reading: image of the temporary withdrawal into oneself — "in loving this inheritance they... turn back to the mother of humanity, to the psyche, which was before consciousness existed... It is the problem of Antaeus" (¶259).
Verbatim: It is the problem of Antaeus, who could only keep his giant strength through contact with mother earth. (cw05 ¶259).

occurrences.title: Anthropos as anima mundi with the four elements — Albertus Magnus, Philosophia naturalis (1650 ed.)
occurrences.label: Anthropos as anima mundi with the four elements
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Deus terrestris, Salvator, or filius macrocosmi… we can only compare with the Gnostic Anthropos
body: Plate 117: "Anthropos as anima mundi, containing the four elements and characterized by the number 10, which represents perfection (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)." Jung cites it in the vessel chapter as the goal-figure toward which the one vas tends — the stone as "an altogether mystical being… Deus terrestris, Salvator, or filius macrocosmi, a figure we can only compare with the Gnostic Anthropos, the divine original man" (¶335).
The decad (1+2+3+4) stamps the original man with the completed quaternity — the same 1-2-3-4 arithmetic as the Axiom of Maria in this very chunk (¶209).

occurrences.title: The Primordial Man as bait for the powers of darkness — Manichaean hook myth
occurrences.label: The Primordial Man as bait for the powers…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Manichaean myth behind Dorn's allegory: God threw out a hook — the Prim ordial Man him self as bait for catching the pow ers of darkness. "The Prim ordial Man was nam ed 'Psyche,' and in Titus of Bostra he is the world soul (psyche apanton). This psyche corresponds to the collective unconscious, which, itself of unitary nature, is represented by the unitary Prim ordial Man" (cw13 ¶450; Bousset, Hauptproblem e der Gnosis p. 178).

In the Valentinian revision (cw13 ¶452) it is no longer the Prim ordial Man but the fem inine Sophia-Acham oth who is cast in to the darkness — see sophia-achamoth-fall-plenum-2c. The hook with which God the Father catches the Leviathan is, in m edieval allegory, the crucifix (cw13 ¶450).
Verbatim: he used the Prim ordial Man as a bait for catching the pow ers of darkness. (cw13 ¶450ocr)

occurrences.title: Basilides: three sonships and the Passion as discrimination of natures
occurrences.label: Basilides — three sonships and the Passion…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Alexandria? (Basilides; reported in Hippolytus, Elenchos VII, 26-30)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Hippolytus reports Basilides: "Now Jesus became the first sacrifice in the discrimination of the natures, and the Passion came to pass for no other reason than the discrimination of composite things" — the motto of Aion itself (Elenchos VII, 27, 8).

The non-existent God begot a threefold sonship (spirit/soul/body), mirrored by three Christ-figures of Ogdoad, Hebdomad, and Jesus son of Mary. The third sonship lies hidden in amorphia — "formlessness," which Jung reads as practically the equivalent of "unconsciousness" (par. 119). Jesus is the prototype "awakener" of the seed slumbering in unconscious humanity.

occurrences.title: The man of light (phos) in Zosimos
occurrences.label: The man of light (phos) in Zosimos
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Zosimos the "man of light"... is simply called φως. He is the spiritual man who has clothed him self in Adam's body.
body: The man of light (ἄνθρωπος φωτεινός) imprisoned in Adam, whom Jung places behind both the Cabalistic Adam Kadmon and the alchemical filius philosophorum: "Originally this figure may have been the ανθρωπος φωτεινος, the 'man of light' who was imprisoned in Adam, and whom we encounter in Zosimos of Panopolis (third century)" (¶166). In Zosimos he is simply called φώς (man = ἄνθρωπος, light = φως, a wordplay Jung notes); "He is the spiritual man who has clothed himself in Adam's body. Christ let Adam approach and accepted him into paradise" (¶166 n.52; cf. Psychology and Alchemy ¶456).
The man of light is "an echo of the pre-Christian doctrine of the Primordial Man," popularized in the fifteenth century by Ficino and Pico della Mirandola and absorbed into alchemy.

occurrences.title: The man rising from the river — Splendor Solis, Plate VIII
occurrences.label: The man rising from the river
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: he is the "m an rising from the river," probably a reference to the vision of Ezra.
body: In the very old "Dicta Belini" (Belinus = pseudo-Apollonius of Tyana), Mercurius is "the man rising from the river" — "probably a reference to the vision of Ezra" (IV Ezra 13: the man coming up from the midst of the sea). "In Trismosin's Splendor solis (sixteenth century) there is an illustration of this" (¶268 n.33: Aureum vellus 1598, Tract 3, Pl. VIII of the 1920 facsimile).

Jung: "The idea itself may go back to the Babylonian teacher of wisdom, Oannes" — the Anthropos rising from the waters, one of Mercurius's avatars; he is also "the 'high man'" and the "Philosophic ambisexual Man."

image.title: Splendor Solis 08 resurrection out of swamp

occurrences.title: 'Gloria mundi': man the little world (microcosm, Musaeum hermeticum)
occurrences.label: Gloria mundi: man the little world
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Man is to be esteemed a little world, and in all respects he is to be compared to a world. The bones under his skin are likened to mountains, for by them is the body strengthened, even as the earth is by rocks, and the flesh is taken for earth, and the great blood vessels for great rivers, and the little ones for small streams that pour into the great rivers. The bladder is the sea, wherein the great as well as the small streams congregate. The hair is compared to sprouting herbs..." (cw13 ¶122).

Jung: the idea of man as microcosm "is a remnant of an original psychic identity which reflected a twilight state of consciousness"; personification and microcosm thinking underlie all alchemical projection (¶122, ¶123).

occurrences.title: The Anthropos beholding his reflection: shadow on earth, image in water
occurrences.label: The Anthropos beholding his reflection
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His shadow falls upon the earth, but his image is reflected in the water.
body: The Poimandres-type myth Jung rehearses from the Neopythagoreans: Nous, the god Anthropos, appears alongside the demiurge as adversary of the planetary spheres; he rends the sphere-circle and leans down to earth and water. His shadow falls on the earth, his image is reflected in the water; the elements kindle with love, and he, charmed by his own reflected beauty, descends — whereupon Physis locks him in her embrace, and from the union are born the seven hermaphroditic beings: the seven planets, the seven metals, the hermaphrodite Mercurius.

Jung: "In such visionary images … there is expressed the whole phenomenon of the unconscious projection of autonomous contents. These myth-pictures are like dreams, telling us that a projection has taken place and also what has been projected."

occurrences.title: Purusha, the Person 'no bigger than a thumb' — Shvetashvatara Upanishad
occurrences.label: Purusha, the Person 'no bigger than a thumb'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Upanishadic Person behind the sun: "There is one Rudra only, they do not allow a second, who rules all the worlds by his powers" (¶176); "I know this mighty Person (purusha), who is like to the sun, transcendent over darkness"; and the dwarf-formula: "That Person, no bigger than a thumb, the inner Self, seated forever in the heart of man" (¶178), matched by the Katha Upanishad: "burning like flame without smoke... that is Self" (¶179). The paradox completes: "Without feet, without hands, he moves, he grasps... Smaller than small, greater than great" (¶182).

Jung's reading: the All-Creator behind the winged sun (fig. 11, Bes with Horus-eyes); the thumb-sized creative Person belongs with "Tom Thumbs, dactyls, and Cabiri" — personifications of creative forces with phallic aspect (¶180). The same disparity of great and small reappears in Faust's key that "leads you to the Mothers."

occurrences.title: Purusha Sukta — the cosmic Man sacrificed to create the worlds (Rig-Veda X,90)
occurrences.label: Purusha Sukta — the cosmic Man sacrificed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Purusha Sukta: the primal Man who "encompassed the earth on all sides and ruled over the ten-finger place" is itself sacrificed — "the gods sacrificed with him, and the saints and the sages" — and from the offering arise the hymns, metres, animals, and the cosmos ("from his mind the moon; from his eye the sun; from his breath Vayu; from his navel the atmosphere; from his head the sky; from his feet the earth"). Adjacent, Vishvakarman makes the world from an unknown tree ("What was the wood, what was the tree, from which heaven and earth were hewn?" ¶646).

Jung reads it as a psychological cosmogony (¶652): Purusha is "a sort of Platonic world-soul" (¶649) with maternal character — "the encompasser and the encompassed, mother and unborn child, an undifferentiated, unconscious state of primal being" (¶650) that must be sacrificed so that "discriminated entities—i.e., conscious contents—may come into being." Anchors the cosmic-sacrifice argument of ch. VIII.
Verbatim: "The world comes into being when man discovers it. But he only discovers it when he sacrifices his containment in the primal mother" (¶652).

occurrences.title: The three manifestations of the Anthropos: body, soul, spirit — Ripley Scrowle
occurrences.label: The three manifestations of the Anthropos
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 196. The three manifestations of the Anthropos during his transformation: body, soul, spirit. Below, dragon and toad as preliminary forms.
body: Plate from the English Ripley Scrowle rolls (1588): the Anthropos shown in his three transformations — body, soul, spirit — with dragon and toad beneath as the preliminary (animal) forms.

Jung sets it against Zosimos' doctrine of the Man of Light who puts on the earthly Adam, and against the homo philosophicus "who is the One, i.e., the tincture or elixir of life, but … also the everlasting inner man, identical or at least connected with the Anthropos" (¶476). The same Scrowle carries the plumed king plucking his own feathers for food (fig. 228).

occurrences.title: Abarbanel: Messiah expected at the Jupiter-Saturn conjunction in Pisces
occurrences.label: Abarbanel — Messiah expected…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Ferrara (Ma'yene ha-Yeshu'ah on Daniel, 1551); Abarbanel b. Lisbon 1437, d. Venice 1508

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Abarbanel's commentary on Daniel expects the Messiah "when there is a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in Pisces": in anno mundi 2365 such a great conjunction stood three years before Moses' birth (legendary); the House of the Fishes is "the house of justice and of brilliant splendour". Saturn is the star of Israel, Jupiter the "king (of justice)."
At par. 168 Jung adds that in Abarbanel's Mashmi'a Yeshu'ah the Messiah ben Joseph "actually is the Antichrist." Cf. R. Abraham ben Hiyya (Messiah in 1464) and Solomon ben Gabirol.

occurrences.title: Nostradamus, letter to Henry II: the second Antichrist and the year 1792
occurrences.label: Nostradamus, letter to Henry II
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: France (letter of June 27, 1558, to Henry II)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Nostradamus' astrological letter: from 1792, "the infernal power shall rise against the Church of Jesus Christ. This shall be the second Antichrist" — a Northern king, an eleven-year persecution, the sanctuary destroyed by paganism (cw09ii pars. 151-152).

Jung (par. 150): the course of Christian religious history "could have been predicted more or less accurately... from the precession of the equinoxes through the constellation of Pisces." With Nostradamus' prediction "he placed himself firmly in the antichristian phase and served as its mouthpiece" (par. 159).

occurrences.title: Pierre d'Ailly, Concordantia: change of sects and the coming of Antichrist
occurrences.label: Pierre d'Ailly, Concordantia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Basing himself on Albumasar, d'Ailly tied the eighth coniunctio maxima (calculated for 1693) and the completion of ten Saturn revolutions in 1789 to "many and great and marvellous changes... especially as concerns law-giving and religious sects": "after the sect of Mahomet none other will come save the law of the Antichrist".

Jung: "Fantasy could do the rest, for the archetype had long been ready and was only waiting for the time to be fulfilled" (par. 156). Saturn periods: 289 Manichaeism, 589 Islam, 1189 Innocent III, 1489 schism.

occurrences.title: Jackal-headed Anubis bending over a mummy — Thebes, XX Dynasty
occurrences.label: Jackal-headed Anubis bending over a mummy
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXXIIa: Anubis the corpse-devourer and psychopomp ministering to the dead.

Jung's reading: "Here the dogs and jackals, devourers of corpses by night, assist in the reconstitution or reproduction of Osiris" (¶354) — the necrophagous helper whose deeper meaning Creuzer reads in the dog-star at solstice: "death being made equal to the sun at its highest point", i.e. entry into the mother's womb for rebirth (¶354).
Verbatim: Actually Isis collected the pieces together again with the help of the jackal-headed Anubis. (cw05 ¶354).

occurrences.title: The initiate elected Helios — Apuleius' Isis-mysteries apotheosis
occurrences.label: The initiate elected Helios
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome/Corinth (Isis mysteries as narrated in Metamorphoses XI)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: In the Metamorphosis of Apuleius, the initiate — "an ordinary human being" — is elected to be Helios: "he is crowned with a crown of palms and clad in the mystic mantle, whereupon the assembled crowd pays homage to him" (¶229). "The suggestion of the crowd brings about his identity with the god."

Jung's reading: prime example of identification with the cult-hero within the transformation experience; and in the 1936 essay, the ritual transformation into the Deity "is attested by Apuleius in the Isis mysteries, and moreover in the form of a Helios apotheosis" (¶107) — the frame for reading his 1906 solar-phallus patient, who felt himself the sun-god creating the wind.

occurrences.title: Apuleius' prayer to the Queen of Heaven (Isis as Venus and Proserpina)
occurrences.label: Apuleius' prayer to the Queen of Heaven
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: he associates "heavenly Venus" with "Proserpina, who strikest terror with midnight ululations
body: Apuleius' "magnificent prayer to the Queen of Heaven" in the Isis book of the Metamorphoses, which associates "heavenly Venus" with "Proserpina, who strikest terror with midnight ululations" ("Nocturnis ululatibus horrenda Proserpina").

Jung's reading: "it was the terrifying paradox of the primordial mother-image" — the loving and the terrible mother united in one figure; entering the realm of the syzygies leads "directly to the experience of individuation, the attainment of the self" (¶194).

occurrences.title: Ardhanari: Shiva and Parvati united — polychrome clay figure
occurrences.label: Ardhanari — Shiva and Parvati united
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXIII: the half-male, half-female Ardhanari — Shiva has "given one half of his body to his wife Parvati as a dwelling-place".
Jung's reading: the god as both male and female, image of continuous cohabitation whose architectural form is the lingam-in-yoni (¶306).
Verbatim: The god Shiva, as Mahadeva and Parvati, is both male and female: he has even given one half of his body to his wife Parvati as a dwelling-place (pl. XXIII). (cw05 ¶306).

occurrences.title: Philoctetes wounded at the shrine of Chryse — the wounded-king prototype
occurrences.label: Philoctetes wounded at the shrine of Chryse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Chryse (island and nymph of the same name)
occurrences.quote: the prototype of the wounded and ailing king, a motif that is continued in the legend of the Grail and in alchemical symbolism
body: Sailing for Troy, the Greeks must sacrifice at the hidden shrine of the nymph Chryse; only Philoctetes knows the way. A scholiast records what the island cost him: Chryse offered the hero her love, and on being scorned cursed him — the snake-bit, unhealing foot-wound whose stench makes his companions maroon him.

Jung draws the line forward explicitly: "Philoctetes, like his forerunner Heracles, is the prototype of the wounded and ailing king, a motif that is continued in the legend of the Grail and in alchemical symbolism." The rejected goddess and the incurable wound are one complex — the wounded king as the land's sickness.

occurrences.title: Heart pierced by triple beams ending in arrows — stigmatization of Anne Catharine Emmerich
occurrences.label: Heart pierced by triple beams ending in arrows
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The wounding and painful shafts do not come from outside, through gossip, which only pricks us on the surface, but from the ambush of our own unconscious.
body: The nun's heart-trouble "as if her heart were continually pierced by arrows" (¶435); Jung reads stigmatization as "an incubation with the Saviour, a slight modification of the ancient conception of the unio mystica as cohabitation with the god" (¶438) — the wounding shafts "do not come from outside … but from the ambush of our own unconscious. It is our own repressed desires that stick like arrows in our flesh."

occurrences.title: Dorn's 'Tour of the World' and 'Way of Truth' — Speculativae philosophiae
occurrences.label: Dorn's 'Tour of the World' and 'Way of Truth'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Hence it has come about that men have built for themselves a great Workshop on the left-hand side of the road... presided over by Industry.
body: In his Speculativae philosophiae (Theatrum chemicum I, 1602, pp. 286ff) the Frankfurt physician Gerard Dorn describes the "Mundi peregrinatio, quam erroris viam appellamus" — the tour of the world which we call the way of error: mankind builds a great Workshop on the left-hand side of the road, presided over by Industry, then crosses "the bridge of infirmity" to a great Hospital presided over by Medicine. The "way of truth", the right way, leads to "the camp of Wisdom" where the traveller is "refreshed with food far more powerful than before", beside "a stream of living water flowing with such wonderful artifice from the mountain peak. (From the Fountain of Wisdom the waters gush forth.)" Jung found in Dorn the exact map of his own mountain dream (¶335-337) — the archetype of the two ways verified in a text he had never read.

occurrences.title: Celestial seed fetched by the ascending elements — Dorn, Physica genesis
occurrences.label: Celestial seed fetched by the ascending elements
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)
jung.locator: tail of ch. XIV, before ¶421 (pdf p281)

body: Gerhard Dorn's Physica genesis (in Theatr. chem. I; Jung's fn 119 cites p. 391) describes the volatilized elements rising to fetch seed from the stars and carrying it back down into the elements: "But during their ascent the volatilized elements take 'from the higher stars male seeds, which they bring down into the four matrices, the elements, in order to fertilize them spagyrically'" (cw09iiend of "The Structure and Dynamics of the Self"). Jung frames this celestial insemination as the "circular distillation" that closes the opus into a cycle — the physical projection of a psychic to-and-fro between spirit and nature.

occurrences.title: Jung's mountain dream — the brook with metallic shimmer and two serpent paths
occurrences.label: Jung's mountain dream
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I was climbing slowly and toilsomely up a mountain... Night was coming on, and I saw, on the dark slope opposite, a brook flowing down with a metallic shimmer, and two paths leading upwards, one to the left, the other to the right, winding like serpents.
body: Jung's own dream, told to prove the method: climbing a mountain, he finds himself only on the edge of a plateau; the real crest rises far off. Night falls. "On the dark slope opposite, a brook flowed down with a metallic shimmer, and two paths leading upwards, one to the left, the other to the right, winding like serpents"; to the right on the crest a hotel; below, the brook runs left under a bridge. "Not long afterwards" he found the same structure in Gerard Dorn's Speculativae philosophiae as the Mundi peregrinatio and the Via veritatis — Workshop and Hospital on the left, the camp of Wisdom and the Fountain of Wisdom on the right (¶335-336). For Jung the point is methodological: an apparently "individual" image is "an archetypal image such as can be reproduced over and over again in any age and any place" (¶337).

occurrences.title: The heavenly journey — Platonis liber quartorum (Harranite treatise)
occurrences.label: The heavenly journey — Platonis liber quartorum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Harran? → Latin print (Theatrum chemicum V, Strasbourg)
occurrences.yearDisplay: printed 1659 (Theatrum chemicum V, p. 145); Harranite material older

jung.locator: fn 28 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p691)

body: Jung fixes the earliest appearance of the alchemical journey motif: "The earliest appearance of this motif is probably the heavenly journey of Plato (?) in the Harranite treatise 'Platonis liber quartorum' (Theatrum chemicum, V, p. 145)." The heavenly wanderings of the soul — a "special instance of the journeys of the hero" — "was continued as the peregrinatio in alchemy" (cf. Psychology and Alchemy, par. 457). The treatise, spuriously fathered on Plato, carries the Sabian-Harranite astronomy of the soul into Latin alchemy.
Verbatim (fn 28): "The earliest appearance of this motif is probably the heavenly journey of Plato (?) in the Harranite treatise “Platonis liber quartorum” (Theatrum chemicum, V, p. 145)."

occurrences.title: Poliphilo's ascent to the Venus mystery and descent to daily life — Hypnerotomachia
occurrences.label: Poliphilo's ascent to the Venus mystery…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung reads the whole first part of the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili as 'the dreamer's ascent to a world of gods and heroes, of his initiation into a Venus mystery, followed by the illumination and semi-apotheosis of Poliphilo and his Polia'; the smaller second part is disenchantment and 'a descent to earth, to the reality of daily life' (cw14 ¶297). Whether Poliphilo 'preserve[d] in secret the nature of the heavenly centre which he acquired by the ascent' Jung doubts. Still: 'his exciting adventure has left us a psychological document which is a perfect example of the course and the symbolism of the individuation process' (¶297).

occurrences.title: Stages of transformation in the Ripley 'Scrowle'
occurrences.label: Stages of transformation in the Ripley Scrowle
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Ripley Scrowle — the vertically unrolling English picture-scroll (George Ripley, d. ~1490; variants produced into the 17th century) that shows the alchemical stages of transformation as a sequence of images from vessel to hermaphrodite — is Jung's chief example of the opus rendered as pictures: "the stages of transformation have been depicted over and over again, above all in the Ripley 'Scrowle' and its variants. These should be understood as indirect attempts to apprehend the unconscious processes of individuation in the form of pictures" (cw09ii ¶421). The scroll is thus read as a pre-psychological individuation map.

occurrences.title: Circular distillation repeated a thousand times — Rupescissa, quinte essence
occurrences.label: Circular distillation repeated a thousand times
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)
jung.locator: tail of ch. XIV, before ¶421 (pdf p281)

body: The Franciscan prophet-alchemist Johannes de Rupescissa (De consideratione quintae essentiae, ~1351) prescribed that the distillation of the fifth essence be endlessly iterated: "This is the 'circular distillation' [119] which Rupescissa says must be repeated a thousand times" (cw09ii; fn 120 cites the Lyons 1581 quinte essence, p. 56). Jung uses the thousand-fold repetition to mark the difference between a mere technical procedure and the circular opus: the iteration is the practical form of the ascent-descent cycle, the physical shadow of an individuation process that never completes in one pass.

occurrences.title: Ascent and descent in the Tabula Smaragdina (Emerald Tablet)
occurrences.label: Ascent and descent in the Tabula Smaragdina
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabic sources (Balinas tradition) -> Latin Europe (Ars chemica, Strasbourg 1566)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Tabula Smaragdina — the shortest and most-cited text of the Hermetic corpus, known from Arabic sources (pseudo-Apollonius/Balinas) and transmitted to Latin Europe — carries in its "ascend... and again descend" formula the root scheme of the circular opus. Jung names it the locus classicus of the idea: "The basic idea of ascent and descent can be found in the Tabula Smaragdinaj [sic] and the stages of transformation have been depicted over and over again" (cw09ii ¶421). He treats the Tablet not as chemistry but as the textual seed of a picture-series tradition running to the Ripley Scrowle — "indirect attempts to apprehend the unconscious processes of individuation in the form of pictures."

occurrences.title: The ashvattha rooted in heaven — Bhagavadgita XV
occurrences.label: The ashvattha rooted in heaven — Bhagavadgita XV
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Krishna: "I am the Him alaya am ong m ountains and the ashvattha am ong trees"; the Gita's fifteenth chapter sings the fig tree "Rooted in heaven, / Its branches earthward", its leaves songs of the Vedas, its buds the sense-objects, its roots "Reaching dow nward / In to this w orld, / The roots of m an's action" (cw13 ¶412).

Jung: "The ashvattha (Ficus religiosa) pours dow n from above the drink of im m ortality, som a" (¶412); n.12 collects the nyagrodha of the Shatapatha-Brahm ana and Chhandogya Upanishad VIII, 5, 3, and Plato's "heavenly plant" (Tim aeus 90A). The Gita's inverted tree is "a process of enlightenm ent... through know ledge" — the Veda as deliverance (cw13 ¶413).
Verbatim: There is a fig tree In ancient story, The giant Ashvattha, The everlasting, Rooted in heaven, Its branches earthward (cw13 ¶412)

occurrences.title: Gnostic gem — she-ass suckling her foal, sign of Cancer, 'Dei filius'
occurrences.label: Gnostic gem — she-ass suckling her foal, sign…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A Gnostic gem showing "a she-ass suckling her foal, surmounted by the sign of Cancer and the inscription 'D.N.-IHV.XPS.': Dominus noster Jesus Christus, to which is added, 'Dei filius'" (¶622). The Christ-child is figured as an ass's foal at the udder — Cancer, the zodiacal sign of birth/nursing, presiding.

Jung deploys it inside the Dionysus-Christ argument: Justin Martyr's indignant observation that the Christian legend's connections with Dionysus "are unmistakable (e.g., the miracle of the wine)"; the ass as steed of Silenus; the ass pertaining to the "second sun," Saturn, "the star of Israel and therefore to some extent identical with Yahweh" (¶622). The gem sits between the Palatine mock-crucifixion and the Dionysian vine of Hölderlin's "Man" — the god of the vine nursed by the beast of the second sun.
Verbatim: "There is a Gnostic gem showing a she-ass suckling her foal, surmounted by the sign of Cancer and the inscription 'D.N.-IHV.XPS.'" (¶622).

occurrences.title: The three-legged ass in the ocean, with the golden horn — Bundahish XIX
occurrences.label: The three-legged ass in the ocean…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The cosmological unicorn of Zoroastrianism: "it stands amid the wide-formed ocean, and its feet are three, eyes six, mouths nine, ears two, and horn one, body white, food spiritual, and it is righteous … The one horn is as it were of gold and hollow, and a thousand branch horns have grown upon it … With that horn it will vanquish and dissipate all the vile corruption due to the efforts of noxious creatures" (¶535). When it stales, "all the sea-water will become purified"; ambergris is its dung.

Jung: "as a cosmological being, it recalls the monstrous personifications of the prima materia (fig. 256) in Arabic alchemy" (¶536); the ass and the tree Gokard "both represent the power of life, procreation, and healing. This is a truly primitive equation: both are or have mana" (¶537); and "the ass is a daemon triunus, a chthonic trinity … identified with Mercurius, salt, and sulphur" (¶539). With Og, the re'em, Behemoth and Leviathan it personifies "the daemonic forces of nature" (¶547).

occurrences.title: The dogma of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin (1950)
occurrences.label: The dogma of the Assumption of the Blessed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The 1950 dogma that elevated "the Christian version of the mother archetype... to the rank of a dogmatic truth". Jung's ADDENDUM (asterisk-marked, ¶s unnumbered in this OCR): the Queen of Heaven has shed her Olympian qualities; "Isis and the Horus-child [are] iconological exemplars", and "the ascension of Semele, the originally mortal mother of Dionysus, likewise anticipates the Assumption" — her son being a dying and resurgent god, youngest of the Olympians; Semele herself an earth-goddess, as Mary is "the earth from which Christ was born".

Jung's reading: proclaimed in the hydrogen-bomb age, the Assumption is "a compensating symptom" — a heavenly figure split off from the chthonic realm taking counter-position to the titanic forces of the earth; understood symbolically it acknowledges matter ("utriusque capax") and anticipates the union of spirit and matter that alchemy had foreshadowed in the hieros gamos of opposites and science now approaches from the other side (synchronistic phenomena, Rhine).

occurrences.title: Androgyne Atman creates the world and fire by rubbing — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad I.4
occurrences.label: Androgyne Atman creates the world and fire…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Atman, "as big as a man and woman joined together", divides in two; begets men, cattle, horses, goats, sheep, "everything down to the ants"; then rubs hands before mouth and brings forth fire from "the fire-hole (yoni)".
Jung's reading: "a monument of Indian literature which describes this conversion of libido into fire-making" (¶227) — the fire-hole (yoni) in the mouth, fire as child of the conjunctio.
Verbatim: Thereupon he rubbed thus [holding his hands before his mouth]. From his mouth, the fire-hole (yoni), and from his hands, he brought forth fire. (cw05 ¶227).

occurrences.title: Kena Upanishad — 'know that as Brahman'
occurrences.label: Kena Upanishad — know that as Brahman
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'By whom willed and directed does the mind fly forth? By whom commanded does the first breath move?... The hearing of the ear, the thinking of the mind, the speaking of the speech... That which speech cannot express, by which speech is expressed... know that as Brahman' (¶348). Jung sets it beside Yajnavalkya's Brihadaranyaka definition of the inner controller (¶349) and Monoïmos' 'Seek him from out thyself' (¶347) — the purusha/atman teaching as the tradition through which alone the self becomes conscious (¶257). Parallels: atman-self-light-yajnavalkya-brihadaranyaka-700bc, monoimos-monad-iota-2c.

occurrences.title: 'Self is his light' — Yajnavalkya, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
occurrences.label: Self is his light
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Self is his light. It is by the light of the self that a m an rests, goes forth, does his work and returns.
body: The saying of the wise Yajnavalkya with which The Spirit Mercurius ends: "When all visible lights are extinguished one finds... the light of the self. 'What then is the light of man? Self is his light. It is by the light of the self that a man rests, goes forth, does his work and returns.'"

Jung sets it beside Augustine's cognitio matutina and the days of creation: "Thus, with Augustine, the first day of creation begins with self-knowledge, cognitio sui ipsius, by which is meant a knowledge not of the ego but of the self, that objective phenomenon of which the ego is the subject" (¶301). His footnote finds here the source of the lapis designation "filius unius diei" (cf. Mysterium Coniunctionis).

occurrences.title: Attis castrates himself beneath the pine — Phrygian cult
occurrences.label: Attis castrates himself beneath the pine
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Attis, son and lover of Cybele, wearing the pileus of Men, Mithras and the dadophors; driven mad by his mother he mutilates himself under a pine-tree and is hanged there in effigy (fig. 42). Fig. 20: Cybele and Attis, Roman coin.

Jung's reading: "incest leads logically to ritual castration in the Attis-Cybele cult" (¶299); "he did so because the tree has a maternal significance" (¶321); the self-castration as expiation of the incestuous longing.
Verbatim: Hence when Attis castrates himself under a pine-tree, he did so because the tree has a maternal significance. (cw05 ¶321).

occurrences.title: Heliopolitan cosmogony — Atum unites with his shadow (self-fertilization)
occurrences.label: Heliopolitan cosmogony
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'I, even I, had union with my clenched hand, I joined myself in an embrace with my shadow, I poured seed into my mouth, my own; I sent forth issue in the form of Shu, I sent forth moisture in the form of Tefnut' (¶322). Jung cites this beside Amen as Ka-mutef, 'husband of his mother', and the Indian Prajapati who has intercourse with his own split-off feminine half — the world-creator as self-fertilizing hermaphrodite. In the Interrogationes vision world-creation gives place to spiritual renewal: the seed is the logos spermatikos, 'a living water springing up into eternal life' (¶323).

occurrences.title: Augustine — the two fishes of the feeding of the five thousand
occurrences.label: Augustine — the two fishes of the feeding…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Augustine interprets the two miraculous fishes as 'the kingly and the priestly person or power, because, like fishes surviving the tempests of the sea, they outlast the turbulence of the multitude'; both are united in Christ, king and priest after the order of Melchisedek (¶228). Jung uses the exegesis to show that 'the fishes were regarded as ruling powers', though the Cathar two fishes cannot be read uniformly as Christ — they are Satanael and Christ, the yoked pair of the Pisces-aeon (¶229). Parallels: cathar-two-fishes-osob-revelation-1111, lambspringk-two-reversed-fishes-1678.

occurrences.title: Aurora consurgens: Sapientia and the alchemical reading of scripture
occurrences.label: Aurora consurgens — Sapientia…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rheinau (Codex Rhenoviensis, Zurich) / Paris (Codex Parisinus Latinus 14006)
occurrences.quote: I am the only daughter of the wise, utterly unknown to the foolish.
body: The Aurora consurgens opens with the Wisdom of Solomon and Proverbs and identifies alchemy with the Sapientia Dei: Sapientia is the Queen of the South who came from the east "like the rising dawn." Its seven parables run scripture into the opus — the Song of Songs' bridegroom is the filius philosophorum (Christ); the "second Adam, who is called the philosophic man," enters eternity from pure elements; Senior's "One thing that never dieth" carries the lapis into the Creed's resurrection of the flesh.

Jung dates it to the first half of the fourteenth century (latest author quoted: Albertus Magnus), the author a cleric who knows the Vulgate by heart. The 1593 printer Waldkirch suppressed Part I for profaning the incarnation "by turning it into the mystery of the lapis."

occurrences.title: The Ave Praeclara and Albertus Magnus' dream of the Virgin
occurrences.label: The Ave Praeclara and Albertus Magnus' dream…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Osnabrück Register of Santa Maria (via Rémy de Gourmont)
occurrences.yearDisplay: Middle Ages (hymn ascribed to Albertus Magnus)
occurrences.quote: Fac … anguem aeneum in cruce speculari
body: The hymn Ave Praeclara — "Hail, clear-shining star of the sea, Mary, divinely born for the enlightenment of the nations" — weaving the sweet stream from the rock, the sea-bathed loins, the crucified brazen serpent to be gazed upon, and the Virgin made mother "by the sacred fire and the Father's word, which thou didst bear like the Burning Bush."

Rémy de Gourmont's legend from the Osnabrück Register: a virgin in royal raiment appeared to Albertus Magnus in a dream and reproached him for ingratitude to Mary — whereupon he composed the hymn. Jung: "An alchemist would find it full of alluring allusions"; Melchior Cibinensis made the Ave Praeclara the "testament of the art," in which "the whole chemical art is figuratively concealed."

occurrences.title: Axiom of Maria Prophetissa: 'One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth'
occurrences.label: Axiom of Maria Prophetissa
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Maria Prophetissa's saying, "One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the one as the fourth" — for Jung "one of the central axioms of alchemy… which runs like a leitmotiv throughout almost the whole of the lifetime of alchemy, extending over more than seventeen centuries" (cw12 ¶26).

In the even numbers "which signify the feminine principle, earth, the regions under the earth, and evil itself" are interpolated between the uneven numbers of Christian dogma. At ¶31 the axiom returns as τὸ ἕν τέταρτον: the inferior function, becoming conscious, "brings up among others the archetype of the self as well."

occurrences.title: Axiom of Democritus — 'Nature rejoices in nature'
occurrences.label: Axiom of Democritus — Nature rejoices in nature
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd-1st c. BC (revealed to Democritus by Ostanes, per Synesius)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The axiom — 'Nature rejoices in nature; nature subdues nature; nature rules over nature' — was, according to the story, revealed to Democritus by his deceased teacher Ostanes (¶244 n.26). Dorn quotes it: 'nature seeks after a nature like to itself, and rejoices in its own nature; if it is joined to another, the work of nature is destroyed' (¶244). For Jung it grounds the magnes-magnesia pair and the whole like-cures-like logic of the opus — the self as the like that alone can unite the opposites. Parallels: axiom-maria-one-becomes-four, morienus-thing-extracted-from-thee-7c.

occurrences.title: Apparition of the Aztec — Miss Miller
occurrences.label: Apparition of the Aztec — Miss Miller
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The continuing hypnagogic vision: "Suddenly, the apparition of an Aztec, complete in every detail: hand open, with large fingers, head in profile, armoured, with a head-dress resembling the plumed crests of the American Indians."

Jung's reading: confirmation "that a masculine figure was hidden in the Sphinx" (¶266-267); the personification of the masculine component of the woman's personality — later named the animus (¶267); "appears with all its 'heroic' qualities", the demon lover whose exalted spirituality forecloses any mortal marriage (¶273); eagle-feather crest = crown = sun-rays (¶268).

Verbatim: Suddenly, the apparition of an Aztec, complete in every detail: hand open, with large fingers, head in profile, armoured, with a head-dress resembling the plumed crests of the American Indians, etc. (cw05 ¶266).

occurrences.title: The mistletoe that killed Baldur
occurrences.label: The mistletoe that killed Baldur
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: All things pledge not to harm Baldur save the mistletoe, "too young" to be asked; Loki's dart of mistletoe kills him.

Jung's reading: the mistletoe as "child of the tree" — "That which grows on the tree is the child (pl. XXXIX), or oneself in renewed and rejuvenated form; and that is precisely what one cannot have, because the incest prohibition forbids it" (¶392); Baldur the puer aeternus, "only a dream of the mother", taken back into her.
Verbatim: The graceful Baldur is such a figure. This type is granted only a fleeting existence, because he is never anything but an anticipation of something desired and hoped for. (cw05 ¶392).

occurrences.title: 'Allegoria sanctissimae trinitatis et lapidis philosophici' — Basilius Valentinus
occurrences.label: Allegoria sanctissimae trinitatis et lapidis…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: So, too, is the gold without flaw … yet, for the sake of its imperfect and sick brothers and sisters, it dies and rises again, glorious and redeemed.
body: From the 1700 complete edition of the pseudonymous Basilius Valentinus (Johann Thölde of Frankenhausen, c. 1600, is the likely author; Maier's Symbola aureae mensae of 1617 already cites the texts with the remark "Rather than become notorious he preferred to remain unknown to everyone"): the Father begets the Son, God and man, who needs no death yet dies freely for his brothers and sisters; so too the gold, "without flaw … for the sake of its imperfect and sick brothers and sisters, dies and rises again." The Spiritus Solis is Mercurius corporis; the two together are Mercurius duplicatus; God the Son is the homo glorificatus, "like our glorified and fixed gold, the lapis philosophorum; wherefore this lapis is also called trinus."
The author is strongly Paracelsian — Archaeus, astral and elemental spirits.

occurrences.title: 'Unless ye slay me, your understanding will not be perfect' — Dicta Belini
occurrences.label: Unless ye slay me, your understanding will not…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th–12th c. (Dicta Belini; source likely Artefius' Harranite Clavis maioris sapientiae)
occurrences.quote: unless ye slay me, ye cannot be called sages
body: The Dicta Belini's dying speech: "I announce therefore to all you sages, that unless ye slay me, ye cannot be called sages. But if ye slay me, your understanding will be perfect, and it increases in my sister the moon according to the degree of our wisdom, and not with another of my servants, even if ye know my secret" (¶164). The Rosarium's variant ("Unless ye slay me, your understanding will not be perfect, and in my sister the moon the degree of your wisdom increases") is one of its "approximate quotations."

Jung untangles the speaker — "the father-son, whose mother is the son's sister-wife," Sol as reborn father — and reads "unless ye slay me" as "the slaying of the dragon, the mortificatio of the first, dangerous, poisonous stage of the anima (= Mercurius), freed from her imprisonment in the prima materia" (¶168). Sol's stages — dragon, lion, eagle, hermaphrodite — are "a new degree of insight, wisdom, and initiation, just as the Mithraic eagles, lions, and sun-messengers signify grades of initiation."

occurrences.title: Eagle over the concentration camp — dream of 'Y' (The Philosophical Tree, print 342–47)
occurrences.label: Eagle over the concentration camp — dream of 'Y'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: The Philosophical Tree, final dream series — ¶ pin tbd (print 342–47)

body: The closing clinical example of "The Philosophical Tree": an eagle circles over Y's internment/concentration camp and the dreamer thinks of shooting it down from a rocket-propelled aircraft. Jung reads the eagle — the "king of the air", here a war-machine thought — as the spirit-bird (birds as "winged thoughts", print 266; eagle at 343n, 347; "eagle 'eye', 344") that must be caught rather than shot, the same captura spiritus the alchemists staged in their bird-flocks and flasks.
Verbatim: EXAMPLE: An eagle circles over Y's concentration camp; he thinks of shooting it from a rocket-propelled aircraft, 342-47.

occurrences.title: Wingless bird of Hermes with bitterness in its throat — Rosinus ad Sarratantam
occurrences.label: Wingless bird of Hermes with bitterness…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The wingless bird of Hermes: 'Take the stone that is black, white, red, and yellow, and is a wonderful bird that flies without wings in the blackness of the night and the brightness of the day: in the bitterness that is in its throat the colouring will be found' (Rosinus ad Sarratantam, quoted cw14 ¶245). Jung uses it to bridge the salt/amaritudo chapter: the bird is a parallel of salt because salt is a spirit, a volatile substance 'which the alchemists were wont to conceive as a bird' (¶246); its throat-bitterness is the origin of the colours (¶333). The colour sequence black-red-gold-white anticipates the Hermas beast and the Ortus.

occurrences.title: Ibis 'dear to Hermes, the father of words' — Aelian, De natura animalium
occurrences.label: Ibis 'dear to Hermes, the father of words'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Aelian (De natura animalium) reports the ibis 'dear to Hermes, the father of words, since in its form it resembles the nature of the Logos; for its blackness and swift flight could be compared to the silent and introverted Logos, but its whiteness to the Logos already uttered and heard, which is the servant and messenger of the inner word' (quoted cw14 ¶250). Jung cites it for the origin and meaning of the avis Hermetis: the black-to-white moulting of the bird enacts nigredo to albedo, the passage of the inner word into speech — the same sequence the salt-bird of Rosinus carries in its throat.

occurrences.title: Understanding the language of birds (patient: anonymous, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Understanding the language of birds
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [26], ref. book p402 ≈ pdf p369 (harvested from index, pdf p580)

body: A patient "understood the language of birds" (case [26], book p402n) — the archaic gift of decoding the spirit's language, filed by the index beside the schizophrenic's star-relation. Jung elsewhere ties understanding's etymology to inner events ("understand," etymology, 440); the birds speak what the dreamer cannot yet.
Verbatim (case-index): "Patient who understood the language of birds. — 402n"

occurrences.title: The blessed waters awakening the dead — 'Instruction of Cleopatra'
occurrences.label: The blessed waters awakening the dead
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: how the elixir of life comes to them and awakens them, rousing them out of their sleep
body: One of the earliest Greek alchemical dialogues: Ostanes (the already-legendary Persian alchemist) and his companions ask Cleopatra how the highest descends to the lowest "and the midmost draws near to the lowest and the highest, so that they are made one with it; how the blessed waters come down from above to awaken the dead, who lie round about in the midst of Hades, chained in the darkness." Cleopatra answers: when the waters come in, the imprisoned bodies and spirits "bestir themselves, rise up, and clothe themselves in bright colours, glorious as the flowers in spring."

Jung connects the passage with the spring coniunctio of De vita longa: the Aniada as "powers that confer everlasting life," corresponding "to the blessed waters of Komarios and also, apparently, to the Communion substances" (¶193); the opus should begin in spring, in the month of Aries.

occurrences.title: 'The sacrifice is Brahm' — Bhagavad Gita 4.24
occurrences.label: The sacrifice is Brahm' — Bhagavad Gita 4.24
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Krishna: "All's then God! The sacrifice is Brahm, the ghee and grain / Are Brahm, the fire is Brahm, the flesh it eats / Is Brahm..."

Jung's reading: "The affinity between this line of thought and the Christian symbol is obvious" (¶241) — the same self-sacrificing mediator structure as Agni (Max Müller's fire "both the subject and the object of a sacrifice", ¶240).
Verbatim: The sacrifice is Brahm, the ghee and grain / Are Brahm, the fire is Brahm, the flesh it eats / Is Brahm, and unto Brahm attaineth he (cw05 ¶241).

occurrences.title: Cadmus and the dragon of Ares; the sown teeth — Thebes
occurrences.label: Cadmus and the dragon of Ares — the sown teeth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Cadmus holds fast to Harmonia while the opposites in projected form slaughter one another.
body: Cadmus, kinsman of Hermes Ithyphallikos, forbidden to seek his sister Europa (taken by Zeus-bull), follows the moon-marked cow to the founding-site of Thebes, slays the dragon of Ares that guards the spring, and sows its teeth: "Immediately armed men sprang up, who fell to fighting among themselves until only five remained. Cadmus was then given Harmonia to wife" (¶85). Philaletha's addition — the serpent spitted to the hollow oak — "represents the banishment of the dangerous daemon into the oak" (¶85).

Jung's alchemical reading: Cadmus is "Mercurius in his masculine form (Sol)"; the sister-anima "acting as a psychopomp in the shape of a cow" leads him to his destiny as dragon-slayer; the dragon is "disharmony," and the self-slaughtering sown men exemplify "nature subdues nature" — "nothing less than the uroboros conceptually formulated" (¶86). The dragon's skin offered to the hollow oak = return to the mother; Cadmus and Harmonia end as stones, snakes, "and even into a basilisk" (Pernety) (¶87).

occurrences.title: The Cantilena Riplaei: the sterile king's return to the mother's womb
occurrences.label: The Cantilena Riplaei
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He then wished to return to his mother's womb and to dissolve himself in the prima materia.
body: The 'Cantilena Riplaei' legend: a noble king (the caput corporum), sterile though "nurtured under the wings of the sun," learns by the mouth of Christ that he shall be born anew; he resolves to return to his mother's womb and dissolve himself in the prima materia; she conceals him under her robe and incarnates him again; eating peacock's flesh and drinking the green lion's blood she bears the child who resembles the moon and then the splendour of the sun. The Crowned Maid (Virgo redimita) stands amid the four elements, the green lion bleeding in her lap; the king emerges "a supreme victor triumphant, a great healer of the sick and a redeemer of all sins."

Jung's reading: mother-son incest (Ripley) parallels brother-sister incest (Visio Arislei) — both "constitute the prototype of the royal marriage," an "endogamous mating [that] is simply a variant of the Uroboros." The king is "the domineering conscious mind" swallowed by the unconscious into the nigredo and reborn.

occurrences.title: Cathar 'Revelation of John' — two fishes yoked like oxen on the primeval waters
occurrences.label: Cathar 'Revelation of John'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: early 12th c. (Basilius' confession before Alexius Comnenus, 1111)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Christ's favourite John asks what Satan was before his fall. Descending through the elements he finds 'two fishes lying upon the waters, and they were like oxen yoked for ploughing the whole earth from sunset to sunrise' at the command of the invisible Father, and his 'Osob' — his own fire, which he could not pass (¶225). Cast down, Satan creates the world in a week on the model of Genesis 1 (¶226). Jung: the yoked fishes 'can refer only to the zodiacal fishes' — Christ and Satanael, the two principles of the Pisces aeon, whose ploughing begins in the west like the alchemical nigredo (¶229-231). The fishes were found 'in the beginning', when the spirit brooded on the dark face of the waters.

occurrences.title: Hal Saflieni hypogeum initiations — Malta
occurrences.label: Hal Saflieni hypogeum initiations — Malta
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The neophyte dies like the seed-corn, springs up again and gets into the winnowing-basket.
body: The neolithic underground sanctuary as the deep-time background of the spelaeum initiations Jung lists from the Attis spelaeum to San Stefano: the tomb-womb where the neophyte "dies like the seed-corn, springs up again" (¶536).

occurrences.title: Diocletian's crypt of Hecate with 365 steps — Antioch (Malalas)
occurrences.label: Diocletian's crypt of Hecate with 365 steps
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: As the “spirit-mother” she sends madness, the moonsickness.
body: The solar count of the stairs leading down to the spook-goddess: "That this cavern is in fact related to the subterranean mother of death can be seen from a note in Malalas" (¶577). Hecate — night and phantoms, Empusa, lamia, the "Bride of Corinth," key, whip, dagger, torch, dogs — "a real spook-goddess"; as spirit-mother "she sends madness, the moonsickness" (¶577).

occurrences.title: The Holy Sepulchre spelaeum of San Stefano — Bologna
occurrences.label: The Holy Sepulchre spelaeum of San Stefano
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It can scarcely be doubted that the underlying meaning of the Church is the mother’s womb.
body: "The Church is, in a sense, the hero's grave (cf. the catacombs). The believer descends into the grave in order to rise again from the dead with the hero. It can scarcely be doubted that the underlying meaning of the Church is the mother's womb" (¶536) — with the Tantric garbha griha ("seeding-place or uterus") as the architectural parallel.

occurrences.title: Theseus and Peirithous grown fast to the rocks of the underworld — Athens
occurrences.label: Theseus and Peirithous grown fast…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Theseus myth is therefore a representation of the individuation process.
body: Theseus and Peirithous descend through a chasm in the grove of Colonus to abduct Persephone from the underworld. Resting below, they find themselves grown fast to the rocks and cannot rise: "they remained stuck in the mother and were lost to the upper world." Theseus is finally freed by Heracles "in the role of the death-conquering hero"; Peirithous is left.

Jung states the reading in one line: "The Theseus myth is therefore a representation of the individuation process" — the descent that fails when the ego is stuck fast in the chthonic mother, and the rescue as liberation from below.

occurrences.title: The virginity test in the serpent's cave — Greek custom
occurrences.label: The virginity test in the serpent's cave
occurrences.subject: n/a
