occurrences.quote: If they were bitten, it was a sign that they were no longer chaste.
body: The cave-serpent as jealous test-mother — the direct antecedent of the Roman dragon-legends in which girls descend to the cave-dragon and are slain for unchasteness (¶572–574), and the clinical inverse of the patient bitten in the genital region while freeing himself from the mother-complex (¶585).

occurrences.title: The divining cup of Joseph and Anacreon — Hippolytus' Naassenes
occurrences.label: The divining cup of Joseph and Anacreon
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus closes his Naassene report with the cup (κόνδυ) from which "the king, when he drinks, draws his omens" — the cup of Joseph and the tankard of Anacreon: "My tankard tells me / Speaking in mute silence / What I must become." "Anacreon's cup is dumb; yet Anacreon affirms that it tells him in mute language what he must become, that is, spiritual and not carnal" (¶550). The secret in the cup is the water Jesus changed into wine at Cana — "the kingdom of heaven that lies within us as a treasure."

Jung's structural reading: the "third and fourth" members of the quaternity are water and earth, "the lower half of the world in the alchemical retort," and "Hippolytus likens them to a cup (κόνδυ)"; water = content, earth = container; the Jordan as the water = the Logos, "bringing out the analogy with the Chalice" (¶551).

occurrences.title: The cup full of fire-coloured water — IV Ezra 14:39–40
occurrences.label: The cup full of fire-coloured water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Ezra's revelatory dream: "Then I opened my mouth, and Io! there was reached unto me a full cup, which was full as it were with water, but the colour of it was like fire. And I took it and drank; and when I had drunk, My heart poured forth understanding, wisdom grew in my breast, and my spirit retained its memory" (¶551).

Jung cites it for the cup whose "content gives life and healing" — the same trinity the alicorn bestows (strength, health, life) and the alchemists attribute to the stone. Water with the colour of fire: the divine water (hydor theion) of Mercurius in a Jewish-apocalyptic vessel.

occurrences.title: The chen-yen, the true and complete man — Wei Po-yang's Ts'an T'ung Ch'i
occurrences.label: The chen-yen, the true and complete man
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Wei Po-yang, "the oldest Chinese alchemist know n to us (2nd cent. a.d.)", describes the chen-yen, "the true or com plete m an, who is the beginning and end of the work: 'He is and he is not. He resembles avast pool of water, suddenly sinking and suddenly floating'"; in him are "m ixed the squareness, the roundness, the diam eter, and the dim ensions... having been in existence before the beginning of the heavens and the earth: lordly, lordly, high and revered" (cw13 ¶432).

Jung's reading: the "closed region" of intercom m unicating labyrinths protects the work; the black m ass — "the m assa Confusa, the chaos or nigredo of Western alchemy... black outside and white inside, like lead" — is the chen-yen hidden in darkness, "threatened by the ratio n al and correct conduct of life" (cw13 ¶433). Giving way to the self's urgencies and perishing is "a true thysia of the self" (cw13 ¶433).
Verbatim: “He is and he is not. He resembles avast pool of water, suddenly sinking and suddenly floating.” (cw13 ¶432)

occurrences.title: Bereshith Rabbati: the Messiah child plunged into the sea
occurrences.label: Bereshith Rabbati — the Messiah child plunged…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: France? (Moses ha-Darshan of Narbonne; midrash compilation)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Elias finds in Bethlehem "a young woman sitting before her door with a newborn child lying on the ground beside her, flecked with blood" — born at the evil hour when the temple was destroyed; "he neither walks, nor sees, nor speaks, nor hears, but lies there like a stone." Suddenly a wind from the four corners "bore the child away, and plunged him into the sea": 400 years in the great sea, 80 in the rising smoke of the children of Korah, 80 under the gates of Rome, wandering until the end of days (cw09ii par. 167rom Wunsche).
Jung: the sea = the Beyond = the unconscious; the endangered, latent Messiah explains the delay of his appearing — near enough the Talmud's critical 530 years to compare.

occurrences.title: 'Chiwantopel, a hypnagogic drama' — Miss Miller
occurrences.label: Chiwantopel, a hypnagogic drama' — Miss Miller
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Miller's third unconscious creation: after an evening of anxiety, lines, sparks and spirals of fire, an invocation, the sphinx and the Aztec, and finally a name forming "bit by bit" — "Chi-wan-to-pel", son of an Inca of Peru — awaited with "positively mystical expectation".

Jung's reading: the finest symbol of the libido is "the human figure, conceived as a demon or hero" (¶251); the birth of Chiwantopel from Popocatepetl means "I make, produce, invent him out of myself" — anal-birth of the hero-figure (¶279); the name-giving as baptism (¶274).
Verbatim: Lines, sparks, and spirals of fire passed before my eyes, symptoms of nervousness and ocular fatigue (cw05 ¶251).

occurrences.title: The Alexamenos mock-crucifixion graffito — Palatine, Rome
occurrences.label: The Alexamenos mock-crucifixion graffito
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Palatine Hill, Rome (wall of the Imperial page school)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: as is shown by the mock crucifixion scratched on the wall of the Imperial Cadet School on the Palatine
body: Jung (¶463) invokes "the mock crucifixion scratched on the wall of the Imperial Cadet School on the Palatine" (reproduced in Symbols of Transformation, pl. XLIII) as proof of the old vulgar prejudice "that the god of the Jews... was an ass — a prejudice which extended to Christ himself". The graffito — an ass-headed figure on the cross, with the taunting inscription about Alexamenos worshipping his god — is the oldest known depiction of Christ's crucifixion, and for Jung a document of the theriomorphic danger that always shadowed the incarnate God: the trickster-beast at the boundary of the most sacred.

occurrences.title: Christ as 'the sun of the East' — Melito of Sardis, Peri Loutrou (~170 AD)
occurrences.label: Christ as 'the sun of the East'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Melito's treatise Peri Loutrou calls Christ "The sun of the East... As the only sun he rose in the heavens" (¶158) — the sharpest single witness in Jung's dossier on Christ as Sol novus. The dossier runs: Philo Judaeus (sun as image of the divine Logos), Ambrose's "O sol salutis," Pseudo-Cyprian (Christ born "on the same day on which the sun was created, the 28th of March," Malachi's sun of righteousness, ¶159), the Pseudo-Chrysostom De solstitiis (Dec 25 as "the birthday of the Unconquerable One," ¶160), Eusebius of Alexandria (Christians praying to the rising sun into the fifth century, ¶161), Augustine's corrective ("he through whom the sun is made," ¶162), the nimbus and halo, apostles as zodiac signs, Tertullian's heathen, the Manichean sun-God, and the dedication Διὶ Ἡλίῳ θεῷ μεγάλῳ βασιλεῖ Ἰησοῦ (¶163).
Jung's thesis: the sun-coronations of the mystery religions are "the psychological roots" of this imagery — visionary light-processes congealing into liturgy (¶158).

occurrences.title: Pistis Sophia: the spirit like unto Jesus bound to the bed
occurrences.label: Pistis Sophia — the spirit like unto Jesus…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Mary tells Jesus how, when he was a child in the vineyard with Joseph, "the spirit came down from the height, and came unto me in the house, like unto thee, and I knew him not, but thought that he was thou" — she seizes and binds him to the foot of the bed until Jesus finds him; the two gaze at each other, embrace, "and you became one".

Jung's reading: Jesus is "a double personality" — "truth sprouting from the earth" rising from chaos/hyle, and pneuma descending as "justice looking down from heaven" — the Gnostic Redeemer's discrimination of natures exemplified.

occurrences.title: Valentinus: Christ 'cast off the shadow from himself'
occurrences.label: Valentinus — Christ cast off the shadow…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome? (Valentinus; reported by Irenaeus, Adv. haer. I, 11, 1; II, 5, 1)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Irenaeus records the Valentinian teaching that Christ, born of the mother outside the pleroma, came forth "not without a kind of shadow," but "being masculine, cast off the shadow from himself" and returned to the Pleroma; the mother, left in the shadow, bore the Demiurge.

For Jung this is the Gnostics tackling the problem of evil "on a broader basis than the Church Fathers": the cut-off counterpart is recognizable in the figure of Antichrist. At par. 171 he re-reads the shadow as the Yahwistic law under which Christ was born.

occurrences.title: Christ 'compared and united' with the stone — Aquarium sapientum
occurrences.label: Christ 'compared and united' with the stone
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Aquarium sapientum (1608): the raven's-head blackness of the decomposed stone is compared with Christ 'full of griefs and sicknesses... a worm and no man' (Isa 53, Ps 22): 'it is not unfitly compared with Christ when the putrefied body of the Sun lies dead, inactive, like ashes, in the bottom of the phial, until, as a result of greater heat, its soul by degrees and little by little descends to it again, and once more infuses, moistens, and saturates the decaying and all but dead body' (cw14 ¶485). Christ at the Mount of Olives and on the cross was 'roasted by the fire of the divine wrath'; his resurrection and 'roseate Tincture' heal 'us sinful men in body and soul'; the stone's 'material and preparation... an outstanding type and lifelike image of the incarnation of Christ' (¶485). Jung: the adept's Passion 'happens to the alchemist... in the form expressed by the alchemical myth' (¶492); cf. the 'furnace of the cross' passage (¶494).

occurrences.title: Christ in the mandorla with the four evangelists — Saint-Jacques-des-Guérets
occurrences.label: Christ in the mandorla with the four evangelists
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Son of Man is an anticipation of the idea of the self
body: Plate 101: "Christ in the mandorla, surrounded by the symbols of the four evangelists," mural at Saint-Jacques-des-Guérets. It stands in the world-clock commentary's time-symbolism cluster: "There is also a connection with the symbolism of Horus: on the one hand, Christ enthroned with the four emblems of the evangelists—three animals and an angel (fig. 101); on the other, Father Horus with his four sons, or Osiris with the four sons of Horus" (¶314). "The Son of Man is an anticipation of the idea of the self."
Christ-in-mandorla-with-four is the Christian member of the centre-and-quaternity family the world clock vision joins.

occurrences.title: Soul-stones of the Birs cave and Burgaschi lake-dwellings (Switzerland, prehistoric)
occurrences.label: Soul-stones of the Birs cave…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Birs river cave near Basel; Burgaschi lake, Canton Solothurn
body: "A cache of 'soul stones,' similar to churingas, was found in a cave on the river Birs near Basel, and during recent excavations of the pole-dwellings on the little lake at Burgaeschi, in Canton Solothurn, a group of boulders was discovered wrapped in the bark of birch trees" (cw13 ¶129).

Jung's evidence that the magic-stone idea — otherwise Australian, Melanesian, Indian — is found "in Europe itself" (¶129): prehistoric Alpine soul-stone caches, material for the argument that the alchemists' stone-God-image rests on something far older than alchemy.

occurrences.title: Churinga — soul-stones of the Central Australian tribes
occurrences.label: Churinga — soul-stones…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Australian child-stone complex: "the view of the Australian aborigines that children's souls live in a special stone called the 'child-stone.' They can be made to migrate into a uterus by rubbing the 'child-stone' with a churinga. Churingas may be boulders, or oblong stones artificially shaped and decorated... The Australians and the Melanesians maintain that churingas come from the totem ancestor... and are full of arunquiltha or mana. They are taboo, are buried in caches or hidden in clefts... In order to 'charge' them, they are buried among the graves so that they can soak up the mana of the dead. They promote the growth of field-produce, increase the fertility of men and animals, heal wounds" (cw13 ¶128). Daubed with red ochre, anointed with fat, bedded in leaves, copiously spat on ("spittle = mana").
Jung's use: the stone-symbol's prehistory behind the alchemical God-stone (¶128) — matter carrying soul and mana.

occurrences.title: Churning of the Milky Ocean for amrita — Rajput miniature (plate XV)
occurrences.label: Churning of the Milky Ocean for amrita
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The gods churn the ocean of milk with the serpent Vasuki as rope to raise the amrita, the drink of immortality; the stir is "like the fire".

Jung's reading: soma and fire "are united in Agni" — "Soma is also the 'nourishing drink'. Its mythological characteristics coincide with those of fire" (¶246-247); the drink of immortality as libido-symbol parallel to the Eucharistic blood.
Verbatim: The drink of immortality, Amrita, was stirred by the Hindu gods like the fire. (cw05 ¶247).

image.title: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk title QS:P1476,en:"The Churning of the Ocean of Milk " label QS:Len,"The Churning of the Ocean of Milk "

occurrences.title: Clement of Alexandria — 'to know oneself is to know God' (Paedagogus III, 1)
occurrences.label: Clement of Alexandria
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Therefore, as it seems, it is the greatest of all disciplines to know oneself; for when a man knows himself, he knows God' (¶347). Jung quotes it with Hippolytus' Gnostic saying 'knowledge of man is the beginning of wholeness (teleiosis), but knowledge of God is perfect wholeness' and Monoïmos' letter — evidence that 'many of the Gnostics were nothing other than psychologists' (¶347). The gnosis strand that runs into Dorn's self-knowledge and Jung's own method.

occurrences.title: Clementine Homilies — pneuma and soma; the devil as psyche of this world
occurrences.label: Clementine Homilies — pneuma and soma
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'In God, pneuma and soma are one. When they separate, pneuma appears as the Son and "archon of the future Aeon," but soma... divides into four, corresponding to the four elements'; 'from the mixing of the four parts there arose the devil, the "archon of this Aeon," and the psyche of this world' — 'God rules this world as much through the devil as through the Son, for both are in his hands' (¶400). God unfolds in syzygies (heaven/earth, day/night, male/female) down to Adam/Eve, then returns to the beginning (¶400). Jung lists the alchemical parallels: hostile brothers, tetrameria, Mercurius duplex, lapis uniting the opposites (¶401). Cf. god-image-clementine-homilies-two-hands-150 (the two hands).

occurrences.title: The Monad and the Monogenes dwelling in Setheus — Codex Brucianus passage quoted by Jung
occurrences.label: The Monad and the Monogenes dwelling in Setheus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (Coptic codex; Codex Brucianus / Codex Jung portion)
body: Gnostic description of the Monad as ship, field, and walled city with twelve gates — the Mother-City of the Only-begotten (Monogenes). Jung quotes: "From Him it is the Monad came, in the manner of a ship, laden with all good things… and in the manner of a city, filled with all races of mankind." (cw12 ¶138).

His reading (¶139): ship/field/city = the temenos idea; the crowned Monad recalls the dream-hat; as metropolis the Monad is feminine "like the padma or lotus, the basic form of the Lamaic mandala"; Setheus dwells in the Pleroma-city with four gates, equivalent to the City of Brahma on Mount Meru; the Monogenes stands on a tetrapeza, quaternion of the four evangelists.

occurrences.title: Medieval paintings of the Conception: the tube from God's throne
occurrences.label: Medieval paintings of the Conception
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Medieval paintings depicting the fructification of Mary "with a tube or hose-pipe coming down from the throne of God and passing into her body, and we can see the dove or the Christchild flying down it" (¶108). The dove is the fructifying agent, the wind of the Holy Ghost.

Jung's reading: the third independent testimony (with the Mithraic Liturgy tube and the patient's vision) proving "the idea of a wind-tube connected with God or the sun exists independently... at other times and in other places"; the patient could never have seen such a rare picture — there was none in Zurich's public gallery, his native town (¶109). Association of sun and wind "frequently occurs in ancient symbolism".

occurrences.title: The hieros gamos of hierophant and priestess in the dark — Asterius on Eleusis
occurrences.label: The hieros gamos of hierophant and priestess…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The descent into the earth is a piece of womb symbolism and was widespread in the form of cave worship.
body: "This clearly points to a hieros gamos which was celebrated underground. The priestess of Demeter seems to have represented the earth-goddess, or possibly the ploughed furrow" (¶528). The descent into the earth as womb symbolism opens Jung's cave-cult catalogue: Magi sacrificing to Ahriman in a sunless place, Mithrobarzanes, "Sister Fire and Brother Spring," the Attis spelaeum.

occurrences.title: Christ the bridegroom consummating his marriage on the cross — Augustine
occurrences.label: Christ the bridegroom consummating his marriage…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The various forms of the crux ansata have the meaning of “life” and “fruitfulness,” and also of “union,” which can be interpreted as the hieros gamos of the god with his mother for the purpose of conquering death and renewing life.
body: Augustine's nuptial reading of the crucifixion: "Like a bridegroom Christ went forth from his chamber … he lovingly gave himself up to the torment in place of his bride, and he joined himself to the woman for ever." For Jung this shows the old mythologem — the hieros gamos of the god with his mother to conquer death and renew life — "has passed into Christianity" (¶411).

occurrences.title: Christ's marriage-bed of the cross — pseudo-Augustine, Sermo suppositus 120
occurrences.label: Christ's marriage-bed of the cross
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Like a bridegroom Christ went forth from his chamber, he went out with a presage of his nuptials into the field of the world.… He came to the marriage-bed of the cross, and there, in mounting it, he consummated his marriage. And when he perceived the sighs of the creature, he lovingly gave himself up to the torment in place of his bride, and he joined himself to the woman [matrona] for ever" (¶671).

St. Augustine "actually interprets Christ's death as a hieros gamos with the mother, similar to the feast of Adonis, where Venus and Adonis were laid upon the bridal couch" (¶671). Jung: "Matrona in the language of St. Augustine means the Church, the bride of the Lamb. The feeling-tone of the classical hieros gamos has here changed into its opposite: torment instead of lust" (¶672) — the union of God with his congregation, the corpus mysticum, which psychologically "signifies the conjunction of conscious and unconscious, the transcendent function characteristic of the individuation process" (¶672).
Verbatim: "He came to the marriage-bed of the cross, and there, in mounting it, he consummated his marriage" (¶671).

occurrences.title: The royal pair crucified for union and rebirth — George Ripley
occurrences.label: The royal pair crucified for union and rebirth
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Ripley (Opera om nia p. 81) crucifies the royal pair, the suprem e opposites, for the purpose of union and rebirth: "If I be lifted up, [as Christ says,] then I will draw all m en unto m e... From that tim e forward, when both parts, having been crucified and exanim ated, are espoused, m an and wom an shall be buried together and are afterward quickened again by the spirit of life" (cw13 ¶446).

Jung's frame: the tree was brought in to connection with Christ's cross partly by the legend that the cross's wood cam e from the tree of paradise, partly by the quatern ity — "the tree possesses a quaternary quality by reason of the fact that it represents the process by which the four elem ents are united" (cw13 ¶446). A sibling locus holds Ripley's Scrowle with its Melusina-top tree: tree-ripley-scrowle-bm-sloane-5025-london-1588.
Verbatim: when both parts, having been crucified and exanim ated, are espoused, m an and wom an shall be buried together and are afterward quickened again by the spirit of life. (cw13 ¶446ocr)

occurrences.title: Faust with Helen: the coniunctio becomes subjective — Goethe's Faust II
occurrences.label: Faust with Helen — Goethe's Faust II
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The essential Faustian drama is expressed most graphically in the scene between Paris and Helen. To the medieval alchemist this episode would have represented the mysterious coniunctio of Sol and Luna in the retort (fig. 268); but modern man, disguised in the figure of Faust, recognizes the projection and, putting himself in the place of Paris or Sol, takes possession of Helen or Luna, his own inner, feminine counterpart. The objective process of the union thus becomes the subjective experience of the artifex: instead of watching the drama, he has become one of the actors" (¶558).

The price: the goal of the opus is missed — "Euphorion, who is supposed to be the filius philosophorum, imperishable and 'incombustible,' goes up in flames" (¶558); "every archetype, at its first appearance and so long as it remains unconscious, takes possession of the whole man and impels him to play a corresponding role." Yet the identification "brings the coniunctio back from its projected state into … consciousness … the solution of the alchemical riddle" — with inflation as its danger (¶559). Faust's sin: "he identified with the thing to be transformed" (¶560); his perfected figure is named "Marianus" — Morienus.

occurrences.title: Flowing Light pursues Dark Water — Hippolytus' blue woman
occurrences.label: Flowing Light pursues Dark Water
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Behind these figures may be discerned a coniunctio Solis et Lunae, both the sun and the new moon appearing in their unfavourable aspect.
body: In Hippolytus' report, a woman of "celestial" blue hue ([kyanokrokon]) is pursued by "a grey-haired, winged, ithyphallic old man." "He is named [Rhou], Flowing Light, and she is [Kyanokome?], 'which means Dark Water.' Behind these figures may be discerned a coniunctio Solis et Lunae, both the sun and the new moon appearing in their unfavourable aspect. Here too there arises between them the 'harmony' of an intermediary spirit, roughly corresponding to the position of the filius philosophorum" (¶177).

A coniunctio of the darkened luminaries — the sexed pursuit at the bottom of the cosmos whose offspring is the harmonizing third. Greek proper names OCR-garbled in the chunk (flagged in the mention record).

occurrences.title: Gabricus and Beya — brother dissolved into sister, becoming the serpens mercurialis
occurrences.label: Gabricus and Beya — brother dissolved…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin alchemical corpus (legend of Hellenistic origin)
body: "Alchemy has the legend of Gabricus and Beya, the royal brother-sister pair. During the hieros gamos, Gabricus gets right inside the body of his sister and disappears completely; he is buried in her womb, where, dissolved into atoms, he changes into the soul-snake, the serpens mercurialis" (¶676, cf. fig. 6).

The coniunctio in its most radical alchemical form: the male partner's total bodily dissolution into the female, out of which the mercurial serpent-soul is born — brother-sister incest, burial, and transformation into the transformative agent itself. Jung cites it as the culmination of the snake-as-instrument-of-sacrifice survey ("the snake symbolizes the numen of the transformative act as well as the transformative substance itself"), and immediately adds the patient who crawled into her mother as a snake (see serpent-fantasy-enter-mother-anon-patient-cw05). The locus that later anchors his CW14 treatment of the coniunctio.
Verbatim: "dissolved into atoms, he changes into the soul-snake, the serpens mercurialis" (¶676).

occurrences.title: Isis as heavenly cow receiving the seed that begets Horus — Heliopolitan autumn rite
occurrences.label: Isis as heavenly cow receiving the seed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the heavenly cow with the moon-eye, Isis, receives the seed that begets Horus
body: The feast-day of Jusasit, "the arrival of the sister who makes ready to unite herself with her father" — daughter becomes wife, the rejuvenated mother given to the sun-god, "the 'father of his mother,'" for self-reproduction (¶408, ¶496). The moon as guardian of the seed is the key phrase Jung repeats for Nokomis (¶487).

occurrences.title: Bridal mysticism — Mechthild of Magdeburg, The Flowing Light of the Godhead
occurrences.label: Bridal mysticism — Mechthild…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: While, in Church mysticism, the primordial image of the hieros gamos was sublimated on a lofty plane and only occasionally-as for instance with Mechthild of Magdeburg-approached the physical sphere in emotional intensity
body: In Church mysticism the primordial image of the hieros gamos was "sublimated on a lofty plane and only occasionally — as for instance with Mechthild of Magdeburg — approached the physical sphere in emotional intensity" (¶295, fn39: The Flowing Light of the Godhead). Mechthild is Jung's limit-case of the sublimated coniunctio: the sponsus-sponsa union carried so hot it nears the body. The rest of the world kept the image "very much alive" below the official sublimation — a tension the alchemists would inherit as the coniugium solis et lunae.

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 14 — coniunctio of the royal pair over Fifth Avenue (Sept 1929)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 14
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: On the blue flower in the centre the coniunctio of the "royal" pair is represented by the sacrificial fire burning between them.
body: The mandala floats over the lit-up ravine of Fifth Avenue, New York. On the blue flower at its centre the coniunctio of the "royal" pair is represented by sacrificial fire between them; King and Queen assisted by two kneeling figures, a man and a woman — "a typical marriage quaternio," for which Jung refers to his "Psychology of the Transference" (¶613). The inner bond is a compensatory consolidation against disintegrating influences from without, after the shock of New York. Picture 15 answers it: blue snakes penetrate the red flesh — the enantiodromia sets in (¶614).

occurrences.title: Coniunctio solis et lunae — Splendor solis (Harley 3469, 1582)
occurrences.label: Coniunctio solis et lunae — Splendor solis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Splendor Solis plate of the sun-moon coniunctio, cited where Jung discusses the anima standing on the globe worshipping the sun.

Context ¶112: "the sun is a symbol of the source of life and the ultimate wholeness of man… the anima still seems to be a sun-worshipper, that is to say, she belongs to the ancient world." The coniunctio plate stands behind the whole sol/luna row of the volume.

image.title: Splendor Solis 04 solar king and lunar queen meet

occurrences.title: The coniunctio of soul and body as ecclesiastical marriage bath — Grandes heures du duc de Berry
occurrences.label: The coniunctio of soul and body…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Da nobis per huius aquae et vini mysterium, eius divinitatis esse consortes, qui humanitatis nostrae fieri dignatus est particeps.
body: Illumination from the Grandes heures (1413) showing the mingling of water and wine at the Offertory as a bath of the two figures — which Jung captions "an ecclesiastical version of the alchemical marriage bath."

His reading: in the Greek rite after the transubstantiation "a piece of the host is mingled with the wine, thus producing the coniunctio of the soul with the body and establishing the living body of Christ." The transformed bread is Ambrose's medicina, the pharmakon athanasias — the drug of immortality uniting body and soul, exactly what the alchemists sought in their bath and their stone.

occurrences.title: Woman and dragon embracing in the grave at new moon — Maier, Scrutinium
occurrences.label: Woman and dragon embracing in the grave…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung recalls 'the gruesome conjunction at the new moon in Maier's Scrutinium chymicum, where the woman and the dragon embrace in the grave' (cw14 ¶293), illustrating the waning of the soul-Luna into the embrace of terrestrial sulphur — 'which here signifies death and corruption' (¶293). It is the nigredo-face of the coniunctio: union consummated not on the wedding-bed but in the tomb, under the sign of the new moon with its 'uncanniness and snakiness' (¶437).

occurrences.title: Consilium coniugii: the philosophical man of the four natures, the red gum
occurrences.label: Consilium coniugii
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the union of the two is a kind of self-fertilization
body: "The old treatise 'Consilium coniugii' explains that the 'philosophical man' consists of the 'four natures of the stone.' Of these three are earthy or in the earth, but 'the fourth nature is the water of the stone, namely the viscous gold which is called red gum and with which the three earthy natures are tinted.' We learn here that gum is the critical fourth nature: it is duplex, i.e., masculine and feminine, and at the same time the one and only aqua mercurialis. So the union of the two is a kind of self-fertilization, a characteristic always ascribed to the mercurial dragon" (¶209).
The fourth nature "leads straight to the Anthropos idea that stands for man's wholeness… a unitary being who existed before man and at the same time represents man's goal" (¶210).

occurrences.title: Corn as 'the old woman' sprung from a slain grandmother — Cherokee myth
occurrences.label: Corn as 'the old woman' sprung…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This view is corroborated by a legend of the Cherokee Indians
body: The corn as the killed mother: the grain sprouting from her blood — the sacrificial underside of Mondamin's burial in the earth his mother (¶523).

occurrences.title: The mown ear of corn held up at the epopteia — Eleusis
occurrences.label: The mown ear of corn held up at the epopteia
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Brimo has borne Brimos!
body: The final vision of the Eleusinian mysteries: the cut grain as the son of the mother, the Brimo-borne Brimos in vegetable form — the dying-and-rising corn-god contemplated in silence (cf. pl. IVb).

occurrences.title: Hiawatha wrestles and buries Mondamin the maize god — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Hiawatha wrestles and buries Mondamin the maize…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His hunger … his longing for the nourishing mother, calls forth from the unconscious another hero, an edible god, the maize, son of the Earth Mother.
body: After three days' fasting and wrestling in the purple twilight, Hiawatha conquers Mondamin, buries him in the earth his mother, "and soon afterwards, young and fresh, the corn sprouts from his grave for the nourishment of mankind" (¶523). The mystery: "It is not man who is transformed into a god, but the god who undergoes transformation in and through man" (¶524). The Christian parallel is the eucharist; Sahagún's Huitzilopochtli is the ethnographic anchor.

occurrences.title: Tages, the fresh-ploughed boy springing from the furrow — Etruscan legend
occurrences.label: Tages, the fresh-ploughed boy springing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the son being the edible fruit of the field
body: "The plough has a well-known phallic meaning (cf. fig. 15), and the furrow, as in India, stands for woman. Psychologically this image is a symbolical equivalent of copulation, the son being the edible fruit of the field" (¶527). The lexicographers' "Demeter's daimon," identified with Dionysus-Zagreus.

occurrences.title: Corn-god vessel — Chimbote culture, Peru
occurrences.label: Corn-god vessel — Chimbote culture, Peru
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A corn-god Clay vessel, Chimbote culture, Peru
body: Plate caption, the American parallel to Mondamin: the corn-god as vessel-god, the edible divinity of the grain — Jung cites pl. LII for the Mondamin motif (¶522, ¶523).

occurrences.title: Hildegard of Bingen — earth quartered, ringed by ocean, air and heaven (Lucca codex)
occurrences.label: Hildegard of Bingen
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the earth surrounded by the ocean, realm of air, and starry heaven. The actual globe of the earth in the centre is divided into four.
body: Manuscript picture from Hildegard of Bingen (Fig. 48 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism): the earth surrounded by the ocean, the realm of air, and the starry heaven — and the globe of the earth in the centre is divided into four. Jung sets it in his row of collective mandalas between the Egyptian Sky Mother (Fig. 47) and Boehme's XL Questions mandala (¶704), as the Western visionary form of the quartered world-circle.
Distinct from the Liber divinorum operum cosmic-man illumination (CW12 ¶456): same visionary, different picture, here a cosmological quaternio.

occurrences.title: Thoth's annunciation and the crux ansata of Kneph and Hathor — Luxor birth reliefs
occurrences.label: Thoth's annunciation and the crux ansata…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~14th c. BCE (divine-birth cycle of queen Mautmes)
occurrences.quote: the bird-headed Thoth, the Logos and messenger of the gods, is shown announcing to the young queen Mautmes that she will give birth to a son.
body: In an Egyptian picture of the birth of a king at Luxor, the bird-headed Thoth — "the Logos and messenger of the gods" — announces to the young queen Mautmes that she will bear a son; in the next scene Kneph and Hathor hold the crux ansata to her mouth, "thus fertilizing her in a spiritual or symbolic manner" (fig. 27).
An annunciation-type iconography fourteen centuries before the Christian one, with the cross itself as the instrument of divine impregnation — the word announced, the life-sign applied.

occurrences.title: Mock crucifixion with ass's head — Palatine graffito
occurrences.label: Mock crucifixion with ass's head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The mock crucifixion on the Palatine shows the Crucified with an ass's head
body: The famous graffito (pl. XLIII, plate at pdf p289), used by Jung in the horse-and-ass excursus of ¶421: the ass-headed Crucified belongs to the theriomorphic underside of the god-image — the ass as priapic animal and mount of the god (Balaam, Christ on the ass, the ass-headed Jerusalem idol).

occurrences.title: Cross of ropes stretched over water — Muyscas sacrifice
occurrences.label: Cross of ropes stretched over water
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Here the divinity is evidently the water, not the cross, which only signifies the place of sacrifice.
body: The divinity is the water (the womb), not the cross; the intersection is the "point of union where the 'crossing' takes place" — sacrifice offered where the roads of the rite cross, on the analogy that fertility magic increases the things marked for sacrifice (¶407).

occurrences.title: Palenque Cross with child offering — Yucatán
occurrences.label: Palenque Cross with child offering — Yucatán
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: one of them holding out a child for either sacrifice or baptism
body: Mayan relief (pl. XLIa, plate at pdf p286), cited by Jung alongside the Fejérváry codex as proof that hanging victims on crosses was a religious custom in Middle America (¶400). The cross here is "tree of our life or flesh" — a sacrificial and baptismal tree with a bird at its crown.

occurrences.title: The world-soul split in a chi (X) — Plato's Timaeus
occurrences.label: The world-soul split in a chi — Plato's Timaeus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The idea of union expressed in the cross symbol is found in Plato’s Timaeus, where the demiurge joins the parts of the world-soul together by means of two sutures, which form a X (chi).
body: The demiurge joins the parts of the world-soul by two sutures forming a chi; the world-soul "contains the world in itself like a body", an image which "cannot fail to remind us of the mother" (¶404). Jung reads the self-contained bliss of the world-god as the vessel motif — the Indian god in the lotus or the embrace of his Shakti, Diogenes in his tub (¶405) — and notes that the image of the soul "somehow coincides with the mother-imago" (¶406).

occurrences.title: The cross as Mary's stepmother — 'Dispute between Mary and the Cross'
occurrences.label: The cross as Mary's stepmother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the Middle Ages the cross was therefore logically understood as the mother.
body: Middle English debate poem in which the cross, the instrument of her son's death, is a "false tree" that "destroyed Mary's fruit with a deadly drink." Mary laments: "My sonys stepmodir I thee calle." Sancta Crux answers: "Lady, to thee I owe honour... Thi fruyt me florysschith in blood colour" (¶26).

Jung uses it to show that "the moment of the eclipse and mystic marriage is death on the cross. In the Middle Ages the cross was therefore logically understood as the mother" — the wounding of the sponsus (Honorius' "Thou hast wounded my heart," ¶¶24-25) read by the vernacular imagination as a family drama between the mother and the fatal tree.

occurrences.title: Cinedian fish and the dragon's stone — Cyranides
occurrences.label: Cinedian fish and the dragon's stone — Cyranides
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Cyranides describes a round transparent fish, six fingers long, living on the Syrian-Palestine-Libya coasts, carrying two stones in its head and one in the third tail vertebra (spondilo) — the cinedian stone, potent as a love-potion ('ligature of Aphrodite') and pertains to Saturn (¶214). The stone is 'twin or twofold': one opaque black, one black but shining 'like a mirror' — the dragon's stone (dracontius lapis), known to Pliny and the medieval alchemists as draconites (¶214-215). Jung reads its double nature as the polarity of opposites that gives the lapis its uniting significance, extended even to Christ (¶215-216).

occurrences.title: Cautes and Cautopates — the Mithraic dadophors
occurrences.label: Cautes and Cautopates — the Mithraic dadophors
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The bull-sacrifice flanked by two torch-bearers, one with raised, one with lowered torch; sometimes holding bull's head and scorpion (Taurus/Scorpio, equinoctial signs); Cumont connects them with sepulchral Erotes and makes them offshoots of Mithras' triadic nature ("the threefold Mithras").

Jung's reading: "One would stand for death, the other for life" (¶294) — the Dioscuri pattern of the mortal and immortal sun, flanked also in Christ between the two thieves and Baal between Aziz and Monimos.
Verbatim: They form a pair of brothers whose characters are revealed by the symbolic position of the torches. (cw05 ¶294).

occurrences.title: Dante's heavenly rose (Paradiso XXXI)
occurrences.label: Dante's heavenly rose (Paradiso XXXI)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a flower that spreads over the whole starry heaven
body: At the beginning of dream 26 a shooting star falls "in a curious leftward curve," and the dreamer notices the curve "corresponded exactly to the line he drew when sketching the picture of the eightfold flower": "Thus the shooting star traces the outline, so to speak, of a flower that spreads over the whole starry heaven. What is now beginning is the circulation of the light. This cosmic flower corresponds roughly to the rose in Dante's Paradiso (fig. 83)" (¶229).

The rose of the celestial assembly — the mandala of the blessed arranged in petals round the divine centre — is Jung's closest medieval parallel for the cosmic mandala-flower of the dream-series; it also links to the "rose garden of the philosophers" of alchemy (¶155, ¶235) and the rosa mystica of the Litany (¶257).

occurrences.title: 'Thou shalt have become God' — Hippolytus on Christian self-knowledge
occurrences.label: Thou shalt have become God
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus's account of Christian doctrine in the Elenchos (X, 34, 4): "But thou shalt speak with God and be joint heir with Christ... For thou wilt have becom e God. For whatever sufferings thou didst undergo as a m an, thou hast show n that thou art a m an; but whatever is appurtenant to a God, that God has prom ised to bestow... That is the 'Know thyself,' the know ing of the God who m ade thee. For to him who know eth him self it is given to be know n of Him by whom he is called" (cw13 ¶372).

Jung cites it directly after the Theosebeia exhortation as the Christian counterpart of the alchemical self-knowledge: "The m oral equivalent of the physical transm utation in to gold is self-knowledge" (¶372).
Verbatim: For thou wilt have becom e God (cw13 ¶372)

occurrences.title: Demon eating the sun — stone, eastern Java
occurrences.label: Demon eating the sun — stone, eastern Java
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Stone relief of Rahu-type eclipse demon swallowing the solar disc.

Jung's reading: the sun-devouring demon — cf. Hanuman bursting "another sea monster, who was the mother of Rahu, the sun-devouring demon" (¶311); the whale-dragon as Terrible Mother whose conquest wins eternal youth (¶374).
Verbatim: Demon eating the sun Stone, eastern Java, 15th century.

occurrences.title: Deucalion and Pyrrha cast the bones of the Great Mother
occurrences.label: Deucalion and Pyrrha cast the bones…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: After the flood, the oracle bids the sole survivors throw "the bones of the Great Mother" behind them; the stones they throw become human beings. The nymph Anchiale similarly casts dust from which the Dactyls spring.

Jung's reading: the motif of throwing behind one as anal-birth imagery — "The idea of anal birth recalls the motif of throwing something behind one" (¶279); creation of mankind by the infantile route.
Verbatim: They thereupon threw stones behind them, from which mankind sprang. (cw05 ¶279).

occurrences.title: Diana of Ephesus with the mural crown — Roman statuette
occurrences.label: Diana of Ephesus with the mural crown
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXIVb: the many-breasted Ephesian Diana wearing the mural crown.

Jung's reading: the city is "a maternal symbol, a woman who harbours the inhabitants in herself like children", hence Rhea, Cybele and Diana "all wear the mural crown" (¶303); Old Testament cities addressed as women (Isaiah 47; Jeremiah 50:12).
Verbatim: It is therefore understandable that the three mother-goddesses, Rhea, Cybele, and Diana, all wear the mural crown (pl. XXIVb). (cw05 ¶303).

image.title: Artemis of Ephesus MAN Napoli Inv6278

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: the sacrificer and Ion, priest of the inner sanctuaries (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — the sacrificer…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Panopolis / Alexandria, Egypt (Berthelot, Alch. grecs III i 2)
body: The opening vision of the Treatise of Zosimos the Divine concerning the Art: a sacrificer on a bowl-shaped altar with fifteen steps; the voice from above — "I have performed the act of descending the fifteen steps into the darkness, and of ascending the steps into the light... I am Ion, the priest of the inner sanctuaries, and I submit myself to an unendurable torment" (cw13 ¶86). Ion is pierced with the sword, dismembered "in accordance with the rule of harmony," flayed head-first, burnt, "till I perceived by the transformation of the body that I had become spirit" — then changes into "a mutilated anthroparion" that spews its own flesh and tears it with its own teeth.

Jung: the homunculus concept "appears here for the first time in alchemical literature" (fn7); the self-devouring anthroparion stands for the uroboros. Ion = Yunan ben Merqūtilus, son of Mercury, of Sabaean tradition (fn4).

occurrences.title: King boiled, dismembered and revived — Allegoria Merlini
occurrences.label: King boiled, dismembered and revived
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The 'Allegoria Merlini': a king drinks 'the water which is closest to my heart', swells, and appears dead; Egyptian and Alexandrian physicians dispute — the Egyptians dismember and triturate him with moist medicines, the Alexandrians wash, dry, powder him again with sal ammoniac and nitre, and melt the mass, 'whereupon the king rose up from death and cried in a loud voice: "Where are my enemies?"' (cw14 ¶357-358). Jung: 'the primitive motif of the murder or sacrifice of the king for the purpose of renewing his kingly power and increasing the fertility of the land' (¶358); the dismemberment's 'original may be the dismemberment of Osiris and Dionysus' (¶365). The medical quarrel 'may hark back to pre-Islamic times' (¶367).

occurrences.title: Pentheus torn to pieces by the Maenads (Dionysus myth, Thebes)
occurrences.label: Pentheus torn to pieces by the Maenads
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Pentheus, curious to see the orgies of the Maenads, climbed up into a pine-tree but was spotted by his mother; the Maenads cut down the tree, and Pentheus, taken for a wild animal, was torn to pieces by them in their frenzy, his own mother being the first to hurl herself upon him" (¶662).

Jung reads it as a "striking counterpart to the death of Attis and the subsequent lamentation": the phallic meaning of the tree (felling = castration), its maternal nature ("the tree 'bears' Pentheus"), and its identity with the son (felling = slaying) are all present at once — and in the mother-led sparagmos "we have here the counterpart and complement of the Pietà, namely the Terrible Mother." The Pietà mourns the dead son on the mother's lap; the Maenads' fury is the same mother in her devouring aspect.
Verbatim: "his own mother being the first to hurl herself upon him" (¶662).

occurrences.title: Rosinus' vision of the dismembered white man with the golden head — Splendor solis, sixth parable
occurrences.label: Rosinus' vision of the dismembered white man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The sixth parable of the Splendor solis portrays the separatio as a dismembered corpse: "Rosinus says that he would like to make plain a vision that he has seen of a man who was dead, whose body was yet all white like a salt, and whose limbs were divided, and his head was of fine gold but separated from the body" (¶530).

Jung traces the golden head to Osiris, "who is described in a Greek papyrus as 'headless,'" and notes that "the Greek alchemists styled themselves 'Children of the Golden Head'" — the severed, gold apex of the separated body as the alchemist's own badge.

occurrences.title: The Logos as a small boy — vision of Valentinus
occurrences.label: The Logos as a small boy — vision of Valentinus
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung: Ripley's rejuvenated king may derive from 'the conception of the Ancient of Days and his youthful son the Logos, who in the visions of Valentinus the Gnostic and of Meister Eckhart was a small boy' (cw14 ¶379). The boy-Logos belongs with 'Dionysus, youngest of the gods, and of the Horus-child, Harpocrates, Aion' — 'All naturally imply the renewal of the ageing god' (¶380). Valentinus' vision gives the senex-puer pair its Gnostic form: the eternal son appears as a child to the visionary, the new dominant as a birth.

occurrences.title: The dream of Brother Eustachius (medieval German mysticism)
occurrences.label: The dream of Brother Eustachius
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I would mention Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy' and the dream of Brother Eustachius.
body: Paired by Jung with Eckhart's naked boy as a medieval spontaneous experience of the child archetype (¶267). Brother Eustachius' dream appears in the same Dominican-mysticism collection — evidence that the divine child "was not merely a traditional figure, but a vision spontaneously experienced (as a so-called 'irruption of the unconscious')". The pair grounds Jung's claim that archetypal images arrive "autochthonously", independent of tradition.

occurrences.title: Homunculi in swarms — the Schreber case
occurrences.label: Homunculi in swarms — the Schreber case
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The 'imaginary' child is common among women with mental disorders and is usually interpreted in a Christian sense. Homunculi also appear, as in the famous Schreber case, where they come in swarms and plague the sufferer.
body: In the psychopathology of the child motif Jung cites the famous Schreber case: "Homunculi also appear, as in the famous Schreber case, where they come in swarms and plague the sufferer" (¶268). This is the plurality-form of the child: numerous homunculi, dwarfs, boys with no individual characteristics signal dissociation, "the products of its dissolution" (¶278) — schizophrenia as fragmentation of personality. (Schreber's Memoirs already serve c01 as the classic anima-possession document; this note pins the homunculus episode specifically.)

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy'
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I would mention Meister Eckhart's vision of the 'naked boy' and the dream of Brother Eustachius.
body: In "The Psychology of the Child Archetype" Jung cites Meister Eckhart's vision of the "naked boy" (with the dream of Brother Eustachius) as evidence that in the Middle Ages the "child" was not merely a traditional figure "but a vision spontaneously experienced (as a so-called 'irruption of the unconscious')" (¶267). He returns to it in "Phenomenology of the Spirit in Fairytales" (¶407 n8, trans. Evans I, p. 438) as the vision-form of the boy who means the self or filius regius. Source: Spamer, Texte aus der deutschen Mystik des 14. und 15. Jahrhunderts, pp. 143, 150.

occurrences.title: The puer aeternus 'Fa' and his unholy boys — Bruno Goetz, Das Reich ohne Raum
occurrences.label: The puer aeternus 'Fa' and his unholy boys
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: a puer aeternus named Fa (= Buddha) appears with whole troops of 'unholy' boys of evil significance.
body: In Bruno Goetz's strange novel Das Reich ohne Raum a puer aeternus named Fa (= Buddha) appears "with whole troops of 'unholy' boys of evil significance. (Contemporary parallels are better let alone.)" Jung cites it twice (¶268; ¶407 n9, where the "boys" figure as negative spirit-boys beside Eckhart's positive naked boy) "only to demonstrate the enduring vitality of the child archetype". The boys' troops shadow the Hitlerjugend years in which Jung wrote.

occurrences.title: The 'Radiant Boy' seen where Roman remains lie — English ghost-lore
occurrences.label: The 'Radiant Boy' seen where Roman remains lie
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: we read of the vision of a 'Radiant Boy' said to have been seen in a place where there are Roman remains. This apparition was supposed to be of evil omen.
body: From English ghost-stories (Ingram, The Haunted Homes and Family Traditions of Great Britain, pp. 43ff): a "Radiant Boy" seen in a place where there are Roman remains, of evil omen. Jung reads it as a puer aeternus become inauspicious through "metamorphosis" — sharing the fate of the classical and Germanic gods, "who have all become bugbears" (¶267). A radiant child at Roman ruins: the archetype surfacing where an old order lies buried, now numinous-dark.

occurrences.title: Obatala and Odudua — world-parents pressed together in a calabash (Yoruba)
occurrences.label: Obatala and Odudua
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: recorded by Frobenius (early 20th c.); myth undated
body: Yoruba cosmogonic image: "In the beginning, Obatala the Sky and Odudua the Earth, his wife, lay pressed close together in a calabash" (¶620). Jung cites it immediately after the Big Snake legend as the second African witness to the mating-in-the-mother motif — the closed primordial round in which the opposites (Sky/Earth, male/female) are still contained undifferentiated, the condition that must be broken for a world of discriminated things to appear.

It thus instantiates the same "dawn state" Jung attributes to Purusha: an all-enfolding container that is at once womb, vessel, and cosmic egg. The calabash as half-gourd container keeps the family resemblance to the krater and the vessels of the horse-sacrifice.
Verbatim: "Obatala the Sky and Odudua the Earth, his wife, lay pressed close together in a calabash" (¶620).

occurrences.title: The Corascene dog and the Armenian bitch — Kalid's Liber secretorum
occurrences.label: The Corascene dog and the Armenian bitch
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: take a Corascene dog and an Armenian bitch, join them together, and they will beget a dog of celestial hue
body: The passage through which "the 'symbolizatio' by the dog entered Western alchemy": "Hermes said, My son, take a Corascene dog and an Armenian bitch, join them together, and they will beget a dog of celestial hue, and if ever he is thirsty, give him sea water to drink: for he will guard your friend, and he will guard you from your enemy... And by dog and bitch, Hermes meant things which preserve bodies from burning and from the heat of the fire" (¶174). Rosarium variant: "Hali, philosopher and king of Arabia, says in his Secret."

Jung: the filius canis "is the same as the much extolled 'son of the philosophers'... it is at once bright as day and dark as night, a perfect coincidentia oppositorum expressing the divine nature of the self" (¶176). Parallel: the poodle in Faust, Mephistopheles as the familiar of Faust the alchemist (¶177).

occurrences.title: The rabid Corascene dog and the doves of Diana — Philaletha's Introitus apertus
occurrences.label: The rabid Corascene dog and the doves of Diana
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: who is infected from his very cradle by the bite of the rabid Corascene dog
body: Philaletha's mad-dog drama: "This Chamaeleon is the infant hermaphrodite, who is infected from his very cradle by the bite of the rabid Corascene dog, whereby he is maddened and rages with perpetual hydrophobia... Yet in the grove of Diana there is a pair of doves, which assuage his raving madness.... When the moon is at the full, give him wings and he will fly away as an eagle, leaving Diana's birds dead behind him" (¶182).

Jung's reading: "the dark, dangerous, rabid dog changes into an eagle at the time of the plenilunium. His darkness disappears and he becomes a solar animal... this refers to a psychic disturbance" whose worst stage "occurred at the novilunium, i.e., the stage of nigredo" (¶183). The doves are "a love pair, for doves are the birds of Astarte," spirits/souls = the extracted aqua; their appearance "points to the imminent marriage of the filius regius" (¶185). Companion text (¶186): the winged youth espoused to Diana's central Water, beset by the thief armed "with the malignity of arsenic," whose darkness is scattered "by the spirit moving over the waters" (¶¶186-211, Jung's full dream-translation).

occurrences.title: King Domaldi killed for failure of the crops — Ynglinga saga 18
occurrences.label: King Domaldi killed for failure of the crops
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Swedish king Domaldi was actually killed as a result of the failure of the crops — the king's body given to secure the land's fertility.
Jung's reading: at accession "Princes... had to guarantee a good harvest" (¶306) — the king as husband of the land whose fruitlessness unmakes him; the sacrificial logic of the sacred marriage.
Verbatim: The Swedish king Domaldi was actually killed as a result of failure of the crops (Ynglinga Saga, 18). (cw05 ¶306).

occurrences.title: Gerhard Dorn — 'Transmute yourselves from dead stones into living philosophical stones!'
occurrences.label: Gerhard Dorn — Transmute yourselves…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Dorn, Jung's clearest alchemical psychologist: the Veritas is a 'metaphysical substance' hidden in things and in the human body — 'it is to be sought not in us, but in the image of God which is in us' (¶248, ¶265); 'nothing exists beside that One' (¶265). 'See, therefore, that thou goest forth such as thou desirest the work to be which thou seekest'; the experiment is best made 'on ourselves' (¶250). His quis/quid distinction — 'No one can know himself unless he knows what, and not who, he is' (¶252) — separates ego-knowledge from knowledge of the self. The vessel 'should be made from a kind of squaring of the circle' (¶378). 'Transmute yourselves from dead stones into living philosophical stones!' (¶264). Parallels: rosinus-ad-sarratantam-lapis-animalis, morienus-thing-extracted-from-thee-7c.

occurrences.title: Dorn: 'Transmutemini in vivos lapides philosophicos!'
occurrences.label: Dorn: Transmutemini in vivos lapides…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the stone is man
body: "To do them justice, one should not overlook the fact that there is more than a little evidence in the literature that they realized it was a matter of their own transformation. For instance, Gerhard Dorn exclaims: 'Transmutemini in vivos lapides philosophicos!' (Transform yourselves into living philosophical stones!)" (¶187).

Jung returns to the exclamation at the end of the projection argument: "But again, the stone is man. Thus Dorn exclaims… 'Transform yourselves from dead stones into living philosophical stones!' Here he is expressing in the clearest possible way the identity of something in man with something concealed in matter" (¶378). The imperative mood (transmutemini, passive) makes the operator the substance to be transformed.

occurrences.title: 'Come, compassionate mother' — invocations of the Church as virgin mother-wife, Acts of Thomas
occurrences.label: Come, compassionate mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: come, holy dove which hath brought forth twin nestlings; come, secret mother
body: In the apocryphal Acts of Thomas the apostle invokes the Church as the virgin mother-wife of Christ: "Come, compassionate mother; come, thou that hast charge of the male child," and again — "come, spouse of [lit. 'communion with'] man... come, woman who knowest the mystery of the chosen one... come, holy dove which hath brought forth twin nestlings; come, secret mother."

Jung notes that "the connection of the Church with the mother is beyond all doubt" and the mother is read as spouse: the "communion with man" points to continuous cohabitation, while the "twin nestlings" carry the old legend that Jesus and Thomas were twins, "based on the Coptic idea of Jesus and his ka" (Pistis Sophia).

occurrences.title: The cold dragon wraps the woman in her grave — Maier, Scrutinium chymicum, Emblem L
occurrences.label: The cold dragon wraps the woman in her grave
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the secret poisoning that otherwise emanates from the coldness and moisture of the moon is occasionally attributed to the 'cold dragon
body: The "cold dragon" who "contains a 'volatile fiery spirit' and 'spits flames'" given "a masculine role: he wraps the woman in the grave in a deadly embrace" (¶30). Companion Emblem V: "a toad is laid on the breast of the woman so that she, suckling it, may die as it grows. The toad is a cold and damp animal like the dragon. It 'empties' the woman as though the moon were pouring herself into the sun."

Jung reads the pair as the secret poisoning of the moon (and of the woman = Luna) by her own cold, wet daemonism — the dark half of the Sol-Luna embrace that the Church allegory suppressed. Sister locus to mercurius-salamander-maier-1687.md (same emblem book, different plate).

occurrences.title: The dragon whose head is Christ — the eight circles of the 'Scriptum Alberti'
occurrences.label: The dragon whose head is Christ
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The pseudo-Albertine "Scriptum Alberti" describes a picture of heaven in eight concentric circles: the fourth holds "a raging dragon issuing from the seven planets"; the fifth, "the head and the death" of the dragon — the caput draconis "lives in eternity", is nam ed "vita gloriosa", and "the angels serve it" (Matt. 4:11). Jung: "But if the dragon's head is identified with Christ, then the dragon's tail m ust be identical with Antichrist or the devil... the whole of the dragon's body is absorbed by the head, so that the devil is integrated with Christ... 'The whole body obeys the head, and the head hates the body, and slays it beginning from the tail, gnaw ing it with its teeth, until the whole body enters in to the head and rem ains there for ever'" (cw13 ¶416).

The sixth circle holds two storks (vas circulatorium, like the Pelican); the eighth the golden tree shining "like lightning" with the stork as pia avis — "the stork is its spiritual principle and thus a sym bol of the A nthropos" (cw13 ¶417). Sibling locus for Alexander's tree and stork: tree-alexander-hermes-tomb-stork-14c (cw12).
Verbatim: the devil is integrated with Christ. (cw13 ¶416)

occurrences.title: The dragon in the fire — Lambspringk's Symbols, Fig. X (Musaeum hermeticum)
occurrences.label: The dragon in the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Figure 50 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism = Figure X of Lambspringk's Symbols in the Musaeum hermeticum (Waite trans., I, p. 295): the dragon glowing in the fire, becoming volatilized — "illumination comes through the fiery torment." Jung introduces it through the fiery-demon drawing of Fig. 49 (a patient's shadow-figure wrapped in flames like a salamander): "the prima materia in alchemy was symbolized by the salamander in the fire, as the next picture shows." Everything the fire consumes rises up to the seat of the gods.
Distinct from the filius regis figure of the same series.

occurrences.title: Ltn the seven-headed serpent — Ugarit text, Ras Shamra
occurrences.label: Ltn the seven-headed serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Quand tu frapperas Ltn, le serpent brh / Tu acheveras le serpent 'qltn, / Le puissant aux sept tetes" — for Jung the earliest authentication of Leviathan (he dates the Ugarit texts c. 2000 B.C.; Virolleaud notes the two adjectives recur in Isaiah 27:1). Contemporary pictures show Baal fighting the serpent — a god against a monster, not yet monster against monster.

His frame (pars. 183-185): the great "fish" was first the opposite of the highest God, hence his shadow; its later doubling into Leviathan/Behemoth "relieves God of his own inner conflict, which now appears outside him in the form of a hostile pair of brother monsters."

occurrences.title: The mechanical dragon that slew the sacrificed girls — De promissionibus
occurrences.label: The mechanical dragon that slew the sacrificed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is a convenient rationalistic conceit to say that the dragon is only “artificial,” thus banishing the mysterious gods with a word.
body: Girls "consecrated and adorned with flowers" given yearly to the dragon are pierced by its springing sword; a monk examines the steps with a rod, exposes the mechanism, and cuts the dragon to pieces — "thus showing that they are not true gods who are made by the hands of men" (¶574). Jung pairs this rationalizing with the schizophrenic apotropaism "It's all a fake" (¶576).

occurrences.title: The mechanical dragon with the sword, and the monk who split it — Rome
occurrences.label: The mechanical dragon with the sword…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in quo draco mirae magnitudinis mechanica arte formatus, gladium ore gestans, oculis rutilantibus gemmis metuendus ac terribilis apparebat
body: Near Rome was a cave where a dragon of wondrous size, "formed by mechanical art," brandished a sword in its mouth and appeared terrible with eyes of ruddy gems. Each year flower-crowned virgins, unknowing gift-bearers, were sent down to it in sacrifice; touching the stair they met the spring of the sword and shed innocent blood. A monk famous for holiness — well known to the patrician Stilicho — feels his way down step by step with his staff, uncovers the fraud, crosses the threshold, splits the dragon in two, and shows "that the gods made by hand are not gods."
The devouring mother here exposed as human artifice: the two tales (with the Tarpeian dragon) form the Christian demystification of the cave-beast.

occurrences.title: Dragon Poine and the Linus lament — Argos
occurrences.label: Dragon Poine and the Linus lament — Argos
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: mythic; annual lament attested from Homer to Herodotus (II, 79)
occurrences.quote: All these motifs are to be found in Revelation 12: 1f., where the child of the sun-woman was threatened by a dragon and afterwards 'caught up' to God.
body: Linus, child of Psamathe and Apollo, exposed at birth for fear of Crotopus and torn to pieces by dogs; in revenge Apollo sent the dragon Poine into the land, which "had the disagreeable habit of tearing children out of their mothers' wombs." The Delphic oracle commanded a yearly lament by the women and maidens of Argos — the Linus lament, which Herodotus (II, 79) aligns with the laments for Adonis and Tammuz (Maneros in Egypt).

Jung reads the whole cluster into Revelation 12: the child of the sun-woman threatened by the dragon and "caught up" to God, with Herod's massacre of the innocents as "the 'human' form of this primordial image."

occurrences.title: The dragon of the Tarpeian Mount and Pope Silvester — Rome
occurrences.label: The dragon of the Tarpeian Mount…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~4th c. legend (Liber Pontificalis, life of Silvester I)
occurrences.quote: Erat draco immanissimus in monte Tarpeio... magi cum virginibus sacrilegis descendebant semel in mense cum sacrificiis et lustris
body: On the Capitoline a monstrous dragon haunts a cave reached down 365 steps, "as to hell." Once a month the magi descend with sacrilegious virgins and sacrifices to feed it; its breath poisons the air and the mortality of infants and great mourning follow. The pagans challenge Pope Silvester: descend and make the dragon cease killing for a year in the name of your God — and Silvester descends and binds it.

The tale is the devouring cave-mother staged as urban legend: the spiral descent, the sacrificed maidens, the hero who masters the beast from within the Christian church. Its 365 steps echo Diocletian's crypt of Hecate at Antioch.

occurrences.title: St. Sylvester chains the dragon of the Tarpeian Hill — Roman legend
occurrences.label: St. Sylvester chains the dragon…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: legend from the end of the 5th c.
occurrences.quote: St. Peter then appeared to Sylvester in a dream, and counselled him to close this door to the underworld with a chain
body: The dragon poisons the air and kills children until Sylvester, counselled by Peter in a dream, closes "this door to the underworld with a chain, as in the vision of the Apocalypse" — the angel binding the dragon of the bottomless pit for a thousand years (¶573). "The descent of the 365 steps refers to the course of the sun, and hence to the cavern of death and rebirth" (¶577).

occurrences.title: Marduk fighting Tiamat — Assyrian cylinder seal
occurrences.label: Marduk fighting Tiamat — Assyrian cylinder seal
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Assyrian cylinder seal (~9th-7th c. BCE; myth older)
body: Jung's fig. 41: "Marduk fighting Tiamat — Assyrian cylinder seal." He cites it as the exemplary image of the cosmic sacrifice: "the slaying of Tiamat (fig. 41), the Babylonian mother-dragon, from whose body heaven and earth were made" (¶646). The dragon here is not the hero's obstacle but the world-mother whose dismemberment is creation: "For him who looks backwards the whole world, even the starry sky, becomes the mother who bends over him... and from the renunciation of this image... arises the picture of the world as we know it today" (¶646).

This locates Tiamat on the mother-side of the sacrifice complex — the Terrible Mother whose body is the prima materia of cosmogony — rather than on the serpent/instinct side Jung assigns to Chiwantopel's green viper.
Verbatim: "a good example being the slaying of Tiamat, the Babylonian mother-dragon, from whose body heaven and earth were made" (¶646).

image.title: Chaos Monster and Sun God
image.credit: editor Austen Henry Layard , drawing by L. Gruner

occurrences.title: The great zodiac-bearer dragon — Codex Vat. 190 (Mithraic text)
occurrences.label: The great zodiac-bearer dragon — Codex Vat. 190
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Via Cumont (Textes et monuments figures relatifs aux mysteres de Mithra): "The all-wise God fashioned an immensely great dragon of gigantic length, breadth and thickness, having its dark-coloured head... towards sunrise, and its tail... towards sunset." "Then the all-wise Demiurge, by his highest command, set in motion the great dragon with the spangled crown, I mean the twelve signs of the zodiac which it carried on its back." Eisler connects this zodiacal serpent with Leviathan; the Mythographus Vaticanus III has the dragon as symbol of the year, as does Horapollo. Jung: the primordial image behind the quicksilver-girdled sphere of Picture 3 — the world encircled by the serpent.

occurrences.title: Brother-sister pair bitten by dragons in the 'bath of life' — Theatrum chemicum Britannicum (1652)
occurrences.label: Brother-sister pair bitten by dragons…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For myself two species are sufficient: male and female or brother and sister
body: Plate 118: "Brother-sister pair in the 'bath of life,' being bitten in the calf by dragons while the lunar water, fertilized by the divine breath, is poured over their heads."

Jung cites it within the quoted catalogue of water-synonyms ("Some [alchemists] put three together, others, only two. For myself two species are sufficient: male and female or brother and sister"): the philosophical water as the pair. The dragons biting the calf are the same motif Jung had flagged in dreams 18 and 44 ("he is bitten… cf. fig. 118") — the animal impulse of the unconscious that must be endured in the circumambulatio.

occurrences.title: Dream: the actor smashes the hat — the hat proves to be a mandala (dream 35)
occurrences.label: Dream — the actor smashes the hat
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: So the 'strange' hat was the self
body: An actor smashes his hat against the wall. Jung (drawing on unpublished personal material): the actor is a fiction the dreamer maintained about himself, "it was the actor in him who rejected the self." The smashed hat "proves to be a mandala": the "strange" hat of the very first dream of the series was the self, which "at that time—while he was still playing a fictitious role—seemed like a stranger to him."

This closes the circle opened by dream 1 (¶52) and confirms Jung's retrospective claim that the mandala motif "was always present," only unnoticed — evidence for the archetype as a priori "type" (¶329).

occurrences.title: Black birds plunge joyfully into the fire and turn white — patient's dream
occurrences.label: Black birds plunge joyfully into the fire…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: one of the birds plunged straight into the blaze and was joyfully burnt to death, turning white in the process.
body: The dream: "A large pile of wood was burning at the foot of a high wall of rock; the flames shot up with clouds of smoke. It was a lonely and romantic spot. High in the air, a flock of great black birds circled round the fire. From time to time one of the birds plunged straight into the blaze and was joyfully burnt to death, turning white in the process." The dreamer remarked its numinous quality (¶82).

Jung: "it repeats the miracle of the phoenix, of transformation and rebirth (the transformation of the nigredo into the albedo, of unconsciousness into 'illumination')," quoting the Rosarium's "Two eagles fly up with feathers aflame, / Naked they fall to earth again. / Yet in full feather they rise up soon." A modern person "never remotely concerned with alchemy" producing the corpus' core image.

occurrences.title: Dream: the bleeding Christ and the work of self-redemption (dream 34)
occurrences.label: Dream: the bleeding Christ and the work…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the Anthropos or Poimen figure should emerge, since it is present in his own psyche
body: The dreamer tells a friend: "I must carry on with the figure of the bleeding Christ before me and persevere in the work of selfredemption" (OCR: 'selfredemption'). Jung reads it as the "extraordinary, subtle kind of suffering" (fig. 89, the pelican) caused by the breaking through of an alien spiritual world — "My kingdom is not of this world" — and as evidence that the dreamer continues his task "in deadly earnest."

The passage develops into one of Jung's central statements: individuation "has constantly been held up to Western man in the dogmatic and religious model of the life of Christ"; dogma works by its symbolic nature, so there is "a 'pre-Christian' as well as a 'non-Christian' Christ, in so far as he is an autonomous psychological fact" — hence the Anthropos/Poimen figure emerges even in modern man without religious assumptions (¶253).

occurrences.title: Dream 17: the dreamer finds a blue flower
occurrences.label: Dream 17: the dreamer finds a blue flower
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The dreamer goes for a long walk, and finds a blue flower on the way." (cw12 ¶100).

Jung reads it as "a numinous emanation from the unconscious" connecting the dreamer with the Romantic past — while "the dreamer knows nothing as yet of the old solar gold which connects the innocent flower with the obnoxious black art of alchemy and with the blasphemous pagan idea of the solificatio." The bridge: "For the 'golden flower of alchemy' (fig. 30) can sometimes be a blue flower: 'The sapphire blue flower of the hermaphrodite.'" (¶101).

occurrences.title: Dream: the chemist's shop and the special water (dream 14 — aqua nostra)
occurrences.label: Dream: the chemist's shop and the special water
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The 'special water' is literally the aqua nostra non vulgi.
body: The dreamer goes with his father into a chemist's shop where "valuable things can be got there quite cheap, above all a special water"; the father tells him of the country it comes from; the dreamer crosses the Rubicon by train. Jung: the apothecary's shop with "its carboys and gallipots, its waters, its lapis divinus and infernalis and its magisteries, is the last visible remnant of the kitchen paraphernalia of those alchemists"; the "special water" is "literally the aqua nostra non vulgi"; the father leads to the source of life as "transmitter of the traditional wisdom," appearing "as the archetypal father figure, the 'wise old man'" (¶159).

Like the lapis, the water of life is "pretio quoque vilis," despised and flung into the street (Spitteler's jewel picked up by Ahasuerus); the dreamer crosses the Rubicon: "the flux and fire of life… absolutely necessary for the achievement of wholeness" (¶161).

occurrences.title: Ten-year-old girl — dream of the horned animal and the four Gods (1939-40)
occurrences.label: Ten-year-old girl — dream of the horned animal…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (sent to Jung by an acquaintance)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Then God came) but there were really four Gods in the four corners.
body: Reported in Jung's 1939/40 seminar on children's dreams; written down by the child herself, who "had absolutely no possibility of ever hearing about the quaternity of God." A horned animal spikes up little animals and lives by wriggling like a snake; a blue fog comes out of all the four corners and it stops eating; God comes — "but there were really four Gods in the four corners"; the animal dies and all the eaten animals come out alive again. Jung: an unconscious individulation process — integration gathers many into one; the dragon changes into pneuma (divine quaternity); then the apocatastasis, resurrection of the dead (¶625).

occurrences.title: Dream: 'The circulation can begin' — shooting star and cosmic flower (dream 26)
occurrences.label: Dream — 'The circulation can begin'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: What is now beginning is the circulation of the light.
body: Night, stars; a voice: "Now it will begin." — "The circulation can begin." A shooting star falls in a leftward curve. The scene drops to a squalid night club where the proprietor quarrels about left and right; the dreamer answers that "The left is the mirror-image of the right… There is no right and no left side to human society, but there are symmetrical and lopsided people," and drives a taxi round the perimeter of a square (magical circumambulatio).

Jung: the star's curve "formed the edge of the petals" of the eightfold flower sketched after dream 23 — "a flower that spreads over the whole starry heaven. What is now beginning is the circulation of the light. This cosmic flower corresponds roughly to the rose in Dante's Paradiso" (¶229). The cosmic aspect is then compensated "downward" into social symbolism (¶230).
