occurrences.title: Dream: the clergyman's fallen choir wall overgrown with vines
occurrences.label: Dream: the clergyman's fallen choir wall…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the whole wall of the choir had collapsed. The altar and ruins were overgrown with vines
body: "I encountered something very similar in the dream of a clergyman who had a rather problematical attitude to his faith: Coming into his church at night, he found that the whole wall of the choir had collapsed. The altar and ruins were overgrown with vines hanging full of grapes, and the moon was shining in through the gap."

Jung sets it beside the universal-church dream as Dionysian irruption into the Christian temenos — grapes and wine, moonlight where the wall of dogma stood. Paired with the next dream of a Gothic cathedral shattered open by sunlight and "a large herd of bulls and cows," which he calls "more Mithraic, but Mithras is associated with the early Church in much the same way Dionysos is" (¶180).

occurrences.title: Dream of the excremental Crucifix in a chamber-pot
occurrences.label: Dream of the excremental Crucifix…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A dream: "she saw the Crucifix formed of excrement on the bottom of a blue-flowered chamber-pot."

Jung's reading: "The contrast is so enormous that one can only assume that the valuations of childhood are totally different from ours" (¶279) — the excrement-gold identity, prima materia found "in stercore", the lowest value wedded to the highest.
Verbatim: A very religiously brought-up young patient once dreamt that she saw the Crucifix formed of excrement on the bottom of a blueflowered chamber-pot. (cw05 ¶279).

occurrences.title: Dream: the 'disturbed' mandala — oblongs and the four coloured waters (dream 51)
occurrences.label: Dream — the 'disturbed' mandala
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: So we are dealing with a 'disturbed' mandala.
body: People circulate leftward round a large central oblong with four smaller oblongs (rightward circulation); an eight-rayed star in the middle; bowls of red, yellow, green, and colourless water; "The disquieting question arises: Is there enough water?" Jung: the question is "whether there is enough water of life—aqua nostra, energy, libido—to reach the central star"; the blue is missing, the square ground-plan abandoned, the horizontal extended at the cost of the vertical: "So we are dealing with a 'disturbed' mandala" (¶287), the ego-consciousness uppermost, "a loss of height and depth."

Dreams 52–53 crack the "hard nuts," lengthen the vertical, and re-establish the square; after them "the dreamer worked out six mandalas in which he tried to determine the right length of the vertical, the form of 'circulation,' and the distribution of colour" (¶292).

occurrences.title: Dream: four children carry the dark ring at the solstice (dream 56)
occurrences.label: Dream: four children carry the dark ring…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the symbol of wholeness is still under the sway of childlike creative powers
body: "Four children are carrying a large dark ring. They move in a circle. The dark unknown woman appears and says she will come again, for it is the festival of the solstice." Jung: the elements of dream 44 (children, the formerly wicked witch-woman) reunite; the solstice is the turning-point; "the symbol of wholeness is still under the sway of childlike creative powers." Children belong to the opus itself: "a certain portion of the work is called ludus puerorum" — since the unanimous testimony of the adepts calls the work exceedingly difficult, the phrase must be "a euphemistic and probably also a symbolical definition" pointing to "co-operation on the part of 'infantile' or unconscious forces represented as Cabiri and hobgoblins (homunculi)" (¶302).

occurrences.title: Dream: the gibbon to be reconstructed in the square (second dream series, dream 16)
occurrences.label: Dream: the gibbon to be reconstructed…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the anthropoid—man as an archaic fact—is to be put together again
body: Crowds walk leftward around a square; the dreamer stands off-centre; "a gibbon is to be reconstructed." Jung reads the square as arising from the circle via the four people — squaring of the circle, symbol of the opus — and the gibbon as the anthropoid, "man as an archaic fact," to be put together again in the sacred precincts: "the left-hand path does not lead upwards to the kingdom of the gods and eternal ideas, but down into natural history" — "a Dionysian mystery" (¶169). The ego, "not in the centre but to one side," must accept a satellite position (¶175).
The ape links Thoth's cynocephalus (godlike) and the simia Dei (devilish): the archetype spans layers below and above consciousness.

occurrences.title: Dream: the round table and the glass of gelatinous mass (dream 31 — the unum vas)
occurrences.label: Dream: the round table and the glass…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The glass corresponds to the unum vas of alchemy
body: The dreamer sits with "a certain man of unpleasant aspect" at a round table on which stands a glass filled with a gelatinous mass. Jung reads the dream as the shadow being accepted as the dreamer's own darkness, freeing the anima "of the moral inferiority projected upon her" to resume "the living and creative function which is properly her own" (¶242).

The glass corresponds to the unum vas of alchemy; its contents to the "living, semi-organic mixture from which the body of the lapis, endowed with spirit and life, will emerge" — or the Faustian figures (Boy Charioteer, Homunculus, Euphorion) bursting into flame. The lapis is "composed 'de re animali, vegetabili et minerali'" and "grows from flesh and blood" (¶243); its birth from an amorphous mass parallels the prima materia as massa informis impregnated with the seeds of life (¶244).

occurrences.title: Dream 18: golden coins offered and indignantly thrown away
occurrences.label: Dream 18 — golden coins offered…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A man offers him some golden coins in his outstretched hand. The dreamer indignantly throws them to the ground and immediately afterwards deeply regrets his action." (cw12 ¶102).

A misreading of the aurum philosophicum, matched in Meyrink's Golem (the spurned grain). Jung then delivers the lapis-exilis doctrine: "it is exilis, uncomely, it is thrown out into the street or on the dunghill… 'in planitie, in montibus et aquis'" — like Spitteler's jewel, like "the stone which the builders rejected" (¶103).

occurrences.title: Dream — the golden fish and the four realms (young woman, Limmat)
occurrences.label: Dream — the golden fish and the four realms
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: A young woman dreamt at six or seven that 'God had promised her a golden fish'; later, standing on the bank of the Limmat, she watches a man throw a gold coin into the river — the water clears, revealing a coral reef and fishes, one with silver belly and golden back (¶232-233). In treatment she fishes the same fish from a broad river; as she draws it to land the dead landscape comes alive, and a voice: 'The patient ones in the innermost realm are given the fish, the food of the deep' (¶233). Four realms are announced, 'the fourth realm joins on to the first... the highest and the lowest come together. They are at bottom one' (¶234). Jung: circles produce a mandala recalling 'God is a circle whose centre is everywhere'; the dream 'sums up in condensed form the whole symbolism of the individuation process' in a person ignorant of the historical fish symbol (¶234-235). Parallels: dream-jellyfish-round-pool-student-1951c, fish-round-fish-allegoriae-turba-11c.

occurrences.title: Dream: the Gothic cathedral burst open by sunlight and bulls
occurrences.label: Dream: the Gothic cathedral burst open…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Blinding sunlight bursts into the interior together with a large herd of bulls and cows.
body: "Again, a man who was much occupied with religious problems had the following dream: An immense Gothic cathedral, almost completely dark. High Mass is being celebrated. Suddenly the whole wall of the aisle collapses. Blinding sunlight bursts into the interior together with a large herd of bulls and cows."

Jung's one-line reading: "This setting is evidently more Mithraic, but Mithras is associated with the early Church in much the same way Dionysos is" (¶180) — the bull-herd as Mithraic irruption paralleling the Dionysian vines of the clergyman's dream (¶179). Recorded as evidence for the pattern of pre-Christian contents breaking back into the Christian temenos (cf. ¶178's "systematic descent ad inferos").

occurrences.title: Dream: the 'House of the Gathering' — religion is no substitute (dream 54)
occurrences.label: Dream — the 'House of the Gathering'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Out of the fulness of life shall you bring forth your religion; only then shall you be blessed!
body: A solemn house — "the 'House of the Gathering'" — with candles arranged in "a peculiar pattern with four points running upward"; an old man at the door: "When they come out again they are cleansed." A voice thunders: "Religion is not a tax to be paid so that you can rid yourself of the woman's image… Religion is no substitute; it is to be added to the other activities of the soul as the ultimate completion." Leaving, the dreamer sees a burning mountain: "The fire that is not put out is a holy fire" (Shaw, St. Joan); distant organ chords recall Wagner's Fire Music.

Jung treats this numinous dream as "a new climax of insight": the square is a "gathering place"; wholeness requires the anima-image of the fourth function; and "man as a whole being casts a shadow" (¶297).

occurrences.title: Dream — the jelly-fish in the round pool (20-year-old student)
occurrences.label: Dream — the jelly-fish in the round pool
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: A student in professional confusion walks into a darkening primeval forest and finds a circular pool of crystal-clear water, in the middle of which floats a pearly, faintly luminous organism about eighteen inches in diameter — a jelly-fish. He wakes 'with a violent emotion' and decides to study science (¶208). Jung: a 'big' dream, archetypal, in no way suggested; the round pool with the medusa is 'a three-dimensional mandala, the self: wholeness as the goal to which the "archetic appetite" points, the magnetic north which gives the traveller his bearings on the "sea of the world"' (¶208). Parallels the fish-symbolism of the alchemists.

occurrences.title: Dream: hotel lift, the note of salvation, the eight-spoked wheel (dream 22)
occurrences.label: Dream: hotel lift, the note of salvation,…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Salvation comes from complete surrender, with one's eyes always turned to the centre.
body: In an American hotel the lift stops "about the third or fourth floor"; a friend reproaches the dreamer for keeping "the dark unknown woman waiting so long below," and hands him an unsealed note: "Salvation does not come from refusing to take part or from running away… Salvation comes from complete surrender, with one's eyes always turned to the centre." On the margin, a drawing: "a wheel or wreath with eight spokes." Soldiers with ramrods prepare to shoot at the centre — but do not shoot.

Jung: the lift rises as something comes "up" from the subconscious; the mandala of the number four waits at the fourth floor because the fourth function is taboo; the "red-haired man" (= Mephisto, the man with the pointed beard) commands "completely throttling the left" (¶201, ¶211).

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of removing the black fleck from the animus's eye (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of removing the black fleck…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A little golden lamp then became visible in the centre of the puPil.
body: Four days before Picture 8: she draws a young man to the window and, with a brush dipped in white oil, removes a black fleck from his cornea; a little golden lamp becomes visible in the pupil; he is relieved; she wakes saying "If therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light" (Matt. 6:22). The young man is her animus, now become her patient, who "has seen things too blackly" (¶592). The dream marks the change: the mandala is an "eye," the structure symbolizing the centre of order in the unconscious; the eye is also a symbol for God (Boehme's "Eye of Eternity").

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of the golden snake demanding sacrifice (~early 1920s)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of the golden snake demanding…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It demanded the sacrifice... of a young man... The dream was repeated a little later, but this time the snake picked on the dreamer herself.
body: The second "big" dream, a year before the narcosis dream: a golden snake in the sky demands, from a great crowd, the sacrifice of a young man, who obeys with sorrow; the assembled people regard him compassionately. Repeated shortly after — this time the snake picks the dreamer herself, who takes her fate "proudly" upon her. The golden snake is the direct ancestor of the golden lightning-snake of Pictures 2-3 (the Nous-serpent, Mercurius Philosophorum). Jung connects the mood to her birth "at the twelfth hour" and to the birth of the self as distinct from the ego (¶548).

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of the mother sleeping in the father's-room bed (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of the mother sleeping…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: my mother had moved my bed away from the wall into the middle of the room and had slept in it
body: Two days before Picture 7 (four days before Picture 8's eye-dream): the mother has moved Miss X's bed from the wall into the middle of the father's room and slept in it; furious, she pushes it back. The red bed-cover is "exactly the red reproduced in the picture." Jung: her sphere is the father's spiritual sphere, usurped as she usurped his room — identification with the "spirit." The mother (physis vs spirit) intrudes and installs herself in the centre, so the dark chthonic principle penetrates to the mandala's centre — "e tenebris lux!" (¶586). The collision of paternal and maternal principles works like a shock.

occurrences.title: Miss X — narcosis dream of the world-globe with vibrating silver band (~mid-1920s)
occurrences.label: Miss X — narcosis dream of the world-globe…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: She saw a grey globe of the world. A silver band rotated about the equator
body: One of the two "big" dreams of Miss X's life, dreamed under narcosis during an operation. A grey globe of the world; a silver band rotating about the equator forms zones of condensation and evaporation; in the condensation-zones appear numbers 1 to 3, tending to increase to 12 — "nodal points" or "great personalities" of historical development; 12 = the culminating point still to come. The dream is one of the two components amalgamated in Picture 3, where the band becomes the quicksilver girdle of the sphere (¶549: cosmic analogy of the birth of the self). It matches the 1916 world-creation picture (Fig. 2).

occurrences.title: Miss X — dream of the tree growing in the workroom (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X — dream of the tree growing…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: To her astonishment she found a tree growing in the middle of the room where she worked.
body: Days before Picture 6: returning from holiday she finds a tree growing in the middle of the room where she works — "with its thick bark this tree can withstand the heat of an apartment." Associations led to the tree's maternal significance; it explains the plant motif of the swastika-mandala and represents "the higher level or freeing of consciousness induced by the movement to the right." The "thick bark" anticipates the protective cortices/skins of Pictures 7-8 (¶572, ¶576). Jung: "the 'philosophical' tree is a symbol of the alchemical opus, which as we know is an individuation process" (¶570).

occurrences.title: Dream 15: the mother pours the water of life into the sister's basin
occurrences.label: Dream 15 — the mother pours the water…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: same series as dream 1 (dreamer a Roman Catholic)
body: "The dreamer's mother is pouring water from one basin into another… This action is performed with great solemnity: it is of the highest significance for the outside world. Then the dreamer is rejected by his father." (cw12 ¶91).

Jung: the father = collective consciousness, traditional spirit; the mother = the collective unconscious, "the source of the water of life"; the sister later proves "the carrier of the anima-image" — "the mother has been replaced by the anima" (¶92). The father's rejection amounts to excommunication. The alchemists' water-synonyms (aqua nostra, mercurius vivus, succus lunariae, acetum fontis) frame it (¶94).

occurrences.title: Mandala dream 9: the pendulum clock that goes forever
occurrences.label: Mandala dream 9 — the pendulum clock…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A pendulum clock that goes forever without the weights running down." (cw12 ¶134).

"This is a species of clock whose hands move unceasingly, and, since there is obviously no loss due to friction, it is a perpetuum mobile, an everlasting movement in a circle" (¶135). 'Metaphysical' — eternity as a quality predicated by the unconscious: "the other centre of personality lies on a different plane from the ego since, unlike this, it has the quality of 'eternity' or relative timelessness." Precursor of the world-clock vision treated later in the same chapter.

occurrences.title: Mandala dream 10: four figures in the Peterhofstatt, Zurich — the four functions round the self
occurrences.label: Mandala dream 10 — four figures…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The dreamer is in the Peterhofstatt in Zurich with the doctor, the man with the pointed beard, and the 'doll woman.'… Question: To which of the three does the woman belong?" (cw12 ¶136).

The church precinct is "a temenos in the truest sense of the word"; St. Peter's clock dial "is divided into four quarters, like the horizon." The four persons read as the four functions: dreamer = ego, pointed beard = the 'employed' Mephisto-intellect, doll woman = anima, doctor = non-ego ("he probably contains a faint allusion to myself," Jung notes). "Therefore the centre of the circle which expresses such a totality would correspond not to the ego but to the self as the summation of the total personality." (¶137).

occurrences.title: Dream of the poisoned Paradise tree — young woman patient
occurrences.label: Dream of the poisoned Paradise tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Dream: in a garden she finds an exotic tree with strange red fleshy flowers or fruits, picks and eats them, then feels to her horror that she is poisoned.

Jung's reading: after sexual difficulties in marriage, "The tree is the same tree that stood in Paradise... It is the tree of libido, which here represents the feminine as well as the masculine side, because it simply expresses the relationship of the two to one another" (¶326).

Verbatim: She was in a garden, where she found an exotic-looking tree with strange red fleshy flowers or fruits. She picked and ate them. Then, to her horror, she felt that she was poisoned. (cw05 ¶325).

occurrences.title: Dream: discovering the Pole under guidance of the unknown woman (dream 40)
occurrences.label: Dream: discovering the Pole under guidance…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The Pole is the point round which everything turns—hence another symbol of the self.
body: "Under the guidance of the unknown woman the dreamer has to discover the Pole at the risk of his life." Jung: "The Pole is the point round which everything turns—hence another symbol of the self." Alchemy had already taken up the analogy: "In the Pole is the heart of Mercurius, who is the true fire, wherein his master rests… he sets his course by the aspect of the North star" (¶265). "Mercurius is the world-soul, and the Pole is its heart. The idea of the anima mundi coincides with that of the collective unconscious whose centre is the self. The symbol of the sea is another synonym for the unconscious."
Dreams 42–43 (the old master's red-illuminated spot; the murky yellow sun with eight rays) continue the place-and-time determination toward the centre.

occurrences.title: Dream: the portrait that becomes four-colour clovers; the wheel drawings (dream 23)
occurrences.label: Dream — the wheel drawings
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: what the dream represents in personified form the dreamer reproduces as an abstract ideogram
body: In the square space the dreamer sits opposite the unknown woman, commissioned to draw her portrait; what appears instead are "three-leaved clovers or distorted crosses in four different colours: red, yellow, green, and blue." He then spontaneously draws the wheel with eight spokes and a four-petalled blue flower, and "a great many drawings now followed at short intervals, all dealing with the curious structure of the 'centre'" (¶213).

Jung: what the dream personifies the dreamer "reproduces as an abstract ideogram" (¶220); the Trinity symbol is "overshadowed or 'coloured' by the alchemical quaternity" — the four colours as concretization of the tetraktys, the transition from trinity to quaternity, preliminary stage of the lapis that unites omnes colores.

occurrences.title: Dream: the prince gives the diamond ring on the fourth finger of the left hand (dream 37)
occurrences.label: Dream: the prince gives the diamond ring…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The self is made manifest in the opposites and in the conflict between them; it is a coincidentia oppositorum. Hence the way to the self begins with conflict.
body: Curves of light around a dark centre; a dark cave where good and evil battle; "a prince who knows everything" gives the dreamer a ring set with a diamond "and places it on the fourth finger of his left hand." Jung: the gift "means nothing less than the dreamer's vow to the self—for as a rule the wedding ring is worn on the fourth finger of the left hand"; the left hand marks the unconscious situation; the prince is "the representative of the aenigma regis." The dark cave "corresponds to the vessel containing the warring opposites."
Dream 38 confirms it: a circular table with four empty chairs — "The mandala is not yet 'in use'" (¶261).

occurrences.title: Dream of the fourth chair and the laurel (patient-anon, ~1930s)
occurrences.label: Dream of the fourth chair and the laurel
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: For this purpose she fetched a fourth chair that stood fw,ther off.
body: A patient dreams: a drawing-room, a table with three chairs; an unknown man invites her to sit; she fetches a fourth chair from further off; she turns the pages of a book with pictures of blue and red cubes, as for a building game; leaving for a yellow house, she shelters from torrential rain under a green laurel tree. Jung: table, three-plus-fourth chairs, cubes, building game = a process of composition in stages; the four colours = four qualities; the green laurel = the inferior (sensation) function, "contaminated with the collective unconscious and... used as a bridge." The laurel, like the alchemical tree, is a symbol of the self (¶583).

occurrences.title: The six mandalas worked out by the dreamer (between dreams 53 and 54)
occurrences.label: The six mandalas worked out by the dreamer
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the dreamer worked out six mandalas in which he tried to determine the right length of the vertical
body: "After this dream the dreamer worked out six mandalas in which he tried to determine the right length of the vertical, the form of 'circulation,' and the distribution of colour. At the end of this work came the following dream (given unabridged)" — the House of the Gathering (dream 54, ¶293).

The patient's own drawing series is the synthetic opus in miniature: correcting the "disturbed" mandala of dream 51 (oblong, missing blue) toward the squared, right-circulating, four-coloured form — and the work is immediately answered by the series' most numinous dream. It is the clearest documentation in the chunk of the patient as co-worker, not merely dreamer.

occurrences.title: Dream 1: the stranger's hat — first mandala allusion of the 1930s dream series
occurrences.label: Dream 1 — the stranger's hat
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: observed via Jung's woman-doctor pupil (355 of 400 dreams away from Jung)
body: Opening dream of the series: "The dreamer is at a social gathering. On leaving, he puts on a stranger's hat instead of his own." (cw12 ¶52).

Jung: the hat, covering the head, is "a sort of leading idea" covering the whole personality — "a stranger's hat imparts a strange personality." He amplifies with Meyrink's Golem (the hat of Athanasius Pernath) and concludes: "Encircling the head, the hat is round like the sun-disc of a crown and therefore contains the first allusion to the mandala" (¶53). The exchange of hats inaugurates the emergence of the unconscious.

occurrences.title: Dream: transformation of animals into men, snakes in the four corners (dream 18)
occurrences.label: Dream: transformation of animals…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: we have to expose ourselves to the animal impulses of the unconscious without identifying with them and without 'running away
body: In a square space, animals are to be transformed into men. Two snakes fleeing in opposite directions are removed at once; the people circumambulate and are bitten in the calf at each of the four corners; four snakes then settle into the corners; sacrificial priests touch a shapeless "life-mass" with a huge reptile, "and out of it there instantly rises a human head, transfigured. A voice proclaims: 'These are attempts at being.'"

Jung reads the life-mass as the inherited unconscious (alchemical chaos, massa informis; midrashic Adam), the serpent rite as the "well-substantiated archetype" of renewal by serpent (Sabazius, Ophites, Kundalini), and the circumambulatio as exclusive concentration on the centre while being "bitten" — exposing oneself to animal impulses without running away. The four-corner arrangement reveals "an order in the unconscious… a kind of Pythagorean tetraktys" (¶189).

occurrences.title: Dream: treasure in the sea, the walled garden with fountain (second dream series, dream 13)
occurrences.label: Dream: treasure in the sea, the walled garden…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The 'treasure hard to attain' lies hidden in the ocean of the unconscious, and only the brave can reach it.
body: The dreamer must dive through a narrow, dangerous opening to reach a treasure lying in the sea; below he finds "a beautiful garden in the depths, symmetrically laid out, with a fountain in the centre." Jung reads the treasure as the "treasure hard to attain" hidden in the ocean of the unconscious, and conjectures that treasure, companion, and garden-fountain "are all one and the same thing: the self" — the lonely ego finding its mate in the self, "at first the strange non-ego" (¶155).
The garden is "another temenos"; the fountain the source of "living water" (John 7:38); centre and circle are "analogues of the lapis."

occurrences.title: Woman patient's dream: two dogs copulating, the male disappears into the female
occurrences.label: Woman patient's dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The male went head first into the female and disappeared in her belly.
body: The incest dream: "Two dogs were copulating. The male went head first into the female and disappeared in her belly." Jung: "Theriomorphic symbolism is always an indication of a psychic process occurring on an animal level, i.e., in the instinctual sphere. The dream depicts a reversed birth as the goal of a sexual act" (¶178).

It anchors the chapter's thesis on incest: "The archetype of incest is also at the back of the primitive notion that the father is reborn in the son, and of the heirosgamos of mother and son in its pagan and Christian form; it signifies the highest and the lowest, the brightest and the darkest, the best and the most detestable. It represents the pattern of renewal and rebirth" (¶178).

occurrences.title: Dream: the universal Catholic Church (Hagia Sophia, 'Soldiers!' proclamation) (dream 17)
occurrences.label: Dream: the universal Catholic Church
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: it does not lose its sacramental character
body: Given unabridged: a future-dated stage-set church, "This is the universal Catholic Church… founded by Jesus and Paul"; a proclamation forbidding direct address to the ineffable Lord; interior like the Hagia Sophia, only framed texts on the walls; a Bach fugue whose original text is omitted ("Everything else is paper"); then the "gemütlich" part — wine, ragtime, "Charles is also with us now" — an "anti-ascetic" American-flavoured church.

Jung: the temenos "has become a sacred building"; the grotesque-humorous side is Dionysian (cf. the shrine inscription μόνον μὴ ὕδωρ); the regression is "not a relapse but a kind of systematic descent ad inferos, a psychological nekyia" (¶178) that retreads the historical path to the pre-Christian level, joining Church and Dionysian sanctuary without destroying either (¶181).

occurrences.title: Dream: letter from the unknown woman — the uterus drawing, spiral, glaciers (dream 32)
occurrences.label: Dream — letter from the unknown woman
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the uterus… is a synonym frequently employed for the alchemical vessel
body: The dreamer receives a letter from an unknown woman complaining of pains "in the uterus," with an attached drawing: a spiral line through primeval forest full of monkeys, opening onto "a panorama of white glaciers." Jung reads the life-creating centre now designated "uterus" — "a synonym frequently employed for the alchemical vessel, just as it is one of the basic meanings of the Eastern mandala" (¶246). The serpentine line recalls the healing serpent of Aesculapius and Shiva bindu encircled three and a half times by the Kundalini serpent.

The dream ends by returning the cosmic aspect with "interest and compound interest": the glaciers recall an earlier Milky Way dream and "a conversation about immortality. Immortality is a clock that never runs down, a mandala that revolves eternally like the heavens" (¶246).

occurrences.title: The Druid's cutting of the mistletoe — Pliny, Natural History
occurrences.label: The Druid's cutting of the mistletoe
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: After sacrifice, the Druid climbs the sacred oak on the sixth day of the moon and cuts the mistletoe with a golden sickle; two white bulls are sacrificed; the plant is a sovereign remedy against barrenness.

Jung's reading: "when the Druid cuts it, he kills it and by this act symbolically repeats the fatal self-castration of Attis and the wounding of Adonis by the boar's tusk" (¶392) — the matriarchal dream of the son killed by separation from the tree-mother.
Verbatim: In Gaul, it was only after offering sacrifice that the Druid was allowed, amid solemn ceremonies, to climb the sacred oak and cut the ritual branch of mistletoe. (cw05 ¶392).

occurrences.title: The toddler's 'two Mamas' (Karl Abraham's case, Berlin)
occurrences.label: The toddler's 'two Mamas'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: fn 27 to ch. IV, The Hymn of Creation (pdf p677)

body: Abraham's girl of three and a half, watching her baby brother suckle, told her mother: "You are two Mamas. You are my Mama, and your breast is little brother's Mama." Jung appends the philological sting: "Mamma is Latin for 'breast'" — "characteristic of the archaic thinking of the child to call the breast 'Mama.'" The dual-mother formula appears here from the child's mouth, the analytic observation confirming the mythologem (cf. index: "mother: two, 295n, 317ff").
Verbatim (fn 27): "You are two Mamas. You are my Mama, and your breast is little brother’s Mama."

occurrences.title: The Oedipus legend — Thebes (Greek myth)
occurrences.label: The Oedipus legend — Thebes (Greek myth)
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The monumental drama of the ancient world at whose root Freud placed "an individual conflict... the incest fantasy" (¶1). Jung opens the whole volume with it: to meet the Oedipus material in one's own psyche is to bridge the gulf to antiquity and learn "that there is an identity of fundamental human conflicts which is independent of time and place" — "Oedipus is still alive for us" (¶1).

Later in the volume the legend becomes the paradigm of the dual-mother motif (the unknowing marriage with the mother); here it already carries the Sphinx as its monster-riddle wing. Burckhardt's word, quoted by Jung: "every Greek of the classical period carries in himself a little bit of Oedipus, and every German a little bit of Faust" (¶45). Jung adds that Faust formulates the same problem for the German sphere that Oedipus did for the Greek (¶121).

occurrences.title: Double-headed eagle covered with eyes, crowned by Pope and Emperor — Codex Palatinus Latinus 412
occurrences.label: Double-headed eagle covered with eyes, crowned…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Vatican, Biblioteca (Wynandi de Stega, 'Adamas colluctancium aquilarum')
body: "266. Double-headed eagle with crowns of Pope and Emperor, symbolizing the kingdoms of both worlds. The eagle is covered with eyes (enlightenment!)" (fig. 266; verified on plate p0452). The imperial-ecclesiastical two-headed bird of the two worlds, its plumage an eyelike field — Jung's own parenthetical gloss "(enlightenment!)" marks his reading of the many-eyed body as vision, consciousness multiplied across the whole animal.

Jung sets it in the chapter's closing series of figures (figs. 265–266) where the unicorn's reflection ("De moy je m'epouvante") and the two-worlds eagle frame the transition to the Epilogue's psychology of enlightenment and inflation.

occurrences.title: Eagle and toad of Avicenna — Maier, Symbola aureae mensae
occurrences.label: Eagle and toad of Avicenna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I would mention the eagle and toad ('the eagle flying through the air and the toad crawling on the ground'), which are the 'emblem' of Avicenna in Michael Maier
body: The emblem pair Avicenna hands the alchemists through Michael Maier: the eagle "flying through the air" and the toad "crawling on the ground" — the volatile and the fixed as theriomorphic opposites. The eagle is Luna "or Juno, Venus, Beya, who is fugitive and winged like the eagle, which flies up to the clouds and receives the rays of the sun in his eyes"; the toad is the contrary element, earth, "which cannot fly [i.e., cannot be sublimated]," the philosophic earth on which "the golden house is to be built" (¶2).

Jung opens Mysterium Coniunctionis with this pair as the classic case of opposites personified in animals: "Theriomorphic symbols are equally common." The toad recurs at ¶30 (Scrutinium Emblem V, suckled by the woman until she dies) and in ¶172's list of the union's poisonous progeny.

occurrences.title: The nourishing earth-mother — Limburg Cathedral vault painting
occurrences.label: The nourishing earth-mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Limburg an der Lahn, Germany (vault painting)
body: Pl. XIVa: the nursing earth-mother of the Limburg vault (with the classical Gaia-type streaming water/milk motif).

Jung's reading: "The ideal example of such an object is the nurturing earth-mother" (¶226) — the object invested by desexualized, regressed libido; "the psychology of the presexual stage accounts for her nourishing character, and sexuality for her most typical form of worship, the hieros gamos."
Verbatim: The ideal example of such an object is the nurturing earth-mother. (cw05 ¶226).

occurrences.title: Echidna, mother of monsters — Hesiodic genealogy
occurrences.label: Echidna, mother of monsters — Hesiodic genealogy
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Echidna, lovely maiden above and hideous serpent below, daughter of Gaia and Tartarus; mother of Chimera, Scylla, the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Nemean lion, Prometheus' eagle and "a number of dragons"; with her own son Orthrus she incestuously begets the Sphinx.

Jung's reading: "This double being corresponds to the mother-imago: above, the lovely and attractive human half; below, the horrible animal half, changed into a fear-animal by the incest prohibition" (¶265). Revelation's woman-on-dragon revives her: "In this primordial image of the woman on the dragon we recognize Echidna" (¶315).

Verbatim: Echidna herself was the mother of all terrors, of the Chimera, Scylla, the Gorgon (pl. XIVb), of frightful Cerberus, of the Nemean lion, and of the eagle that devoured the liver of Prometheus. (cw05 ¶265).

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart — the Godhead 'of forms formless'; the poor in spirit
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart — the poor in spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Eckhart's Godhead 'of which no qualities, except unity and being, can be predicated' — 'of forms formless; of becoming becomingless; of beings beingless; of things thingless' — an 'absolute coincidence of opposites', hence unconscious: 'Union of opposites is equivalent to unconsciousness' (¶301). The poor man 'is so quit and empty of all knowing that no knowledge of God is alive in him'; love God 'as a not-God... a sheer, pure, clear One... sundered from all secondness' (¶301). Jung: Eckhart knew 'the primordial mystical experience of India as well as of the Gnostics', finest flower of the Free Spirit (¶302). His God is the Godhead as agnosia.

occurrences.title: Edem: virgin above, serpent below — the Gnosis of Justin
occurrences.label: Edem — virgin above, serpent below
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Justinian Gnosis depicts her as Edem, virgin above, serpent below.
body: In the Justinian Gnosis, Edem — the body of the world — is "virgin above, serpent below": the upper half the pneumatic virgin, the lower a serpent. She longs for the embrace of the Monad; the demiurge, her faithless lover, abandons her; she strives vengefully against the pneuma. She is "the divine soul imprisoned in the elements, whom it is the task of alchemy to redeem."

Jung's frame: the pagan projection goes beyond man into the unknown substance of the material world, where the Godhead hides "in the uncomely stone" as in Christianity it hides in the man of low degree. Edem names the feminine, matter-pole of the Nous-Physis drama.

occurrences.title: Rig-Veda X,129 (Nasadiya hymn) — the One hidden in the shell
occurrences.label: Rig-Veda X,129 — the One hidden in the shell
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Quoted under Fig. 21 (a patient's picture of a fish making a whirlpool in the sea of the unconscious, the precious pearl forming in its midst): "Darkness there was, concealed in darkness, A lightless ocean lost in night. Then the One, that was hidden in the shell, was born through the power of fiery torment. From it arose in the beginning love, Which is the germ and the seed of knowledge." The creation-hymn of the Rig-Veda gives the oldest text-form of the germ-in-the-shell — the world-egg of the mandala centre — arising from the dark watery beginning.

occurrences.title: The eight-petalled flower — 'Recueil de figures astrologiques' (MS., 18th c.)
occurrences.label: The eight-petalled flower
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the eighth or the first of seven
body: Plate 85: "The eight-petalled flower as the eighth or the first of seven." It illustrates visual impression 29, where the dreamer sees "a bunch of roses, then the sign… but it should be [the eightfold flower]" — a mistake corrected "which somehow impaired the wholeness of the rose. The aim of the reconstruction is to bring the problem of the mandala—the correct valuation and interpretation of the 'centre'—once more into the field of consciousness" (¶237).

The historical figure certifies the spontaneous drawing: the eightfold flower as "the eighth or the first of seven" is the same number-structure as the Cabiri scene's eighth-on-Olympus and the world clock's eight spokes.

occurrences.title: Moses and El-Khidr at the source of life (Koran, Sura 18)
occurrences.label: Moses and El-Khidr at the source of life
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the ground round about El-Khidr blossomed with spring flowers, although it was desert
body: Third companion-example: in Sura 18 Moses seeks the place "where the two seas meet" and meets "one of Our servants whom We had endowed with Our grace and wisdom" — El-Khidr, the Green One. "And the legend has it that the ground round about El-Khidr blossomed with spring flowers, although it was desert" (¶155). Jung notes Moses "found to his cost" that the source of life "is not without its dangers" (¶157).

El-Khidr doubles the companion with the well-spring: "The source of life is, like El-Khidr, a good companion" — the eternally renewing life-force, "the clock that never runs down," sought underground: "only down below can we find the fiery source of life" (¶157).

occurrences.title: Eleusinian mysteries — 'The Mistress has borne the divine boy, Brimo has borne Brimos!'
occurrences.label: Eleusinian mysteries
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Proteus is likened to the green ear of corn of the Eleusinian mysteries; to him the celebrants cry: 'The Mistress has borne the divine boy, Brimo has borne Brimos!' (¶339). The 'lower' correspondence is 'the dark path of Persephone... to the grove of adored Aphrodite, who rouses the sickness of love'; initiates become bridegrooms 'robbed of their virility by the virgin spirit' (Rev. 14:4 motif) (¶339). Jung's footnote records his interview at Turukalukundram on why erotic sculptures guard the path to the adyton — see turukalukundram-erotic-temple-pundit-1937.

occurrences.title: 'Blessed is he among men who has seen these mysteries' — Homeric Hymn to Demeter 480-82
occurrences.label: Blessed is he among men who has seen these…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The testimonium of the Eleusinian initiate quoted from the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, vv. 480-82 (Evelyn-White trans.): "Blessed is he among men who has seen these mysteries; but he who is uninitiate and has no part in them, never has lot of like good things once he is dead, down in the darkness and gloom." Joined to an Eleusinian epitaph: "Truly the blessed gods have proclaimed a most beautiful secret: Death comes not as a curse, but as a blessing to men" (fn 2).

Jung's reading: exemplar of the fifth form of rebirth — participation in a transformation rite outside oneself; through witnessed mystery "the hope of immortality" is conferred as grace (cf. ¶208 on Osiris and the phoenix).

occurrences.title: The 'maker of fear' of the Elgonyi
occurrences.label: The 'maker of fear' of the Elgonyi
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: He comes to you," they said, "like acold gust of wind, and you shudder, or he goes whistling round in the tall grass
body: Jung's field datum from the Elgonyi elders in Kenya: their nocturnal god, the "maker of fear", comes "like a cold gust of wind, and you shudder, or he goes whistling round in the tall grass" — "an African Pan who glides among the reeds in the haunted noontide hour, playing on his pipes and frightening the shepherds" (¶33).

Jung's reading: exact parallel to the pneuma rushing over the dark water in the theologian's dream — the numen's unseen presence, "like everything whose cause we do not know — since it is not ourselves"; the erstwhile fiery spirit has descended into "the trees and rocks and the waters of the psyche".

occurrences.title: 'I know the tree of emerald green' — Book of the Dead
occurrences.label: I know the tree of emerald green
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt ('Gate of Knowledge of the Souls of the East')
body: "I am the pilot in the holy keel... I know the tree of emerald green from whose midst Ra rises to the height of the clouds."

Jung's reading: "Ship and tree (i.e., the ship of death and tree of death) are closely related here... The idea is that Ra rises up, born from the tree" (¶368) — Mithras half-risen from a tree (Heddernheim) is the same conglomeration.
Verbatim: I know the tree of emerald green from whose midst Ra rises to the height of the clouds. (cw05 ¶367).

occurrences.title: The disciples on the road to Emmaus — the unrecognized companion
occurrences.label: The disciples on the road to Emmaus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is the theme of the magical travelling companion, of whom I will give three famous examples: the disciples on the road to Emmaus…
body: First of Jung's three "famous examples" of "the theme of the magical travelling companion": the risen Christ joins the disciples on the road to Emmaus, unrecognized until the breaking of bread (Luke 24). Jung lists it with Krishna–Arjuna and Moses–El-Khidr as analogues of the dream-companion found in the depths of the sea — "a close analogy to the lonely ego who finds a mate in the self, for at first the self is the strange non-ego" (¶155).
The unrecognized-then-vanishing companion precisely figures the self as "strange non-ego": present beside the ego, known only in retrospect.

occurrences.title: Ephrem the Syrian — Christ 'clothed in figures'
occurrences.label: Ephrem the Syrian — Christ clothed in figures
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The principle of 'outward uncomeliness' said of the lead and the lapis is applied to Christ by Ephrem (d. 373): 'He is clothed in figures, he is the bearer of types.... His treasure is hidden and of small account, but when it is laid open, it is wonderful to look upon' (¶216). Jung cites this in the sequence draconite–lapis–Christ to show that the alchemical fish symbol 'points ultimately to an archetype of the order of magnitude of the self' and that the lapis-Christ parallel (Psychology and Alchemy) is an old, living equation.

occurrences.title: The Ethiopian treatise: watching the Creation in rainwater (Ch. VIII 'The Creation')
occurrences.label: The Ethiopian treatise
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: you will see with your own eyes… how God created all things in six days
body: Rainwater sealed ten days in glass; poured into a round wooden vessel cut through the middle, one-third full, set in the noon sun; a drop of consecrated red wine falls in — "you will instantly perceive a fog and thick darkness on top of the water, such as also was at the first creation." Drop by drop: "you will see with your own eyes one thing after another… how God created all things in six days… Fall on your knees before you undertake this operation." Chapter IX: seven planetary metals melted in a darkened chamber; a flame lights it "more brightly than sun and moon, and over your heads you shall behold the whole firmament as it is in the starry heavens above" (¶348).
Jung's key witness that "in point of fact there are one or two unmistakable accounts" of the alchemists' own visionary experiences in the work (¶347).

occurrences.title: Indra's yonis changed into eyes — Indian legend
occurrences.label: Indra's yonis changed into eyes — Indian legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The little image reflected in the eye, the “pupilla,” is a “child.
body: The eye stands for the female genitals; the "pupilla" reflected in the eye is a "child": "The great god becomes a child again: he enters into the mother's womb for self-renewal" (¶408). The pun that carries Jung's whole eye–womb–child chain.

occurrences.title: siddhaśila, the spiritual eye of the Jain universe
occurrences.label: siddhaśila, the spiritual eye…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: may be called the spiritual eye of the universe
body: Jain cosmography's world-shape: "The loka [world] is held in the middle of the aloka [void], in the form of the trunk of a man, with siddhaśila at the top, the place where the head should be. This siddhaśila is the abode of the omniscient souls, and may be called the spiritual eye of the universe" (¶46).

Jung adduces it as the non-Western twin of the alchemists' fishes' eyes and the one eye of God: "a similar nexus of ideas" to the "particles of light imprisoned in the dark Physis, whose reconstitution was one of the chief aims of Gnosticism and Manichaeism." The universe as Anthropos whose crown is the eye where all souls converge.

occurrences.title: Faust II: the Cabiri scene — 'the fourth refused to call'
occurrences.label: Faust II — the Cabiri scene
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Though they have the Fleece of Gold, / Ye have the Cabiri.
body: In the Classical Walpurgis Night, Nereids and Tritons carry the Cabiri over the sea in Chelone's giant shell: "In Chelone's giant shield / Gleams a form severe revealed." Three Cabiri "followed where we led, / But the fourth refused to call; / He the rightful seer, he said, / His to think for one and all." The Sirens sing the Cabiris' prize over the Argonauts': "Though they have the Fleece of Gold, / Ye have the Cabiri."

Jung: Goethe's feeling-toned nature made thinking the fourth, taboo function — "Because of its contamination with the unconscious it takes on the grotesque form of the Cabiri, for the Cabiri, as dwarfs, are chthonic gods and misshapen accordingly" (¶204). They strive "from the depths to the heights and are therefore always to be found both below and above"; the "severe image" is "the treasure hard to attain" (¶205). The tortoise (Chelone) "symbolizes the instinctual side of the unconscious" (¶203).

occurrences.title: The filius macrocosmi correlated with Christ — Aquarium sapientum
occurrences.label: The filius macrocosmi correlated with Christ
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The "Aquarium sapientum " (Siebmacher's Hydrolithus sophicus) correlates the "son of the great world" (filius m acrocosm i, the lapis) with Christ, "who is the filius m icrocosm i", his blood the quintessence, the red tincture: "the true and authentic duplex Mercurius or Giant of twofold substance... God by nature, m an, hero" (cw13 ¶384). The author adds that since the stone has "alm ost a thousand" nam es, all these titles apply "m uch m ore properly... to Alm ighty God and the Suprem e Good" (¶385).

Jung: "It obviously never occurred to the author... th at he had sim ply transferred God's attributes to the stone" (cw13 ¶385) — the stone as "a prim ordial religious experience" (¶386). The 'giant of twofold substance' (gigas gem inae substantiae) goes back to Ambrose's hymn (n.5).
Verbatim: the “son of the great world” (filius m acrocosm i, the lapis) is correlated with C hrist, who is the filius m icrocosm i, and his blood is the quintessence, the red tincture. (cw13 ¶384ocr)

occurrences.title: The filius macrocosmi as symbol of Christ — Khunrath's Amphitheatrum
occurrences.label: The filius macrocosmi as symbol of Christ
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Without blasphemy I say: In the Book or Mirror of Nature, the Stone of the Philosophers, the Preserver of the Macrocosm, is the symbol of Christ Jesus Crucified.
body: Khunrath's "confession without blasphemy": the filius philosophorum is "the Son of the Macrocosm... God and creature," just as Christ is the son of God, the θεάνθρωπος — "the one conceived in the womb of the Macrocosm, the other in the womb of the Microcosm, and both of a virginal womb." The Stone of the Philosophers is "the symbol of Christ Jesus Crucified, Saviour of the whole race of men": "From the stone you shall know in natural wise Christ, and from Christ the stone."

Jung: Khunrath was as unconscious of the full implications as Paracelsus — yet in this equation "Medieval alchemy prepared the way for the greatest intervention in the divine world order that man has ever attempted" (¶163); whereas in Christ God became man, the filius philosophorum is "extracted from matter by human art" — "I under God" versus "God under me."

occurrences.title: The King's Son and the mystagogue Hermes on the mountain — Lambspringk fig. XII
occurrences.label: The King's Son and the mystagogue Hermes…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Th eKing's Son (filius regis) and the mystagogue Hermes on am ountain, an obvious allusion to th e T em ptation (Luke, ch. 4).
body: Plate B6 of CW13: the King's Son (filius regis) together with the mystagogue Hermes standing on a mountain — "an obvious allusion to the Temptation (Luke, ch. 4)." The accompanying text: "Another mountain of India lies in the vessel, which the Spirit and Soul, as son and guide, have together ascended." The two are called spirit and soul because they represent volatile substances rising up during the heating of the prima materia.

Jung's reading: Hermes/Mercurius as psychopomp and "mystagogue, as in the Corpus Hermeticum or the visions of Zosimos" (¶273); Maier found on his mystic peregrination "a statue of Mercurius pointing the way to paradise" (¶278).

occurrences.title: The filius regius crying from the depths — Maier's Symbola aureae mensae
occurrences.label: The filius regius crying from the depths
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He lives and calls from the depths: Who shall deliver me from the waters and lead me to dry land?
body: Michael Maier's lament of the kingly substance hidden in the sea: "Who shall deliver me from the waters and lead me to dry land?" Few believe the cry; most take it for "the crashing and roaring of Scylla and Charybdis" and stay at home. In Maier's usage filius regius / Rex marinus means antimony — but only the name, Jung stresses: in reality it is "the secret transformative substance, which fell from the highest place into the darkest depths of matter where it awaits deliverance" (¶183). "The sea (mare nostrum) of the alchemists is their own darkness, the unconscious."

Jung lines the passage up with the Naassene king in the flood (Hippolytus, Elenchos V, 8) and with the Rosarium's promise: "At the end of the work the king will go forth for thee, crowned with his diadem... constant in the fire" (¶183).

occurrences.title: Fire-boring with a Priapus simulacrum against cattle plague — Fentone, Lotharingia
occurrences.label: Fire-boring with a Priapus simulacrum…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: docebant idiotas patriae ignem confrictione de lignis educere et simulacrum Priapi statuere, et per haec bestiis succurrere
body: A plague-year rite among cattle, performed by a Cistercian lay brother "cloistered in habit, not in mind": fire kindled by friction from wood, a simulacrum of Priapus set up, and a dog's testicles dipped in holy water and sprinkled over the sick beasts.

Jung cites it beside Charlemagne's ban on the niedfyr (need-fire) as proof that the fire-boring magic of the pramantha — sexual generation by friction — lived on inside Christendom, practiced by and against the Church. The Priest's blessing and the phallic fire-drill operate in one gesture.

occurrences.title: Brünnhilde asleep behind the wall of fire — Wagner's Ring
occurrences.label: Brünnhilde asleep behind the wall of fire
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the fiery longing of the hero for the forbidden goal
body: The fire-maiden on the mountain: the ring of fire as the barrier and the lure at once — the forbidden mother behind flame. Siegfried's terror before the sleeping armour ("Mother! Mother!", ¶602) breaks against it; the kiss "Even though I die in a kiss!" consummates the love-death (¶602, ¶610–611).

image.title: Brünnhilde slowly and silently leads her horse down the path to the cave

occurrences.title: Hearth-spirit Chi, the fire as lovely maiden — Chuang-tzu commentary
occurrences.label: Hearth-spirit Chi, the fire as lovely maiden
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: commentary on Chuang-tzu (c. 350 BCE); Book of Rites older
body: "Like the sacrificial bull, fire... has a feminine nature in Chinese philosophy, according to one of the commentators on the Chuang-tzu (350 B.C.): 'The hearth spirit is called Chi. He is dressed in bright red, resembling fire, and in appearance is like a lovely, attractive maiden.' The Book of Rites says: 'Wood is burnt in the flames for the Au spirit. This sacrifice to Au is a sacrifice to the old women who are dead'" (¶663).

Jung reads these hearth- and fire-spirits as "the souls of departed cooks" — "old women" — from whom the god of kitchens later grew, who "as a man, became the ruler of the family and the link between it and heaven. In this way the original female fire-spirit became a sort of Logos and mediator" (¶663). A small but exact witness for his claim that sacrificial fire belongs to the maternal-feminine pole, paralleling the bull's hidden femininity (Gosh) in the Gayomart myth (¶662).
Verbatim: "in appearance is like a lovely, attractive maiden" (¶663).

occurrences.title: Izanagi lights his comb and loses Izanami — the Japanese Orpheus
occurrences.label: Izanagi lights his comb and loses Izanami
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For 'wife' read 'mother,' 'anima,' 'unconscious.' Instead of the mother, the hero brings back fire, just as Hiawatha produced the corn, Odin the runes, etc.
body: Izanagi, the Japanese Orpheus, follows his dead wife to the underworld and begs her to return; she consents but forbids him to look. Impatient, he kindles a light "with one of the 'masculine' prongs of his comb and immediately lost his wife."

Jung's gloss does the work of the image tier: "For 'wife' read 'mother,' 'anima,' 'unconscious.'" What the hero retrieves instead of the woman is fire — "just as Hiawatha produced the corn, Odin the runes, etc." — the beloved's place taken by the boon of culture.

image.title: Illustration of (Izanami and Izanagi) exploring the blue sea with the heavenly spear.

occurrences.title: Fire-sticks as bride and bridegroom — Rig-Veda Agni hymn
occurrences.label: Fire-sticks as bride and bridegroom
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The friction-hymn: "Bring the mistress of the people: we will rub Agni in ancient fashion forth"; Jatavedas lies in the fire-sticks "safe as the seed in pregnant women"; the staff enters the outstretched (wood) and "Straightway she conceives, has given birth to the fructifier... With his red pillar lighting his path, the son of Ila is born."
Jung's reading: "the pramantha is also Agni, the begotten son: the phallus is the son, or the son is the phallus" (¶212) — the sexual symbolism of fire-making "unmistakable".
Verbatim: Let this (staff) enter into her as she lies there outstretched, O you skilled ones; Straightway she conceives, has given birth to the fructifier: (cw05 ¶211).

occurrences.title: The Abercius inscription — the 'giant' fish of the Christian aeon (c. AD 200)
occurrences.label: The Abercius inscription
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Cited as the concrete locus of the "great" Fish of the Christian aeon: in Jung's run of world-period images — Parsee world periods, the yugas and avatars of Hinduism, the Platonic months with their bull and ram deities — the fish is the Christian aeon's animal, "born through the power of fiery torment" of the age. The Abercius epitaph (c. AD 200), with Christ as the great fish caught by the holy virgin, is the classic early witness (cf. Aion, par. 127, n. 4). Here it anchors the claim that the patient's number-symbolism (3, 12) is not merely individual but aeon-conditioned: the aeon of the Fishes is drawing to its end and is at the same time the twelfth house of the zodiac (¶552).

occurrences.title: Abercius inscription — the great pure fish caught by a virgin
occurrences.label: Abercius inscription
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The epitaph of Abercius of Hierapolis, the most-discussed early Christian(?) fish text: "everywhere he set before me for food a fish from the source, exceeding great and pure, which a holy virgin had caught". Jung returns to it at pars. 145, 149, 162, 179-180, where — with Scheftelowitz — he identifies the great pure fish with Leviathan.
Jung stresses its doubleness: Dieterich argued the "holy shepherd" is Attis and the inscription commemorates the hieros gamos journey to Rome after A.D. 216; Christian origin is doubtful.

occurrences.title: Denderah zodiac: both fishes facing the same way
occurrences.label: Denderah zodiac: both fishes facing the same way
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The zodiac of the temple of Hathor at Denderah "shows the fishes, but they both face the same way" — evidence for Jung that the contrary movement of the two fishes, so emphasized in Christian astrological speculation, is not ancient: the planisphere of Timochares even shows only one fish where Pisces should be.
Coins and gems of the emperors and Mithraic monuments show fishes either facing the same way or moving oppositely — polarity cannot be demonstrated for pre-Christian times.

occurrences.title: Farnese Atlas globe: the two fishes of Pisces
occurrences.label: Farnese Atlas globe: the two fishes of Pisces
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Naples, Museo Archeologico (Roman copy of Hellenistic original)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The globe of the heavens carried by the Farnese Atlas — for Jung one representation of the fishes "near the beginning of our era... certainly free from Christian influence": "The first fish, depicted north of the equator, is vertical, with its head pointing to the celestial Pole; the second fish, south of the equator, is horizontal, with its head pointing West". Naturalistic, following the astronomical configuration.

Later pictorial polarity of the fishes — "They move almost at right angles to one another and hence form a cross" — was "much emphasized in Christian times," which "leads one to suspect a certain tendentiousness."

occurrences.title: The fish of Manu — Vishnu as the redeemer-fish
occurrences.label: The fish of Manu — Vishnu as the redeemer-fish
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Vishnu, "in the form of a small goldfish," begs Manu to take him home for fear of the water monsters; "He then grows mightily, fairytale fashion, and in the end rescues Manu from the great flood" (cw09ii par. 176; "I will save thee," Shatapatha Brahmana). Jung also cites the ritual echo: a golden fish placed in a bowl of water on the twelfth day of the first month — "As thou, O God, in the form of a fish, hast saved the Vedas... so save me also, O Keshava!"
Jung rejects de Gubernatis' derivation of the Christian fish from India: Western fish symbolism is "so rich and at the same time so archaic that we may safely regard it as autochthonous."

occurrences.title: The forgotten fish of Moses and Joshua ben Nun at the meeting of the two seas — Qur'an 18
occurrences.label: The forgotten fish of Moses and Joshua ben Nun…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabia (Qur'anic recension); isthmus of Suez per commentators

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: But when they had reached the place where the two seas meet, they forgot their fish, and it took its way through astream to the sea.
body: In Sura 18 Moses travels with his servant Joshua ben Nun to "the place where the two seas meet"; there they forget their breakfast-fish, which slips back to the sea alive. Where it vanished, the sea turns to solid ground, Khidr sits enthroned "between the upper and the lower sea", and Moses takes him for a teacher, enduring three incomprehensible deeds (the scuttled ship, the slain youth, the rebuilt wall). Jung reads the fish as the unconscious instinctual basis — Joshua is "son of Nun", "fish" — whose loss is the primitive "loss of soul", abaissement du niveau mental (¶244-245). The reanimated fish is identified with the Second Adam; Khidr's birthplace is exactly where the fish disappeared (¶247-248). Alchemical parallels: the "round fish lacking bones and skin", aqua permanens, nigredo after the coniunctio, and the Stone appearing "like fish's eyes".

occurrences.title: Pectorios inscription, Autun: 'divine descendants of the heavenly fish'
occurrences.label: Pectorios inscription, Autun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In the Pectorios inscription the believers are "the divine descendants of the heavenly fish": "holding the fish in the hands... Nourish now with the fish, I yearn, Lord Saviour" — the first three distichs make the acrostic Ichthys (Doelger I; Pohl, Das Ichthysmonument von Autun).
Like the Abercius inscription, its Christianity is doubted. Jung reads the family of fish-inscriptions against the question whether Ichthys derived from the zodiac — which he denies (par. 177).

occurrences.title: The round fish 'lacking bones and cortex' — Allegoriae super librum Turbae
occurrences.label: The round fish 'lacking bones and cortex'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin West (Artis auriferae I, pp. 139ff.; Harran-Alexandrian ancestry)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Est in mari piscis rotundus, ossibus et corticibus carens": "There is in the sea a round fish, lacking bones and cortex, and having in itself a fatness, a wondrous virtue" — cooked slowly till it shines, yielding at the citrinitas the ironic "collyrium of the philosophers". Our earliest source for alchemical fish symbolism; nothing suggests Christian origin.

Through the transformation of the arcane substance the fish became "a symbol of the lapis" — prima materia and end product (lapis philosophorum, elixir vitae, filius philosophorum, Hermaphroditus); Jung adds: "The filius philosophorum (or macrocosmi), otherwise the lapis, means nothing other than the self" (par. 194).
Jung identifies the creature as a scyphomedusa of radial construction, "divided into eight sections by means of four perradials and four interradials" (par. 196).

occurrences.title: Fish as soul-symbol — late Hellenistic Egyptian sarcophagus
occurrences.label: Fish as soul-symbol
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: On a late Hellenistic sarcophagus painting the mummy "lies on a lion-shaped bier," the four Canopic jars below (four sons of Horus, three animal-headed, one human), and "over the mummy there floats a fish, instead of the usual soul-bird" — an oxyrhynchus or barbel, one of the three most abominated fishes, said to have devoured the phallus of Osiris after Typhon dismembered him.

Jung: the fish as Egyptian soul-symbol is "all the more remarkable" given the ambivalence — barbels sacred to Typhon, "that part of the soul which is passionate, impulsive, irrational, and truculent"; in the Middle Ages fishes allegorized the damned.

occurrences.title: Sibylline acrostic ICHTHYS — 'Iudicii signum'
occurrences.label: Sibylline acrostic ICHTHYS — Iudicii signum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (book of the Erythraean Sibyl shown by Flaccianus to Augustine)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c.? (via Augustine, City of God XVIII)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Augustine (City of God XVIII.23) reports the ex-proconsul Flaccianus producing the songs of the Erythraean Sibyl, whose verses form the acrostic ICHTHYS (Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour): "Iudicii signum tellus sudore madescet, / E coelo Rex adveniet per saecla futurus".

Jung cites it while arguing ICHTHYS is unlikely to be "simply an anagrammatic abbreviation" — the fish was "the symbolical designation for something far more complex" with a long Near-Eastern prehistory.

occurrences.title: Talmudic prophecy of the war of the tanninim — Rashi: the fishes
occurrences.label: Talmudic prophecy of the war of the tanninim
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Babylon (Sanhedrin 97b; prophecy of R. Hanan ben Tahlifa, 2nd c.)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Four thousand two hundred and ninety-one years after the Creation [A.D. 530], the world will be orphaned. There will follow the war of the tanninim [sea-monsters], the war of Gog and Magog, and then the Messianic era". Rashi (1039-1105) remarks that the tanninim are fishes, evidently on older authority.

Jung: "probably the oldest testimony to the antithetical nature of the fishes," an eschatological battle like Behemoth vs Leviathan; the date matches the founding era of Monte Cassino and Joachim's calculations. Gog and Magog likewise antithetical (tectum / de tecto, Augustine).

occurrences.title: Vishnu becomes the fish and recaptures the Vedas — Indian myth
occurrences.label: Vishnu becomes the fish and recaptures the Vedas
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This is a primitive way of describing the libido’s entry into the interior world of the psyche, the unconscious.
body: Vishnu's trance brings forth Brahma on the lotus of his navel — "Birth of creative thought from introversion" — but the ecstatic absorption unleashes the world-flood ("Devouring and destruction of the world through introversion"), and the fish-avatar dives to rescue the Vedas from the demon (¶449, pls. XLVIa–XLVII, plates at pdf pp292–293).

image.title: Matsya Avatar of Vishnu
image.credit: Image: http://collections.lacma.org/sites/default/files/remote_images/piction/ma-31965721-O3.jpg Gallery: http://collections.lacma.org/node/242261 archive copy at the Wayback Machine

occurrences.title: Zohar: the fish that swallowed Jonah dies and revives after three days
occurrences.label: Zohar: the fish that swallowed Jonah dies…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "According to the Zohar, the fish that swallowed Jonah died, but revived after three days and then spewed him out again. 'Through the fish we shall find a medicament for the whole world'".

Jung's frame: "Always the hope of a Messiah is connected with the appearance of a star" (Balaam, Num. 24:17); Scheftelowitz identifies the Abercius inscription's "very great and pure fish" with Leviathan — the biggest fish, held to be pure.

occurrences.title: Fountain of life as fons mercurialis — Rosarium philosophorum (1550)
occurrences.label: Fountain of life as fons mercurialis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Rosarium's fountain-of-life cut, captioned by Jung "The fountain of life as fons mercurialis".

It illustrates ¶92: "the mother stands for the collective unconscious, the source of the water of life (fig. 25)." Jung adds the maternal πηγή and the fons signatus of the Virgin Mary as parallels, and reads the dream's transfer of the water to the sister as "the mother has been replaced by the anima."

occurrences.title: Fountain of youth — Codex de Sphaera (Modena, 15th c.)
occurrences.label: Fountain of youth — Codex de Sphaera
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the symbol of the life force that eternally renews itself
body: Plate 56: a walled garden in which bathers crowd round a great many-tiered fountain — the Fountain of youth (plate verified against p0144.jpg). Jung sets it opposite dream 13, where the crash into the sea-deeps lands the dreamer in "a beautiful garden in the depths, symmetrically laid out, with a fountain in the centre": "The source of life… is the symbol of the life force that eternally renews itself… and of the clock that never runs down" (¶157).
The fountain stands "underground and therefore the way leads underneath: only down below can we find the fiery source of life" (¶157) — rejuvenation through descent into the unconscious.

image.title: La Fontaine de jouvence, miniature extraite du De Sphaera
image.credit: Formerly attributed to Cristoforo de Predis

occurrences.title: Diagram of the four functions of consciousness — Jung's own diagram (via Jacobi, The Psychology of Jung)
occurrences.label: Diagram of the four functions of consciousness
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Jung's diagram: "Thinking, the superior function in this case, occupies the centre of the light half of the circle, whereas feeling, the inferior function, occupies the dark half. The two auxiliary functions are partly in the light and partly in the dark."

It is brought in at ¶137 to gloss the Peterhofstatt dream's four persons: ego, doctor, pointed-beard (Mephisto-intellect), doll-woman (anima) — "the four persons in the dream to represent the four functions as components of the total personality."

occurrences.title: Four season-goddesses around the round table — Stolcius, Viridarium chymicum
occurrences.label: Four season-goddesses around the round table
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1624 (fig. XLII; also Mylius, Philosophia reformata 1622, p.117)
occurrences.quote: The arrangement of the opposites in a quaternity is shown in an interesting illustration in Stolcenberg's Viridarium chymicum (Fig. XLII).
body: Stolcius von Stolcenberg's engraving of four goddesses seated around a circular table: "The goddesses represent the four seasons of the sun in the circle of the Zodiac (Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn) and at the same time the four degrees of heating, as well as the four elements 'combined' around the circular table" (¶5).

Jung reads it as the quaternio of opposites arranged spatially, whose synthesis is "effected by means of the circular movement in time (circulatio, rota) of the sun through the houses of the Zodiac," the aim being "the production (or rather, reproduction) of the Original Man, who was a sphere." It anchors the book's opening argument that dualities default to fourfold structure.

occurrences.title: The fourth man in the fiery furnace — Daniel 3 / Biblia pauperum
occurrences.label: The fourth man in the fiery furnace
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Nebuchadnezzar sees "four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire... and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God." The Biblia pauperum comments: "The three signify for us the Holy Trinity of the person, and the fourth the unity of being."

Jung's reading: the legend is "a magical procedure during which a 'fourth' is produced" (¶245); the fiery furnace is a mother-symbol (like Faust's tripod), the Hermetic vessel a uterus, and the fourth "a son of God made visible in the fire".
Verbatim: The three signify for us the Holy Trinity of the person, and the fourth the unity of being. (cw05 ¶244).

occurrences.title: Sancta Maria, closed gate, sealed fountain — the Melk hymn
occurrences.label: Sancta Maria, closed gate, sealed fountain
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Sancta Maria, / Closed gate / Opened at God's command— / Sealed fountain, / Locked garden, / Gate of Paradise.
body: The 12th-century Melk hymn to Mary folds Song of Solomon 4:12 into liturgy: "Sancta Maria, / Closed gate / Opened at God's command— / Sealed fountain, / Locked garden, / Gate of Paradise."

Jung sets it immediately beside the erotic verse — "Maiden, let me enter with you / Into your rose garden / Where the red rosebuds grow... / And the deep cool well / That lies below" — to show that the same symbolism (enclosed garden, sealed fountain, low door) serves mystic and profane love alike: the hymn to Mary and the seduction song are one vocabulary.

occurrences.title: Gayomart — the metals grow from the Original Man's blood
occurrences.label: Gayomart — the metals grow…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'The metals grow from Gayomart's blood' (¶389). Gayomart is the Original Man of the theosophical Zarathustra system; Yima ('the shining Yima') the Original Man of ancient Aryan legend, whose body, per the Bundahishn, consisted of metals (¶389 n.77). Jung uses this to close the uroboros of his four quaternios: 'the heavy darkness of the earth, metal, has a secret relationship to the Anthropos' — the lowest, most material thing identical with the highest and most spiritual (¶389). Parallels: ostanes-nile-stone-zosimos-3c, uroboros-codex-marcianus-venice-11c.

occurrences.title: The serpent steals the herb of immortality — Gilgamesh epic
occurrences.label: The serpent steals the herb of immortality
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Gilgamesh crosses the waters of death to Utnapishtim, dives to the sea-bottom for the magic herb, and on the return journey — escorted by the banished immortal mariner — a serpent steals it and sloughs its skin.

Jung's reading: "a serpent steals the magic herb from him (i.e., the fish slips back into the sea)" — the treasure regained and lost; the mariner is Jensen's prototype of Ahasuerus (¶293). Plate XIX: Gilgamesh with the herb of immortality, relief from the palace of Assurnasirpal II, Nimrud.
Verbatim: But when Gilgamesh arrives home, a serpent steals the magic herb from him (i.e., the fish slips back into the sea). (cw05 ¶293).

occurrences.title: Christ as Anthropos on the globe — Glanville, Le Propriétaire des choses (1482)
occurrences.label: Christ as Anthropos on the globe
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Gnostic quadripartite original man… as well as Christ Pantokrator is an imago lapidis
body: Plate 64: "Christ as Anthropos, standing on the globe, flanked by the four elements." Jung reads it beside the Gnostic quadripartite original man: "Consequently the Gnostic quadripartite original man (fig. 64) as well as Christ Pantokrator is an imago lapidis" (¶173) — the original-man figure and the philosopher's stone are one archetype in different theologies.

The plate shows the translation chain Jung traces in the ape commentary: Thoth → Hermes Trismegistus → Mercurius → the transforming substance as totality of four, culminating in the mystical homo maximus (¶173).

occurrences.title: 'In this fire God himself glows in divine love' — Gloria mundi
occurrences.label: In this fire God himself glows in divine love
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)
