body: The anonymous Gloria mundi describes the philosophers' unquenchable fire in which 'God himself glows in divine love' together with the sun — fire that 'purifies, as purgatory does in the lower regions' (¶201). 'The Philosophers call this fire the fire of the Holy Ghost'; it unites Mercurius with the sun 'so that all three make but one thing', just as the Trinity is three Persons in one God (¶202). The same fire is 'the dragon that burns furiously like hell-fire' (¶203). Jung: God glows in the subterranean fire — the unity of the symbol implies the identity of the opposites (¶199).

occurrences.title: Justin's gnosis — Elohim and Edem, twelve and twelve angels, Baruch and Naas (Elenchos V, 26)
occurrences.label: Justin's gnosis — Elohim and Edem, twelve…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The passage of Justin's gnosis Jung mines in the Miss X commentary: the "Father" (Elohim) begets with Edem — half woman, half snake — twelve "fatherly" angels; Edem bears besides twelve "motherly" angels, the shadows of the fatherly ones; the motherly divide into four categories of three, corresponding to the four rivers of Paradise, and dance round in a circle (¶552). Third of the fatherly angels is Baruch, the tree of life; his counterpart Naas (the serpent), the tree of knowledge, torments the pneuma left by Elohim in man (¶560). Edem is the soul, Elohim the spirit; "Naas is the same as the snakelike Nous and mercurial serpent of alchemy"; her snake-maiden figure became the androgynous Mercurius of medieval alchemy.

occurrences.title: Unas lives on his fathers and feeds on his mothers — Pyramid Texts
occurrences.label: Unas lives on his fathers and feeds…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Unas rising as a soul, like a god who liveth upon his fathers and feedeth upon his mothers.
body: The oldest Egyptian god-eating text, cited by Jung as parallel to the Aztec teoqualo and to the Consilium coniugii's "the parents are the food of the son": "Unas rising as a soul, like a god who liveth upon his fathers and feedeth upon his mothers" (¶22).

Jung's point is typological: the same archetypal structure — the new thing born from the consumed opposites — appears in a funerary liturgy of the third millennium BCE, in Aztec ritual, and in the 15th-century Latin alchemical allegory, without historical filiation. Distinct from the existing Unas locus (the ladder to heaven in god-image-unas-ladder-pyramid-texts-2350-bce.md); this is the cannibalistic Unas of Utterance 217ff.

occurrences.title: R. Ishmael's vision: Akathriel Jah Yahweh Zebaoth asks for man's blessing
occurrences.label: R. Ishmael's vision
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Palestine (setting of R. Ishmael b. Elisha, 2nd c.); redacted in Bavli, Berakoth 7a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "I once entered the innermost sanctuary to offer incense, and there I saw Akathriel Jah Yahweh Zebaoth seated upon a high and exalted throne. He said to me, Ishmael, my son, bless me!". Ishmael blesses God: "May it be Thy will that Thy mercy may suppress Thy anger."

Jung sets this at the end of a midrash chain showing the effect of Job's contradictory God-image: Yahweh's justice and love as his two hands, the destroyer who "even begins with the righteous," God praying to himself that his mercy prevail, sinners hidden under his throne (pars. 106-111).

occurrences.title: 'Before Christ was imagined in us, God was more terrible' — Aquarium sapientum
occurrences.label: Before Christ was imagined in us, God was more…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Deus, antequam Christus filius eius in nobis formatus imaginatusque fuit, nobis potius terribilis Deus
body: The Aquarium sapientum states the alchemical psychology of the God-image with startling economy: "Deus, antequam Christus filius eius in nobis formatus imaginatusque fuit, nobis potius terribilis Deus" — before Christ his son was formed and imagined in us, God was more terrible to us. The divine image is not given ready-made; it must be formed and imagined in the soul, and until then the numen is pure terror.

Jung cites this in the chapter on the mental prerequisites of the work: it is the alchemists' version of his thesis that God-image contents undergo projection and must be consciously realized (cf. cw12 Part I on the God-image in the psyche). The phrase "in nobis formatus imaginatusque fuit" also grounds his later active-imagination vocabulary: imagination as opus.

occurrences.title: Triumphal song of the ascending soul — 'I am the god Atum' (Egypt)
occurrences.label: Triumphal song of the ascending soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Egyptian funerary text (New Kingdom?, dating inferred)
body: An ancient Egyptian funerary text cited by Jung as representing deification "very beautifully, as the triumphal song of the ascending soul": "I am the god Atum, I who alone was. I am the god Ra at his first appearing. I am the great god who created himself... I was yesterday and know tomorrow; the battle-ground of the gods was made when I spoke" (¶133).

The dead soul washes in the two great pools of Heracleopolis, enters "the land of the glorified," and joins the fathers: "I am daily together with my father Atum... I am become one of you." Jung reads the refrain through the parental-imago lens: religious feeling is rooted in "memories of archetypal intuitions" of earliest infancy — "I am in my country, I come into my city. I am daily together with my father Atum" (¶¶134, 139... the hymn recurs in the discussion of regressive reactivation, ¶134).

occurrences.title: Ascension of Isaiah: Sammael and the graded seven heavens
occurrences.label: Ascension of Isaiah
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Isaiah's rapture through the seven heavens: first "Sammael and his hosts, against whom a 'great battle' was raging in the firmament"; then thrones whose right-hand angels sing more beautifully than the left, splendour rising heaven by heaven.

Jung's reading: the devil, like the Gnostic archons, dwells in the firmament (astrological gods); his sphere interpenetrates the divine sphere, "complementary opposites balancing one another like right and left hands" — "a genuine yang-yin relationship... which the Jesuits quite logically translated as 'God'" (Tao). Pre-Manichaean, hence free of defensive dualism.

occurrences.title: Clementine Homilies: good and evil as the two hands of God
occurrences.label: Clementine Homilies
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The unknown author of the Clementine Homilies "understands good and evil as the right and left hand of God, and views the whole of creation in terms of syzygies, or pairs of opposites". God appointed two kingdoms and two ages; he kills with the left hand and saves with the right (Deut. 32:39); body and spirit are "two triads," and the mixing of the four elements begot choice "as a child" (pars. 100-101).
For Jung this pre-Manichaean, reflective God-image "guarantees that unity on a plane beyond" the Yahweh/Christian split and comes "closer to the actual truth than the privatio boni."

occurrences.title: 'Glory to God' dream poem — Miss Frank Miller (at sea, 1898)
occurrences.label: Glory to God' dream poem — Miss Frank Miller
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The founding locus of Symbols of Transformation: the dream that ended with a three-stanza hymn in which the Creator makes Sound, then Light, then Love, each answered by "All glory to the God of Sound/Light/Love!" Its prelude: "when the morning stars sang together" (Job 38:7), mixed with Paradise Lost and Handel's Creation (¶¶60-61).

Jung's reading: after a deliberate introversion on the voyage, the erotic impression of the night-watching singer — underappreciated, half-repressed — regressed to the father-imago and produced the Creator-God: "by the devious route of the father-imago relationship, the night-watching singer becomes the Creator, the God of Sound, of Light and of Love" (¶83). Hence the chain "the singer — the singing morning star — the God of Sound — the Creator — the God of Light — of the sun — of fire — and of Love" (¶65). Her parting "Only this, and nothing more!" quotes Poe's raven of lost Lenore (¶¶81-83).

occurrences.title: Light, wind, and the visited heart — Riklin's paranoid megalomania case (Zürich)
occurrences.label: Light, wind, and the visited heart
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: fn 51 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p692); index 'Riklin ... megalomanic phase, 102n'

body: Jung records a case from "my late colleague Dr. Franz Riklin": a paranoid woman passing into manifest megalomania. "She suddenly saw a strong light, a wind blew upon her, she felt as if her 'heart turned over,' and from that moment she knew that God had visited her and was in her." The pneuma-formula — light plus wind as divine insemination — the same equation Jung traces through Anaxagoras, the Stoic primal warmth, and the Mithraic liturgy in the surrounding footnotes.
Verbatim (fn 51): "She suddenly saw a strong light, a wind blew upon her, she felt as if her “heart turned over,” and from that moment she knew that God had visited her and was in her."

occurrences.title: Pyramid Texts of Unas: Horus and Set lead the dead up the ladder
occurrences.label: Pyramid Texts of Unas
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Saqqara (pyramid of Unas; via Budge, Gods of the Egyptians II)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: "Unas cometh forth upon the Ladder which his father Ra hath made for him, and Horus and Set take the hand of Unas, and they lead him into the Tuat". Heaven's floor is an iron plate resting on four pillars at the cardinal points; Pepi I's texts praise "the ladder of the twin gods."

Jung (par. 188): Horus/Set "represent the latent opposites contained in Osiris... just as Behemoth and Leviathan do in relation to Yahweh" — and the opposites cooperate to bring the one god to "the heavenly quaternity," personified by the four sons of Horus behind the thigh of the northern heaven, analogues of Ezekiel's cherubim and the evangelists' symbols.

occurrences.title: The golden bough of Diana at Aricia — rex Nemorensis
occurrences.label: The golden bough of Diana at Aricia
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: cult attested classical era (recorded 1st c. BCE-CE)
body: Only the runaway slave who could pluck the golden bough from the sacred grove of Diana and kill the reigning priest became her priest-king at Nemi.

Jung's reading: grouped with the robbery motifs of the "treasure hard to attain" — sun-cattle of Geryon, apples of the Hesperides, herb of immortality (¶250) — the stolen branch as regressive treasure torn from the goddess.
Verbatim: in the cult of Diana at Aricia only he could become her priest who plucked the golden bough from the sacred grove of the goddess. (cw05 ¶250).

occurrences.title: Red-and-white rose, the 'golden flower' of alchemy — Ripley Scrowle (1588)
occurrences.label: Red-and-white rose, the 'golden flower'…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: London, British Museum (MS Add. 5025, No. 1 detail)
body: Caption: "The red-and-white rose, the 'golden flower' of alchemy, as birthplace of the filius philosophorum.". The Western twin of the Chinese golden flower: the solar essence descended into the flower.

Jung at ¶101: "For the 'golden flower of alchemy' (fig. 30) can sometimes be a blue flower: 'The sapphire blue flower of the hermaphrodite.'" — binding the dreamer's blue flower (dream 17) to the alchemical rose and hermaphrodite.

occurrences.title: Vision of the Holy Grail — Roman de Lancelot du lac (Paris MS, 15th c.)
occurrences.label: Vision of the Holy Grail
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Paris MS (Roman de Lancelot du lac)
occurrences.quote: a bewildering profusion of semblances for that obscure thing we call the mandala or 'self
body: Plate 88: "Vision of the Holy Grail" from the Roman de Lancelot du lac. Jung sets it at the head of the passage where the unconscious "puts forth a bewildering profusion of semblances for that obscure thing we call the mandala or 'self'" (¶247) — grail, lapis, and mandala as one family of the treasure hard to attain.
The plate belongs with the Grail-stone lore Jung cites later in the series: "According to the legend the Grail-stone comes from the east and must return there again" (¶263).

image.title: Holy-grail-round-table-bnf-ms-120-f524v-14th
image.credit: Attributed to Maître des cleres femmes.

occurrences.title: The green lion devouring the sun — Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: The green lion devouring the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 169. The 'green lion' devouring the sun.—Rosarium philosophorum (1550)
body: Rosarium woodcut: the green lion swallowing the sun disc — the most famous single image of the prima materia consuming the perfected substance.

Jung's context: among the versions of the King's Son's death, "in another version he is eaten by his father …, or the Sun is drowned in Mercurius or swallowed by the lion." The green lion is a form of Mercurius (¶498); in the Cantilena the virgin-mother drinks "the blood of the green lion" that lies bleeding in her lap — communion and Pietà symbols at once.

occurrences.title: God as King and Queen of Heaven on two thrones — Digulleville's Pelerinage de l'ame
occurrences.label: God as King and Queen of Heaven on two thrones
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Chalis, Normandy (Cistercian priory; author prior there)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: In Guillaume de Digulleville's Le Pelerinage de l'ame — three pilgrimage allegories written in the manner of the Divine Comedy but independently of Dante, 1330-1350 — the visionary "saw God in the highest heaven as the King on a shining round throne, and beside him sat the Queen of Heaven on a throne of brown crystal" (¶133).

Jung's reading: "For a monk of the Cistercian Order, which as we know is distinguished for its severity, this vision is exceedingly heretical" — the condition for genuine (untraditional) projection is fulfilled; the vision belongs with Brother Klaus's God-Father-and-God-Mother theophany as an autonomous uprising of the syzygy archetype against dogma that had "eliminated the feminine element from the Trinity".

occurrences.title: Guillaume de Digulleville: the calendar-circle in the golden heaven (Pélerinage de l'âme)
occurrences.label: Guillaume de Digulleville
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Châlis, Normandy (Cistercian priory; author prior there)
occurrences.quote: Cette cercle que tu vois est le calendrier / Qui en faisant son tour entier
body: The last canto of the Pélerinage de l'âme: Paradise as seven large spheres each containing seven smaller spheres, "all the spheres rotate, and this movement is called a siècle (saeculum)." In the highest heaven of pure gold the King sits on a round throne, the Queen on one "made of brown crystal" (¶315). "The pilgrim perceived a marvellous circle… three feet across" — the sapphire calendrier that "spinning round the course entire / Shows the feast day of each saint" (¶316–317). Three crowned spirits enter with it; the angel expounds the Trinity through gold, red, and green — blue, the Virgin's colour, is missing (¶319–320).

Jung offers this as the chief historical parallel to the world-clock vision: rotating spheres + calendar-circle + three mysterious rhythms = "the moment of time in eternity" (¶318). The missing blue = the forgotten reyne, the feminine vertical.

occurrences.title: The young man with the black pointed beard among the philosophers — Parabolae of the Güldenen Tractat vom philosophischen Stein (1625)
occurrences.label: The young man with the black pointed beard…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "the 'man with a pointed beard' also crops up in alchemical literature, in one of the 'Parabolae' contained in the 'Güldenen Tractat vom philosophischen Stein,' written in 1625, which Herbert Silberer has analysed from a psychological point of view. Among the company of old white-bearded philosophers there is a young man with a black pointed beard. Silberer is uncertain whether he should assume this figure to be the devil." (cw12 ¶89).
The dream's Mephisto-employee (¶88) thus has a dated literary double in the alchemical corpus — the ambiguous junior spirit among the senes.

occurrences.title: Hanuman swallowed by the mother of Rahu — Ramayana
occurrences.label: Hanuman swallowed by the mother of Rahu
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The sun travelling with Hanuman casts a shadow on the sea; a sea-monster seizes it; Hanuman shrinks, enters the body, and passes through. A second monster — "the mother of Rahu, the sun-devouring demon" — draws him down; he swells inside and bursts her.

Jung's reading: Frobenius' devouring-and-birth sequence, with conquest of the devouring mother; "We now understand why the Indian fire-bringer Matarisvan is called 'he who swells in the mother'" (¶311).

Verbatim: Once more he had recourse to his earlier stratagem, made himself small, and slipped into her body; but scarcely was he inside than he swelled up to gigantic size, burst her, and killed her, and so made his escape. (cw05 ¶311).

occurrences.title: Three hares in rotation — Gothic window, Paderborn cathedral
occurrences.label: Three hares in rotation
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 39 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: the same motif as the three-dogs mandala (Fig. 38) "but represented by hares. From a Gothic window in the cathedral at Paderborn. There is no recognizable centre though the rotation presupposes one." The triad circling an implicit centre embodies the sesquitertian proportion (3:4) — the incomplete, triadic state turning around the complete, tetradic one — known in alchemy as the axiom of Maria. The famous three-hares motif of German church windows, harvested by Jung directly into the sesquitertian series.

occurrences.title: The cow-headed Hathor — bronze, Serapeum of Sakkara
occurrences.label: The cow-headed Hathor
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXXb: bronze cow-headed Hathor.

Jung's reading: "The cow as a mother-symbol (cf. pl. Ia) appears in all the innumerable forms and variations of Hathor-Isis" (¶358); she it is who receives the wounded Ra: "the cow was the cow-headed mother-goddess, just as Osiris was the bull Apis" (¶351) — the mother who wounds and heals.
Verbatim: But the cow was the cow-headed mother-goddess (pl. XXXb), just as Osiris was the bull Apis. (cw05 ¶351).

occurrences.title: Heb-Sed festival — the king turns to the four cardinal points
occurrences.label: Heb-Sed festival — the king turns…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: New Kingdom (~14th c. BC; Amenhotep III)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The royal renewal rite: the king comes from the sanctuary and 'ascends into a pavilion open at the four sides, with four staircases leading up to it. Carrying the emblems of Osiris, he takes his seat on a throne, and turns to the four cardinal points in succession... he acts as a priest, making offerings to himself... the climax of the deification of the king' (¶309). Jung: 'all kingship is rooted in this psychology' — every king, for his subjects, carries the symbol of the self as cosmic Anthropos, homo maximus (¶310). Parallels: mandala-hasjelti-dailjis-navaho-sand-painting-1887, mandala-madura-temple-floor-1938.

occurrences.title: Hera's annual disappearance into the lygos-tree — Samos
occurrences.label: Hera's annual disappearance into the lygos-tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Each year Hera's image vanishes from the temple, attaches itself to a lygos (willow) tree on the seashore, is entwined, then "found" and regaled with wedding-cakes; wedding processions at Plataea and Argos; Argive Hera renews her virginity in the fountain of Kanathos.
Jung's reading: the hieros gamos as rejuvenation magic — "its twining-about by the lygos-tree... all this points to death and rebirth" (¶363).
Verbatim: Every year her image “disappeared” from the temple, attached itself to a lygos-tree somewhere on the seashore, and was entwined in its branches. (cw05 ¶363).

occurrences.title: Heracles threatens Helios and wins the sun-ship — journey to Geryon
occurrences.label: Heracles threatens Helios and wins the sun-ship
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: On the way to the sun-cattle of Geryon the burning sun so provokes Heracles that he draws his invincible arrows; Helios yields and lends him the golden sun-ship for crossing Ocean.
Jung's reading: the hero's "bold attitude" toward the sun parallels Mithras as patron of Helios and Peter's investiture as Miles of Christ (¶288-289) — the mortal who commands the luminary.
Verbatim: on his way to fight the monster Geryon the sun burned too fiercely, so Heracles wrathfully threatened him with his invincible arrows. (cw05 ¶288).

occurrences.title: Hercules on the night sea journey in the vessel of the sun — Attic vase base
occurrences.label: Hercules on the night sea journey…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 171. Hercules on the night sea journey in the vessel of the sun.—Base of an Attic vase (5th cent. B.C.)
body: Vase-base relief of Herakles riding the sun-barque through the night — the Greek hero assimilated to the sun's nocturnal voyage.

Jung gathers this with the labours of Herakles as one of the journey-forms of the quaternity-cross motif (¶457) and with the sun-hero who "submits to arduous labours and to the passion of self-cremation, like Herakles" (¶469). Hercules is "a favourite symbol because of his opera" even inside the alchemical Mutus liber (fig. 215).

image.title: Heracles on the sea in the bowl of Helios

occurrences.title: Epigram of the Hermaphrodite — Mathieu de Vendôme
occurrences.label: Epigram of the Hermaphrodite
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And I—male, female, and neither—suffered by water, weapon, and cross.
body: The schoolman's riddling epitaph: "When my pregnant mother bore me in her womb, they said she asked the gods what she would bear. A boy, said Phoebus, a girl, said Mars, neither, said Juno. And when I was born, I was a hermaphrodite. Asked how I was to meet my end, the goddess replied: By arms; Mars: On the cross; Phoebus: By water. All were right. A tree overshadowed the waters, I climbed it; the sword I had with me slipped, and I with it. My foot caught in the branches, my head hung down in the stream; And I — male, female, and neither — suffered by water, weapon, and cross" (¶89).

Jung treats it as the serious relative of the Aelia inscription — "the most important item" of the triple-death motif (Vita Merlini and its 15th-century imitations) — and notes the alchemists strangely never took it up, "though it might have been a more suitable subject for exegesis." Also kin: the Platonic riddle of the one-eyed eunuch and the bat (¶90), and the Hindu paradox "Awakener to Myself is my name."

occurrences.title: Symbolical drawings of Opicinus de Canistris (Pavia/Vercelli)
occurrences.label: Symbolical drawings of Opicinus de Canistris
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the symbolical drawings of Opicinus de Canistris afford us an interesting glimpse of the way in which this primordial image was instrumental in uniting opposites, even in a pathological state.
body: The priest Opicinus de Canistris left symbolical drawings (Salomon, Opicinus de Canistris, fn40) in which, Jung says, the primordial image of the male-female union was "instrumental in uniting opposites, even in a pathological state" (¶295). Opicinus' visionary diagrams — cartographic body-mandalas in which his own figure, Europe, and the divine interpenetrate — show the hermaphrodite as uniting symbol at work under psychic strain: the medieval coniunctio performed not in glass but in ink and suffering.

occurrences.title: Phanes in the egg — Orphic relief, Modena Museum
occurrences.label: Phanes in the egg — Orphic relief, Modena Museum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Roman relief, ~2nd c. AD (Orphic, Hellenistic original?)
body: The Orphic Phanes reproduced as Plate XII: "The Shining One, the First-Created, the 'Father of Eros.'" Jung lists him among the "mythological and philosophical attempts... to formulate and visualize the creative force which man knows only by subjective experience" (¶198), beside the cosmogonic Eros of Hesiod.

His attributes per Jung: Orphically he has "the significance of Priapus; he is bisexual and equated with the Theban Dionysus Lysius" — and "the Orphic significance of Phanes is akin to that of the Indian Kama, the god of love, who is likewise a cosmogonic principle" (¶198). The egg-birth makes him a first-form of the philosophic egg; the bisexuality a first-form of the rebis.

occurrences.title: Fish meal with hermaphrodite statue — British Museum MS Add. 15268
occurrences.label: Fish meal with hermaphrodite statue
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Th e significance of the herm aphrodite in this context is unknow n to me.
body: Plate B1 of CW13: "A fish meal, with accompanying statue of the hermaphrodite. Though the picture is undoubtedly secular, it contains echoes of early Christian motifs. The significance of the hermaphrodite in this context is unknown to me."

Jung's caption is a documented refusal: he reproduces the locus and expressly leaves its meaning open — worth preserving as a marker of where the field still needs work (the fish meal belongs to the early Christian ichthys/eucharist complex he treats in Aion). The hermaphrodite statue co-manifests the rebis family in a secular 13th-century context.

occurrences.title: Hermaphrodite with three serpents and one serpent; the three-headed Mercurial dragon — Rosarium philosophorum (Artis auriferae, 1593)
occurrences.label: Hermaphrodite with three serpents…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The rebis of the Rosarium: hermaphrodite with three serpents and one serpent, above the three-headed Mercurial dragon — the ternary/quaternary uncertainty in a single image.

Jung cites it at ¶142 for the aenigma regis: "the final production of the lapis in the form of the crowned hermaphrodite is called the aenigma regis," with the German verse: "Here now is born the emperor of all honour / Than whom there cannot be born any higher."

occurrences.title: The hermaphroditic-mother drawings of the castration-complex patient
occurrences.label: The hermaphroditic-mother drawings…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: A man with a still-unresolved high-grade mother and castration complex, "without any hint from me", made drawings showing the mother first "as a superhuman being", then as a figure of woe with bloody mutilations — before her genitals lay the cut-off male organ: a castration obviously performed on the mother (¶138).

Jung's reading: "the mother was a divine hermaphrodite, who then, through the son's disappointing experience of reality, was robbed of her androgynous, Platonic perfection and changed into the woeful figure of an ordinary old woman" (fn 26: conforms to the bisexual Original Man of Plato's Symposium and hermaphroditic Primal Beings generally). The "castration complex" was really the fall from the childhood Olympus of the syzygy-mother — fear of real life, a "godless" existence.

occurrences.title: Prayer of Astrampsychos — 'Come to me, Lord Hermes... I am thou and thou art I'
occurrences.label: Prayer of Astrampsychos
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Come to me, Lord Hermes... I am thou and thou art I.
body: Jung closes the footnote on Hermes-as-inner-friend (¶238) with "the beautiful prayer of Astrampsychos", which begins "Come to me, Lord Hermes" and ends "I am thou and thou art I" (Reitzenstein, Poimandres, p. 21). It is the purest formula of the identity-colloquy: the invoker takes the god as the partner within, the voice that answers in one's own heart. In Jung's frame this is the "inner friend of the soul" before its alchemical projection into the Stone — the devotional twin of the alchemist's meditatio with aliquem alium internum.

occurrences.title: Hymn to Hermes 'ruler of the world' — Magic Papyrus
occurrences.label: Hymn to Hermes 'ruler of the world'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: (Hermes, ruler of the world, dweller in the heart, circle of the mo on, Ro un da n d square...
body: The epigraph Jung chose for the entire Spirit Mercurius monograph: "Hermes, ruler of the world, dweller in the heart, circle of the moon, Round and square, inventor of the words of the tongue, Obedient to justice, wearer of the chlamys, shod in winged sandals, Guardian of the many-sounding tongue, prophet to mortals."

Every theme of the essay is prefigured: Hermes as world-ruler and psychopomp ("dweller in the heart" — cf. the centre ¶186-189), and above all the paradoxical "circle of the moon, Round and square" — a mandala-like self-description uniting the opposites in one figure.

occurrences.title: Hermes conjuring the winged soul out of an urn — Attic funeral lekythos
occurrences.label: Hermes conjuring the winged soul out of an urn
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 139. Hermes conjuring the winged soul out of an urn.—Attic funeral lekythos
body: White-ground funeral lekythos showing Hermes Psychopompos drawing the winged soul — a small bird — up out of the burial urn.

Jung uses it as the Greek counterpart of the alchemical soul-release: the pneuma or soul hidden in matter (in the vessel, the stone, the body) that the opus must "draw out," as Ostanes draws the heart from the Nile stone (¶405) and as the fig-tree of the artifex's imaginatio releases spirits (¶394-396). The soul-bird is the representable form of what the alchemists called the spiritus in materia.

image.title: Classical lekythos ARV extra - Hermes psychopompos and bearded man (01)

occurrences.title: 'When the two shall be one' — logion of the Gospel according to the Egyptians (2 Clement)
occurrences.label: When the two shall be one
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. logion; quoted by Clement of Alexandria

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: When the two shall be one, the outside as the inside, and the male with the female neither male nor female.
body: In ¶295 Jung traces the coniunctio of male and female through Gnosticism's mysterium iniquitatis back to the Old Testament "divine marriage" (Hosea), and forward through the logion Clement of Alexandria quotes from the Gospel according to the Egyptians: "When the two shall be one, the outside as the inside, and the male with the female neither male nor female." Clement introduces it with "When ye have trampled on the garment of shame" — the body. Clement, Cassian, and pseudo-Clement read it spiritually; the Gnostics "would seem to have taken the coniunctio all too literally" (practising abortion and other restrictions to keep the biological meaning from swamping the religious rite).

occurrences.title: The widow Malchuth awaiting Tifereth — Zohar hierosgamos
occurrences.label: The widow Malchuth awaiting Tifereth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~13th c. (Zohar; via Knorr von Rosenroth, Kabbala denudata 1677)
occurrences.quote: the coming Messiah will reunite the King with the Queen, and this mating will restore to God his original unity
body: The Cabala's widow: "[Almanah] Widow. This is Malchuth, when Tifereth is not with her" (Knorr von Rosenroth). Malchuth is Domina, the Shekinah, the virago; Tifereth is the King, the Microcosm; Yesod "signifies the genital region of the Original Man, whose head is Kether" (¶18). "In this wicked world ruled by evil Tifereth is not united with Malchuth. But the coming Messiah will reunite the King with the Queen, and this mating will restore to God his original unity" (¶18).

Jung: "The Cabala develops an elaborate hierosgamos fantasy which expatiates on the union of the soul with the Sefiroth of the worlds of light and darkness"; the Shekinah is present in the sexual act, the absconditus sponsus joined with the abscondita sponsa, "neither male nor female" (¶18); Yesod acts as paranymphus at the nuptial canopy (¶19). Vigenerus' alchemical citation of the Zohar (Malchuth = Luna) forms "a link with alchemy" (¶19).

occurrences.title: Creator, macrocosm, and microcosm in human form — Hildegard of Bingen, Liber divinorum operum
occurrences.label: Creator, macrocosm, and microcosm in human form
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 195. Creator, macrocosm, and microcosm in human form, the microcosm surrounded by the elements.—St. Hildegarde of Bingen, 'Liber divinorum operum' (MS., 12th cent.)
body: Visionary illumination from Hildegard's Liber divinorum operum: the Creator enthroned within the cosmic man, the microcosm surrounded by the elements and the zones of the world.

Jung reproduces it beside the Zosimos passages on the Anthropos — the first man, symbolized by the four elements, whose body is the whole heavenly sphere. Hildegard's Christian visionary microcosm shows the same figure the alchemists would call the homo philosophicus, the Microcosm (¶476).

occurrences.title: Hoghelande's iridescent colours on the decoctio (1594) — 'Ut vidi, ut perii'
occurrences.label: Hoghelande's iridescent colours on the decoctio
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Ut vidi, ut perii, ut me malus abstulit error
body: "In his biographical notes (1594), Hoghelande describes how, on the third day of the decoctio, he saw the surface of the substance cover itself with colours, 'chiefly green, red, grey, and for the rest iridescent.' Whenever he remembered that day a verse of Virgil's came into his mind: 'Ut vidi, ut perii, ut me malus abstulit error.'… he had believed that he was on the point of attaining the nigredo. But a few days later his fire went out in the night, which led to an irreparabile damnum" (¶353).

Jung's reading: not necessarily hallucination, but "a remarkable willingness on the part of the author to suspect something of the sort" — projection in the laboratory, the opus mirroring the operator's psyche.

occurrences.title: Joachim of Flora: the third aeon of the Holy Ghost
occurrences.label: Joachim of Flora — the third aeon…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Joachim expected "the opening of the seventh seal... the advent of the 'everlasting gospel' and the reign of the 'intellectus spiritualis,' the age of the Holy Ghost" — secretly begun with St. Benedict (~529), the year the Talmud had prophesied as critical. Gerard of Borgo San Donnino proclaimed 1260 as its public inauguration (Paris, 1254).

Jung's psychological re-reading (par. 142): "Joachim could have been seized by the archetype of the spirit," an ambivalent dualistic figure whose era coincided with the beginning of the second Fish — Holy Ghost movement and antichristian dawning in one. The spirit degenerated into rationalism and doctrinairism, "the most unspiritual of all the spirit's manifestations."

occurrences.title: 'Come, secret mother' — the Holy Ghost in feminine form
occurrences.label: Come, secret mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in the Acts of Thomas the Holy Ghost is addressed as the mother, and it is always the mother-imago which proves to be the hero’s greatest danger but is for that very reason the prime source of his deeds and of his ascent.
body: The Third Person invoked as mother: against the Ophite "first word," "Mother of All Living," and the Valentinian "Word of the Mother from Above" (¶563). With the Acts of Thomas addressing the Holy Ghost as the mother (¶558), the Logos-cow of the Rig-Veda, and the Kore-hymn, the feminine spirit trinity within the godhead.

occurrences.title: Souls of the calcined prima materia escaping as homunculi — Codex Rhenoviensis (15th c.)
occurrences.label: Souls of the calcined prima materia escaping…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 54 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: from the Codex Rhenoviensis (fifteenth century), Zurich — the souls of the calcined prima materia escape as vapours, in the form of human figures looking like children (homunculi); in the fire is the dragon, "the chthonic form of the anima mundi, which is being transmuted."

Jung's astonishing caveat (¶708): the parallel patient pictures (Figs 52-53, a woman painting flames with a soul rising from them) were made when neither patient knew alchemy nor he himself the alchemical picture material — evidence that "similar psychological situations make use of the same symbols, which on their side rest on archetypal foundations."

occurrences.title: The vulture conceiving by wind — Horapollo's Hieroglyphica
occurrences.label: The vulture conceiving by wind
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~5th c. CE (much used in Leonardo's time)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Horapollo's Hieroglyphica: "vultures are female only and symbolize the mother. They conceive through the wind (Pneuma)" — a word that took on the meaning of "spirit" chiefly under Christian influence (Pentecost's pneuma still double: wind and spirit). The vulture also symbolizes Athene, who "sprang, unbegotten, directly from the head of Zeus, was a virgin, and knew only spiritual motherhood" (¶96).

Jung's reading: "All this is really an allusion to Mary" — the virgin who conceived through the pneuma, like a vulture; hence "There is not a shadow of evidence that Leonardo meant anything else by his picture" (the vulture of his childhood fantasy) — the mythological dual-mother motif, not personal prehistory.

occurrences.title: The horn as remedy against hereditary disease — Atharva-Veda III, 7
occurrences.label: The horn as remedy against hereditary disease
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Vedic root of the alicorn-as-medicine, a "charm against kshetriya, hereditary disease": "Upon the head of the nimble antelope a remedy grows! He has driven the kshetriya in all directions by means of the horn. … O horn, loosen the kshetriya that is knitted into his heart! … (The horn) that glistens yonder like a roof with four wings (sides), with that do we drive out every kshetriya from thy limbs" (¶532).

Jung follows the track east ("The track of the unicorn in pre-Christian days leads us to the East") to the horned fish of Manu and the one-horned hermit Rishyashringa — the horn as the healing, saving point of an Anthropos-like figure.

occurrences.title: The horned Alexander coin of Lysimachus (~297–281 BCE)
occurrences.label: The horned Alexander coin of Lysimachus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: pl. XXa; index 'Lysimachus, coin of, pl. XXa' (pdf p590)

body: The two-horned head on Lysimachus' tetradrachms — Alexander with the ram-horns of Ammon — is Jung's pl. XXa for the "two-horned" motif: "horns: two-horned, 194n, 198n, pl. XXa" (index p566). It belongs to his solar-hero row (cf. book p227, pdf 260, where c02 recorded the coin at ¶285 beside Khidr "of the two horns", 198n — the homology of Alexander-Dhulqarnayn-Khidr).
Verbatim (index): "horns: two-horned, 194n, 198n, pl. XXa"

image.title: Thrace - king Lysimachos - 297-281 BC - siver tetradrachm - head of Alexander III with ram´s horn - Athena Nikephoros - Berlin MK BM

occurrences.title: Ashvamedha — the world as the sacrificial horse (Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1,1)
occurrences.label: Ashvamedha — the world as the sacrificial horse
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The horse-sacrifice cosmogony: "Verily, dawn is the head of the sacrificial horse, the sun his eye, the wind his breath, universal fire his open mouth. The year is the body of the sacrificial horse..." Day and night stand before and behind him "as the two sacrificial vessels"; "as a steed he carried the gods, as a charger the Gandharvas, as a racer the demons, as a horse men." In BU 3,3 Yajnavalkya tells where the offerers of the horse-sacrifice go: to the razor-edge gap between the shells of the world-egg, whither Indra as falcon, having stolen the soma, delivered the Parikshitas — the psychopomp saving them from "repeated death" (¶659).

Jung: the horse "signifies a quantum of energy at man's disposal... the libido which has passed into the world" (¶658); horse between two vessels = "the birth-giving and the devouring mother," life in the ovum. With Deussen he reads the ashvamedha as renunciation of the world — the same libido that created the world by sacrifice destroys it by renewed sacrifice (¶658). In the Miller drama the horse is "the animal brother of the hero" dying first (¶659).
Verbatim: "The sacrifice of the horse can only produce another phase of introversion similar to that which prevailed before the creation of the world" (¶658).

occurrences.title: The cosmic sacrificial horse — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
occurrences.label: The cosmic sacrificial horse
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The ocean is his kinsman, the sea his cradle.
body: The ashvamedha cosmology: the horse as time-symbol and the whole world — "his kinsman and cradle is the sea, the mother, who is the equivalent of the world-soul" (¶426). The libido in the mother, "dying and rising again in the unconscious" (¶426).

occurrences.title: Horses with 'half-moons' under their skins — dementia praecox patient, Zurich
occurrences.label: Horses with 'half-moons' under their skins
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: declared that her horses had 'half-moons' under their skins 'like little curls.
body: A schizophrenic patient declared that her horses had "half-moons" under their skins, "like little curls." Jung calls it "a special motif which must have something typical about it" and lines it up with three star-skinned beasts: the horse that carried the "river map" on its coat and so brought the I Ching to China; the Egyptian sky-goddess, the heavenly cow dotted with stars (fig. 25); and the Mithraic Aion bearing the zodiac on his skin (pl. XLIV).
The clinical image and the cult image share one grammar: the animal as carrier of the astral order, the cosmos worn as hide.

occurrences.title: The three-legged and four-legged magic horses — 'The Princess in the Tree' (German fairytale)
occurrences.label: The three-legged and four-legged magic horses
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the young man, who has hidden himself under the bed, learns that about an hour's journey from the hunting-lodge there dwells a witch who breeds magic horses.
body: From the witch who breeds magic horses the hero wins the four-legged horse by guarding the foals three days, helped by wolf, bear, and lion, and paying tribute of twelve lambs to the twelve wolves. The hunter's own mount is three-legged — a hoof torn off at the border of the witch's realm. The horses talk: "Sister, throw him off!" — and trample the magician. Jung's analysis (¶425-426, 430, 441-445): the horses "represent the unconscious spirit"; "the spirit can be somebody's property"; three-leggedness is "the unconscious masculinity immanent in a female creature" (the bewitched mare-princess, i.e. the animus/shadow), four-leggedness the wholeness of the quaternity. "When the third produces the fourth it at once produces unity" — the axiom of Maria in harness.

occurrences.title: Tishtriya the white horse defeats Apaosha at the rain-lake — Avesta
occurrences.label: Tishtriya the white horse defeats Apaosha…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In this symbolism we can see very clearly how libido fights against libido, instinct against instinct, how the unconscious is in conflict with itself
body: The black horse Apaosha blocks the sources of the rain-lake; the white Tishtriya conquers him at the third attempt. Jung's reading: "libido fights against libido, instinct against instinct, how the unconscious is in conflict with itself" (¶395) — the dragon-horse as guardian of the fertilizing waters.

occurrences.title: Wotan riding the eight-legged Sleipnir — Gotland tombstone
occurrences.label: Wotan riding the eight-legged Sleipnir
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Legend attributes properties to the horse which psychologically belong to the unconscious of man
body: Fig. 28 in the great horse excursus (¶421–428): the god on his steed as god-and-animal unity (Drosselbart, "half man, half horse"); the horse as the unconscious of man — mantic, clairvoyant, path-finding — and as devil's beast (horse's hoof, nightmare), psychopomp (Valkyries, "St. Michael's Horse" as bier, the Persian "wooden horse" coffin).

occurrences.title: Hui Ming Ching, stage 4 — the centre amid the spirit-fire multiplication (China)
occurrences.label: Hui Ming Ching, stage 4
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Hui Ming Ching (Book of Consciousness and Life)
body: The fourth meditation picture (reproduced pdf p47): "a sage sunk in contemplation, his head surrounded by tongues of fire, out of which five human figures emerge; these five again split up into twenty-five smaller figures" (cw13 ¶46). Jung: "This would be a schizophrenic process if it were to become a permanent state." The Hui Ming Ching warns: "The shapes formed by the spirit-fire are only empty colours and forms. The light of human nature (hsing) shines back on the primordial, the true" (¶46); footnote — the figures are recollections of earlier incarnations.
Jung's reading: the protective circle (mandala) exists to prevent the "outflowing" and to keep the unity of consciousness from being burst asunder by the autonomous figures (¶47).

occurrences.title: Hymn of Hibis: the ram of Mendes, 'the phallus, lord of the gods'
occurrences.label: Hymn of Hibis — the ram of Mendes, the…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Amon-Ra invoked: "Thy Ram dwelleth in Mendes... He is the phallus, lord of the gods. The bull of his mother rejoiceth in the cow, and the husband maketh fruitful through his seed."
Jung's reading: Khnum-Ra as ram, consort of Hatmehit ("mother of Mendes", fish on her head) — divine fecundation as phallic godhead (¶357-358).
Verbatim: He is the phallus, lord of the gods. (cw05 ¶358).

occurrences.title: Hymn of the Pearl — the Gnostic song of the soul
occurrences.label: Hymn of the Pearl — the Gnostic song of the soul
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Syria/Edessa? (preserved in the Acts of Thomas)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It lies at the bot tom of adeep well, guarded by a dragon, in the land of the Egyptians
body: The Gnostic hymn to the soul (James, Apocryphal New Testament, pp. 411-15), ascribed to Bardesanes: the son is sent by his parents to seek the pearl that fell from the King's crown; it lies at the bottom of a deep well, guarded by a dragon, in Egypt — "that land of fleshpots and drunkenness". The heir forgets himself in Egyptian worldliness until a letter from his father reminds him; he plunges into the dark depths, finds the pearl, and offers it to the highest divinity.

Jung's reading: an age "that resembled ours" — the way of the waters that raises up "the treasure, the precious heritage of the father"; from this same matrix "it was a fish — 'levatus de profundo' — that became the symbol of the saviour, the bringer of healing" (¶38).

occurrences.title: Poliphilo meets his anima Polia at the court of Queen Venus — Hypnerotomachia Poliphili (1499)
occurrences.label: Poliphilo meets his anima Polia at the court…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1499 (French version 1600 used by Jung: Le Songe de Poliphile)
body: Francesco Colonna's Hypnerotomachia: "Poliphilo meets his anima, the lady Polia, at the court of Queen Venus, quite untouched by Christianity and graced with all the 'virtues' of antiquity. The book was rightly regarded as a mystery text." (cw12 ¶112).

Jung reads it as Renaissance evidence that scholastic intellectualism "drove the anima to regress to the ancient world" — the same regression his dreamer's sun-worshipping anima displays. Seductive maidens also open the Poliphilo's nekyia (¶61; fig. 33).

occurrences.title: Poliphilo's conjuring of Queen Venus (Hypnerotomachia Poliphili)
occurrences.label: Poliphilo's conjuring of Queen Venus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Poliphilo conjured up Queen Venus; Goethe, Helen of Tray.
body: The Renaissance dream-romance Hypnerotomachia of Poliphilo — with Goethe's Faust — "reach deep into antiquity in order to find 'le vrai mot' for the situation. Poliphilo conjured up Queen Venus; Goethe, Helen of Troy" (¶60). Linda Fierz-David's study is cited in the footnote; a kindred Aldrovandus passage on the anima-dryad appears later in the Rebirth essay (¶224 fn).

Jung's reading: the anima "is conservative and clings in the most exasperating fashion to the ways of earlier humanity. She likes to appear in historic dress, with a predilection for Greece and Egypt" — the classic anima stories of Rider Haggard and Pierre Benoit stand in the same row.

occurrences.title: Ignatius Loyola — the Foundation of the Spiritual Exercises
occurrences.label: Ignatius Loyola — the Foundation…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Man was created to praise, do reverence to, and serve God our Lord, and thereby to save his soul.' Jung sets this beside Dorn's quis/quid: man's end is the 'what' not the 'who'. Stripped of theology: 'Man's consciousness was created to the end that it may (1) recognize its descent from a higher unity (Deum); (2) pay due and careful regard to this source; (3) execute its commands intelligently and responsibly; and (4) thereby afford the psyche as a whole the optimum degree of life and development' (¶253). A quaternity of function, transposing dogma into psychological terms.

occurrences.title: Instructio de arbore solari — catching the Echeneis in the world-sea
occurrences.label: Instructio de arbore solari
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The anonymous French father teaches his son to catch the Echeneis-remora, 'shut up in that deep mid region of the great universal sea', using the 'magnet of the wise'; caught, it becomes first water then earth, dissolving and purifying all bodies (¶217). Jung: the ocean is the 'spirit of the world', a projection of the unconscious; 'our sea' is the unconscious 'just as it is in dreams'; the extremely small fish in its centre is the self as unconscious content, catchable only because a 'magnet' — the theoria — exists in the conscious subject (¶218). The treatise marks alchemy's turn from laboratory to philosophy.

occurrences.title: Interrogationes maiores Mariae — Christ produces a woman from his side on the mountain
occurrences.label: Interrogationes maiores Mariae
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Christ takes Mary up a mountain, 'produced a woman from his side and began to have intercourse with her... partaking of his flowing seed he showed that this was to be done, that we might live' (¶314). Mary falls to the ground in shock; Christ: 'Wherefore do you doubt me, O you of little faith?' Jung's symbol-by-symbol reading (¶316-320): the mountain = spiritual ascent; Christ = Archanthropos and 'squared circle of the self'; the woman from the side = second Adam playing the Creator-god, androgyny ('I am both, man and woman'); the splitting = 'an act of nascent consciousness'. The counterpart vision: mechthild-rocky-mountain-child-13c.

occurrences.title: Isis invoked as 'the One, who art All' — aretalogy inscription
occurrences.label: Isis invoked as 'the One, who art All'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Hellenistic-Roman Isis aretalogy (~2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE)
occurrences.quote: All these statements apply just as well to the prima materia in its feminine aspect: it is the moon, the mother of all things, the vessel, it consists of opposites, has a thousand names
body: An inscription of the Isis cult invokes her as "the One, who art All" — the same hen-to-pan formula the Greek alchemists give the uroboros and the arcane substance. Jung assembles the aretalogy's evidence for Isis as the feminine prima materia: the Black One ([Kemet], with Apuleius' palla nigerrima), healer of Ra, "redemptrix," "thousand-named," "the nature of the Aeon, whence all things grew and by which all things are" (Athenagoras), whore in Tyre (Epiphanius), teacher of alchemy in "Isis the Prophetess to her Son Horus" (cross-link water-isis-amnael-vessel-egypt-1c.md), collector of Osiris' scattered limbs, "bathed... with her tears and laid... in a secret grave beneath the bank of the Nile" (¶14).

occurrences.title: Isis wounds Ra with the serpent — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.label: Isis wounds Ra with the serpent — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Isis fashions a poisonous snake and sets it in the sun-god's path; from the bite "he never recovered", and must retire on the back of the heavenly cow. In the parallel tradition she also frees Set, whom Horus has bound, and loses her diadem for a cow's head (¶374).

Jung's reading: the mother both wounds and cures — "the real cause of the wound is the incest-taboo, which cuts a man off from the security of childhood" (¶351); the son flees to the mother from the wound she herself inflicted.
Verbatim: The hymn describes how Isis fashioned a poisonous snake and set it in his path, and how the snake wounded the sun-god with its bite. (cw05 ¶351).

occurrences.title: Joachim of Flora — Trinity diagram (Zurich manuscript)
occurrences.label: Joachim of Flora — Trinity diagram
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Plate II of Aion: the Trinity figure from a Joachimite manuscript, which Jung reads as 'a similar motif' to the stacked quaternities of his own diagrams (¶399, cf. ¶390). Footnote 81: Sabellius' 'silent and unacting God' with three prosopa bequeathed 'the first beginnings of a quaternary view of the Deity' — the basis of Joachim's accusation at Lateran IV (1215) that Peter Lombard posited 'not Trinity, but Quaternity... three persons, and that common Something as a fourth'. The 3+1 dilemma of the God-image in an actual medieval diagram.

occurrences.title: Jonah in the whale — early Christian earthenware lamp
occurrences.label: Jonah in the whale
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 174. Jonah in the whale.—Early Christian earthenware lamp
body: Early Christian lamp with Jonah cast up in the sea-monster — among the oldest Christian images, from the catacomb repertoire Jung surveys.

In the hero myth, writes Jung, the swallowed state "is known as being swallowed up in the belly of the whale or dragon. The heat there is usually so intense that the hero loses his hair, i.e., he is reborn bald as a babe." Jonah is the canonical Christian form of the alchemical mortificatio: three days in the dark belly as the precondition of emission and mission.

occurrences.title: The cook's chicken-saviour — Jung family kitchen, Basel
occurrences.label: The cook's chicken-saviour
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.quote: When the Saviour of men came down to earth, the chicken saviour also came to the chickens.
body: Jung's childhood anecdote: the Swabian cook, returning with the decapitated bantam cock, consoles the household — "He died like a Christian, although he was so wicked … so now he'll go to heaven." Challenged by Jung's mother, she insists animals have souls and their special heavens, "because when the Saviour of men came down to earth, the chicken saviour also came to the chickens, and that's why they must repent of their sins before they die if they want to go to heaven."

Jung's point: "The theology of our cook is a remnant of that folklore mentality which saw the drama of redemption going on at all levels and could therefore discover it even in the mysterious and incomprehensible transformations of matter" (¶495) — the living substrate beneath the alchemical lapis-Christ parallel.

occurrences.title: The theological student's dream of the two magicians and the keys of paradise
occurrences.label: The theological student's dream…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: sent to Jung (student unknown to him personally)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
jung.locator: reused in 'Phenomenology of the Spirit in Fairytales' ¶398 — pin tbd

occurrences.quote: But there lie the keys o.f paradise.
body: A young theological student, "in great straits because of his religious beliefs", dreamt (¶70-71): a handsome old man dressed entirely in black — the white magician — whose closing words were "And for this we need the help of the black magician"; then a double in white; then the black magician's tale of an old king who chose for his tomb the grave of a buried virgin — the bones took on life and changed into a black horse which fled into the desert; pursuing it, the magician found the lost keys of paradise. Dreamer woke at the climax.

Jung's reading (¶72-79): the old king is the ruling symbol seeking its rest in the grave of the anima-Sleeping-Beauty; the black horse is Plato's unruly passions; paradise — Eden and the apocalyptic city — "is conceived as a mandala... the mandala is a symbol of individuation"; the dream paraphrases the Oxyrhynchus sayings and the Ophitic serpent-Saviour; the two magicians are two aspects of the wise old man, "the archetype of the spirit" (¶74), going back in direct line to the medicine man; good and evil work together (nirdvandva).

occurrences.title: Khidr as white light at the door — dream of Jung's Somali headman (Kenya)
occurrences.label: Khidr as white light at the door
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: One 'night, while he slept, he dreamt he saw a bright white light near the door and he knew it was Khidr.
body: During the 1925-26 safari through Kenya the headman, a Somali raised in the Sufi faith, told Jung that Khidr was for him a living person who might be met in the street, as pure white light in the night, or even as a blade of grass. Out of want after the war he dreamt of a bright white light near the door, knew it was Khidr, rose in the dream and saluted him salem aleikum — and a few days later was offered the post of safari headman in Nairobi (¶250). Jung's point: the self-symbol still functions as "friend, adviser, comforter, and teacher of revealed wisdom", dogmatically ranked as maleika kwanza-yamungu, "First Angel of God" (¶251).

occurrences.title: Khidr the Verdant One — Qur'an, Sura 18
occurrences.label: Khidr the Verdant One — Qur'an, Sura 18
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Khidr may well be a symbol of the self. His qualities signalize him as such: he is said to have been born in a cave, Le., in darkness.
body: Khidr, "the Verdant One", appears in Sura 18 as the mysterious servant of Allah whom Moses begs to teach him: he scuttles a fishing-boat, kills a youth, rebuilds a falling wall, then explains the hidden mercy of each act. Jung treats the whole Sura as a rebirth mystery and Khidr as a symbol of the self: born in a cave (darkness), the "Long-lived One" who continually renews himself like Elijah, dismembered at the end of time by Antichrist like Osiris yet restoring himself to life, counsellor and Paraclete (¶247). Khidr stands for "not only the higher wisdom but also a way of acting which is in accord with this wisdom and transcends reason" (¶247); he is paired with Dhulqarnein like the Dioscuri, and still lives in popular religion as "First Angel of God" (¶251) — as Jung's Somali headman attested.

occurrences.title: Khunrath: the Circumrotation of the Quaternarius into the Catholic Monad
occurrences.label: Khunrath — the Circumrotation…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the basic mandala of alchemy
body: "Through Circumrotation or a Circular Philosophical revolving of the Quaternarius, it is brought back to the highest and purest Simplicity of the plusquamperfect Catholic Monad. … Out of the gross and impure One there cometh an exceeding pure and subtile One" (¶165). Khunrath adds the Pauline "Cupio dissolvi, et esse cum Christo" and the command to "catch the Spirit and Soul of the Magnesia."

Jung: spirit (ternarius) must be separated from body (the fourth) and re-infused; Khunrath's Pseudo-Aristotle passage has "the circle re-emerges from a triangle set in a square. This circular figure, together with the Uroboros—the dragon devouring itself tail first—is the basic mandala of alchemy" (¶165).

occurrences.title: Kihe Wahine, goddess of goblins and lizards — Hawaiian wood figure
occurrences.label: Kihe Wahine, goddess of goblins and lizards
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XVI: kou-wood figure with human teeth, "goddess of goblins and lizards" — the devouring mother of Polynesia.

Jung's reading: cited (¶254) as visual embodiment of the Terrible Mother, "the mother of innumerable evils", whose stagnant-pool phantasmagorias veil reality; cf. the lamias and Frobenius' devouring whale-dragon (¶365, 369).
Verbatim: This dangerous passion is what lies hidden beneath the hazardous mask of incest. It confronts us in the guise of the Terrible Mother (pl. XVI...) (cw05 ¶254).

occurrences.title: Copper as earthly sun, a king upon earth — Zosimos, True Book of Sophe
occurrences.label: Copper as earthly sun, a king upon earth
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: From Zosimos' 'True Book of Sophe the Egyptian and Divine Lord of the Hebrews, and of the Powers of Sabaoth': 'as the sun is the blossom of fire, and the heavenly sun is the right eye of the world, so also the copper, when purification makes it to blossom, is an earthly sun, a king upon earth, like the sun in heaven' (cw14 ¶353). Jung: 'the above passage from Zosimos is, to my knowledge, the earliest reference to the king in alchemy' (¶354). The king-gold is born only through liberation of the divine soul or pneuma 'chained in the elements'; chrysopoeia runs as a psychic operation parallel to the chemical one, 'actually... its causa efficiens' (¶354).

occurrences.title: King and Lord of Lords reborn from his glassy sepulchre — Khunrath
occurrences.label: King and Lord of Lords reborn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Khunrath (Amphitheatrum, 1595): 'When at last... the ash-colour, the whitening, and the yellowing are over, you will see the Philosophical Stone, our King and Lord of Lords, come forth from the couch and throne of his glassy sepulchre onto the stage of this world, in his glorified body, regenerated and more than perfect, shining like a carbuncle, and crying out, Behold, I make all things new' (cw14 ¶355). Jung unfolds the mystic birth: Ruach Elohim penetrates 'the meditullium of the virginal massa confusa'; the son of the Macrocosm and the son of God are 'a mysterium typicum' — 'the one in the womb of the Macrocosm, the other in the womb of the Microcosm', both virginal (¶355). The triune stone: 'earthly, heavenly, and divine... Sal-Mercurius-Sulphur' — the Egyptian sequence Pharaoh, ka, God.

occurrences.title: The King of Glory, 'a worm and no man' — Naassene psalm exegesis in Hippolytus
occurrences.label: The King of Glory, 'a worm and no man'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: But who, say the Naassenes, is this King of Glory? A worm and no man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.
body: Hippolytus, reporting the mysteries of the Naassenes: the form that "comes down from above, from the Uncharacterized" is found in earthly clay and none recognize it; "that is the god who dwells in the great flood," calling and crying out from the many waters (identified with the multitude of mortal men). To the Uncharacterized Man: "Save mine Only-Begotten from the lions" (a feminine μονογενη, read as the soul). Psalm 23's "King of Glory" gates-of-ascent passage is referred to Adam's regeneration (αναγεννησις), and the King is "A worm and no man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people."
Jung: Maier can have had no access to the long-lost Philosophumena, "and yet it might well have served him as a model for the king's lament" (¶182) — an amplificatio row across thirteen centuries.

occurrences.title: The sunken king renewed with three crowns and seven stars — Splendor Solis
occurrences.label: The sunken king renewed with three crowns…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Trismosin's Splendor Solis narrative: philosophers 'saw a Fog rise... the impetuosity of the Sea... and how these same became foul and stinking in the darkness. They further saw the king of the Earth sink, and heard him cry out with eager voice, "Whoever saves me shall live and reign with me for ever in my brightness on my royal throne," and Night enveloped all things'; next morning a star appears, the sun clears the clouds, and the king is 'released and renewed', crowned 'with three costly crowns, the one of Iron, the other of Silver, and the third of pure Gold', sceptre with seven stars (cw14 ¶465). Jung: 'The king sinking in the sea is the arcane substance... The arcane substance corresponds to the Christian dominant, which was originally alive and present in consciousness but then sank into the unconscious and must now be restored in renewed form' (¶466).

occurrences.title: Kircher — the four monads of the Arithmologia
occurrences.label: Kircher — the four monads of the Arithmologia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Kircher's quaternity: Unum = Monas monadike = Deus = Radix omnium; the tenth (1+2+3+4) = mundus intellectualis, 'composition from opposites'; the hundredth = Anima; the thousandth = omnia sensibilia, Corpus (¶416). When the senses are raised through reason to intelligence and 'absolute unity', 'then the Stone too is not so much a Stone as no Stone, but everything is the simplest unity' (¶417); the lapis 'is the arcanum that contains God or that part of God which is hidden in matter' (¶417). Kircher's cycle — God unfolding and returning through human understanding — is another opus circulare (¶418). Communication from M.-L. von Franz.

occurrences.title: The hero in the belly of Kombili the King Fish — Polynesian myth
occurrences.label: The hero in the belly of Kombili the King Fish
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Swallowed by the King Fish, the hero lights a fire in its belly, cuts out a piece of the heart, then cuts the belly open with his obsidian knife, slips out and beholds a splendour: "Then the sun rose up with a bound."

Jung's reading: one of Frobenius' devouring/sea-journey/opening/slipping-out sequences — rebirth from the whale-dragon (¶310-311); the fire in the belly "kills" the dark state of union with the mother.
Verbatim: the hero, in the belly of Kombili, the King Fish, seized his obsidian knife and cut open the fish’s belly. (cw05 ¶311).

occurrences.title: Case X — Kore vision series (blue mother, golden pig, youth with cymbals, Earth Mother in the snake den)
occurrences.label: Case X — Kore vision series
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I saw a white bird with outstretched wings. It alighted on the figure of a woman, clad in blue, who sat there like an antique statue. The bird perched on her hand, and in it she held a grain of wheat.
body: A series of spontaneous visual impressions (with X's paintings), presented in the Kore essay as the clearest modern Demeter-Kore material: a white bird alights on a blue-clad archaic mother holding a grain of wheat; a bull lifts a child like Europa; a golden pig on a pedestal; a man in a golden carriage leaps from a hole, rapes the girl and begets a child; a beautiful youth with golden cymbals dances, dissolves into a swarm of bees, sinks exhausted into the lap of a very old mother, sports like a dolphin and falls into a gorge; sacrifice of sheep with a ball-game and blood-bath; X transformed into a plant; a den of snakes; and in the den beneath the sea a sleeping divine woman in a blood-red garment — the Earth Mother — who kisses X and hands her to the men. Emergence brings illumination: white flames playing about her head in waving fields of grain (¶333). Jung: "not the slightest trace of any known myth being repeated", yet every motif familiar from mythology (¶334).

occurrences.title: Case Y iv — the dancer who becomes bees, leopard, octopus; the lily and the white lady
occurrences.label: Case Y iv — the lily and the white lady
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Jung's practice (dream-space: magician's show for an Indian prince)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: During the dance she dissolves with the music into aswarm of bees. Then she changes into a leopard, then into a jet of water, then into an octopus that has twined itself about a young pearl-fisher.
body: Part dream, part visual imagination: a magician demonstrates his tricks to an Indian prince, producing from under a cloth a beautiful dancer. During the dance "she dissolves with the music into a swarm of bees. Then she changes into a leopard, then into a jet of water, then into an octopus that has twined itself about a young pearl-fisher"; again human; then a she-ass with baskets of wonderful fruits; a many-coloured peacock; naked, she tears the skin from her body and falls down — a naked skeleton. Buried by night, "a lily grows out of the grave, and from its cup there rises a white lady, who floats slowly up to the sky". Jung reads the series as "the successive transformations of the illusionist... until she becomes a transfigured personality" (¶350) — artistry in illusion as "a specifically feminine talent".

occurrences.title: Case Y iii — two pictures by 'Hermann Christian Lund': the witchlike humpback and the faceless girl in the dragon's power
occurrences.label: Case Y iii — two pictures…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Jung's practice (dream-space: gallery of invented paintings)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The second picture shows a dragon with its neck stretched out over the whole picture and especially over a girl, who is in the dragon's power and cannot move... Strangely enough, the girl has no face, at least I couldn't see it.
body: Y sees two pictures by the Scandinavian painter Hermann Christian Lund — an invention of the dream. In the first, peasant girls walk arm in arm, the middle one smaller, humpbacked, "keeps turning her head back... gives her a witchlike look". In the second, "a dragon with its neck stretched out over the whole picture and especially over a girl, who is in the dragon's power and cannot move... Strangely enough, the girl has no face, at least I couldn't see it" (¶349). Jung reads the painter motif through the animus as projection apparatus, and the two pictures as the maiden demonic (evil glance — hence amulets worn on the nape) and the maiden as innocent victim of the monster, the girl-dragon relation of identity "which in practical life is often rather more than just a bad joke".

occurrences.title: Case Y v — the girl in the red dress hanging on the stone cross
occurrences.label: Case Y v — the girl in the red dress hanging…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Near the tabernacle a girl in a red dress is hanging on the stone cross of the window. (Suicide?)
body: "I am in a church made of grey sandstone. The apse is built rather high. Near the tabernacle a girl in a red dress is hanging on the stone cross of the window. (Suicide?)" (¶351). Jung reads it with the sacrifice of children and sheep in the earlier material: "the sacrifice of the maiden hanging on the 'cross'" — the doomed maiden whose exclusive domination of the feminine psyche hinders the maturation of personality. The Kore crucified in the church's own architecture: the maiden fixed where the redeemer belongs.

occurrences.title: The maiden-goddess in purest white carrying a black monkey (case vision)
occurrences.label: The maiden-goddess in purest white carrying…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I remember a case, in fact, where a maiden-goddess appears clad all in purest white, but carrying a black monkey in her arms.
body: Among "very few cases where Demeter's own noble figure in its pure form breaks through as an image rising spontaneously from the unconscious" Jung recalls one where "a maiden-goddess appears clad all in purest white, but carrying a black monkey in her arms" (¶311). Kore in her celestial purity, with the chthonic animal tucked in her arm — the maiden-mother ambivalence in a single image, kin to the white-bird/black-monster alternations of the other Kore material.

occurrences.title: Koschei the Deathless and Queen Maria Morevna — Russian variant of the spirit-fairytale
occurrences.label: Koschei the Deathless and Queen Maria Morevna
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 19th c. collection ('Maria Morevna', 'daughter of the sea')

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The evil spirit is an old man who is often shown naked and is called Koschei the Deathless. The corresponding witch is the well-known Baba Yaga.
body: Jung's postscript (¶435) adds the Russian variant found only after completing the essay: Czarevitch Ivan, his three sisters married to bird-men ("a species of angel" = auxiliary unconscious functions), the evil spirit as Koschei the Deathless — an old man often shown naked, chained with twelve chains in the forbidden room — and the witch Baba Yaga. Ivan, unlike the German swineherd, is killed and dismembered: "The old man puts the dismembered body into a barrel which he throws into the sea. This is reminiscent of the fate of Osiris (head and phallus)" (n55). The princess is Queen Maria Morevna, a martial leader — "Mary the queen of heaven is lauded in the Russian Orthodox hymnal as 'leader of hosts!'". "This Russian story has a distinctly more primitive character."

occurrences.title: Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot — the divine companion
occurrences.label: Krishna and Arjuna on the chariot
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. BCE–2nd c. CE (Gita layers, inferred)
occurrences.quote: the disciples on the road to Emmaus, Krishna and Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita, Moses and El-Khidr in Sura 18 of the Koran
body: Second of the three companion-examples: Krishna as charioteer guiding Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita — the divine companion who drives while the hero fights, then reveals himself as the Lord "whose body is the whole universe."

Jung's use is typological rather than exegetical: the companion "who goes through life at our side" is "in all probability a close analogy to the lonely ego who finds a mate in the self" (¶155). The Gita supplies the Indian branch of the companion motif alongside the Christian (Emmaus) and Islamic (El-Khidr) ones.

occurrences.title: St. Brendan's sacrifice of the immaculate lamb on the island of sheep
occurrences.label: St. Brendan's sacrifice of the immaculate lamb…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Atlantic island of the navigatio (Land of Sheep); legend from Irish monastic tradition
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th–13th c. MSS (La Légende latine de S. Brandaines)
occurrences.quote: Faciamus hic opus divinum, et sacrificemus Deo agnum immaculatum, quia hodie cena Domini est.
body: In the Latin legend of St. Brendan's voyage, the monks land on an island covered with flocks of white sheep so numerous "they could not see the ground," and Brendan commands a Mass: "Let us perform here the divine work and sacrifice to God an immaculate lamb, for today is the supper of the Lord." A ewe follows the brothers "as if it were a domestic animal"; the chosen lamb is sacrificed and its blood taken "for life eternal."

Jung quotes the passage (Part II ch. 2, n. 42) as a naive survival of the archaic identification of god, sacrificial animal, and meal — the same structure the alchemical Mass analogies (Melchior Cibinensis, the opus as missa) transpose into the laboratory. The sheep/land-of-sheep motif also belongs to the biblical vision-material of the Book of Enoch (cw12 Part I ch. 2, nn. 14–15).

occurrences.title: Lambspringk — two reversed fishes swimming in our sea
occurrences.label: Lambspringk — two reversed fishes swimming…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Lambspringk's emblem shows two fishes swimming in opposite directions in the sea — 'nostro mari', the aqua permanens or arcane substance — designated 'spiritus et anima' (¶224 n.82, ¶231). With the stag and unicorn, the two lions, the dog and wolf, and the two fighting birds, they indicate the double nature of Mercurius (¶231). Jung dates the symbol to the end of the sixteenth century, 'a revitalization of the archetype', and declines to prove Catharist descent: the reversed fishes visualize 'the antithetical nature of the self'. Parallels: cathar-two-fishes-osob-revelation-1111, fish-round-fish-allegoriae-turba-11c.

occurrences.title: The Andalusian prince who desires the torment of the seekers — 'Book of Ostanes'
occurrences.label: The Andalusian prince who desires the torment…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: m edieval Arabic (Berthelot, Chimie au moyen age III, p. 117)
body: The Arabic "Book of Ostanes" (Kitab el-Ful) describes the arcane substance in its forms — water white, black, red, then fire struck from stones — and then: "It is a tree that grow s on the tops of the m ountains, a young m an born in Egypt, a prince from Andalusia, who desires the torment of the seekers. He has slain their leaders... Th e sages are pow erless to oppose him. I can see no weapon against him save resignation, no charger bu t know ledge, no buckler bu t understanding" (cw13 ¶424). Slain with these three weapons, "he will com e to life again after his death... and will give the seeker the highest pow er".

Jung reads the hostile prince with Enkidu — "the chthonic m an and shadow of G ilgam esh, created by the gods... so that he m ay kill the hero" (cw13 ¶425) — and with the K hidr legend: at first m eeting the self appears negative (cw13 ¶428). 'Unless thy stone shall be an enemy, thou wilt not attain to thy desire' (cw13 ¶426).
Verbatim: a young m an born in Egypt, a prince from Andalusia, who desires the torment of the seekers. (cw13 ¶424ocr)
