occurrences.title: Ostanes to Cleopatra: 'In you is hidden the whole terrible and marvellous secret' (Greek alchemy)
occurrences.label: Ostanes to Cleopatra
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: text ~1st c. A.D. (Ostanes legendary, possibly 4th c. BCE)
body: Jung quotes the saying again in the stone-symbolism chapter: "Thus the legendary Ostanes, speaking of the secret of the 'philosophy,' says to his pupil Cleopatra: 'In you is hidden the whole terrible and marvellous secret... Make known to us how the highest descends to the lowest, and how the lowest ascends to the highest, and how the midmost draws near to the highest, and is made one with it'" (cw13 ¶131).

His comment: "This 'midmost' is the stone, the mediator which unites the opposites. Such sayings have no meaning unless they are understood in a profoundly psychological sense" (¶131) — the stone hidden in man, quoted here against the anima-figure of the turquoise goddess who "contains the secret of the precious stone."

occurrences.title: The Yellow Man and the Red Man — dialogue of the Cardinal of Brixen (Aureum vellus)
occurrences.label: The Yellow Man and the Red Man
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Aureum vellus printing (attrib. Melchior, Cardinal of Brixen, d. 1459)
body: An alchemical folk-tale of personified metals, quoted at length: the seeker goes to the house with two shut doors, until one comes out — "that will be a Yellow Man, and is not pretty to look upon, but you should not fear him, because he is unshapely, but he is sweet of word" — who asks what he seeks; the answer: "I have come here and seek the Lapidem Philosophorum." Deeper in, at a running fountain, meets the Red Man, "he is Fiery Red and has Red eyes," equally gentle of word (cw13 ¶123).

Footnote 5: "After the Red Man he finds the Black Raven, and from this comes the White Dove." Jung's frame: alchemical projections "are only a special instance of the mode of thinking typified by the idea of the microcosm" (¶123) — personification as participation mystique (¶122).

occurrences.title: Leonardo's St. Anne with the Virgin and Child (the dual-mother picture)
occurrences.label: Leonardo's St. Anne with the Virgin and Child
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

jung.year: Leonardo da Vinci and a Memory of His Childhood

occurrences.quote: Surely not all of them had two mothers?
body: Leonardo's St. Anne with the Virgin Mary and the Christ-child — the picture Freud interpreted through Leonardo's two mothers. Jung's counter-reading: "interwoven with the apparently personal psychology there is an impersonal motif well known to us from other fields. This is th e motif of th e dual mother)" (¶94) — an archetype "to be found in many variants in the field of mythology and comparative religion", whatever Leonardo's biography; the vulture symbol (Freud's other plank) comes from Horapollo's Hieroglyphica, current among educated artists of the day.
The fn to ¶140 adds: Freud assimilated the painting to his theory — "the 'religious inhibition of thought'... proved true of the author himself".

image.title: Leonardo da Vinci - Virgin and Child with St Anne C2RMF retouched
image.credit: original file: C2RMF: Galerie de tableaux en très haute définition : image page

occurrences.title: Diagram of the stages of the opus — Libavius, Alchymia (1606)
occurrences.label: Diagram of the stages of the opus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Q A vision of heaven, where a dragon lies on his back and devours his own tail: he is an image of the second coagulation.
body: A full synoptic picture of the opus with Libavius' own lettered explicatio: two Atlases; a four-headed dragon of the four fires; Mercurius with a silver chain; green lion and one-headed dragon (both the mercurial materia prima); a three-headed eagle spitting the white water; black stream of putrefactio; the black-white mountain; ravens in the sea; silver rain; the dragon in heaven "that lies on his back and devours his own tail"; the Ethiopian pair as nigredo; the swan as white elixir; eclipses of sun and moon each flanked by rainbows (the peacock's tail); the king with red lily and golden lion beside the queen with white lily and silver eagle; and the phoenix cremating itself with birds flying from the ashes.

One plate carrying nearly the whole image-inventory of the spagyric process; Jung reproduces it to show the method's density. Parallels: uroboros-codex-marcianus-venice-11c · sol-luna-allegory-rosarium-1550.

occurrences.title: Mercurius made equal to the Virgin Mary — Liber de arte chymica
occurrences.label: Mercurius made equal to the Virgin Mary
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: it is not without good reason that Mercurius is made equal [non immerito … aequiparatur] to the most glorious and worshipful Virgin Mary.
body: The anonymous Liber de arte chymica sets an aequiparatio of Mercurius with the Virgin Mary: Christ unlocked the gate of the ethereal Olympus; correspondingly the virginal Mercurius — who "has never increased any kind of metallic body" — opens the gold, leads out the soul (a divinity), carries it in his belly, and brings forth the puer, the lapis, by whose blood the lower bodies are tinctured.

Jung: as anima mundi, Mercurius can be compared with the Gnostic parthenos tou photos (virgin of light) and with the Virgin Mary; the puer is then the filius macrocosmi, an analogy of Christ. The author also argues Christ's body would never have died had he not sought death freely — the same incorruptibility the stone derives from the alliance of its elements.

occurrences.title: Liber Platonis quartorum: the occiput as vessel of transformation
occurrences.label: Liber Platonis quartorum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the use of the occiput… as the vessel of transformation
body: "The 'Liber Platonis quartorum' accordingly recommends the use of the occiput as the vessel of transformation, because it is the container of thought and intellect. For we need the brain as the seat of the 'divine part.'… on account of its proximity to the anima rationalis the brain had to be assimilated to the amalgam" (¶376).

The recommendation makes literal the treatise's premise of "an unconscious identity between the psyche of the alchemist and the arcane substance, i.e., the spirit imprisoned in matter" (¶376): the container of the opus is the operator's own head, the skull as vas (cf. fig. 135, the skull of Eve with the tree growing from it).

occurrences.title: 'Res ex qua sunt res, est Deus invisibilis' — Liber Platonis quartorum
occurrences.label: Res ex qua sunt res, est Deus invisibilis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Res ex qua sunt res, est Deus invisibilis et immobilis.
body: The Arabic-derived Liber Platonis quartorum states the terminus of the prima materia speculations: "That from which things arise is the invisible and immovable God." Jung quotes it after the Aquarium sapientum had applied Micah 5:2 and John 8:58 ("Before Abraham was made, I am") to the stone.

His reading: "the alchemists came to project even the highest value—God—into matter," which gave the starting-point for genuine chemistry and, later, philosophical materialism. Psychologically the identification is compelled because unconscious contents, "lacking all recognizable qualities," are indiscriminable from one another.

occurrences.title: Lilith, Adam's demon-wife — Jewish legend
occurrences.label: Lilith, Adam's demon-wife — Jewish legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Adam's first wife Lilith strives with him for supremacy, rises into the air by the magic of God's name and hides in the sea; forced back by three angels, she becomes the lamia who haunts pregnant women and kidnaps infants.

Jung's reading: the Terrible Mother betrayed into nightmare — cf. Lamia, whom jealous Hera cursed to bear only dead children; "a well-known German paradigm is the story of Hansel and Gretel" (¶369); Lamia is also "a large, voracious fish", the whale-dragon.
Verbatim: whereupon Lilith changed into a nightmare or lamia (pl. XXXVIIIa) who haunted pregnant women and kidnapped new-born infants. (cw05 ¶369).

occurrences.title: Lingam with yoni — Angkor Wat
occurrences.label: Lingam with yoni — Angkor Wat
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXV: the aniconic lingam standing within its spouted yoni-base, "found everywhere in Indian temples" (cf. also the 'Goddess in the Lingam', Cambodia 14th c.).

Jung's reading: form of the motif of "continuous cohabitation" of Shiva and Parvati — "the base is a female symbol, and within it stands the phallus" (¶306); akin to the Greek phallic baskets and chests.

Verbatim: The motif of continuous cohabitation is expressed in the wellknown lingam symbol found everywhere in Indian temples: the base is a female symbol, and within it stands the phallus. (cw05 ¶306).

image.credit: Greg Willis from Denver, CO, usa

occurrences.title: Jung's 1938 conversation with the rimpoche Lingdam Gomchen on the khilkor (mandala)
occurrences.label: Jung's 1938 conversation with the rimpoche…
occurrences.subject: jung
body: "In 1938, I had the opportunity, in the monastery of Bhutia Busty, near Darjeeling, of talking with a Lamaic rimpoche, Lingdam Gomchen by name, about the khilkor or mandala." (cw12 ¶123).

The lama explained the khilkor as a dmigs-pa ("migpa"), a mental image built up only by a fully instructed lama through the power of imagination: "The true mandala is always an inner image… at such times when psychic equilibrium is disturbed or when a thought cannot be found… because it is not contained in holy doctrine." Jung's caveat: Lamaic mandalas nonetheless share "a quaternary system, a quadratura circuli," with contents from dogma; the khilkor is strictly distinct from the sidpe-korlo World Wheel with its ternary centre.

occurrences.title: Green lion bleeding in the queen's lap — Ripley
occurrences.label: Green lion bleeding in the queen's lap — Ripley
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: green lion lying in the queen’s lap with blood flowing from his side
body: Ripley's image of the "green lion lying in the queen's lap with blood flowing from his side." Jung reads it as a double allusion: "on the one hand to the Pieta, on the other to the unicorn wounded by the hunter and caught in the lap of a virgin (figs. 241, 242), a frequent theme in medieval pictures." That the green lion replaces the unicorn "did not present any difficulty to the alchemist since the lion is likewise a symbol of Mercurius"; the virgin is Mercurius' "passive, feminine aspect," while the beast is "the wild, rampant, masculine, penetrating force of the spiritus mercurialis" (¶519). The side-wound ties the image to the lance-wound of Christ.

occurrences.title: Mithraic god Aion (leontocephalic) — Vatican
occurrences.label: Mithraic god Aion (leontocephalic) — Vatican
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The leontocephalic Aion — lion-headed, winged, entwined by a serpent, often holding keys — is the frontispiece and namesake of Aion: the volume on the phenomenology of the self takes its title from this figure of eternal time. Jung's working of the leontocephalic god lies in "A Psychological Approach to the Dogma of the Trinity" and later Aion chapters (ch. XIV falls outside chunk c01).
Caption (OCR-damaged): "The Mithraic god Aion / Roman,:nd-jrd century."

The figure condenses time, fire, and the pole: cf. cw09ii par. 190, where the Mithraic Liturgy's bull-shoulder Bear turns the heavens from the fiery north. Parallels: god-image-unas-ladder-pyramid-texts-2350-bce, fish-farnese-atlas-pisces-naples.

image.title: Mithraic relief of Chronos-Aion (Vienne, Mus St-Pierre R 2001-5-131) - 19th c. drawing
image.credit: Unknown artist Unknown artist , perhaps Félix Lajard

occurrences.title: Lion hunt of Marchos — lion swallowed by the woman-stone (Senior)
occurrences.label: Lion hunt of Marchos
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Senior's 'lion hunt' the lion takes the king's place: lured by a sweet-smelling eye-charm stone, it falls into a trap under a 'glass roof' — 'the "cucurbita," is here called the "thalamus" (bridal chamber)' — and is swallowed (transglutit) by the stone: 'And this stone, which the lion loves, is a woman' (cw14 ¶409). Jung: 'This is a parallel of the Arisleus vision, where Beya causes Gabricus to disappear into her body' (¶409). The royal incest is 'projected on the lion, the animal nature or "accrescent soul" of the king... it is enacted in his unconscious' (¶410) — the sacral act performed 'outside oneself' in the glasshouse.

occurrences.title: The lion lured from the Saturnine mountain with rose-coloured blood — Khunrath
occurrences.label: The lion lured from the Saturnine mountain…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Khunrath's Hyl. Chaos gives the "lion lured forth from the Saturnine m ountain" rose-coloured blood: "the costly Catholick Rosy-Coloured Blood and Aetheric Water that flows forth Azothically from the side of the innate Son of the Great World when opened by the pow er of the Art" (cw13 ¶383).

Jung: the lion "signifying 'all and conquering all,' corresponds to the pan or panta of Zosim os, i.e., totality" (cw13 ¶383) — the blood of the lion equated elsewhere with the lion of the tribe of Judah, i.e., Christ (n.18 on ¶390).
Verbatim: the “lion lured forth from the Saturnine m ountain” had rose-coloured blood. (cw13 ¶383ocr)

occurrences.title: Lion and unicorn together — Chymical Wedding and the royal arms
occurrences.label: Lion and unicorn together
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In the Chymical Wedding, as in the royal arms of England, lion and unicorn are combined (fig. 258); both are symbols of Mercurius in alchemy, just as they are allegories of Christ in the Church" (¶547). The pairing is not decorative: "Lion and unicorn stand for the inner tension of opposites in Mercurius. The lion, being a dangerous animal, is akin to the dragon; the dragon must be slain and the lion at least have his paws cut off. The unicorn too must be tamed; as a monster he has a higher symbolical significance and is of a more spiritual nature than the lion" (¶547).
The English royal arms make the same heraldic pair — church and state both holding the two beasts of the one substance.

occurrences.title: The Logos is a dog: Kyon the Begetter — Aratus via Hippolytus
occurrences.label: The Logos is a dog — Kyon the Begetter
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For the Logos is a dog... and begets all things. For Cyon, they say, means the Begetter.
body: The Naassene-Aratus astronomy: "Cynosura is the [little] Bear, the Second Creation, the small, narrow way... For the Logos is a dog who guards and protects the sheep against the wiles of the wolves, and chases the wild beasts from Creation and slays them, and begets all things. For Cyon, they say, means the Begetter." The Dog-star rises "judge of the quick and the dead," star of the plants; "between the two Creations stretches the Dragon, hindering anything of the Great Creation from entering the lesser" (¶176).
Jung sets it beside Kalid's filius canis: the dog as divine Logos-Begetter is the archetype's most startling form, millennia before the alchemists' puppy "of celestial hue."

occurrences.title: The lapis-Christ parallel of Raymond Lully's Codicillus
occurrences.label: The lapis-Christ parallel of Raymond Lully's…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And as Jesus Christ, of the house of David, took on human nature for the deliverance and redemption of mankind, who were in the bonds of sin on account of Adam's disobedience, so likewise in our art that which has been wrongfully defiled by one thing is absolved by its opposite; cleansed, and delivered from that stain.
body: The oldest lapis-Christ testimony Jung could discover: chapter IX of the Codicillus ascribed to Raymond Lully (1235–1315) — against A. E. Waite's claim that Khunrath (Amphitheatrum, 1598) first identified stone with Christ.

Jung's frame: the roots of the parallel are pagan-Gnostic, not ecclesiastical — "it is far truer to say that Christianity was assimilated through Gnosticism" (¶453) — and a mid-2nd-century Chinese text shows the same ideas where Christian influence is impossible.

occurrences.title: Der Wasserstein der Weysen: the inner light that cannot be placed in man from without (1619)
occurrences.label: Der Wasserstein der Weysen
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany (German treatise, trans. R. T. Llewellyn)
body: The passage Jung quotes to illustrate the medieval doctrine of the inner man: "Behold, the kingdom of God is within you — from which it is clearly seen that knowledge of the light in man must emerge in the first place from within and cannot be placed there from without" (cw13 ¶141). The boards example: knowledge of white and black "does not come from the boards themselves (for they are mute and inanimate), but originates in and flows forth from your innate faculties." And the flint: "likewise hidden in man, there exists such a heavenly and divine light which... cannot be placed in man from without, but must emerge from within".
Jung's frame: the alchemists' inner light = the divine water as corpus mysticum; the withdrawal of projection as "an extremely difficult affair from the very beginning".

occurrences.title: Adolphus' vision: the crowned psychopomp of the Aurelia occulta (late medieval)
occurrences.label: Adolphus' vision — the crowned psychopomp…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The "Declaratio et Explanatio Adolphi" reports a dream-vision Jung judges genuine ("certain features that are not traditional but are entirely original"): "a shining male figure wearing a crown of stars. His robe is of white linen, dotted with many-coloured flowers, those of green predominating. He assuages the anxious doubts of the adept, saying: 'Adolphus, follow me. I shall show thee what is prepared for thee, so that thou canst pass out of the darkness into the light'" (cw13 ¶106).

"This figure, therefore, is a true Hermes Psychopompos and initiator, who directs the spiritual transitus of the adept"; the book shown with the "parabolic figure" of the Old Adam indicates "the psychopomp is the second Adam, a parallel figure to Christ" (¶106).

occurrences.title: Megissogwon the Pearl-Feather magician, guarded by fiery serpents — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Megissogwon the Pearl-Feather magician, guarded…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The magician, we are told, had killed the father of Nokomis. Now she sends her son forth to avenge her father.
body: The danger in the West: snake and water are "mother attributes"; the black Stygian water "is the place where the sun sinks down for rebirth, the maternal sea of death and night" (¶541). The woodpecker "Mama" reveals the one vulnerable spot under the topknot — "the point where the mythical 'head-birth' takes place" (¶547) — and the wampum belt passes to the hero.

occurrences.title: Meister Eckhart's 'daughter': neither virgin nor spouse
occurrences.label: Meister Eckhart's 'daughter'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~14th c. (anecdote attached to Meister Eckhart, d. 1327)
occurrences.quote: Of all these things I am no single one, and am the one thing and the other running thither.
body: A daughter comes to the convent asking for Meister Eckhart and answers the porter: "I am neither virgin nor spouse, nor man nor wife nor widow nor lady nor lord nor wench nor thrall." To the Master she explains each refusal — virgin, "I were in my first innocence"; spouse, "bearing the eternal word within my soul unceasingly"; widow, "ever yearning for my one and only love" — until: "Of all these things I am no single one, and am the one thing and the other running thither." Eckhart: "I have been listening to the most perfect person I ween I ever met" (¶102).

Jung reads her as "the divine maiden (anima)," paired with Eckhart's vision of the naked boy as "the divine child (the self)": "these primordial images can rise up anywhere at any time quite spontaneously, without the least evidence of any external tradition" (¶103). She is the Aelia Laelia Crispis figure two centuries before Bologna — the paradoxical one beyond every predicate.

occurrences.title: Erythraean Sibyl as feminine psychopomp — Maier's peregrinatio
occurrences.label: Erythraean Sibyl as feminine psychopomp
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabia Felix (Maier's narrative); cave of the Sibyl
body: Near the Red Sea Maier 'heard a rumour' of the Erythraean Sibyl dwelling in a cave — the sibyl who foretold Christ (via Augustine, De civitate dei, and the Sibylline acrostic IHΣOYΣ XPEIΣTOΣ ΘEOY YIOΣ ΣΩTHP ΣTAYPOΣ) (cw14 ¶277-278). Jung: 'by the Red Sea, he met the animal soul... and, at the same time and in the same place, the meeting with the anima, a feminine psychopomp who showed him the way to Mercurius' (¶282). Where Hermas' maiden meant the Church, Maier's means the sibyl: 'the newer is the older' (¶303). The scandal: at the start of the 17th c. he asks the sibyl not for Christ but for Mercurius — 'striking proof of the parallelism between Mercurius and Christ' (¶285).

occurrences.title: Maier — the four elements as four stages of fire (Scrutinium chymicum, Emblem XVII)
occurrences.label: Maier — the four elements as four stages of fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Four spheres filled with fire: 'Imus Vulcanum referat... Mercurium, Lunam tertius orbis habet: Quartus, Apollo' — the lowest is Vulcan's earthly fire, the second Mercurius the vegetative life-spirit, the third the moon, female psychic principle, the fourth the sun, male spiritual principle (¶393). Jung tabulates the Vigenère, Ripley and Maier fire-series against the states of aggregation — solid, liquid, gas, flame — and reads the whole as an adumbrated phlogiston theory: 'fire is peculiar to all the states of aggregation' (¶394-395). The alchemical lapis-quaternity as proto-physics. Cf. mercurius-salamander-maier-1687 (same work).

occurrences.title: Edward Maitland's vision of the dual God
occurrences.label: Edward Maitland's vision of the dual God
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1870s-80s (published in Maitland's biography of Anna Kingsford, I, pp. 130)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Edward Maitland — biographer and collaborator of Anna Kingsford — described his own experience of God, "which, like that of Brother Klaus, consisted in a vision of light": "This was... God as the Lord, proving by His duality that God is Substance as well as Force, Love as well as Will, feminine as well as masculine, Mother as well a Father" (¶134).

Jung's reading: another "impressive account of the syzygy vision" whose dual God cannot be derived from tradition (the footnote compares the male-female light of the Poimandres, adding "I do not know whether Maitland was acquainted with the Poimandres; probably not") — spontaneous projection of the divine pair.

occurrences.title: 1916 patient — world-creation picture: sun, twelve-part halo, four lines (Fig. 2)
occurrences.label: 1916 patient — world-creation picture
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The nodes are "great personalities and founders of religions," as my erstwhile patient told me.
body: In 1916 Jung observed a similar individuation process, illustrated by pictures, in another woman patient: a world creation. Fig. 2: at the top the sun, surrounded by a rainbow-coloured halo divided into twelve parts like the zodiac; to the left, three drops fall from an unknown source, dissolve into four lines (two pairs, painted in the classical four colours), which move, form four paths, and unite periodically in a node — building a system of vibrations. The nodes are "great personalities and founders of religions." The same conception as Miss X's narcosis dream; archetypal, grounded in world-period ideas (Parsees, yugas, Platonic months).

occurrences.title: Jakob Boehme's mandala — XL Questions concerning the Soule (1620)
occurrences.label: Jakob Boehme's mandala
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Gorlitz, Germany (picture from the 1647 English edition)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Boehme's diagram of the divine quaternity in the XL (=Forty) Questions concerning the Soule: Father, H. Ghost, Sonne, and Earth or Earthly Man — with the two semicircles turned back to back instead of closing. Jung uses it twice: as the anticipation of Miss X's divided mandalas (cross, quaternity, lower hell-half, upper "Salniter" realm, ¶535), and in Concerning Mandala Symbolism as "un-united opposites, which presumably should be bound together by the heart standing between them" (¶704). The outermost ring is labelled "will of ye Devill Lucifer," "Abysse (of) Eternity," "Hell of Devills" (¶578). The soul is "an Eye in the Eternal Abyss... a fiery Eye."
Jung: Boehme "was the first to try to organize the Christian cosmos, as a total reality, into a mandala" — and failed, unable to unite the halves (¶601).

occurrences.title: Mandala of opposites in Boehme's XL Questions concerning the Soule
occurrences.label: Mandala of opposites in Boehme's XL Questions…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: London (1647 English printing of Boehme's treatise)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The mandala is divided into a dark and alight half, and the semicircles that are drawn round them, instead of joining up to form a ring, are turned back to back.
body: Jakob Boehme knew a God of the "Wrath-fire", a real Deus absconditus; he bridged the agonizing contradiction through the Christian formula of Father and Son and — "undoubtedly alchemy, long brewing the union of opposites in secret" (¶21). The mandala appended to his XL Questions concerning the Soule (London, 1647; CW9i Fig. 1, anchored at ¶297) shows the nature of the divinity with the opposites still visible.

Jung's reading: the semicircles turned back to back record the un-reconciled opposites in Boehme's God-image — had they formed a ring, the union would be achieved. Otherwise Boehme "would have become a dualist".

occurrences.title: Cor altum, the 'high heart' as quaternary mandala — Liber de spiritu et anima
occurrences.label: Cor altum, the 'high heart' as quaternary…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon ¶301 n18 (pdf p281)

body: The medieval treatise Liber de spiritu et anima (chs. LI-LII) makes self-knowledge the condition of union with God through a threefold ascent: "Let us therefore return to ourselves... At first we ascend to ourselves from these outward and inferior things. Secondly, we ascend to the high heart.... In the third ascent we ascend to God" (cw13 ¶301 n18).

Jung's gloss closes the Paracelsus essay: the "high heart" (cor altum, also "deep heart") "is the mandala divided into four, the imago Dei, or self" — Augustinian interiority as proto-mandala. Augustine himself: "Go not outside, return into yourself; truth dwells in the inner man" (De vera religione LXXII).
Verbatim: The “high heart” (cor altum; also “deep heart”) is the mandala divided into four, the imago Dei, or self. (cw13 ¶301 n18)

occurrences.title: Depressed young woman — black sun-swallowing serpent, eight-rayed black mandala (Fig. 3)
occurrences.label: Depressed young woman
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: There then followed an eight-rayed, completely black mandala with a wreath of eight silver stars. In the centre was a black homunculus.
body: Sketch of a drawing by a young woman with psychogenic depression at the beginning of treatment. Two phases: a black sphere (profound depression) and the lightning striking into it. The earlier pictures: the sphere lay at the bottom of the sea because a black snake had swallowed the sun; then an eight-rayed, completely black mandala with a wreath of eight silver stars, in its centre a black homunculus; the sphere then developed a red centre with blood-rays into tentacle-like extremities, like a crab or octopus; the patient herself was shut up in the sphere. Ordinary speech uses the same imagery: something "strikes home" in a "flash of revelation" (¶558).

occurrences.title: Dream mandala of the embroidery pattern, stone and kundalini-spiral (Fig. 4, ~1930s)
occurrences.label: Dream mandala of the embroidery pattern, stone…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: One must go around and around the sqilare until near the centre, then go in circles.
body: A woman patient in her middle years first saw this mandala in a dream: trying to decipher an embroidery pattern, she learns one "must go around and around the square until near the centre, then go in circles." The painted spiral is in the four colours; the central square represents a stone with four facets; the inner spiral is the snake that, like Kundalini, winds three and a half times round the centre. She knew nothing of the Eastern parallels (¶649). Jung: the snake in angles and circles = circumambulation, the way to the centre; the stone-cube is "the quaternary form of the lapis philosophorum" and signifies the new centre of personality, the self, "also symbolized by a vessel" (¶651).

occurrences.title: Mandala pavement with stag, lion, griffin, unicorn — St. Urban's Monastery
occurrences.label: Mandala pavement with stag, lion, griffin…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "246. Mandala with four ornamental medallions containing a stag, lion, griffin, and unicorn. — Pavement from St. Urban's Monastery, Lucerne" (fig. 246; verified on plate p0427): four roundels of beasts bound by interlacing foliage in a square field — the Mercurius-beasts (stag, lion, unicorn, griffin) arranged in quaternio.

Jung cites it precisely where the ecclesiastical taming of the unicorn "has its parallel in the alchemical taming of the lion and the dragon" (¶522): the monastery floor holds the same fourfold beast-mandala the alchemists paint in their retorts.

occurrences.title: European mandala fig. A9 — the germinal vesicle nourished from the cosmos, solar plexus
occurrences.label: European mandala fig. A9
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Plate A9: "In the centre, the germinal vesicle with a human figure nourished by blood vessels which have their origin in the cosmos. The cosmos rotates around the centre, which attracts its emanations. Around the outside is spread nerve tissue indicating that the process takes place in the solar plexus."

A European patient's spontaneous version of the Hui Ming Ching's germinal vesicle — "the dragon castle at the bottom of the sea," where consciousness and life "are still a unity, inseparably mixed like the sparks in the refining furnace" (cw13 ¶33-34) — with the somatic localization in the solar plexus that echoes "Zeus no longer rules Olympus but rather the solar plexus" (¶54).

occurrences.title: Eleven-year-old girl — mandalas against the devil; sun-eyes in the uroboros (Figs. 34-35)
occurrences.label: Eleven-year-old girl — sun-eyes in the uroboros
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Round the sun is a circle with eyes, and round this an uroboros.
body: An eleven-year-old girl with divorced parents, in a time of great difficulties, drew a series of clearly mandala-structured pictures — magic circles keeping the adversities of the outer world out of the inner psychic space (¶688). As on the Tibetan World Wheel, horns and slanting eye-slits appear at the sides: "Behind the mandala lurks the devil" (¶689). Another drawing (Fig. 35): round the sun a circle with eyes, and round this an uroboros — polyophthalmia. The eyes signify the observing consciousness, yet texts and pictures alike attribute them to a mythic figure, an Anthropos "who does the seeing" (¶690).

occurrences.title: European mandala fig. A1 — 'The Golden Flower represented as the most splendid of all flowers'
occurrences.label: European mandala fig. A1
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Plate A1 of the ten European mandalas following the Golden Flower commentary, captioned "The Golden Flower represented as the most splendid of all flowers." Jung: the pictures "were produced in the way described in the text, by patients during the course of treatment. The earliest picture dates from 1916. All the pictures were done independently of any Eastern influence".

A European patient spontaneously producing the central symbol of the Taoist text — the exact parallelism the mandala plates were chosen to show: "they ought, as a whole, to illustrate clearly the parallelism between Eastern philosophy and the unconscious mental processes in the West".

occurrences.title: Hasjelti Dailjis — Navaho sand-painting ceremony (Stevenson, 8th Rep. BE, 1886–87)
occurrences.label: Hasjelti Dailjis — Navaho sand-painting ceremony
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: Commentary on The Secret of the Golden Flower — ¶ pin tbd (print 22)

body: The Navaho healing ceremony with its mythical sand painting, documented by James Stevenson in the Eighth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology (1886–87, pp. 235–85), which Jung's bibliography lists and whose painted sacred precincts he places alongside the magic circle and mandala material of the Golden Flower commentary (print p22; cf. "magic circle, 22, 24, 90, fig. 17", "temenos, 24f, 244"). A ritual instance of the protected-circle family, outside the Buddhist-Christian mandala traditions.
Verbatim: St ev en so n, J am es. "Ceremonial of Hasjelti Dailjis and Mythical Sand Painting of the Navajo Indians." Eighth Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology, 1886-87. Washington, 1891.

occurrences.title: European mandala fig. A3 — aluminous flower with eight-gated walls (Jung's own)
occurrences.label: European mandala fig. A3
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Plate A3: "A luminous flower in the centre, with stars rotating about it. Around the flower, walls with eight gates. The whole conceived as a transparent window." The editorial note records that Jung himself painted it — Memories, Dreams, Reflections (N.Y. edn., p. 197 and Pl. XI).
The eight-gated circular wall is the temple/city form of the mandala — the same circumvallatio Jung reads into Zosimos' round temple of one stone and into the Chinese 'yellow castle' (cw13 ¶31, ¶38).

occurrences.title: European mandala fig. A10 — mandala as fortified city with golden temple (Jung's own)
occurrences.label: European mandala fig. A10
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Plate A10: "A mandala as a fortified city with wall and moat. Within, a broad moat surrounding a wall fortified with sixteen towers and with another inner moat. This moat encloses a central castle with golden roofs whose centre is a golden temple." The editorial note: Jung tells of painting it in Memories, Dreams, Reflections.

The concentric wall-moat-temple is the sulcus primigenius made visible — "a magical furrow around the centre, the temple or temenos... of the innermost personality" (cw13 ¶36) — and the sixteen-towered city recalls Zosimos' temple and the later domus thesaurorum.

occurrences.title: European mandala fig. A6 — white light, life-seeds, light and dark souls (Jung's own)
occurrences.label: European mandala fig. A6
occurrences.subject: jung
body: Plate A6: "In the centre, the white light, shining in the firmament; in the first circle, protoplasmic life-seeds; in the second, rotating cosmic principles which contain the four primary colours; in the third and fourth, creative forces working inward and outward. At the cardinal points, the masculine and feminine souls, both again divided into light and dark." The editorial note says Jung painted this picture too (cross-ref, 'Concerning Mandala Symbolism').
The central white light is the Tao-symbol of cw13 ¶37; the masculine/feminine souls split light/dark enact the yang-yin doubling Jung reads in the Chinese text (¶37, ¶38).

occurrences.title: The Liverpool dream mandala — magnolia island, ruby rose (Jung, ~1927)
occurrences.label: The Liverpool dream mandala
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: On it there was a single tree) a red-fiowering magnolia) which miraculously stood in everlasting sunshine.
body: Published anonymously as by "a male patient" — but the editors note Jung acknowledged in Memories, Dreams, Reflections (pp. 197f.) having painted this mandala (Fig. 6). With three younger companions in night-time, rainy, soot-black Liverpool, he reaches a square public garden with a pool; on a little island stands a single red-flowering magnolia "in everlasting sunshine," unseen by the others. Painting it, the magnolia became a rose of ruby-coloured glass shining like a four-rayed star, the square a wall with gates, eight streets radiating like the Etoile. "The whole thing seemed like a window opening on to eternity." (Note Jung's own pun on "Liver-pool," the seat of life.)

occurrences.title: Floor mandala drawn in chalk by a woman — Madura temple, southern India
occurrences.label: Floor mandala drawn in chalk by a woman
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Madura, southern India (mandapam / porch of the great temple)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Jung's eyewitness account: in the great temple of Madura he watched a woman draw a mandala-picture on the floor of the mandapam (porch) in coloured chalks, about ten feet across. The accompanying pandit could give no information ("Only the women who drew such pictures knew what they meant"), and the woman herself was non-committal. Elaborate mandalas in red chalk are also found on the whitewashed walls of many huts. Jung opens Concerning Mandala Symbolism with this — the living ritual use of the circle-drawing, of which "the best and most significant mandalas are found in the sphere of Tibetan Buddhism."

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 1 — caught in the rock, the sorcerer's wand (Oct 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 1 — caught in the rock,…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: Zurich (fantasy begun in Denmark, mother's country)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: she saw herself with the lower half of her body in the earth, stuck fast in ab lock of rock.
body: First picture of the Miss X series (American, 55, "fille à papa"). Painting a Danish landscape from memory, she was interrupted by a vision: herself half-embedded in a boulder on a beach, freed by Jung-as-medieval-sorcerer whose touch splits the stone. Jung reads it as being caught in the unconscious/mother (¶527): still partly identical with the mother, "through that part of the body which contains just that secret of the mother."
Her inability to draw let the unconscious insinuate itself: the boulders became eggs cut in two and pointed pyramids (¶526) — the egg-germ that later unfolds through the whole series.

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 10 — moon phases, two crabs, the solstice (Jan 1929)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 10
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A notable innovation is the appearance of two crabs in the lower, chthonic hemisphere
body: Begun in Zurich, finished in the motherland. Soul-flower in a night sky with the four moon-phases; the goat become two horned semi-humans; and, new, two crabs in the lower chthonic hemisphere. Jung devotes pages to the crab: Cancer, house of the moon; resurrection (the crab sheds its shell); Karkinos who bit Heracles; the Panchatantra crab killing the black snake (¶604-606). Miss X was born ~3° Cancer and set her ascendent into the mandala. The picture is a solstice/climax — "a path sharp as the edge of a razor" — at which synchronistic phenomena occur: sixteen years later she died of cancer of the breast (¶607).

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 2 — lightning blasts the rotundum from the massa confusa (Oct 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 2 — lightning blasts…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: One of the round forms has been blasted out of its place by a gol den flash of lightning.
body: The magician is gone; an impersonal golden lightning-flash has blasted one round form out of the dark rock. Jung: the eggs have become abstract circles — she has "rediscovered the historical synonym of the philosophical egg, namely the rotundum, the round, original form of the Anthropos" (¶532). The sphere = the self as wholeness; Jung himself is reduced to "the fraction of a second, the duration of a lightning flash" (¶540). Jung appears as Hermes Kyllenios, "originator of souls," fourfold god (¶538); the lightning anticipates the quaternity-pictures. This picture gave Jung "the definitive incentive" toward alchemy (¶544).

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 3 — sphere, quicksilver band, golden snake, number 12 (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 3 — sphere, quicksilver band…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: its head pointing at the sphere-an obvious development of the golden lightning in Picture 2.
body: A dark blue sphere floats among clouds, girdled by a vibrating silver (quicksilver) band with the number 12; a golden-ring snake aims at it — "a planet in the making." Two "big" dreams amalgamated in it: the narcosis world-globe dream and the golden-snake sacrifice dream. Miss X: the silver is quicksilver, "Mercury, that is Hermes, is the Nous... the animus... like a veil that hides the true personality" (¶546). Jung reads the primordial image as the world egg encoiled by the mercurial serpent, Mercurius duplex split into mercurius vulgi (band) and Mercurius Philosophorum (lightning-snake) (¶554). The hour of the self's birth (¶548).

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 4 — black serpent fecundates the sphere (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 4 — black serpent fecundates…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the snake is black, dark, chthonic, a subterranean and ithyphallic Hermes; but it has the golden wings of Mercury
body: The sphere divides into membrane and ternary-structured nucleus; a black, chthonic, ithyphallic Hermes-serpent with Mercury's golden wings penetrates it — fecundation, fire (emotion) breaking out at the point of entry. Miss X felt it the turning point: the ego "circled round a sun" (¶559). Jung amplifies with Mercurius duplex as winged/wingless dragon (feminine/masculine), Leone Ebreo's Mercury-membrum-virile, and the hierogamy of sun and moon (¶557). The serpent, "contrary to expectation," proves a pneumatic symbol, Mercurius spiritualis — the classical "most spiritual animal," symbol of Nous and Redeemer (¶562).

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 5 — quaternity of eddies, benedicta viriditas (Oct 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 5 — quaternity…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: In this picture we have the quaternity, the archetypal 4
body: The fecundated sphere blossoms; its nucleus has segmented into four left-turning eddies around a green centre — "the 'benedicta viriditas' of the alchemists" (¶567). Jung's cross-cultural quaternity series: four sons of Horus, four seraphim of Ezekiel, four Aeons from the Metra in Barbelo-gnosis, Boehme's lightning-cross, the tetrameria of the opus (¶565). The leftward turn means movement toward the unconscious (¶565). The black snake stays outside the circle: it "represents the shadow... could therefore best be compared with a principle, such as the principle of evil" (¶567) — the colossal shadow of our age.

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 7 — night mandala, black centre, golden cross (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 7 — night mandala, black…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: the blackness of the snake and of the sombre surroundings has been assimilated by the nucleus and... is compensated by a golden light radiating out from the centre.
body: The whole sheet is black; all light concentrated in the sphere. The blackness of the snake has been assimilated into the nucleus, compensated by golden rays forming an equal-armed cross (replacing Picture 6's swastika) — the cross with its connotation of suffering, suspension "over the dark abyss of inner loneliness" (¶575). Jung's Tibetan informant Lingdam Gomchen confirmed the reading: the swastika is what "cannot be broken, divided, or spoilt" — an inner consolidation (¶575 n. 111). The cortices/skins (cf. the thick-barked tree dream) seal the mandala against the disintegrating outer blackness (¶576).

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 8 — inner and outer quaternity, twelve, the golden lamp (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 8 — inner and outer quaternity…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The inner, undifferentiated quaternity is balanced by an outer, differentiated one
body: The interior filled with black; a dark blue quaternity (each quarter divided into three — the number 12 again); the golden centre-light now turning anti-clockwise: the bird comes down to earth. The undifferentiated inner quaternity is balanced by an outer differentiated one equated with the four functions (yellow = intuition, light blue = thinking, flesh pink = feeling, brown = sensation) — cabalistic parallel: Merkabah quaternity vs Achurayim; in Boehme, four Spirits of God vs four elements (¶588). Linked to the eye-healing dream: the mandala is "an eye," symbol of the centre of order in the unconscious (¶592). Accepting the dark principle in practice (¶593).

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 9 — soul-flower, cauda pavonis, four I Ching hexagrams (Nov 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 9 — soul-flower, cauda pavonis…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The connection with the East is deliberately stressed by the patient, through her painting into the mandala four hexagrams from the I Ching.
body: First appearance of the blue "soul-flower"; rainbow light like the cauda pavonis; upper half with three white birds (Pneumata, Trinity), lower half a goat rising with Wotan's two ravens and twining snakes — no white without black (¶595). Into it Miss X deliberately painted four hexagrams of the I Ching: Yü (16, Enthusiasm), Sun (41, Decrease), Sheng (46, Pushing Upward), Ting (50, the Cauldron) — "fire over wood," like the alchemical vessel (¶598). Unlike Boehme's mandala, whose halves turn back to back, this one comprises the opposites — helped, Jung surmises, by the Chinese doctrine of Yang and Yin (¶600-602).

occurrences.title: Mandala of a Modern Man — Jung's own mandala
occurrences.label: Mandala of a Modern Man — Jung's own mandala
occurrences.subject: jung
occurrences.place: Zurich (painted); published in Du, Zurich, April 1955

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Macrocosm, top: boy in the winged egg, Erikapaios or P hanes... bottom, his dark adversary Abraxas, ruler of the physical world
body: Jung's own tempera, painted 1916, reproduced as CW9i frontispiece and in Du (Zurich, April 1955) with his short appendix article "Mandalas". The editorial caption: "The microcosmic enclosed within the macrocosmic system of opposites." Macrocosm, top: boy in the winged egg, Erikapaios or Phanes with triadic fire-symbol; bottom, his dark adversary Abraxas, ruler of the physical world, with double pentadic star. Microcosm: snake with phallus (procreative principle) and dove of Holy Ghost with double beaker of Sophia; inner sun (jagged circle) encloses repetitions on a diminishing scale.

Jung's engagement: he acknowledged painting it (and four other mandalas in the volume) in Memories, Dreams, Reflections p. 195 (editorial noten.1). The 1916 date places it in the Liber Novus aftermath, just before "The Transcendent Function".

occurrences.title: Navaho sand-painting — four horned heads in the four colours (Male Shooting Chant)
occurrences.label: Navaho sand-painting
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Navaho country, SW USA (via Mrs Margaret Schevill)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 46 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: another sand-painting by the Navahos, from the Male Shooting Chant. The four horned heads are painted in the four colours that correspond to the four directions — the same colour-direction-function quaternio Jung unpacks in the Tibetan mandala (¶630). Jung's footnote also records the Navajo Shooting Chant sandpainting of a white snake coiled round a cross-shaped centre in four colours (Newcomb & Reichard) as the American Indian parallel to a patient's mandala (¶652 n. 6).

occurrences.title: Navaho sand-mandala of the Mountain Chant — body of the Rainbow Goddess
occurrences.label: Navaho sand-mandala of the Mountain Chant
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Navaho country, SW USA (via Mrs Margaret Schevill)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 45 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: a mandala the Navaho prepare with great toil from coloured sand for curative purposes, part of the Mountain Chant Rite performed for the sick. Around the centre runs, in a wide arc, the body of the Rainbow Goddess; a square head denotes a female deity, a round one a male. The four pairs of deities on the arms of the cross suggest a swastika wheeling to the right, and the four male deities surrounding it make the same movement. (Variant of the sandpainting in Psychology and Alchemy, fig. 110.)

occurrences.title: Palaeolithic 'sun-wheel' mandala — Rhodesia
occurrences.label: Palaeolithic 'sun-wheel' mandala — Rhodesia
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The oldest mandala drawing known to me is a palaeolithic 'sun-wheel,' recently discovered in Rhodesia. It, too, is based on the quaternary principle" (cw13 ¶45).

Jung's point: things reaching so far back into human history "touch upon the deepest layers of the unconscious, and can have a powerful effect on it even when our conscious language proves itself to be quite impotent" — symbols of the highest insights "must grow again from the forgotten depths" (¶45).

occurrences.title: Woven rug as magic circle — woman doctor in distress (Fig. 13, ~1930s)
occurrences.label: Woven rug as magic circle
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: she wove this magic circle round herself
body: Photograph of a rug woven by a middle-aged woman doctor, "Penelope-like," at a time of great inner and outer distress: "she wove this magic circle round herself, working at it every day for months, as a counterbalance to the difficulties of her life." Jung stresses she was not his patient "and could not have been influenced by me" — an uninfluenced product of the mandala archetype. The rug bears an eight-petalled flower and a real "above and below" (above light, below relative darkness); in the lower darkness, a beetle-like creature — an unconscious content comparable with the sun in the form of Khepera.

occurrences.title: Mandala of the somnambulist girl, 15 1/2 — spring of 'Primary Force' (~1899)
occurrences.label: Mandala of the somnambulist girl, 15 1/2
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A mandala Jung names as mentioned before the Golden Flower commentary: "The afore-mentioned mandala of a somnambulist girl, aged fifteen and a half, whom I had under observation some thirty years ago, shows in its centre a spring of 'Primary Force,' or life energy without extension, whose emanations clash with a contrary spatial principle — in complete analogy with the basic idea of our Chinese text" (cw13 ¶37). Reproduced in Psychiatric Studies, p. 40 (footnote 11); the CW13 index lists her as case 2, "not illus. here."

Her drawing thus predates any Eastern suggestion and matches the germinal vesicle / square-inch-field structure: centre as intensity without extension against a field of extensity (yang/yin, hsing/ming).

occurrences.title: Mandala of the university-trained woman (CW13 fig. A4)
occurrences.label: Mandala of the university-trained woman
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: Commentary on The Secret of the Golden Flower — ¶ pin tbd (print 56, fig. A4)

body: Case 3 of the five clinical summaries the CW13 index numbers: a university-trained woman patient of Jung's drew the mandala reproduced as fig. A4 in the Golden Flower commentary (print p56), where Jung's discussion of European mandalas stands ("European mandalas, 2, 22n, 24, 56"; "Eastern mandalas, 56"). The index distinguishes her from case 2, the 15½-year-old somnambulist girl whose mandala is "not illus. here" (print 23n, 25) — a separate locus.
Verbatim: ¶3 University-trained wo ma n, d re w ma n da la, fig. A4.—56 (the ¶N marks are the index's own case numbers, not CW paragraphs).

occurrences.title: Mani the son of the widow, adopted heir — legendary biography
occurrences.label: Mani the son of the widow, adopted heir
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Mani is the best-known example of the 'son of the widow.
body: The biographical legend: born Cubricus in Babylonia, "As a four-year-old boy he was sold as a slave to a rich widow. She came to love him, and later adopted him and made him her heir. Together with her wealth he inherited the 'serpent's poison' of his doctrine — the four books of Scythianos" (¶31). Later "he changed it to Manes, a Babylonian word meaning 'vessel'"; the Arabic kibrit means sulphur, kin to the alchemical name-family Gabricus/Kybrius/Kibrit.

Jung's argument: the Manichaeans called themselves "children of the widow" (¶14), and Mani is "the best-known example of the 'son of the widow'" — the archetype behind the lapis' name "orphan" and behind alchemy's widow-imagery. His master Scythianos' dualism of pairs ("white and black, yellow and green, moist and dry... soul and body, good and evil") seeds the whole doctrine of opposites.

occurrences.title: Marduk slays Tiamat and splits her like a flat fish — Enuma Elish
occurrences.label: Marduk slays Tiamat and splits her like a flat…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Babylon (text from library of Assurbanipal, Kuyunjik)
body: Ea overthrows Apsu the father; Tiamat, "Mother Hubur, who created everything", breeds giant snakes, dragons, sphinxes, scorpion-men, fish-men, centaurs; Marduk the spring-sun fills her belly with the winds, hews her in pieces and splits her "like a flat fish into two parts", covering the sky with half.

Jung's reading: "Evidently the killing of the mother-dragon here takes the form of a negative wind-fertilization. The world is created from the mother" (¶379); Gunkel's OT parallels: Rahab, Leviathan, the dragon of the waters.
Verbatim: He split her like a flat fish into two parts, One half he set up and with it he covered the sky. (cw05 ¶378).

occurrences.title: Maria Prophetissa: the Interrogationes — the woman from Christ's side
occurrences.label: Maria Prophetissa — the Interrogationes
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Christ, on a mountain, caused a woman to come forth from his side and… he mingled himself with her
body: "Epiphanius testifies to the existence of writings by this Maria, namely the 'Interrogationes magnae' and 'Interrogationes parvae,' said to describe a vision of how Christ, on a mountain, caused a woman to come forth from his side and how he mingled himself with her" (¶209). Jung adds: "It is probably no accident that the treatise of Maria… deals with the theme of the matrimonium alchymicum in a dialogue with the philosopher Aros," source of the saying "Marry gum with gum in true marriage."

The passage roots the alchemical coniunctio and the axiom "One becomes two, two becomes three, and out of the third comes the One as the fourth" in a Gnostic-Christian side-opening vision — the androgynous Anthropos dividing into pair.

occurrences.title: Maria Prophetissa: 'Unum est vas' — the whole secret of the Hermetic vessel
occurrences.label: Maria Prophetissa — 'Unum est vas'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is a kind of matrix or uterus from which the filius philosophorum… is to be born
body: "Maria Prophetissa (fig. 78) says that the whole secret lies in knowing about the Hermetic vessel. 'Unum est vas' (the vessel is one) is emphasized again and again. It must be completely round, in imitation of the spherical cosmos… It is a kind of matrix or uterus from which the filius philosophorum, the miraculous stone, is to be born. Hence it is required that the vessel be not only round but egg-shaped" (¶338).

Jung concludes the vessel is "more a mystical idea, a true symbol like all the central ideas of alchemy": it is the aqua permanens, and equally its opposite, fire (¶338). The one vessel is the womb of the stone — the psychological container.

occurrences.title: The Marriage of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6-10
occurrences.label: The Marriage of the Lamb — Revelation 19:6-10
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: for the m arriage of the Lam b is com e, and his wife hath m ade herself ready.
body: Jung quotes the Apocalyptic marriage of the Lamb in full: "for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready... Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb." Union with the feminine personification of the unconscious "is a well-nigh eschatological experience, a reflection of which is to be found in the Apocalyptic Marriage of the Lamb, the Christian form of the hierosgamos" (¶225).

The angel who refuses John's worship — "I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren" — is read through Paracelsus: "in the language of Paracelsus, he is the homo maior, Adech.... Adech is not my self, he is also that of my brothers" (¶226). The participants' virginity (Rev 14:4) parallels "the year Aniadin," when the One Man reigns for ever (¶227, ¶235).

occurrences.title: Queen Maya's delivery beneath the sala tree — Buddha's birth
occurrences.label: Queen Maya's delivery beneath the sala tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The conscious tree bent down its boughs to make / A bower about Queen Maya's majesty"; the rock gives forth a stream for the bath, and she brings forth her child.

Jung's reading: the embracing-entwining motif — tree as birth-giving mother (¶362, pl. XXXIX); the same motif in Sleeping Beauty, the sun-hero freed from a creeping plant, Ra's barge entwined by the nocturnal serpent.
Verbatim: And, knowing the time come—for all things knew— The conscious tree bent down its boughs to make A bower about Queen Maya’s majesty (cw05 ¶362).

occurrences.title: Maya, weaver, encircled by the Uroboros — Brahminic vignette
occurrences.label: Maya, weaver, encircled by the Uroboros
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the centre is (in other cases) often pictured as a spider in its web
body: Plate 108: "Maya, eternal weaver of the illusory world of the senses, encircled by the Uroboros.—Damaged vignette from a collection of Brahminic sayings."

Jung cites it for the image of the centre "often pictured as a spider in its web, especially when the conscious attitude is still dominated by fear of unconscious processes" (¶325) — Maya weaving the world at the centre of the encircling serpent, the self's creativity seen from the frightened ego's side as illusion and trap.

occurrences.title: Mayan ritual tree with serpent — Dresden Codex
occurrences.label: Mayan ritual tree with serpent — Dresden Codex
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 190. Mayan ritual tree with serpent.—Dresden Codex
body: Page of the Maya Dresden Codex showing the ritual tree with the serpent — the world-tree and snake in an American tradition wholly outside the Western alchemical line.

Jung prints it in the series of tree-pictures (coral tree, Hesperides tree with dragon, tree of the philosophers) that amplify the fructus arboris immortalis of the Visio Arislei: the food of life hanging on a tree guarded by a serpent. Its presence argues the complex is archetypal rather than transmitted.

occurrences.title: Mechthild of Magdeburg — the bearded-less Lord and the birth on the rocky mountain
occurrences.label: Mechthild of Magdeburg
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The soul remarks that when the Lord kissed her 'he had, contrary to expectation, no beard' — the tokens of masculinity lacking (¶320). In a vision Mechthild is transported to a 'rocky mountain' (allegory of the spiritualis habitus) where the Virgin awaits the birth of the divine child; she embraces and kisses it three times; the Son is 'the innermost core [medulla] of the Father's heart' (¶320). Jung: 'that sweetest thing' is the self, indistinguishable from the God-image; the daughter-bride has become a mother who bears the Father as Son — a new millennium speaking, where 'God is born from the soul' (¶321). Counterpart: interrogationes-mary-mountain-vision-2c.

occurrences.title: Melchior Cibinensis: the alchemical paraphrase of the Mass
occurrences.label: Melchior Cibinensis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hungary (Nicholas Melchior of Hermannstadt; addressed to King Ladislaus)
occurrences.quote: Behold a wondrous restoration and renewal of the Ethiopian! Because of the bath of rebirth he takes a new name, which the philosophers call the natural sulphur and their son.
body: Nicholas Melchior of Hermannstadt, court alchemist, expounded the opus as a Mass addressed to Ladislaus, King of Hungary and Bohemia: Introitus ("Fundamentum vero artis est corporum solutio"), a Kyrie to the "blessed stone of the art of the science … for the extirpation of the Turk," the Graduale's south wind, an Ave Praeclara to the Virgin, and the paraphrase of the hymn: the lamp of heaven united with the moon, the band of Mars, the conjunction of Mercury; from the three, in mercurial water, "the strong giant whom a thousand times a thousand seek"; the mighty Ethiopian dead in the vessel, then raised by the bath of rebirth and renamed the philosophers' son — the stone.

Jung: the Consecration is conspicuously missing — "a conflict of conscience," the rite acting from without set against the individual experience acting from within; yet "the alchemical process [is] the equivalent of the transubstantiation in the Mass."

occurrences.title: The anima as Melusina embracing the man from the sea — Ripley Scrowle variant
occurrences.label: The anima as Melusina embracing the man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The anima as Melusina, embracing a man rising out of the sea (= unconscious): a coniunctio animae cum cor pore.
body: Plate B5 of CW13, from a variant of the Ripley Scrowle: "The anima as Melusina, embracing a man rising out of the sea (= unconscious): a coniunctio animae cum corpore. The gnomes are the planetary spirits in the form of paredroi (familiars)."

Jung's reading: Melusina belongs to the Aquaster, the watery realm of the "Nymphidida"; she is "clearly an anima figure" and a variant of the mercurial serpent (¶181). The picture states pictorially what ¶223 formulates: union with the feminine personification of the unconscious as "a well-nigh eschatological experience." Mercurius in the form of Lilith or Melusina also appears in the tree of the Ripley Scrowle (¶247 n.1).

occurrences.title: Melusina's transmutation — final chapter of De vita longa
occurrences.label: Melusina's transmutation
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: And in this m anner, through the intervention of the Scaiolae, Melosine departs from her nymphididic nature, to remain in another transmutation if that difficult Adech permit, who rules over both the death and life of the Scaiolae.
body: The deliberately obscure closing chapter of Paracelsus's treatise on longevity, given by Jung in the original Latin with his English translation, followed by Gerard Dorn's commentary of 1583. Through the "intervening" Scaiolae (the four spiritual powers of the homo maximus), Melusina departs from her "nymphididic nature" into another transmutation — if "that difficult Adech" (the inner man, ruler of the death and life of the Scaiolae) permits. The adept then takes the "characters of Venus" to attain the "year Aniadin" of immortality.

Jung reads the whole chapter as a coded account of the ego's problematic relation to the self (¶214, ¶221) and of the anima's assimilation: the "gesta Melusinae" are a "veritable veil of Maya" from which the "supermonic" elements must be distilled (¶221).

occurrences.title: Melusina, ancestress of the counts of Lusignan
occurrences.label: Melusina, ancestress of the counts of Lusignan
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: When her husband once surprised her in her fish-tail, which she had to wear only on Saturdays, her secret was o ut and she was forced to disappear again into the watery realm.
body: The water-nymph with the fish- or snake-tail, forced to disappear into the watery realm when her husband surprised her secret (the tail she wore only on Saturdays); she reappears only as a presage of disaster. In the Raymond-of-Poitiers episode she appears to a man whose whole life-form has collapsed — the classic situation, Jung says, in which "the harbinger of fate, the anima, an archetype of the collective unconscious, appears" (¶217).

Jung's reading: Melusina is "clearly an anima figure," a variant of the mercurial serpent sometimes shown as a snake-woman; her birthplace "is the womb of the mysteries, obviously what we today would call the unconscious" (¶180). She dwells in the blood, has no genitals (paradisal being), and was seduced by Beelzebub into witchcraft.

occurrences.title: Melusina with the lance of Longinus — Pandora woodcut
occurrences.label: Melusina with the lance of Longinus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Melusina as the aqua permanens, opening the side of the {tlius (an allegory of Christ) with the lance of Longinus.
body: Plate B4 of CW13: Melusina as the aqua permanens opening the side of the filius (an allegory of Christ) with the lance of Longinus; Eve (earth) in the middle is reunited with Adam (Christ) in the coniunctio, and from their union is born the hermaphrodite, "the incarnate Primordial Man." To the right the athanor with the vessel in the centre from which the lapis will arise; the vessels on either side contain Sol and Luna.

Jung's reading (¶181): the snake-woman form expresses "the monstrous, double nature of Mercurius," and "the redemption of this monstrosity was depicted as the assumption and coronation of the Virgin Mary." His posthumous note on Pandora (¶181 n.52) values its eighteen symbolic pictures, one of them the Echidna symbol of Mercurius.

occurrences.title: Melusina in Paracelsus's De vita longa (fig. B5)
occurrences.label: Melusina in Paracelsus's De vita longa (fig. B5)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon — ¶ pin tbd (print 138–183)

body: In Paracelsus's treatise on longevity the water-spirit Melusina appears "in the mind" as an animating figure of the Aquaster region; Jung's commentary (1942) makes her the central exhibit of the Paracelsan anima: "Melusina as anima, fig. B5, 144", "vision appearing in mind, 144, 174", "psychic reality of, 176", "transformation of, 179", "as tree-numen, 315". Illustration CW13 fig. B5.

Verbatim: Melusina, 138, 142/f, 145, fig. B5, 163, 173-80, 182, 183, 199, 240, 303, 315, 317, 321; as anima, fig. B5, 144; Isis has form of, 318; psychic reality of, 176 — Isis has form of Melusina (318); counts of Lusignan (143); the Melusinian Ares (138, 142).

occurrences.title: Spiritus Mercurialis as monstrous dragon-quaternion — German alchemical ms. c. 1600
occurrences.label: Spiritus Mercurialis as monstrous…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany (Mellon Collection, now Yale University Library)
body: The CW13 frontispiece: the spiritus mercurialis and his transformations as a monstrous dragon, "a quaternity, in which the fourth is at the same time the unity of the three, the unity being symbolized by the mystagogue Hermes. The three (above) are (left to right): Luna, Sol, and coniunctio Solis et Lunae in Taurus, the House of Venus. Together they form ~ = Mercurius." The editors note it replaces an almost identical woodcut from Nazari, Della tramutatione metallica sogni tre (Brescia, 1599) which Jung had published in Paracelsica (1942); the ms. replica was found in the Mellon Collection.
Hermes as mystagogue uniting the three: the dragon as the many-in-one body of Mercurius — the same mercurial monster Jung analyzes in "The Spirit Mercurius" (¶191ff).

occurrences.title: 'I am the poison-dripping dragon' — the Aurelia occulta monologue
occurrences.label: I am the poison-dripping dragon
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I am the egg of nature, known only to the wise, who in piety and modesty bring forth from me the microcosm
body: The most complete self-description of Mercurius in the literature, quoted entire by Jung: "I am the poison-dripping dragon, who is everywhere and can be cheaply had... My water and fire destroy and put together; from my body you may extract the green lion and the red... I am the egg of nature... By the philosophers I am named Mercurius; my spouse is the [philosophic] gold; I am the old dragon, found everywhere on the globe of the earth, father and mother, young and old, very strong and very weak, death and resurrection, visible and invisible, hard and soft... I contain the light of nature; I am dark and light... I am the carbuncle of the sun."
Jung uses it as exhibit A for Mercurius's antinomian dual nature (¶266-267), for the egg of nature (¶268), and for the whole six-point summary (¶285).

occurrences.title: Fourfold Hermes of the four quarters — invocation of Astrampsychos (PGM)
occurrences.label: Fourfold Hermes of the four quarters
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the love-magic of Astrampsychos the invocation to Hermes catalogues the god's four forms at the four corners of heaven: ibis (East), dog-headed baboon (West), serpent (North), wolf (South); his plant is the grape (elsewhere the olive), his wood ebony (cw13 ¶359).

Jung uses it to show the fourfold Mercurius: "Th e fourfold Mercurius is also the tree or its spiritus vegetativus" (cw13 ¶360), the four forms derived from the four sons of Horus (see osiris-four-sons-horus-lotus). A sibling locus holds the same prayer's identity-formula "I am thou and thou art I" (hermes-astrampsychos-prayer-egypt-hellenistic, cw9i ¶238n31).

Verbatim: in the East you have the form of an ibis, in the West you have the form of a dog-headed baboon, in the North you have the form of a serpent, but in the South you have the form of a wolf. (cw13 ¶359)

occurrences.title: Mercurius bound to his mother's breast — Septem tractatus aurei (1566)
occurrences.label: Mercurius bound to his mother's breast
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Ego vinctus ulnis et pectori meae matris... et invisibile ex visibili compono.
body: The arcane substance speaks: "Ego vinctus ulnis et pectori meae matris et substantiae eius continere et quiescere meam substantiam facio, et invisibile ex visibili compono" — "Bound to the arms and breast of my mother, and of her substance, I make my substance to contain itself and rest, and I compose the invisible from the visible."

Jung opens the Dual Mother chapter with it: the subject of the sentence (Mercurius, the arcane substance) "can be interpreted as inner fantasy activity," while the original text's anagogic meaning "naturally has a much more comprehensive... meaning... while making use of the primordial image of relationship to the mother" (cf. Psychology and Alchemy, par. 141). The alchemical opus speaking the mother-bond as its engine.

occurrences.title: Nine eagles shooting arrows at Hermes Trismegistus — Senior's vision
occurrences.label: Nine eagles shooting arrows at Hermes…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: 'This image occurs again in Senior's vision of Hermes Trismegistus, at whom nine eagles shot their arrows. Mercurius is the archer who, chemically, dissolves the gold, and, morally, pierces the soul with the dart of passion' (cw14 ¶416). The vision parallels the Book of Krates, where Venus appears surrounded by Indians shooting arrows at him; as Kyllenios, Mercurius is Cupid, who also shoots arrows in the Chymical Wedding (¶416). The god of the stone appears in vision as the target-and-source of the piercing arrow — the dart of passion that both wounds and tinctures.

occurrences.title: 'That I may be reborn a king' — Mercurius transformation poem, Verus Hermes
occurrences.label: That I may be reborn a king
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Th at I m ay be reborn a king.
body: The poem Jung quotes entire ("A rather deplorable but picturesque poem") in which Mercurius describes his own transformation: "A weakling babe, a greybeard old, / Surnamed the Dragon: me they hold / In darkest dungeon languishing / That I may be reborn a king... To a black crow am I akin... In deepest dust I lie alone, / O that the Three would make the One!... Hero of peace, come forth from me, / Whom the whole world would like to see!"

Jung: "Mercurius is describing his own transformation, which at the same time signifies the mystic transformation of the artifex; for not only Mercurius but also what happens to him is a projection of the collective unconscious... the projection of the individuation process" (¶277).

occurrences.title: The Mercurial spirit of the prima materia as a salamander in the fire
occurrences.label: The Mercurial spirit of the prima materia…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 138. The Mercurial spirit of the prima materia, in the shape of a salamander, frolicking in the fire.—Maier, Scrutinium chymicum (1687)
body: Emblem from Michael Maier's Scrutinium chymicum pictura XXI: the spirit of the prima materia as a salamander frolicking in the flames — fire as its element rather than its destroyer.

Jung sets it beside a French alchemist's vision of the Sacerdotes Aegyptiorum revealing "the Hermetic vessel, the salamander, the full moon and the rising sun" (¶391), and beside the hidden elemental fire of the hyle (¶433): the salamander shows the spirit dwelling IN the burning matter of the opus, not consumed by it.

occurrences.title: Six planets united in the seventh, Mercury, as Uroboros — pseudo-Aquinas, De alchimia (Codex Vossianus 29)
occurrences.label: Six planets united in the seventh, Mercury…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Caption: "The six planets united in the seventh, Mercury, depicted as the Uroboros, and the red-and-white (hermaphroditic) double eagle.". The seven planetary gods gathered into Mercurius — the dream's "That is the seventh!" made pictorial.

Jung's commentary at ¶84: "In the alchemical hierarchy of gods Mercurius comes lowest as prima materia and highest as lapis philosophorum… His dual nature enables him to be not only the seventh but also the eighth."

occurrences.title: The Spirit in the Bottle — Grimm, KHM 99 ('Der Geist im Glas')
occurrences.label: The Spirit in the Bottle — Grimm, KHM 99
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fairy tale: a spirit shut in a bottle under an oak (its roots wrapped around the flask) proves to be the dangerous, ambivalent Mercurius — a "spellbound spirit" whom the boy outwits rather than a wish-fulfilling genie. Jung makes it the opening exhibit of "The Spirit Mercurius" (1943/48), retelling it across print pp. 193–201 and returning to it at 239n and 258, where the motif "spellbound spirit, 198" anchors his argument that the alchemist's quicksilver-spirit is the same autonomous complex the tale knows.
Verbatim: bottle, spirit in (tale), 193, 194*2, 195, 197. i99> 2 0 a> 239/^ 258 — and the Grimm entry: "fairy tale of spirit in bottle, 193, 194n, 258."

occurrences.title: Quadriga Aminadab — Suger's window, Abbey of Saint-Denis
occurrences.label: Quadriga Aminadab — Suger's window, Abbey…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A stained-glass medallion by Abbot Suger (Saint-Denis, ~1140-44): God the Father standing on a four-wheeled chariot, crucifix before him, the four evangelist emblems in the corners; inscription 'QUADRIGE AMINADAB' after Song of Songs 6:11 (cw14 ¶267). Jung reads it with Ezekiel's Merkabah and the Christian tetramorph: 'The four gospels form, as it were, a quaternary podium on which the Redeemer stands' (¶267). Alongside the Tractatus Aristotelis chariot and Puri it shows the quadriga as vehicle of divinity — the functions carrying the god-image.

occurrences.title: Serpent of Hermes in the four-wheeled chariot — Tractatus Aristotelis
occurrences.label: Serpent of Hermes in the four-wheeled chariot
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A recipe in the Tractatus Aristotelis ad Alexandrum Magnum: 'Take the serpent, and place it in the chariot with four wheels... until it is immersed in the depths of the sea, and nothing more is visible but the blackest dead sea' (cw14 ¶260); the goal is the Red Sea, 'running without running, moving without motion' (¶260). Jung glosses: the Serpens Hermetis / Agathodaimon, 'the Nous that animates the cold part of nature — that is, the unconscious — is enclosed in the spherical vessel of diaphanous glass which... represents the world and the soul' (¶261). The four wheels are the four elements or functions; incubation (tapas) spins the mandala of the total personality (¶262). 'The "chariot of Aristotle" can be understood in this sense as a symbol of the self' (¶261).

occurrences.title: Zohar — Metatron, the central column of the Sephiroth
occurrences.label: Zohar — Metatron, the central column…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In the Zohar the Messiah is the 'central column' of the Sephiroth system: 'The column of the centre is Metatron, whose name is like that of the Lord. It is created and constituted to be his image and likeness, and it includes all gradations from Above to Below and from Below to Above, and binds them together in the centre' (¶335). Jung cites it as the cabalistic counterpart of the Paracelsian Mumia and the Naassene Protanthropos — the Original Man as mediator-column running through all gradations of the self. Parallels: paracelsus-mumia-de-vita-longa-1562, naassene-hymn-polymorphous-attis-2c.

occurrences.title: Michelspacher: the Mountain of the Adepts (Cabala, 1654)
occurrences.label: Michelspacher: the Mountain of the Adepts
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Augsburg (Stephan Michelspacher, Cabala, spec. ed. cited 1654)
occurrences.quote: the philosophers' stone lies buried in the earth and must be extracted and cleansed
