body: Plate 93: "The Mountain of the Adepts. The temple of the wise ('House of the Gathering' or of 'Self-Collection'), lit by sun and moon, stands on the seven stages, surmounted by the phoenix. The temple is hidden in the mountain—a hint that the philosophers' stone lies buried in the earth and must be extracted and cleansed. The zodiac in the background symbolizes the duration of the opus, while the four elements indicate wholeness. In foreground, blindfolded man and the investigator who follows his natural instinct."
Jung pairs it with dream 54's "House of the Gathering": the square as "'gathering place'"; the temple hidden in the mountain is the centre buried in the natural man, reached only by the gathered.

occurrences.title: Midrash: Adam fashioned from the shapeless mass in hourly stages
occurrences.label: Midrash — Adam fashioned…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: in the first hour God collected the dust, in the second made a shapeless mass out of it, in the third fashioned the limbs
body: "According to a midrashic view, Adam was created in much the same way: in the first hour God collected the dust, in the second made a shapeless mass out of it, in the third fashioned the limbs, and so on" (¶185) — illustrated by fig. 71, Schedel's Buch der Chroniken (1493): the creation of Adam from the clay of the prima materia.

Jung uses it to gloss dream 18's "shapeless life-mass": the human form rises from the massa informis "which has contained the divine seeds of life ever since the Creation." The anthropogony from chaos is the same pattern the alchemists projected into the vessel.

occurrences.title: The 'Mill of the Host' — high altar, Tribsees, Pomerania
occurrences.label: The 'Mill of the Host'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Word, in the form of scrolls, is poured into a mill by the four evangelists, to reappear as the Infant Christ in the chalice.
body: Fifteenth-century altar painting: the four evangelists pour the Word — as scrolls — into a mill; from the mill issues the Infant Christ in the chalice. The caption Jung supplies: John 1:14, "And the word was made flesh."

His use: a churchly transformation-machine standing exactly where the alchemists set their opus — mechanical processing of a sacred substance into the God-man, with the quaternity of the evangelists as millers. It opens Jung's comparison of the Mass's transubstantiation with the alchemical transmutation (¶417).

occurrences.title: The Mithraic sacrifice creating fruitfulness — Heddernheim relief
occurrences.label: The Mithraic sacrifice creating fruitfulness
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Rotating stone slab (pl. XXXIII): tauroctony on one side; on the other Sol with grapes, Mithras with cornucopia, dadophors bearing fruits, Silvanus above. From the dead bull "comes all fruitfulness: fruits from his horns, wine from his blood, corn from his tail, cattle from his semen, garlic from his nostrils".

Jung's reading: the sacrifice "should be conceived as the moment of supreme fruitfulness"; the dog leaping on the bull as compensatory sign of the dog-star at solstice, death equated with the sun's highest point (Creuzer, ¶354).
Verbatim: In the light of the Persian legend, and on the evidence of the monuments themselves, this sacrifice should be conceived as the moment of supreme fruitfulness. (cw05 ¶354).

occurrences.title: Mithras crowning Helios — Klagenfurt relief
occurrences.label: Mithras crowning Helios — Klagenfurt relief
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Marble relief (pl. XXIVa): Mithras crowns the kneeling Helios with a ray-crown, shakes his hand in farewell, and mounts his chariot for the ascension; the Osterburken monument shows the bull's shoulder held over Helios' head with a crown on the ground.

Jung's reading: "the divine prototype of initiation into the degree of Miles" (Cumont, ¶288) — the setting sun invests a successor with solar power, the pattern of Khidr-Dhulqarnein and Peter-Christ; "the Pope is a symbolical 'solis invicti comes'" (¶289).
Verbatim: On the marble relief at Klagenfurt, Mithras is shown crowning Helios with a crown of rays, as he kneels before him or floats up to him from below. (cw05 ¶288).

occurrences.title: Monoïmos — the Monad that wars with itself; the jot of the iota
occurrences.label: Monoïmos — the Monad that wars with itself
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'This Man is a single Monad, uncompounded and indivisible, yet compounded and divisible; loving and at peace with all things, yet warring with all things and at war with itself in all things... as it were a musical harmony containing all things... It is its own mother, its own father' (¶340). Its emblem is 'the jot or tittle' — the many-faced, thousand-eyed jot of the iota; the Son of the Man is 'the one iota flowing from on high' (¶340). Jung: this 2nd-c. Monad 'describes the psychological nature of the self' (¶341); footnote links iota to the Hebrew Yod of the lapis, Adam as the hook of the Yod. 'Seek him from out thyself... thou wilt find Him in thyself, the One and the Many' (¶347).

occurrences.title: Four-coloured beast and the maiden — Shepherd of Hermas
occurrences.label: Four-coloured beast and the maiden
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Shepherd of Hermas (Vision IV) the hero travelling the Via Campana meets 'a monster resembling a dragon of the sea': 'the beast had on its head four colours, black, then the colour of flame and blood, then golden, then white. After I had passed the beast by... lo! a maiden met me, "adorned as if coming forth from the bridal chamber," all in white... but her hair was white' (cw14 ¶301). 'The similarity between the two stories is so complete' with Maier's Ortus-Sibyl sequence that Jung suspects a shared archetypal source rather than literary dependence (¶302). Hermas' mistress decodes the colours: black = this world, fire and blood = its destruction, gold = the tried soul, white = the world to come (¶303).

occurrences.title: Vidarr's fight with the Fenris-Wolf — Gosforth cross relief
occurrences.label: Vidarr's fight with the Fenris-Wolf
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The rescue of the hero is at the same time a sunrise, the triumph of consciousness.
body: Fig. 33 beside the "rescue of the hero … at the same time a sunrise, the triumph of consciousness" (¶539): the Norse monster-slaying carved on an English cross — Christ sphere and Norse myth fused on the same stone, the monster of death overcome at the world's end.

occurrences.title: The moon, author of mortal bodies — Macrobius
occurrences.label: The moon, author of mortal bodies — Macrobius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There is no doubt that the moon is the author and contriver of mortal bodies.
body: Macrobius on the lunar border: "The realm of the perishable begins with the moon and goes downwards. Souls coming into this region begin to be subject to the numbering of days and to time.... There is no doubt that the moon is the author and contriver of mortal bodies" (¶173).

Jung uses it to fix the ancient psychology of the moon's position: "Because of her moist nature, the moon is also the cause of decay. The loveliness of the new moon, hymned by the poets and Church Fathers, veils her dark side, which however could not remain hidden from the fact-finding eye of the empiricist.... She partakes not only of the earth's sufferings but of its daemonic darkness as well" (¶173).

occurrences.title: The moon as eye of the basilisk of heaven — Paracelsus, De pestilitate
occurrences.label: The moon as eye of the basilisk of heaven
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the moon in the sky is the eye of the basilisk of heaven
body: Paracelsus' lunar pathology: "the moon in heaven is the corpus to bring this about" for the timid man's imagination, which makes his eyes basilisk-like and poisons "the speculum venenosum magnum naturae [great poisonous mirror of nature]"; conversely "the sidereal spirit and body draw poison out of the mirror of the moon into which you have looked." The clinching clause: "Quia ex menstruo et venenoso sanguine mulieris causatur et nascitur basiliscus, ita luna in coelo est oculus basilisci coeli [Because as the basilisk is caused and born from the menstrual and poisonous blood of a woman, thus the moon in the sky is the eye of the basilisk of heaven]" (¶215). "Menstruating women do poison the moon and the stars much more readily and also more intensely than any man."
Jung: the passage "catches very aptly the atmosphere which hangs round the pale moonlight" — imagination and mirror poisoning each other, magnetic reciprocity of sidereal body and sky.

occurrences.title: 'The disc of the moon is filled with souls' — Epiphanius, Firmicus, Lydus
occurrences.label: The disc of the moon is filled with souls
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the disc of the moon is filled with souls
body: A standing late-antique doctrine of the lunar gate: Firmicus — "The soul is believed to descend through the disc of the sun, but its ascent is prepared through the disc of the moon"; Lydus reports the hierophant Praetextus saying Janus "sends the diviner souls to the lunar throng"; Epiphanius — "the disc of the moon is filled with souls." Jung adds "It is the same in exotic myths" (Frobenius) and, in ch. V, reads the Egyptian "left eye" as the moon, "the gathering-place of souls" (fig. 31).
The moon as the collecting vessel of the dead between death and rebirth — the counter-gate to the sun's.

occurrences.title: The fool changed as the moon is Adam — Augustine's moon exegesis
occurrences.label: The fool changed as the moon is Adam
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The moon and death significantly reveal their affinity.
body: Augustine on the unfavourable aspect of the moon: "The wise man remaineth stable as the sun, but a fool is changed as the moon" — "Who then is that fool who changeth as the moon, but Adam, in whom all have sinned?" (¶20). He attaches the Church as Luna (Ep. LV, 10), the arrows "to shoot in the darkness of the moon at the upright of heart," and Psalm 71's "until the moon shall be destroyed," glossed: "the abundance of peace shall grow until it consumes all changefulness of mortality... the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed" (¶20).

Jung reads a disguised fear here: "the destruction of the moon is manifestly equivalent to the destruction of death... To eliminate the moon from Creation is therefore as desirable as the elimination of death" — Augustine's "cautious and perhaps not altogether unconscious disguising of the sinister aspect of the moon" (¶20, p34). Alchemy, "all the more ruthlessly," insists on the dangerousness of the new moon (¶21).

occurrences.title: 'Luna is diminished that she may fill the elements' — Ambrose's kenosis
occurrences.label: Luna is diminished that she may fill…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thus has Luna proclaimed the mystery of Christ.
body: Ambrose's lunar kenosis, the heart of Hugo Rahner's "Mysterium Lunae": "Luna is diminished that she may fill the elements. Therefore is this a great mystery.... He emptied her that he might fill her, as he also emptied himself that he might fill all things. He emptied himself that he might come down to us. He came down to us that he might rise again for all.... Thus has Luna proclaimed the mystery of Christ" (¶28).

Jung reads the changefulness of the moon as causally dependent on the transformation of the bridegroom (Philippians 2:6), the patristic root of the Sol-Luna allegory's darkening: the sponsa is "black but comely" because she reflects his kenosis. St. Hilary's lapidary paradox follows — "Deus homo, immortalis mortuus, aeternus sepultus" — and Ephraem Syrus' image of creation unburdened of "the prefigurations of his glory" (¶29).

occurrences.title: Luna's sudden intervention with the child — Mutus liber
occurrences.label: Luna's sudden intervention with the child
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Mutus liber (1702) the goddess 'who suddenly intervenes in the opus... appears equally suddenly during the procedure, as a naked female figure crowned with the sign of the moon and bearing a child in her arms' (cw14 ¶436). 'The miracle is there described as an intervention of the gods, who, like god-parents, take the place of the earthly parents and arrange for the spiritual procreation of the foetus spagyricus' (¶436); there follows adoption by Sol and a coniunctio Solis et Lunae including the adoptive child (¶436). The Cantilena's Luna who takes the dissolved king into her own solution repeats the same motif: the matrix itself becomes the divine mother.

occurrences.title: Nokomis falls from the moon and bears Wenonah — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Nokomis falls from the moon and bears Wenonah
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the moon is the gathering-place of departed souls (fig. 31) a guardian of the seed, and hence a source of life with a feminine significance.
body: The moon as "the gathering-place of departed souls … a guardian of the seed, and hence a source of life with a feminine significance" (¶487); the plucking of the grape-vine branch as infringement of the incest-taboo. Nokomis' fall and birth-pangs are "something altogether typical"; the rejuvenated mother is to be thrown up to the sky to bear a daughter-wife for the sun-god, "the 'father of his mother'" (¶496).

occurrences.title: The blood-bearing moon-sponge of the lunar sea — Allegoriae super librum Turbae
occurrences.label: The blood-bearing moon-sponge of the lunar sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a sponge planted, having blood and sentience [sensum], in the manner of a tree that is rooted in the sea
body: The moon-plant in the lunar sea: "In the lunar sea there is a sponge planted, having blood and sentience [sensum], in the manner of a tree that is rooted in the sea and moveth not from its place. If thou wouldst handle the plant, take a sickle to cut it with, but have good care that the blood floweth not out, for it is the poison of the Philosophers" (¶157).

Jung: "it would seem that the moon-plant is a kind of mandrake and has nothing to do with the botanical Lunaria (honesty)," though kin to Galen's arbor philosophica Lunatica/Berissa (thirty flowers for the moon's age) and Khunrath's "red and white coral-tree of our sea." Ruland: the sponge "has understanding." It belongs to the family of the tree of the sea in Arabian alchemy and the arbor philosophica, "which in turn has parallels with the Cabalistic tree of the Sefiroth and with the tree of Christian mysticism and Hindu philosophy" (¶158).

occurrences.title: The moon slays the sun: the Tyriac serpent — Consilium coniugii
occurrences.label: The moon slays the sun — the Tyriac serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the two opposites cancel each other out, their impact resulting—in accordance with the laws of energetics—in the birth of a third and new thing
body: The Consilium coniugii's darkest Sol-Luna text: the lion, the lower sun, "grows corrupt through the flesh... For the moon is the shadow of the sun, and with corruptible bodies she is consumed, and through her corruption is the lion eclipsed." The substance "is named the Tyriac of the Philosophers, and it is also called the poisonous serpent, because, like this, it bites off the head of the male in the lustful heat of conception, and giving birth it dies and is divided through the midst. So also the moisture of the moon, when she receives his light, slays the sun, and at the birth of the child of the Philosophers she dies likewise, and at death the two parents yield up their souls to the son... And the parents are the food of the son" (¶21).

Jung: "In this psychologem all the implications of the Sol-Luna allegory are carried to their logical conclusion" — the parents cancel out, the son is "a united double nature" — and the god-eating ending (teoqualo, Unas) shows it was never conscious of its kinship with transubstantiation (¶22).

occurrences.title: Morienus to Kalid: the introduction to the art — 'none may enter save through affliction of the soul'
occurrences.label: Morienus to Kalid — the introduction to the art
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Jerusalem? (Morienus the hermit) → Latin transl. by Robert of Chester, 1144
occurrences.quote: Exceeding narrow is the gateway to peace, and none may enter save through affliction of the soul
body: "Particularly instructive is the introduction to the art given by Morienus to Kalid: 'This thing for which you have sought so long is not to be acquired or accomplished by force or passion. It is to be won only by patience and humility and by a determined and most perfect love. For God bestows this divine and immaculate science on his faithful servants…'" Asked why he lives in mountains and deserts rather than hermitages, Morienus answers: "no one reaps who does not sow.… Exceeding narrow is the gateway to peace, and none may enter save through affliction of the soul" (¶386).
Jung's capstone to the "mental attitude" chapter: the divine science "draws its master away from the suffering of this world and leads to the knowledge of future good" — the opus as via purgativa.

occurrences.title: Morienus — the stone extracted from man, 'thou art its ore'
occurrences.label: Morienus — the stone extracted…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Morienus (7th-8th c.), writing on the rim of the Hermetic vessel 'All those who have all things with them have no need of outside aid' — not chemistry but a moral matter (¶256). 'This thing is extracted from thee, for thou art its ore; in thee they find it, and... from thee they take it.' The lapis contains the four elements and is likened to the cosmos; the procedure 'cannot be performed with hands' but is a 'human attitude' (dispositio hominum), accomplished through the coniunctio which forms the essence of the work (¶256). Jung: self-knowledge as the oldest layer of the opus. Parallels: rosinus-ad-sarratantam-lapis-animalis.

occurrences.title: Apotropaic mosaic against the evil eye — Moknine, Tunis (Roman)
occurrences.label: Apotropaic mosaic against the evil eye
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Moknine, Tunis (floor mosaic of a house)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 44 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism: a motif from a Roman mosaic on the floor of a house in Moknine, Tunis, which Jung himself photographed — "It represents an apotropaism against the evil eye." Placed among the eye-mandala parallels (eye motif, polyophthalmia, observing consciousness), it shows the apotropaic, magical-protective function that patient mandalas spontaneously reproduce.

occurrences.title: The all-devouring mother in a depressive psychosis (patient: mother, Zürich)
occurrences.label: The all-devouring mother in a depressive…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [20], ref. book p328 ≈ pdf p295 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A depressed mother "became symbol of the all-devouring mother in her depressive psychosis" (case [20], book p328) — the Terrible Mother manifesting as diagnosis. The index cross-files it under psychoses: "mother as symbol of all-devouring mother, 328", and under "Terrible Mother: as death-symbol, 328".
Verbatim (case-index): "Mother who became symbol of the all-devouring mother in her depressive psychosis. — 328"

occurrences.title: The king's daughter buried in a gilded wooden cow — Mykerinos
occurrences.label: The king's daughter buried in a gilded wooden…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Egyptian king Men-kau-Re (Mykerinos) had his daughter buried in a gilded wooden cow, as a guarantee of rebirth.
body: Herodotus (II, 129) records that the Egyptian king Men-kau-Re — Mykerinos — had his daughter buried in a gilded wooden cow, "as a guarantee of rebirth": the cow stood in a gorgeous apartment with offerings made to it, and in an adjoining room stood the images of the king's concubines.

Jung cites it under "Death is a re-entry into the mother": the hollow cow as the womb-tomb of royalty, the gilded beast both mourning monument and rebirth machine. It is the monumental form of the cow-rebirth rites (Ra's retreat on the heavenly cow; the Hindu crawl through the artificial cow).

occurrences.title: Hecate of Samothrace with cross on her head — Gnostic gem
occurrences.label: Hecate of Samothrace with cross on her head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Where the roads cross and enter into one another, thereby symbolizing the union of opposites, there is the “mother,” the object and epitome of all union.
body: Fig. 34: the triple-bodied goddess of dogs and gate of Hades, "more or less identical with Cerberus" — Heracles bringing up Cerberus "was really bringing the vanquished mother of death to the upper world" (¶577). She is kourotrophos and birth-goddess, "the patron goddess of Medea, because the power of the Terrible Mother is irresistible, coming as it does from the unconscious" (¶577); in Orphic cosmogony she occupies the centre of the world as Aphrodite, Gaia, or the world-soul itself.

occurrences.title: Matuta, the Etruscan Pietà — ossuary vessel of the death-mother
occurrences.label: Matuta, the Etruscan Pietà
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Matuta is the mother. Her chair is adorned with sphinxes, a fitting symbol of the mother of death.
body: An Etruscan ossuary that is at once statue and urn (pl. LIV, plate at pdf p301): the goddess of death as hollow mother receiving the dead, "her chair … adorned with sphinxes, a fitting symbol of the mother of death. (Cf. the Oedipus myth.)" (¶536). The Pietà iconography a millennium early.

occurrences.title: Maui creeps into the jaws of Hine-nui-te-po — Maori myth
occurrences.label: Maui creeps into the jaws of Hine-nui-te-po
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: My little friends, when I creep into the jaws of the old woman, you must not laugh...
body: The monster to be overcome is Grandmother Hine-nui-te-po, the great-woman-of-night. Maui instructs the birds who accompany him: "when I creep into the jaws of the old woman, you must not laugh, but once I have been in and have come out of her mouth again, you may welcome me with shouts of laughter." Then Maui creeps into the mouth of the old woman as she sleeps.

The hero's victory consists in a voluntary re-entry into, and exit from, the devouring mother's body — the night-side of rebirth, with laughter as the fatal boundary (in the full myth, the birds' laughter wakes her and Maui dies: the venture's shadow Jung leaves unspoken in this footnote).

occurrences.title: The moon-lady at the landing-stage — recurrent childhood dream
occurrences.label: The moon-lady at the landing-stage
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The moon-lady was always waiting for me down by the water at the landing-stage, to take me to her island.
body: A girl who grew up in peculiarly difficult psychic circumstances had a recurrent dream between her seventh and tenth years: "The moon-lady was always waiting for me down by the water at the landing-stage, to take me to her island." She never remembered what happened there, "but it was so beautiful that she often prayed she might have this dream again" (¶344). Jung: "The moon-goddess also appears in children's dreams." Thirty years later the same figure returned in a dramatic fantasy — proof of the image's persistence across a lifetime (¶345-346).

occurrences.title: The horned moon-lady, the nine suns, and the Earth Mother of clay — fantasy thirty years later
occurrences.label: The horned moon-lady, the nine suns…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: same dreamer as moon-lady childhood dream

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I see a black tentacle like that of an octopus groping towards me from underneath the sun. I step back in fright and plunge into the abyss. But instead of being dashed to pieces I lie in the arms of the Earth Mother. When I try to look into her face, she turns to clay
body: Thirty years after the moon-lady dream, the same woman, climbing a steep dark mountain in fantasy, finds a domed castle; within, a woman with a head-dress of cow's horns whom she recognizes as the moon-lady of her childhood. At her behest she crosses a narrow transparent bridge toward a dazzling sun — "If you can approach me nine times without being burned, all will be well" — but looking down sees "a black tentacle like that of an octopus groping towards me from underneath the sun", steps back and plunges into the abyss. "But instead of being dashed to pieces I lie in the arms of the Earth Mother. When I try to look into her face, she turns to clay, and I find myself lying on the earth." Jung: moon-lady above, Earth Mother below; the dreamer is in the role of the Kore (¶347).

occurrences.title: Racial-mother fantasy of the fifteen-year-old girl (clinical case, ~1899)
occurrences.label: Racial-mother fantasy of the fifteen-year-old…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jung's own clinical precedent for the Miller material, observed "during the latter part of my medical studies": a fifteen-year-old girl whose outward demeanour gave no hint of the contents of her unconscious fantasy. "They were far-reaching fantasies of a positively mythical nature: the girl saw herself, in her split-off fantasy, as the racial mother of uncounted generations of men" (¶75).

Jung's generalization: elements of this fantasy are "probably common to all girls of her age," for "the unconscious is infinitely more common to all men than are the contents of their individual consciousnesses" — indeed "the unconscious is, in fact, the condensation of the average run of historical experience" (¶75). It anchors the volume's argument that individual fantasy draws on the collective creative substratum.

occurrences.title: Case Y i — the sky-woman and the bear (Diana / Dea Artio)
occurrences.label: Case Y i — the sky-woman and the bear
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A woman comes down from the sky to accompany and help me. She is all bright with light hair and shining eyes... at her look the bear lies down quietly and lets us pass.
body: Case Y's first dream: on a lonely wild mountain the dreamer meets a bear-monster she must pass twice; a radiant woman "comes down from the sky to accompany and help me", vanishes, and returns — "at her look the bear lies down quietly and lets us pass". Jung: "a maternally protective goddess related to bears, a kind of Diana or the Gallo-Roman Dea Artio"; the sky-woman the positive, the bear the negative aspect of the supraordinate personality, extending the human being "upwards into the celestial and downwards into the animal regions" (¶340).

occurrences.title: The Sleeper of Hal Saflieni — hypogeum figurine, Malta
occurrences.label: The Sleeper of Hal Saflieni
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: In form she not infrequently resembles the neolithic ideal of the 'Venus' of Brassempouy or that of Willendorf, or again the sleeper of Hal Saflieni.
body: Jung names the corporeal ideal of the modern Earth Mother as she appears in women's unconscious: "In form she not infrequently resembles the neolithic ideal of the 'Venus' of Brassempouy or that of Willendorf, or again the sleeper of Hal Saflieni" (¶311, fn6 → Neumann, The Great Mother, pls. 1a, 1b). The Hal Saflieni "Sleeping Lady" — the obese reclining terracotta from the Maltese underground sanctuary — stands for Jung (with the two Venuses, mentioned only) as the a-temporal, purely somatic figure of the chthonic Great Mother.

occurrences.title: Case Y ii — the shrine of Ursanna: red stone temple, moon-bowl, 'Vis ut sis'
occurrences.label: Case Y ii — the shrine of Ursanna
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It is the shrine of Ursanna, the bear-goddess and Mother of God in one. The temple is of red stone.
body: Case Y's second dream climbs a tower of steps inscribed "Vis ut sis" ("wish to be" / "may you be as...") to a temple on a wooded crest: the shrine of Ursanna, "the bear-goddess and Mother of God in one". Red stone; bloody sacrifices; entry only by transformation into a beast of the forest. The temple has "the form of a cross with equal arms and a circular space in the middle, which is not roofed, so that one can look straight up at the sky and the constellation of the Bear", with the moon-bowl steaming on the altar. Jung: the relation to the self is shown "not only by the oracle 'Vis ut sis' but by the quaternity and the circular central precinct of the temple"; stars symbolize eternity, the soul coming "from the stars" and returning (¶343); the bear-goddess expresses itself also in Cybele-Artemis.

occurrences.title: The mother who became wolf and pig in psychosis — clinical case
occurrences.label: The mother who became wolf and pig in psychosis
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In her psychosis she had herself become the symbol of the all-devouring mother.
body: A mother who "kept her children tied to her with unnatural love and devotion" breaks into the devouring-mother identity at the climacteric: "In her psychosis she had herself become the symbol of the all-devouring mother" (¶504). The clinical root of Jung's animal-as-Terrible-Mother reading of the bear, the roebuck, and the dragon.

occurrences.title: The Mothers and the fiery tripod — Goethe, Faust II
occurrences.label: The Mothers and the fiery tripod
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mephistopheles sends Faust down "To the untrodden, / Untreadable regions" to the Mothers, throned "in no place, still less in any time", around a fiery tripod: "Formation, transformation, / Eternal Mind's eternal recreation."

Jung's reading: the fiery tripod is a mother-symbol from which Paris and Helen arise (the alchemical royal pair, ¶245); the Mothers are "thronged round with images of all creation" (¶373) — the primordial image of the mother as matrix of all forms.
Verbatim: They are the Mothers!... Formation, transformation, Eternal Mind's eternal recreation. (cw05 ¶245 / 373).

occurrences.title: The realm of the Mothers — Faust II, the key and the Mothers
occurrences.label: The realm of the Mothers
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mephistopheles presses the key on Faust: "Here, take this key... The key will smell the right place from all others: Follow it down, it leads you to the Mothers!" (¶180). Jung reads the key as libido's "intuitive faculty, a strange power to 'smell the right place,' almost as if it were a live creature with an independent life of its own (which is why it is so easily personified)" (¶182) — "the dark creative power of the unconscious."

His reading of the realm: "The 'realm of the Mothers' has not a few connections with the womb (fig. 12), with the matrix, which frequently symbolizes the creative aspect of the unconscious" (¶182). There Faust finds the tripod, "the Hermetic vessel in which the 'royal marriage' is consummated," and with the phallic wand works "the greatest wonder of all — the creation of Paris and Helen" (¶182). The devil, as ever, is "part of that power which would / Ever work evil, but engenders good" (¶181).

occurrences.title: Naassene hymn — the polymorphous Attis, 'dark rumour of Rhea'
occurrences.label: Naassene hymn — the polymorphous Attis, dark…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes call the central figure the 'polymorphous Attis', young dying son of the Great Mother, 'the dark rumour of Rhea'; in the hymn his synonyms are Adonis, Osiris, Adam, Korybas, Pan, Bacchus, and 'shepherd of white stars' (¶311). He is the 'undivided point', 'present in the body' (¶310), the Naas as moist substance that 'contains within itself, like the horn of the one-horned bull, the beauty of all things' (¶311). Hippolytus objects that a point cannot have human form — precisely the objection the transcendent self always provokes. Parallels: monoimos-monad-iota-2c, naassene-water-above-firmament-2c.

occurrences.title: Naassene triad — the 'kingless race': Moses, Sephora, Mariam, Jothor
occurrences.label: Naassene triad — the 'kingless race'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes derive all things from a triad: the 'blessed nature of the blessed Man on high, Adamas'; the mortal lower man; and 'the kingless race begotten from above' — 'Mariam the sought-for one, and Jothor the great wise one, and Sephora the seer, and Moses whose generation was not in Egypt' (¶328). Jung reads a marriage quaternio (husband Moses / wife Sephora / sister Mariam / brother Jethro) whose synonyms are mother-queen-anima and father-king-animus; its senarius extension gives the Shadow Quaternio (Ethiopian woman, Miriam the 'white' leper) (¶328-330). Basis of Jung's Moses Quaternio schema (¶359ff.).

occurrences.title: Naassenes — the water above the firmament and the Heracleian stone
occurrences.label: Naassenes — the water above the firmament…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes map the four rivers of Paradise onto the senses — Pison = sight, Gihon = hearing, Tigris = smell, and the Euphrates = the mouth, 'through which prayers go out and food goes in' (¶288, ¶311). This fourth is the 'water above the firmament' of which the Saviour spoke: 'To this water comes every nature to choose its own substances... more certainly than iron to the Heracleian stone' (¶288). Jung: the water is the aqua doctrinae which 'perfects every nature in its individuality and thus makes man whole too', a magnetic power of integration — 'the doctrine is the magnet' (¶289). Eden is 'the brain' (¶311).

occurrences.title: Nodfyr need-fire with Priapus image — Chronicle of Lanercost
occurrences.label: Nodfyr need-fire with Priapus image
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: To stop cattle murrain, monastery folk taught rustics to kindle fire by rubbing wood and to set up an image of Priapus; a Cistercian lay brother dipped a dog's testicles in holy water and sprinkled the herd.

Jung's reading: the rite "plainly reveals the sexual symbolism of the ceremonies" (¶212) — fire-making and sexuality are one symbolic act across cultures (with the Indian pramantha and the Wachandi dance).

Verbatim: certain cattle-breeders, monastery folk by habit or dress but not by disposition, taught the ignorant rustics to make fire by rubbing pieces of wood together, and to set up an image of Priapus (cw05 ¶212).

occurrences.title: Neith, 'Father of Fathers, Mother of Mothers' — Esne invocation
occurrences.label: Neith, 'Father of Fathers, Mother of Mothers'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Invocations to Nit/Neith: "the mother who bore Ra... who, brought forth when there was nothing which brought forth. The Cow, the Ancient, who bore the sun and set the seeds of gods and men."
Jung's reading: Neith as feminine aspect of Nun-Amon, the primordial water "which was in the beginning" — "father of fathers, the mother of mothers" — the androgynous primary substance (¶358).
Verbatim: Nit, the Ancient, the Mother of God, Mistress of Esne, Father of Fathers, Mother of Mothers, who is the Scarab and the Vulture, who was in the beginning. (cw05 ¶358).

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's Noontide Vision at Surlei
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's Noontide Vision at Surlei
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Surlei, Engadine, Switzerland ('6000 feet beyond man and time')

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

jung.year: Nietzsches Lehre von der ewigen Wiederkehr

body: Nietzsche's "classic example" of an immediate (ritual-less) experience of the transcendence of life: standing by the pyramid-shaped rock at Surlei, he suddenly saw. Zarathustra's Noontide Vision: "Hath time flown away? Do I not fall? Have I not fallen — hark! — into the well of eternity?"; even the "golden ring", the "ring of return", appears "as a promise of resurrection and life" (¶211).

Jung's reading: Nietzsche substitutes for the Christian mystery the myth of Dionysus-Zagreus, dismembered and come to life again; the Deity appears in the garb of Nature as antiquity saw it, the moment of eternity is the noonday hour sacred to Pan — "It is just as if Nietzsche had been present at a performance of the mysteries."

occurrences.title: Joseph in the cistern, Christ in the sepulchre, Jonah in the whale — Biblia pauperum
occurrences.label: Joseph in the cistern, Christ…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 170. The night sea journey. Joseph in the cistern, Christ in the sepulchre, Jonah swallowed by the whale.
body: Typological blockbook page setting the three descents side by side: Joseph thrown in the cistern, Christ laid in the sepulchre, Jonah swallowed by the whale — the night sea journey as prefiguration-chain.

Jung's reading: the "ritual katabasis eis antron, the perilous adventure of the night sea journey," images the descent of the conscious mind into the unconscious, "whose end and aim is the restoration of life, resurrection, and the triumph over death" (¶436). The belly-heat is the ignis gehennalis, the hell Christ entered "in order to conquer death as part of his opus" (¶440).

occurrences.title: Hiawatha swallowed by Mishe-Nahma the fish-king — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Hiawatha swallowed by Mishe-Nahma the fish-king
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Often the monster is killed by the hero lighting a fire inside him—that is to say, in the very womb of death he secretly creates life, the rising sun.
body: The eighth-canto battle: swallowed with his canoe, the hero smites the heart of Nahma, crosses the canoe for safety, and the fish dies and drifts ashore, where a bird helps him out. Jung's worldwide formula: "in the very womb of death he secretly creates life, the rising sun"; the rescue "is at the same time a sunrise, the triumph of consciousness" (¶538–539).

occurrences.title: Nganaoa in the whale's belly with his parents — the Rata cycle, Polynesia
occurrences.label: Nganaoa in the whale's belly with his parents
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: oral tradition (published Frobenius, Zeitalter des Sonnengottes, 1904)
occurrences.quote: Then Nganaoa leapt into the maw of the great whale (devouring of the hero) and peered down into his belly... There sat his two parents
body: The watchful Nganaoa defeats a giant clam, an octopus, and finally a great whale whose jaws close around the boat. Leaping into the maw, he finds his two parents — swallowed long before while fishing — sitting alive in the belly. He breaks his spear into fire-sticks, kindles fire inside the monster with his father's help, heats the heart-fat, and the dying whale swims to land, where father, mother, and son step out through the open gullet.

Jung prints the tale whole in the dual-mother chapter: devouring, discovery of the parents within, fire-boring inside the monster, and release — the dragon-whale mythogram complete, with the hero's rebirth achieved as a family delivery.

occurrences.title: 'Accipe hominem, tonde eum' — the torture of the anthropos in the Allegoriae
occurrences.label: Accipe hominem, tonde eum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Accipe hominem, tonde eum, et trahe super lapidem … donec corpus eius moriatur …
body: The rawest formulation of the opus as torture of the human substance: "Take a man, shave him, and drag him over a stone … until his body dies …" — the anthropos himself is the material of the mortification. The same note preserves the Rosarium's admission: "Nonnulli perierunt in opere nostro" (not a few have perished in our work).

Jung adduces it (Part II ch. 4, n. 46) where the Visio Arislei's Thabritius is killed and reborn in Beya's womb: the alchemical suffering of the king's son is not metaphor but a ritual dismemberment of the ego-figure, the psychic danger the dreams of the "perishing" seeker echo. Fear of ghosts here means "the overpowering of consciousness by the autonomous contents of the unconscious" (n. 43).

occurrences.title: 'I am black and swarthy' — Aurora Consurgens, Parable VII
occurrences.label: I am black and swarthy
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Aurora Consurgens, Parable VII: 'Be turned to me with all your heart and do not cast me aside because I am black and swarthy, because the sun hath changed my colour and the waters have covered my face... for I stick fast in the mire of the deep and my substance is not disclosed. Wherefore out of the depths have I cried... if any shall find one like unto me, I will give into his hand the morning star' (cw14 ¶468). Jung: 'the sunken king forms a parallel to Parable VII of Aurora Consurgens' (¶468). Sophia-as-nigredo speaks in the first person — the despised substance crying from the depths, promising the morning star to her finder.

occurrences.title: Disaster from a technical blunder — Wei Po-yang's opus
occurrences.label: Disaster from a technical blunder
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Wei Po-yang (Ts'an t'ung ch'i, ~142 CE), 'quite uninfluenced by Western alchemy', on a technical blunder in the opus: 'Disaster will come to the black mass... The right essence will be exhaled and the evil one inhaled. Days and nights will be passed without sleep, moon after moon. The body will then be tired out, giving rise to an appearance of insanity. The hundred pulses will stir and boil so violently as to drive away peace of mind and body... Ghostly things will make their appearance... all of a sudden he is seized by an untimely death' (cw14 ¶495). The Chinese parallel proves the nigredo's psychic dangers are archetypal, not a medieval Latin fantasy — the same 'appearance of insanity' Dorn's vesania names.

occurrences.title: The nigredo standing on the rotundum, i.e. sol niger — Mylius, Philosophia reformata (1622)
occurrences.label: The nigredo standing on the rotundum, i.e. sol…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mylius's blackened figure standing on the round chaos — Jung's caption: "The nigredo standing on the rotundum, i.e., sol niger.".

Cited at ¶140 where Jung links gnostic and alchemical black suns: "the Monogenes is called the 'dark light,' a reminder of the sol niger, the black sun of alchemy (fig. 34)." The nigredo is "the first stage of the work, which was felt as 'melancholia' in alchemy and corresponds to the encounter with the shadow in psychology" (¶41).

occurrences.title: Noah in the Ark — enamelled altar of Nicholas of Verdun
occurrences.label: Noah in the Ark — enamelled altar…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fig. 21: Noah's ark on the enamelled altar (1186) — the chest floating on the Flood that kills all living things, saving one family and the animals for a new creation.

Jung's reading: the ark is "an analogy of the womb, like the sea into which the sun sinks for rebirth" (¶311); a close parallel to the Frobenian night-sea-journey — the chest/barrel floating on the water as the sun's course.
Verbatim: The ark (fig. 21), chest, casket, barrel, ship, etc. is an analogy of the womb, like the sea into which the sun sinks for rebirth. (cw05 ¶311).

occurrences.title: Nut the heavenly cow giving birth to the sun — tomb of Seti I
occurrences.label: Nut the heavenly cow giving birth to the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Valley of the Kings, Thebes (tomb of Seti I); Dendera-type reliefs
body: Figs. 24-25: Nut with starry body as the heavenly cow dotted with stars, swallowing and bearing the sun daily; from Naunet of the primordial flood-waters (nun).

Jung's reading: "when the sun-god Ra retires on the back of the heavenly cow, it means that he is going back into the mother in order to rise again as Horus. In the morning the goddess is the mother, at noon she is the sister-wife, and at evening once more the mother" (¶360).
Verbatim: From her sprang Nut, the sky-goddess, who is represented with a starry body or as a heavenly cow dotted with stars (figs. 24, 25). (cw05 ¶359).

occurrences.title: The King's bath in the hollow oak — Bernard Trevisan's parable
occurrences.label: The King's bath in the hollow oak
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the oak, as the feminine numen, has taken the place of the Queen
body: Trevisan's parable of the adept who finds "a clear spring set about with the finest stone and 'secured to the trunk of an oak-tree,' the whole surrounded by a wall." Hermes the mystagogue explains that the King had his renewal-bath built by placing in it "an old oak, 'cloven in the midst'... first it was enclosed in hard, bright stone, then in a hollow oak" (¶74).

Jung's reading is delicate: the Queen is missing from the nuptial bath, so "the oak, as the feminine numen, has taken the place of the Queen" (¶75). The tree is at once "stock" (source of the fountain), "trough" (vessel) and "protecting tree" (mother); "From ancient times the tree was man's birthplace... The alchemists called both the vessel and the bath the 'womb.'" In the Ripley Scrowle the tree stands in the bath with a snake-tailed mermaid = anima; the Dodonian oak houses the oracle.

occurrences.title: Priest with fish-mask representing Oannes — Nimrud relief
occurrences.label: Priest with fish-mask representing Oannes
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fig. 18: the fish-cloaked priest as Oannes-Ea, who "daily came out of the sea as a fish to teach the people wisdom".

Jung's reading: Khidr born "as a 'son of the watery deep'... like the Babylonian Oannes-Ea" (¶291); Oannes' name "brought into connection with John's" — the Baptist's water-and-fire baptism (Matthew 3:11) (¶292).
Verbatim: who was represented in fish form and daily came out of the sea as a fish to teach the people wisdom. (cw05 ¶291).

occurrences.title: 'Oculatus abis' — Hermes united with artifex and soror — Mutus liber finale
occurrences.label: Oculatus abis' — Mutus liber finale
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Hermes as Anthropos, united with the artifex and soror through the threefold cord.
body: The final plate of the wordless book: Hermes as Anthropos united with the artifex and his soror mystica by the threefold cord; Hercules below (a favourite symbol "because of his opera"); the ladder in the background, no longer needed. Inscription: "oculatus abis" — provided with eyes, thou goest thy way.

Jung reads the Mutus liber as the opus stripped to pure image: the ladder of ascent discarded once the threefold cord (body, soul, spirit of the transforming substance) holds the union — the filius philosophorum comparable to the mystical body of the Church.

image.title: Alchemical scene showing two putti holding philosopher's stone containing image of Hermes, below which are a man and a woman kneeling before furnace where trans
image.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress

occurrences.title: Oedipus and the Sphinx of Thebes
occurrences.label: Oedipus and the Sphinx of Thebes
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hera sends the Sphinx against Thebes; whoever solves her riddle wins the throne and the widowed queen. Oedipus solves it "merely because he had solved her childishly simple riddle", marries Jocasta, and falls into matriarchal incest.

Jung's reading: "The riddle of the Sphinx was herself—the terrible mother-imago" (¶265); overestimating his intellect "in a typically masculine way", Oedipus walks into the trap; the riddle "can never be solved merely by the wit of man" (¶264).
Verbatim: The riddle was, in fact, the trap which the Sphinx laid for the unwary wanderer. (cw05 ¶265).

occurrences.title: The Ophites: Christ as the serpent
occurrences.label: The Ophites: Christ as the serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt/Syria (Ophite sect; reported by Hippolytus, Rome)
occurrences.quote: Among the Ophites, Christ was the serpent.
body: "Among the Ophites, Christ was the serpent." Jung gives this one line in the dream-18 commentary, ranking serpent-renewal developments: the healing serpent of the mysteries, the Ophite identification of Christ with the serpent, and "Probably the most significant development of serpent symbolism as regards renewal of personality… in Kundalini yoga" (¶184).
The Ophite equation belongs with the corpus's Christ–serpent–lapis cluster: the redeeming principle taking the form of the despised chthonic animal (cf. Mercurius' devil-attributes, ¶173).

occurrences.title: Ophites — eucharistic feast with a live snake
occurrences.label: Ophites — eucharistic feast with a live snake
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'The emphasis falls so much on the "serpent" that the Ophites celebrated their eucharistic feast with a live snake, no less realistic than the Aesculapian snake at Epidaurus' (¶294). Jung's point is the degree of hypostatization: real water in ritual, a real snake on the table, real fish-monuments — the symbols of the incarnate God were not metaphors but numinous presences (¶294). The Gnostic tier of Christ's serpent-form, 'an old-established symbol for the "good" genius loci, the Agathodaimon' (¶291).

occurrences.title: The alchemical Mass of Melchior Cibinensis
occurrences.label: The alchemical Mass of Melchior Cibinensis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: M elchior Cibinensis, at the beginning of the sixteenth century, could still represent it in the form of a M ass
body: The Hungarian alchemist Nicolaus Melchior Szebeny, court astrologer to King Ladislaus II (1471-1516), sent the king a chemical process "in the form of a Mass" (Addam et processum sub forma missae). Jung cites it twice: as proof that the opus alchymicum "was always understood as a kind of rite after the manner of an opus divinum" (¶158), and as the "bold attempt" showing how far the nature-mystery of alchemy was at odds with the Church "despite the superficial analogies" (¶195). The author was condemned to death under Ferdinand I and executed in Prague, May 2, 1531.

The Mass-form presupposes the long-standing equation of the filius / lapis philosophorum with Christ: "If the opus alchymicum claimed equality with the opus divinum of the Mass, the reason... was not grotesque presumption but the fact that a vast, unknown Nature... was imperiously demanding recognition" (¶196).

occurrences.title: Origen — 'thou thyself art even another little world': sun, moon and stars within (In Leviticum, Hom. V,2)
occurrences.label: Origen — sun, moon and stars within
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Origen on the sacrificial animals, quoted by Jung after the ten-year-old girl's animal-quaternity dream: "Seek these sacrifices within thyself... Understand that thou hast within thyself flocks of cattle... flocks of sheep and flocks of goats.... Understand that the birds of the sky are also within thee. Marvel not if we say that these are within thee, but understand that thou thyself art even another little world, and hast within thee the sun and the moon, and also the stars." Jung: the many animals are the affective states; individuation subordinates the many to the One — the imago Dei, which "expresses itself in the mandala" (¶626).
The companion passage (In libros Regnorum I,4): "Each of us is not one, but many" — man "changed as the moon" until the unus et ipse.

occurrences.title: The 'orphan' stone — Albertus Magnus
occurrences.label: The 'orphan' stone — Albertus Magnus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Orphan' as the name of a precious stone is found in Albertus Magnus.
body: "Orphan" as the name of a precious stone in Albertus Magnus: called orphan "because of its uniqueness — 'it was never seen elsewhere'" — said to be set in the Emperor's crown, wine-coloured, and once luminous at night, "but nowadays it does not shine [any more] in the darkness" (¶13). Jung glosses it as the medieval "solitaire" — "a very apt name for the unique lapis Philosophorum" — and traces Dorn's and Petrus Bonus' use of the name to this source; in the Carmina Heliodori the orphan is the [parentless one] "slain at the beginning of the work for purposes of transformation."

The orphan's absent father opens the whole son-of-the-widow complex of ¶¶13-35: Mani sold as a child to a rich widow, the Manichaeans as "children of the widow," Beya marrying her son Gabritius, and the Cabala's Malchuth widowed when Tifereth is not with her.

occurrences.title: Orthelius: verbum scriptum and verbum factum, the spiritus mundi
occurrences.label: Orthelius — verbum scriptum…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The spirit of God filled the whole world.
body: Orthelius' theology of the lapis: "There are said to be two treasures: one is the written word and the other is the word become fact. In the verbum scriptum Christ is still in swaddling clothes in his cradle; but in the verbum dictum et factum the word is incarnate in God's creatures, and there … we may touch it with our hands." The spiritus mundi that brooded on the waters, impregnated them, and "hatched a seed within them, like a hen upon the egg," dwells in the inward parts of the earth, above all in the metals; the task of the art is to separate the Archaeus and produce a quintessence "whose action may be compared with that of Christ upon mankind." Some, he notes, made this world-spirit the third person of the Godhead — forgetting that "Elohim" is plural.

Jung: "Once more the Gnostic vision of Nous entangled in the embrace of Physis flashes forth in the work of this latecomer" — but the philosopher-Hercules has become a laboratory worker seeking a tonic.

occurrences.title: Osiris in the cedar-coffin at Byblos — Dendera relief
occurrences.label: Osiris in the cedar-coffin at Byblos
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The coffer with Osiris floats to Byblos; a cedar shoots up enclosing it; the king fells the tree for a roof-pillar. His absence = winter solstice, lament for the dead god; his heuresis (finding) a feast of joy. Fig. 23: Osiris in the cedar-coffin, Dendera.

Jung's reading: "he enters into the mother's womb, into the coffer, the sea, the tree, the Astarte column; is dismembered, put together again, and reappears in his son Horpichrud" (¶361) — the tree as maternal container.
Verbatim: the coffer containing Osiris was cast ashore at Byblos and came to rest in the branches of a cedar-tree, which shot up and enclosed the coffer in its trunk (cw05 ¶353).

occurrences.title: The ritual enactment of the slaying, dismemberment, and resurrection of Osiris
occurrences.label: The ritual enactment of the slaying…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "The initiate who ritually enacts the slaying, dismemberment, and scattering of Osiris, and afterwards his resurrection in the green wheat, experiences in this way the permanence and continuity of life, which outlasts all changes of form and, phoenix-like, continually rises anew from its own ashes" (¶208).

Jung's reading: ritual-induced transcendence of life — the transformation occurs objectively, in the god, while the initiate is "influenced, impressed, 'consecrated', or granted 'divine grace' on the mere ground of his presence". Later (¶229): the Osiris cult's democratization — first only Pharaoh "had an Osiris", then the nobles of the Empire, finally "the Christian idea that everyone has an immortal soul and shares directly in the Godhead"; the totem-meal logic of the One eaten in many (one Christ-child, one Santa Claus) anticipates it.

occurrences.title: Osiris enters Selene at the new moon of Phamenoth — Plutarch
occurrences.label: Osiris enters Selene at the new moon…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (calendar rite, reported by Plutarch of Chaeronea)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1st–2nd c. CE (De Iside et Osiride); Egyptian festival far older
occurrences.quote: the unconscious is pregnant with consciousness and gives birth to it
body: The synodos rite: "On the first day of the month of Phamenoth, Osiris enters into Selene, and this is evidently equivalent to the synodos in the spring. 'Thus they make the power of Osiris to be fixed in the moon.' Selene, Plutarch says, is male-female and is impregnated by Helios" (¶219).

Jung draws the consequence for his lunar psychology: the moon has "a double light, outside a feminine one but inside a masculine one which is hidden in it as a fire. Luna is really the mother of the sun, which means, psychologically, that the unconscious is pregnant with consciousness and gives birth to it. It is the night, which is older than the day" — capped with Shelley's "Part of the darkness which gave birth to light."

occurrences.title: Osiris with the four sons of Horus on the lotus (Book of the Dead)
occurrences.label: Osiris with the four sons of Horus on the lotus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Father Horus with his four sons, or Osiris with the four sons of Horus
body: Plate 102: "Osiris, with the four sons of Horus on the lotus.—The Book of the Dead." Jung sets it parallel to Christ with the evangelists in the world-clock commentary: the Egyptian quaternity of Amset, Hapi, Duamutef, Qebehsenuf around the enthroned Osiris is the oldest documented form of the deity-with-four arrangement that reappears in the Christian mandorla and, transformed, in the modern patient's world clock.
Horus is also "the ἣλιος ἀνατολῆς (rising sun), and Christ was still worshipped as such by the early Christians" (¶314).

image.title: BD Ani before Osiris
image.credit: Published by James Wasserman; facsimile made by E. A. Wallis Budge; original artist unknown

occurrences.title: Ostanes' stone with a spirit in the Nile — quoted by Zosimos
occurrences.label: Ostanes' stone with a spirit in the Nile
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (via Zosimos, 'Concerning the Art and Its Interpretation')
occurrences.yearDisplay: Ostanes ~4th c. B.C.?; Zosimos ~3rd c. A.D.
occurrences.quote: Go to the waters of the Nile and there you will find a stone that has a spirit. Take this, divide it, thrust in your hand and draw out its heart: for its soul is in its heart.
body: The saying of Ostanes — "known even to Pliny," among the dawn-figures of alchemy — preserved in Zosimos: go to the Nile, find the stone that has a spirit (pneuma), divide it, thrust in the hand, draw out its heart: its soul is in its heart. An interpolator glosses it as the expulsion of quicksilver.

Jung's reading: the pneumatic stone is the carrier of projected psychic content — the divine slumbering in matter which the opus must liberate. Nietzsche's Zarathustra image, "an image slumbers for me in the stone," "says much the same thing, but the other way round" (¶406). The Easter fire-rite's spark struck from the stone is "yet again an imago Christi" — the same extraction (¶451).

occurrences.title: Oxyrhynchus sayings — fishes and fowls pointing to the kingdom
occurrences.label: Oxyrhynchus sayings
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The logion: 'the fowls of the air and the fishes of the sea and whatsoever is upon or beneath the earth' point the way to the kingdom of heaven — the motif of the helpful animals (¶224). Jung reads the 'kingdom of heaven' or conjectural 'city' like the alchemical arcane substance: it refers to the self, and the cooperation of birds and fishes illustrates that 'wholeness is perforce paradoxical in its manifestations' (¶225). Ripley's fishes and birds that 'bring the storie' continue the same messianic role (¶224). Parallels: ripley-lapis-everywhere-birds-fishes-15c, lambspringk-two-reversed-fishes-1678.

occurrences.title: The voice proclaiming the birth of Osiris — Pamyles at Thebes
occurrences.label: The voice proclaiming the birth of Osiris
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pamyles, drawing water, hears a voice from the temple proclaim that Osiris, "the great and beneficent king", is born; the Pamylia festival resembles the Phallophoria.

Jung's reading: "Pamyles seems, therefore, to have been originally a phallic daimon, like Dionysus. In his phallic form he represents the creative power which 'draws' things out of the unconscious (i.e., the water)" (¶349) — the archetype "drawing up from the depths"; the type recurs in the baptism in the Jordan.
Verbatim: This type of experience recurs in the baptism in the Jordan, Matthew 3:17. (cw05 ¶349).

occurrences.title: Pandora (1588) — three alembics in the cooking-pot, Christ bleeding beside them
occurrences.label: Pandora — three alembics…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Aurora consurgens (Part II) calls the vas naturale the matrix: 'the One in which there are three things, namely water, air, and fire. They are three glass alembics, in which the son of the Philosophers is begotten. Therefore they have named it tincture, blood, and egg' (¶380). The Pandora illustration confirms the Trinitarian allusion: beside the three alembics in the great cooking-pot stands Christ 'with blood pouring from the lance wound in his breast — flumina de ventre Christi!' (¶380). The round Hermetic vessel 'is God himself, the (Platonic) world-soul and man's own wholeness... the universe in its smallest and most material form' (¶380).

occurrences.title: The club-battle of Papremis — Herodotus II.63
occurrences.label: The club-battle of Papremis — Herodotus II.63
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: At sunset, votaries armed with clubs storm the temple gate against the priests defending the god's shrine; "heads are broken and not a few actually die of the wounds". The local aition: Ares came as a man to visit his mother in the temple, was refused, and forced his way in by violence.
Jung's reading: "It is clear that the votaries fight and even kill each other for their share in the mystery of divine incest" (¶392) — participation in the god's action.
Verbatim: the votaries fight and even kill each other for their share in the mystery of divine incest. (cw05 ¶392).

occurrences.title: Hermes identity and womb prayers — London magical papyrus CXXII
occurrences.label: Hermes identity and womb prayers
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: for I am your image
body: A Greek prayer to Hermes from the British Museum papyri, cited twice in CW5 for two different doors it opens. (1) The identity formula — "For you are I and I am you; your name is mine and my name is yours; for I am your image" — Jung's evidence that in the mystery religions "there is no doubt about the identity of the divine hero with the celebrant" (ch. IV n. 20). (2) "Come to me, O Hermes, as children come into the womb of women" (ch. VII n. 76) — the god as the one who enters the womb, the reverse of the hero born from it.

occurrences.title: Papyri Graecae Magicae V: Hermes 'round and square' (line 401)
occurrences.label: Papyri Graecae Magicae V
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: this is round and square, i.e., a totality consisting of four parts
body: "Hermes is associated with the idea of roundness and also of squareness, as can be seen particularly in Papyrus V (line 401) of the Papyri Graecae Magicae, where he is named [Greek lost to OCR], 'round and square.' He is also called [—], 'quadrangular.' He is in general connected with the number four; hence there is a [—], a 'four-headed Hermes'" (¶172; the Greek terms are eaten by OCR in the chunk).

This squareness of Hermes, glossed by Cartari's reading of the square herms ("the Sun is the head of the world… the four quarters of the world or the four seasons"), makes Mercurius "an eminently suitable symbol for the mysterious transforming substance of alchemy; for this is round and square, i.e., a totality consisting of four parts" (¶173).

occurrences.title: The unica materia increata — Paracelsus, Philosophia ad Athenienses
occurrences.label: The unica materia increata
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This uncreated mystery was prepared (praeparatum) by God in such a way that nothing will ever be like it in the future nor will it ever return to what it was.
body: Paracelsus teaches that the unique materia of the work is increatum — uncreated: a great secret with nothing in common with the elements, filling the whole regio aetherea, mother of the elements and of all created things; corrupted beyond reparation (the Fall); prepared by God once and never again.

Jung: such autonomy and everlastingness suggest "a principle equal to the Deity, corresponding to a dea mater"; Dorn, Paracelsus' pupil, renders it the "Adamica," the limbus microcosmicus. The increatum is the psychologicalAbsolute of the prima materia series — the unknown that precedes all opposites.

occurrences.title: Paracelsus — life as an embalmed mummy: the Mumia (De vita longa)
occurrences.label: Paracelsus — life as an embalmed mummy
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Life, verily, is naught but a kind of embalmed mummy, which preserves the mortal body from the mortal worms' (¶334). The body lives from the Mumia, through which the peregrinus microcosmus — the wandering microcosm corresponding to the macrocosm — rules the body; his synonyms are Adech, Archeus, Protothoma, Ides, 'the door whence all created things have come' (¶334). Jung: the Mumia corresponds 'in every way to the Original Man, who forms the microcosm in the mortal man and, as such, shares all the powers of the macrocosm' (¶335) — the Hippolytan Papa/Attis 'buried in the body like a mummy in a tomb'.

occurrences.title: Asenath and the honeycomb of paradise — Joseph and Asenath
occurrences.label: Asenath and the honeycomb of paradise
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hellenistic Egypt (Joseph in Egypt); midrash preserved in Christian revision
occurrences.quote: a male messenger from heaven (in the recension: Michael)—whom she received as a δαίμων πάρεδρος, spiritus familiaris, in truly pagan fashion—gave her a honeycomb of paradise to eat and thus endowed her with immortality.
body: Asenath, daughter of the priest of On (Heliopolis), loves Joseph and is rejected as an unbeliever; after penance a male messenger from heaven (Michael in the recension) — whom she receives "as a δαίμων πάρεδρος, spiritus familiaris, in truly pagan fashion" — feeds her a honeycomb of paradise, endowing her with immortality, and announces that Joseph will come to court her.

Jung cites the episode (Part II ch. 5, n. 36) in the scholarly apparatus to the Zosimos "men of light" material: the hieros-gamos prepared by heavenly food and the paredros-spirit belong to the same syncretistic complex as the alchemical assessor (πάρεδρος) of Mercurius (cw12 Part I, index s.v. "paredros"). Jung speculates the messenger "was originally Hermes."

occurrences.title: Patrizi proposes Hermetic philosophy to Pope Gregory XIV
occurrences.label: Patrizi proposes Hermetic philosophy…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: it was a m om ent of the utmost significance when the hu m anist Patrizi proposed to Pope Gregory XIV that Herm etic philosophy should take the place of Aristotle in ecclesiastical doctrine.
body: The humanist Francesco Patrizi proposed to Pope Gregory XIV that Hermetic philosophy replace Aristotle in ecclesiastical doctrine. Jung calls it "a moment of the utmost significance... At that moment two worlds came into contact, which—after heaven knows what happenings!—must yet be united in the future. At that time it was obviously impossible. A psychological differentiation of religious as well as scientific views is still needed before a union can begin to be brought about."
The event closes the Mercurius-Hermes section: "Hermes is a god of thieves and cheats, but also a god of revelation who gave his name to a whole philosophy" (¶280).

occurrences.title: St. Paul's Christophany on the road to Damascus
occurrences.label: St. Paul's Christophany on the road to Damascus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "Another example is St. Paul, who, on his way to Damascus, was suddenly confronted by Christ" (¶217) — given by Jung as a classic case of the enlargement of personality, alongside Nietzsche's encounter with Zarathustra "which made of the critic and aphorist a tragic poet and prophet".

Jung's reading: "True though it may be that this Christ of St. Paul's would hardly have been possible without the historical Jesus, the apparition of Christ came to St. Paul not from the historical Jesus but from the depths of his own unconscious." In the same paragraph-milieu (¶218): the greater figure appears to the lesser personality "with the force of a revelation" — "the long expected friend of his soul, the immortal one... a moment of deadliest peril"; "Christ himself is the perfect symbol of the hidden immortal within the mortal man."

occurrences.title: Seed like a peacock's egg — Basilides' threefold sonship
occurrences.label: Seed like a peacock's egg
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Basilides (via Hippolytus): the 'God who is not' cast down a seed which, 'like a grain of mustardseed, contained the whole plant, or, "like a peacock's egg, had in itself a varied multitude of colors"'; in it a 'threefold sonship, consubstantial with the God who is not' (cw14 ¶397). Jung lines this up with alchemy: 'In alchemy, the end of the work announced by the cauda pavonis was the birth of the filius regius. The display of colours in the Basilidian doctrine therefore occurred at the right place. Again one must ask: tradition — or spontaneous generation?' (¶397). The egg-totality of all colours pre-contains the son.

occurrences.title: Osiris' chariot drawn by peacocks — bronze tablets at Meroë
occurrences.label: Osiris' chariot drawn by peacocks
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Meroë (Sudan); reported in late alchemical text
occurrences.yearDisplay: late antique (Meroë); reported in late alchemical text
body: 'According to a late alchemical text, the bronze tablets in the labyrinth at Meroë showed Osiris, after his regeneration by Isis, mounting a chariot drawn by peacocks, in which he drives along triumphing in his resurrection, like the sun' (cw14 ¶395). Jung cites it beside Penotus' Table of Symbols, where the peacock correlates with the mysterium coniugii and Venus, and the coniugium with the dii mortui 'presumably because they need resurrecting' (¶395). The peacock is 'an ancient Christian symbol of resurrection, like the phoenix' — here in an Egyptian, pre-Christian key: the resurrected god rides the bird of 'all colours'.

occurrences.title: Peacock as Phoenix rising from the fire — Codex Alchemicus Rhenoviensis (15th c.)
occurrences.label: Peacock as Phoenix rising from the fire
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Fig. 32 of Concerning Mandala Symbolism, reproduced from the Codex Alchemicus Rhenoviensis (Central Library, Zurich): the peacock as the Phoenix rising newborn from the fire. A similar picture exists in a British Museum manuscript, only there the peacock is enclosed in a flask, the vas hermeticum, like the homunculus (cf. John Read, Prelude to Chemistry, frontispiece). In the vessel beside the peacock the colours of the cauda pavonis appear — sign that the transformation process is nearing its goal. The peacock is an old emblem of rebirth and resurrection, quite frequently found on Christian sarcophagi; in the alchemical process "the serpens mercurialis, the dragon, is changed into the eagle, the peacock, the goose of Hermes, or the Phoenix."

occurrences.title: Peacock standing on the two heads of the Rebis — Khunrath
occurrences.label: Peacock standing on the two heads of the Rebis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Khunrath's Amphitheatrum (1595) a peacock stands on the two heads of the Rebis: 'Since the peacock stands for "all colours" (i.e., the integration of all qualities)... it stands on the two heads of the Rebis, whose unity it obviously represents. The inscription calls it the "bird of Hermes" and the "blessed greenness," both of which symbolize the Holy Ghost or the Ruach Elohim' (cw14 ¶391). The cauda pavonis is here 'the soul of the world, nature, the quintessence'; the peacock occupies the highest place, 'in whom the male-female polarity of the hermaphrodite and the Rebis is integrated' (¶391-392). Jung elsewhere: at the hour of conjunction appear 'all the colours in the world... even Iris, the messenger of God, and the peacock's tail' (¶392).

occurrences.title: The pearl of light in the fish's belly — Pirkê de Rabbi Elieser
occurrences.label: The pearl of light in the fish's belly
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the darkness of the unconscious a treasure lies hidden, the same “treasure hard to attain” which in our text, and in many other places too, is described as the shining pearl
body: Jonah "entered its mouth just as a man enters the great synagogue"; the fish's eyes were windows of glass. Paracelsus says he saw "mighty mysteries" there (¶509) — the treasure hard to attain, the fascinosum, shining in the darkness of the unconscious (¶510).

occurrences.title: Pelican vessel uniting superius/inferius, exterius/interius — scholia to the Tractatus aureus
occurrences.label: Pelican vessel uniting superius/inferius…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: early 17th c. (Jung: 'cannot be dated earlier than the beginning of the seventeenth century')
occurrences.quote: For this vessel is the true philosophical Pelican, nor is any other to be sought after in all the world.
body: The scholia's diagram B C D E F G with the central point A: superius/inferius, exterius/interius "united into one thing by means of the circular distillation, named the Pelican." The point A, "as it were the origin and source from which the other letters flow," is the circulus exiguus and "a mediator making peace between the enemies or elements, that they may love one another in a meet embrace" (¶¶8-9).

Jung identifies this little circle with the Mercurial Fountain of the Rosarium (cw12/cw18 cross-ref) and with the vessel of transformation: "the circle and the Hermetic vessel are one and the same, with the result that the mandala, which we find so often in the drawings of our patients, corresponds to the vessel of transformation" (¶12). The Pelican's Christ-allegory (blood that revives, ¶11, p26-27) pulls the text toward Mercurius as Holy Ghost and toward the author's confessed Ecclesia spiritualis scattered "in Turkey, in Persia... and even in farthest India" (¶9-10, p25-26).

occurrences.title: The Pelican vessel of the circulatory distillation — Rhenanus
occurrences.label: The Pelican vessel of the circulatory…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Picture of the Pelican, the vessel in which the circulatory distillation takes place.
body: Plate B7 of CW13: "Picture of the Pelican, the vessel in which the circulatory distillation takes place," from Rhenanus's Solis e puteo emergentis (1613). The Pelican is the vas hermeticum shaped for the distillatio circulatrix: the distillate runs back into the belly of the retort, endlessly recycling — "By means of the 'thousandfold distillation' they hoped to achieve a particularly 'refined' result" (¶185).

Jung conjectures Paracelsus's retorta distillatio took place in such a vessel: a distillation "turned back upon itself," whose psychological analogue is the work upon the Iliaster starting "from the midst of the centre" (ex medio centri) — "This process was a psychic as well as a physical experience" (¶185). The Pelican also appears in the Rosarium hermaphrodite plate (B2).

occurrences.title: Cloven tongues of fire at Pentecost — Acts 2
occurrences.label: Cloven tongues of fire at Pentecost — Acts 2
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Fire appears as parted tongues on the apostles, who are filled with the Holy Ghost and speak with other tongues: "The γλῶσσα of the fire caused the glossolalia of the apostles."

Jung's reading: the mouth-fire-speech fusion of ch. III (¶229-233) at its Christian apotheosis — fire "devouring/consuming" recalls the mouth (Deut 4:24, Ezek 15:4), and speech-fire chains run from II Samuel 22:9 through Isaiah to Revelation 11:5.
Verbatim: And there appeared unto them cloven tongues [γλῶσσαι] like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. (cw05 ¶232).

image.title: The Pentecost label QS:Les," Pentecostés " label QS:Len," The Pentecost "

occurrences.title: Peratae — the Serpent who carries the signs of the Father down and back
occurrences.label: Peratae — the Serpent who carries the signs…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'This is the serpent. For it is he who brought the signs of the Father down from above, and it is he who carries them back again after they have been awakened from sleep' — the 'I am the Door'; naphtha draws fire 'more than the Heracleian stone draws iron'. 'Thus the perfect race of men, made in the image of the Father and of the same substance [homoousion], is drawn from the world by the Serpent' (¶290). Jung: here the magnet is the Son himself, Christ as the brazen serpent of John 3:14; the serpent 'is an equivalent of the fish' and its comparison with Christ is 'more authentic' (¶291).

occurrences.title: Trimalchio's dog for life after death — Petronius, Satyricon 71
occurrences.label: Trimalchio's dog for life after death
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Trimalchio begs the sculptor: "paint a small dog round the foot of my statue... so that by your kindness I may attain to life after death."

Jung's reading: the dog as companion of healing and rebirth — Hecate dog-headed (Canicula), dog sacrifices to Eileithyia, Aesculapius' dog, Cerberus pacified with honey-cakes; the necrophagous helper who "assists in the reconstitution" (¶354-355).
Verbatim: I earnestly beseech you to paint a small dog round the foot of my statue … so that by your kindness I may attain to life after death. (cw05 ¶355).

occurrences.title: Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, Pretiosa margarita novella (1330–39)
occurrences.label: Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, Pretiosa margarita…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Now, since no creature except man can unite with God, on account of their dissimilarity, God must needs become one with man. And this came to pass in Christ Jesus and his virgin mother.
body: The oldest source treating specifically of the stone's connection with Christ. At the end of sublimation germinates "a shining white soul (anima candida) which flies up to heaven with the spirit … This is clearly and manifestly the stone." The secret stone is grasped only by the intellect through inspiration, divine revelation, or an initiate's teaching. Hermes: "It is needful that at the end of the world heaven and earth be united: which is the philosophic Word."
