The old philosophers discerned the Last Judgment and the resurrection of the dead in the art; Alphidius says the stone's mother was a virgin; Balgus: "the father has become the son"; Plato "wrote a gospel which was completed long after by John the Evangelist"; God will become man on the Last Day of this art (in novissima die huius artis).
Jung: this text, "at least a century older than Khunrath," proves the mystery of Christ and the mystery of the lapis were felt as parallel — perhaps continuous — by 1330.

occurrences.title: Phalli and serpent-pastries thrown into the pit — Arrhetophoria
occurrences.label: Phalli and serpent-pastries thrown into the pit
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: pastries shaped like phalli and serpents were thrown into a pit near the Thesmophorion, to invoke the blessing of children and good harvests.
body: Earth-fertilization by the phallus-and-serpent pair thrown back into the mother-pit — the negative of the Gaia-temenos grain offering (¶570–571) and the edible counterpart of Tages' furrow-birth (¶527).

occurrences.title: Priapus with the snake biting his phallus — Verona museum
occurrences.label: Priapus with the snake biting his phallus
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's pl. LXIb: "a statue of Priapus in the archaeological museum at Verona: Priapus, with a sidelong smile, points with his finger to a snake biting his phallus" (¶680). The god of the erect member calmly presenting the serpent that devours it — phallic libido and its castrating chthonic other in a single ironic figure.

Jung introduces it precisely to image the ambivalence of libido discovered in ch. VIII: the conflict of horse and snake or bull and snake "represents a conflict within the libido itself, a striving forwards and backwards at one and the same time"; like the sun, "the libido also wills its own descent, its own involution" (¶680). The Priapus is the comic-monumental form of that doctrine. The same serpent-castration recurs in Jung's next plate, Rubens' Last Judgment (¶681).
Verbatim: "Priapus, with a sidelong smile, points with his finger to a snake biting his phallus" (¶680).

occurrences.title: Anton Unternährer: the devil's communion and the sacred stones — early 19th c. Switzerland
occurrences.label: Anton Unternährer — early 19th c. Switzerland
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: History has numerous examples of how easily the mystery can turn into a sexual orgy just because it grew out of the opposite of the orgy.
body: The blasphemer of the Bernese Oberland: "The communion of the devil is in the brothels … there they have sucked the head of the snake" (¶581); a self-styled priapic divinity preaching nakedness before God, the lap of the daughters of Jerusalem as "the gate of the Lord," and God creating children from stones — "for the seed comes from the stones" (¶583). Jung's exhibit for the enantiodromia by which "the mystery can turn into a sexual orgy just because it grew out of the opposite of the orgy" (¶584).

occurrences.title: Pharaoh's second, divine conception on the temple birth-chamber walls
occurrences.label: Pharaoh's second, divine conception…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (temple birth chambers / mammisi, e.g. Luxor, Deir el-Bahari)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "What was a myth in Greece was actually a ritual in Egypt: Pharaoh was both human and divine by nature. In the birth chambers of the Egyptian temples Pharaoh's second, divine conception and birth is depicted on the walls; he is 'twice-born'" (¶94). The Greek parallel given is Heracles, who "received immortality through being unwittingly adopted by Hera".

Jung's reading: the dual-birth motif underlies all rebirth mysteries, Christianity included — Christ "twice-born" through Jordan baptism; in the Roman liturgy the font is the "uterus ecclesiae" (benediction of the font, Holy Saturday); the early Christian-Gnostic dove = Sophia-Sapientia, Mother of Christ; godparents preserve the motif today.

occurrences.title: The King who 'possesses his mothers' — Pyramid Texts
occurrences.label: The King who 'possesses his mothers'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The dead Pharaoh's fight for supremacy in heaven: "The sky weeps, the stars shake... when they behold the King rising up as a spirit, as a god who lives on his fathers and possesses his mothers."

Jung's reading: divine incest as royal prerogative — "the votaries fight and even kill each other for their share in the mystery of divine incest" (¶392); parallels the Papremis club-battle and Herodotus' aition of Ares forcing his way to his mother (¶390).
Verbatim: as a god who lives on his fathers and possesses his mothers. (cw05 ¶391).

occurrences.title: Philalethes' chalybs — the infernal fire, magnet and the royal child (Introitus apertus)
occurrences.label: Philalethes' chalybs
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In the Introitus apertus the arcane substance is named 'chalybs' (steel), the 'auri minera', a 'secret, infernal, and yet most volatile fire' (¶204). The magnet's hidden centre turns 'with an archetic appetite' towards the Pole, where the heart of Mercurius rests (¶205); the wise man is bidden to follow the star to the cradle and 'honour the royal child' — the filius born in the philosophical East. Jung reads the peregrinatio to the four quarters as a quaternity centred on the Pole, the hidden God who reveals himself through magnetism (¶205, ¶209).

occurrences.title: Philalethes — Mercurius as two-edged sword and hidden vessel
occurrences.label: Philalethes — Mercurius as two-edged sword…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Summing up the synonyms of Mercurius, Philalethes calls him the key of the art, 'that two-edged sword in the hand of the cherub who guards the way to the tree of life', and 'our true, hidden vessel, the Philosophic garden, wherein our Sun rises and sets' (¶379). The vessel is thus identical with its content — the Mercurius non vulgi — and with the guarded way to Paradise; Jung pairs it with Rupescissa's cherub-vessel. Parallels: rupescissa-cherub-vessel-1351, philalethes-chalybs-royal-child-pole-1667.

occurrences.title: Prajapati hatches himself from the world-egg — Rig-Veda and Brahmanas
occurrences.label: Prajapati hatches himself from the world-egg
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Immersion in oneself (introversion) is a penetration into the unconscious and at the same time asceticism.
body: Tapas, "he heated himself with his own heat" — "brooder and brooded being conceived not as separate, but as one and the same thing" (¶589): introversion as cosmogony. "The result, for the philosophy of the Brahmanas, is the creation of the world, and for the mystic the regeneration and spiritual rebirth of the individual" (¶590); "Then the One, that was hidden in the shell, was born through the force of fiery torment" (Rig-Veda X, 129).

occurrences.title: Phoenix reborn as an 'unseemly worm' in one day — Epiphanius, Ancoratus
occurrences.label: Phoenix reborn as an 'unseemly worm' in one day
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Epiphanius (Ancoratus): 'When the bird is dead, indeed utterly consumed... there are left only the crude remnants of the flesh. From this there comes forth in one day an unseemly worm, which puts on wings and becomes as new; but on the third day it matures' (cw14 ¶472). The worm-stage anchors Jung's decoding of Khunrath's 'filius unius (SVI) diei' — the Hermaphrodite of nature, Saturn, 'the ambisexual Philosophic Man', world-egg, green and red lion (¶472-476): the one day of Genesis 1:5, when 'darkness precedes the light and is its mother' (¶476). The phoenix's lowest form is the worm — the renewal beginning from what is most abject.

occurrences.title: Burning starfish of Picinellus — 'Stella maris' (Polyhistor symbolicus)
occurrences.label: Burning starfish of Picinellus — 'Stella maris'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Picinelli's baroque emblem dictionary reads the burning starfish ('stella marina', Pliny) as the fire of the Holy Ghost — Ecclesiasticus 48:1, the Pentecostal tongues, charity that 'many waters cannot quench' (Song of Solomon 8:7). In the next breath he gives the opposite reading: St. Basil's hell-fire, 'fire that has no brightness', the 'scintilla voluptatis' of concupiscence (¶199). Jung's point: the unity of the symbol implies the identity of the opposites, which the medieval symbolists never noticed (¶199). Picinellus even makes the fish man's tongue, 'set on fire by hell' (James 3:6, ¶209).

occurrences.title: Journey through the seven mouths of the Nile — Maier's transitus
occurrences.label: Journey through the seven mouths of the Nile
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Maier's transitus: the seven mouths of the Nile = seven planets, beginning at the Canopic Gate where Saturn is 'domiciled' (cw14 ¶287). The ascent runs 'from darkness and cold to light and warmth, from old age to youth, from death to rebirth', but Mercurius is not found in the sun's region; only on returning to Saturn — now a 'domus barbae' where 'the wisest of all, Thrice-Greatest Hermes, imparts wisdom' — is he met (¶298, ¶303). Jung: the ascent sheds the character 'imprinted by the archons' (¶308), the descent carries light back into darkness (¶309); the opus is 'a "transitus"... in the Gnostic sense' (¶288).

occurrences.title: Gates of the planets — Origen on the soul's descent
occurrences.label: Gates of the planets
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Origen describes the soul's descent through 'the gates of the planets': 'the first gate is of lead and is correlated with Saturn' (cw14 ¶299) — the same lead-gate at which Maier begins and ends his Nile journey. Jung sets it beside Priscillian's soul 'imprinted' by the archons with the 'chirographum' (the bill of debt to fate blotted out by Christ, Col. 2:14) and calls the whole a 'heavenly journey of the soul' 'developed more particularly in Persia' (¶299). The planetary gate-series is the descent-side of the ascent-descent that alchemy reverses.

occurrences.title: The remora that stopped Caligula's ship — Pliny
occurrences.label: The remora that stopped Caligula's ship — Pliny
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Pliny tells how a remora half a foot long 'had sucked fast to the rudder on the return journey from Stura to Entium, and had brought the ship to a standstill'; Caligula was murdered on his return — the fish as omen, the same trick played on Mark Antony before Actium (¶223). This amazement fixed the identification of the 'round fish in our sea' with the remora. Jung: the remora symbolizes 'that extremely small thing in the vastness of the unconscious which is charged with such fateful significance: it is the self, the atman, "smaller than small, greater than great"' (¶223). Parallels: dream-golden-fish-limmat-woman-1951c.

occurrences.title: Plotinus — the soul circles around a centre (Enneads VI, 9, 8)
occurrences.label: Plotinus — the soul circles around a centre
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Self-knowledge reveals the fact that the soul's natural movement is not in a straight line... it circles around something interior, around a centre. Now the centre is that from which proceeds the circle, that is, the soul... divinity consists in being attached to the centre.... Anyone who withdraws from it is a man who has remained un-unified, or who is a brute' (¶342). Jung: the point is 'the centre of a circle that is created, so to speak, by the circumambulation of the soul... a God-image. This is an idea that still underlies the mandala-symbols in modern dreams' (¶343). Parallels: monoimos-monad-iota-2c, mandala-modern-man-jung-zurich-1916.

occurrences.title: Six ithyphallic men carrying an ithyphallic plough — vase, Museo Archeologico, Florence
occurrences.label: Six ithyphallic men carrying an ithyphallic…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Florence, Museo Archeologico (vase 'in [or once in]' the collection)
occurrences.quote: it portrays a row of six naked ithyphallic men carrying a plough which is represented ithyphallically (fig. 15).
body: An archaic Greek vase picture: a row of six naked ithyphallic men carrying a plough that is itself represented ithyphallically — the implement and its bearers one continuous phallus, ploughing as ritualized copulation with the earth.

Jung adduces it (via Dieterich, Mutter Erde, pp. 107ff.) as the "excellent picture" capping his etymology of ploughing as libido: IEur. *ueneti "he ploughs" piercing the ground, Lat. arare with its erotic double sense, and the "bridal bed in the field" custom — "as I make this woman fruitful, so I make the earth fruitful" (ch. III n. 22). The phallic plough is the canalization formula made visible.

occurrences.title: Four lines from a single point — John Dee's Monas hieroglyphica
occurrences.label: Four lines from a single point
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Things and beings have their first origin in the point and the monad.
body: Dee's speculation on the monad: "It is not unreasonable to suppose, that by the four straight lines which run in opposite directions from a single, individual point, the mystery of the four elements is indicated.... Things and beings have their first origin in the point and the monad." The centre of nature is "the point originated by God," the "sun-point" in the egg (¶41).

Jung files Dee with the scintilla-doctrine that runs from Heraclitus' "spark of stellar essence" and the Sethian spark in the dark waters to Khunrath's "fiery sparks of the World-Soul": the geometry of the cross-in-circle as the point's own unfolding, a "double quaternio" whose centre is the germ of the egg in the yolk.

occurrences.title: 'Consider the point in nature' — Sendivogius, Novum lumen chemicum
occurrences.label: Consider the point in nature
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: fire is the life of the metals
body: The admonition that opens the doctrine of the point: "But you, dear reader, you will have above all to consider the point in nature... and you need nothing else, but take care lest you seek that point in the vulgar metals, where it is not. For these metals, the common gold more especially, are dead. But our metals are alive, they have a spirit... For know that fire is the life of the metals" (¶40). The point "is identical with the prima materia of the metals, which is a 'fatty water' (aqua pinguis), the latter being a product of the moist and the hot."

Jung's section II.2 ("The Scintilla") treats the point as "the symbol of a mysterious creative centre in nature," whose epilogue passage ("When a man is illuminated by the light of nature... he may behold the point of our magnet, which corresponds to both centres of the rays, that is, those of the sun and the earth") shows the centre as "a conjunction of male and female" (¶43).

occurrences.title: John Pordage — Paradise rising from the Heart of the New Earth
occurrences.label: John Pordage — Paradise rising…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The alchemist-mystic Pordage (1607-81): divine Wisdom is 'a New Earth, the heavenly Land.... For from this Earth grew all the Trees of Life.... Thus did Paradise... rise up from the Heart and Centre of this New Earth, and thus did the lost Garden of Eden flourish in greenness' (¶373). Jung cites it with the alchemical equation of Paradise = albedo, the regained innocence, whose rivers' source is the aqua permanens; for the Fathers Christ himself is the source, Paradise the 'ground of the soul' (¶373). Parallels: tree-ripley-scrowle-bm-sloane-5025-london-1588, golden-flower-ripley-scrowle-1588.

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: Agathodaimon transformed into a pillar of fire, the leaden man (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — Agathodaimon transformed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Third ascent: "I saw an old man whitened by years, who had become wholly white, with a blinding whiteness. His name was Agathodaimon" — who at the place of punishments "was transformed by the flame into a pillar of fire," groaning: "I am the leaden man, and I submit myself to an unendurable torment" (cw13 ¶86). Zosimos wakes and interprets: "the lead is to be rejected, and in truth the vision refers to the composition of the liquids."

Jung's footnote: "In our text (III, v, 3) it is the Agathodaimon itself that suffers transformation" (pdf p91 n4) — the good daimon as arcane substance imprisoned in lead, the anima media natura in matter. Lead = "the sealed tomb of Osiris".

occurrences.title: Prima materia as the mountain containing all knowledge and all vices — Abu'l Qasim
occurrences.label: Prima materia as the mountain containing all…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabic alchemy (ed. Holmyard, Kitab al-'ilm al-muktasab p. 24)
occurrences.quote: And this prime matter is found in a mountain containing an immense collection of created things. In this mountain is every sort of knowledge that is found in the world.
body: Abu'l Qasim locates the prime matter "in a mountain containing an immense collection of created things. In this mountain is every sort of knowledge that is found in the world" — and, in the same breath, "hatred or malevolence or fraud or villainy or deceit or tyranny or oppression … or blood or killing that is not present there." The prima materia as the total mountain: all wisdom and all evil in one substance.

Jung opens the unicorn chapter's footnote apparatus with this text because it states the moral ambivalence of the arcane substance — the same radical ambivalence he predicates of Mercurius (bestia, ascia, and salvator in one) and of the self as union of good and evil. The mountain is the unfolded massa confusa; the unicorn/stone hunted on the mountain is its liberated core.

occurrences.title: Priscillian — Christ destroying the wheel of generation
occurrences.label: Priscillian — Christ destroying the wheel…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Priscillian, the Gnostic-leaning bishop executed in 385, takes the horoscope as the wheel of birth: 'He alone has the power to join together the Pleiades and to loose the bands of Orion. Knowing the changes of the firmament and destroying the wheel of generation, he has overcome the day of our birth by the renewal of baptism' (¶212). For Jung this proves that in the fourth century the trochos geneseos was 'in fact regarded as the horoscope'; setting fire to the wheel is a catastrophic revolt of the psyche's original components (¶211). Cf. the chirographum of the zodiacal signs on Priscillianist bodies (¶366 n.25).

occurrences.title: Proteus — the Old Man of the Sea, psychopomp of the fish-giving sea
occurrences.label: Proteus — the Old Man of the Sea, psychopomp…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The Naassenes read Aipolos — 'the Pole that turns the cosmos round' — as Homer's Proteus, 'the Old Man of the Sea, immortal Proteus the Egyptian... who always tells the truth' (¶338). Jung: 'Proteus is evidently a personification of the unconscious'; he must be seized and held, lies among his warm-blooded seals — contents capable of becoming conscious — and teaches the hero the way home 'over the fish-giving sea': 'the Old Man proves to be a psychopomp' (¶338). 'He spins round himself and changes his shape' — the revolving image that cannot be grasped; 'il ne se laisse pas rouler'. Cf. his Faust II role with the Homunculus.

occurrences.title: The putissimus homo who sweats rose-coloured blood — Dorn, Congeries Paracelsicae
occurrences.label: The putissimus homo who sweats rose-coloured…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn, "Congeries Paracelsicae chem icae de transm utatione m etallorum " (Theatr. chem. I, 1659, pp. 519ff): the Philosophers' m aterial is "a golden tree with seven branches" enclosing the seven m etals; at the final operations "a dark red liquid, like blood, sweats out drop by drop from their m aterial and their vessel. And for this reason they have prophesied that in the last days a m ost pure m an, through whom the w orld will be freed, will com e to earth and will sweat bloody drops of a rosy or red hue, whereby the w orld will be redeemed from its Fall" (cw13 ¶380-381).

Jung: this is not a future Christ but "the alchem ical servator cosmi, representing the still unconscious idea of the whole and com plete m an, who shall bring about what the sacrificial death of Christ has obviously left unfinished" (cw13 ¶390); putus = 'genuine', unalloyed (n.5).
Verbatim: they have prophesied that in the last days a m ost pure m an, through whom the w orld will be freed, will com e to earth and will sweat bloody drops of a rosy or red hue (cw13 ¶381ocr)

occurrences.title: The Merkebah — Ezekiel's vision of the four cherubim
occurrences.label: The Merkebah — Ezekiel's vision…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Babylon (exilic setting of the vision; text Judah)
body: Ezekiel's throne-vision (chs. 1 and 10): four cherubim "had 'the likeness of am an'", each with four faces — man, lion, ox, eagle — and a wheel; the four wheels were read as the Merkebah, the chariot, under "a firm am ent as the colour of terrible crystal" bearing the throne of him who had "the appearance of am an", "the c o unte rpa rto f Osiris" (cw13 ¶362-363).

Jung: 4x4 faces in all (¶362); the one human head signals consciousness — "H orus as the rising sun is the enlighten er"; the apotropaic tau-mark of Ezekiel 9:4 shows God's own quaternity (¶363). The analogy with the Egyptian four sons of Horus "is at once apparent" (¶361).
Verbatim: Th e analogy with the vision of Ezekiel (chapters 1 and 10) is at once apparent. (cw13 ¶361)

occurrences.title: The four beasts of Daniel's night-vision
occurrences.label: The four beasts of Daniel's night-vision
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~6th c. BCE setting (text perhaps 2nd c. BCE)
body: Daniel 7: four beasts — lion with a man's heart, bear, leopard, and the "dreadful and terrible" fourth with iron teeth and ten horns. Jung: "AU four of them are beasts of prey or, in psychological term s, functions that have succum bed to desire, lost their angelic character, and becom e daem onic in the worst sense" — the negative aspect of the four angels of God (Book of Enoch), "the daemonization of m an" (cw13 ¶365).

Daniel reads them as four kings; the fourth beast "shall devour the whole earth" — "a m onstrous lust for pow er will m ake the hum an quarter unconscious again... It has recurred countless tim es in the history of m ankind" (cw13 ¶365).
Verbatim: a m onstrous lust for pow er will m ake the hum an quarter unconscious again. (cw13 ¶365ocr)

occurrences.title: The Ortus — four-coloured beast at the Red Sea (Maier)
occurrences.label: The Ortus — four-coloured beast at the Red Sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Maier's peregrinatio (Symbola aureae mensae, 1617) the adept reaches the Red Sea and finds the animal 'Ortus' (rising): 'a red head with streaks of gold reaching to its neck, black eyes, a white face, white forepaws, and black hindpaws' (cw14 ¶277), after Avicenna: 'That thing whose head is red, its eyes black and its feet white, is the magistery.' Jung: 'The Ortus is the alchemical "animal" which represents the living quaternity in its first synthesis... the prima materia of the self and, as the phoenix, rebirth' (¶282). The beast is met at the 'ford', the critical fourth direction — 'Africa', the inferior function (¶276-280). 'The animal is the symbolic carrier of the self' (¶283).

occurrences.title: Ostanes between two brilliances and two dim lights — Abu'l-Qasim
occurrences.label: Ostanes between two brilliances…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: each of them has reached me and I know not how to save myself from them
body: Ostanes' cry from Abu'l-Qasim: "Save me, O my God, for I stand between two exalted brilliancies known for their wickedness, and between two dim lights; each of them has reached me and I know not how to save myself from them." Sent up to Agathodaimon, he is told of "somewhat of his nature, which will never be corrupted," and receives the "child of the bird which is mixed with redness," to be sealed in its vessel "whence it has no power to come out except when thou desirest" (¶5).

Jung decodes the quaternio: Mars and Saturn (malefici, rulers of Aries and Capricorn) against the moon and Venus (dim lights of Cancer and Libra) — masculine/feminine crossed with good/evil. The adept stands "subject to Heimarmene, the compulsion of the stars" (¶6), while the incorruptible germ — gold, aurum philosophorum, "the son of the bird... the filius philosophorum" — must be heated until the humidum radicale departs. Same text: Hermes makes the Sun "a crown" of its brothers' spirits (¶6, p23).

occurrences.title: Gitche Manito painted as an egg with points to the four winds — Hiawatha's pictographs
occurrences.label: Gitche Manito painted as an egg with points…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The hieroglyph is at the same time a quaternity-symbol, which psychologically always points to the self.
body: Hiawatha invents writing: the egg with four points is the world enclosed in the egg, "the cosmic birth-giver, a symbol used by Plato and by the Vedas"; "this 'mother' is omnipresent, like the air … so the world-mother is a spirit, the anima mundi. The hieroglyph is at the same time a quaternity-symbol, which psychologically always points to the self" (¶550) — with the atman "no bigger than a thumb" as the centre. The second glyph paints the evil spirit as the serpent Kenabeek (¶550–551).

occurrences.title: Four sons of Horus — three animal-headed, one human-headed (Egyptian representations)
occurrences.label: Four sons of Horus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Egypt (canopic amulets and vignettes of Amset, Hapi, Duamutef, Qebehsenuf)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: there are occasionally representations in which three of the sons have animals' heads and only one a human head, in keeping with the Old Testament visions as well as with the emblems of the seraphim which were transferred to the evangelists
body: Egyptian representations of the four sons of Horus (Amset, Hapi, Duamutef, Qebehsenuf) in which three have animals' heads (man, ape, jackal, falcon — one variant human) and only one a human head. Jung uses this zoomorphic/anthropomorphic differentiation of the divine four as an "interesting differentiation" inside the quaternity-of-the-One schema, and lines it up with the Old Testament throne-visions, the seraphim emblems transferred to the evangelists, and the gospels themselves ("three of which are synoptic and one 'Gnostic'").

Jung's reading: the four sons are an early, materially dated form of the deity-with-four arrangement that runs Ezekiel → seraphim → evangelists → alchemical quaternity; the animal/human head ratio marks the chthonic-natural versus human-spiritual quarter. Index concordance: "Horus... four sons of, 234n, 319, 346n, 366, 388".

occurrences.title: The mystic quadriga of four horses — Dio Chrysostom
occurrences.label: The mystic quadriga of four horses
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The horses represent the four elements.
body: The highest god drives his chariot in a circle with four horses — the four elements; when the fiery one consumes the others, "the division of God into Many ceases, and the divine One is restored." Jung reads the quadriga as "an astronomical symbol of Time" with the same libido symbolism as fate-as-fire (¶423).

occurrences.title: Plato's Timaeus opening — 'One, two, three... but where is the fourth?'
occurrences.label: Plato's Timaeus opening
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: ever since the opening of Plato's Timaeus ('One, two, three... but where, my dear Socrates, is the fourth?') and right up to the Cabiri scene in Faust) the motif of four as three and one was the ever-recurring preoccupation of alchemy.
body: The opening of Plato's Timaeus: Socrates counts his guests of the day before — "One, two, three" — and asks where the fourth has gone (the missing fourth is Timaeus, who supplies the missing speech). Jung cites this as the fountainhead of the "four as three and one" motif: "ever since the opening of Plato's Timaeus... and right up to the Cabiri scene in Faust, the motif of four as three and one was the ever-recurring preoccupation of alchemy."

Jung's reading: the counting-scene is a literary vestige of the archetypal quaternity problem — the conspicuous absence of the fourth — which the appendix sets as the schema behind the visions of Ezekiel, Daniel, and Enoch, Horus with his four sons, the seraphim-evangelist emblems, and the three synoptic gospels plus one "Gnostic." (CW9i Appendix; OCR ¶ markers on the appendix pages are truncated — likely ~¶717 in continuous CW9i numbering.)

occurrences.title: The 'secret square of the sages' with the mediating circle — Tractatus aureus (Gnosius scholium)
occurrences.label: The 'secret square of the sages'…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Tractatus aureus … cum Scholiis Dominici Gnosii (1610), pp. 43–44, 262f.
occurrences.quote: the mediator, making peace between enemies, or [the four] elements; nay rather he alone effects the squaring of the circle
body: A drawing of the "secret square of the sages": in the centre of the square a circle surrounded by rays of light. The scholium explains: "Divide lapidem tuum in quatuor elementa … et coniunge in unum et totum habebis magisterium," and names the central circle "the mediator, making peace between enemies, or [the four] elements; nay rather he alone effects the squaring of the circle." An accompanying drawing of the circulatio shows four rivers flowing in and out of the inner "ocean" — "for this vessel is the true philosophical Pelican, and there is no other to be sought for in all the world."

Jung uses it (Part I ch. 3, n. 44) as the alchemical twin of his dream-mandalas: the centre as mediator making peace among the four, and the circumambulatio/circulatio as the movement in which "all would be one thing in one circle or vessel."

occurrences.title: The triad as unity, the quaternity standing on the binarius — Valentinus, Duodecim claves
occurrences.label: The triad as unity, the quaternity standing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: 185. Below, the triad as unity; above, the quaternity standing on the binarius.—Valentinus, 'Duodecim claves,' in Mus. herm. (1678)
body: Diagram from the Duodecim claves of Basilius Valentinus: below, the triad fused as unity; above, the quaternity standing upon the binarius — the arithmetic of 3-and-4 that Jung made central to his alchemical structural analysis.

His context: the stone is "trinus et unus"; the fourth, "absent and yet present," appears in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3:25) as the completion of the three (¶449). The same figure underlies Böhme's quaternity of the cross in the zodiac (fig. 192).

occurrences.title: Rama marries Sita the furrow — Ramayana
occurrences.label: Rama marries Sita the furrow — Ramayana
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Sita means "furrow": the hero-king marries the ploughed earth; Indra likewise is husband of Urvara, "the fertile land"; Chinese emperors ploughed a furrow on accession.
Jung's reading: "the seizure of a country by the king was regarded as his marriage with the land" (¶306) — the hieros gamos of king and soil; its failure kills the king (Domaldi).
Verbatim: In the Hindu Ramayana, the hero Rama marries Sita, the furrow. (cw05 ¶306).

occurrences.title: Dhulqarnein's iron-and-brass rampart against Gog and Magog — Qur'an 18
occurrences.label: Dhulqarnein's iron-and-brass rampart…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: He dammed up the valley between the Two Mountains, and said: 'Ply your bellows.' And when the iron blocks were red with heat, he said: 'Bring me molten brass to pour on them.
body: Dhulqarnein ("the Two-horned One", Alexander the Great) journeys to the sun's setting in a pool of black mud and to its rising, then dams the valley between the Two Mountains with blocks of iron poured over with molten brass — an unscalable rampart against Gog and Magog, destined to fall to dust when the Lord's promise is fulfilled (¶252-255; cf. Revelation 20:7). Jung reads the rampart as protection thrown around "the place in the middle": "the self, enthroned in the place of the middle... the beloved city (Jerusalem, the centre of the earth). The self is the hero... the jewel... the god who is dismembered" (¶256). Individuation here is opus contra naturam, its wall provisional — it falls "when consciousness sinks back into the darkness... the moment of death" (¶256-256a).

occurrences.title: The raven nailed with three nails on the world-tree — 'The Princess in the Tree' (German fairytale)
occurrences.label: The raven nailed with three nails…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Germany ('The Princess in the Tree', Deutsche Marchen seit Grimm, pp. 1ff)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: there in the room he finds a raven fixed to the wall with three nails. One nail goes through his throat, the two others through the wings.
body: A swineherd climbs a tree whose branches lose themselves in the clouds; in a castle atop it a king's daughter is held by a wicked magician. In the one forbidden room he finds "a raven fixed to the wall with three nails. One nail goes through his throat, the two others through the wings." Out of pity he gives the raven water — at each sip a nail falls out, and the raven flies free. The raven is the hunter-devil who stole the princess (an anima mundi "bewitched up there"); the three nails are "the triune name". Jung reads the whole as an inverted Christian image: "The Saviour who freed the soul of humanity from the dominion of the prince of this world was nailed to a cross down below on earth, just as the thieving raven is nailed to the wall in the celestial branches of the world-tree" (¶427). The raven's release, the theft of the four-legged horse from the witch, and the trampling of the hunter carry the triad-quaternion drama to the hieros-gamos ending.

occurrences.title: Rebirth of water and spirit — the Nicodemus dialogue, John 3
occurrences.label: Rebirth of water and spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Nicodemus asks literally: "Can he enter the second time into his mother's womb?" Jesus answers: "Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit..." — πνεῦμα meaning both spirit and wind.

Jung's reading: "to be born of water simply means to be born of the mother's womb; to be born of the Spirit means to be born of the fructifying breath of the wind" (¶334); symbolical truth "puts water in place of the mother and spirit or fire in place of the father, frees the libido from the channel of the incest tendency" (¶335); the Church becomes the mother (¶335).
Verbatim: Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. (cw05 ¶333).

occurrences.title: The Rebis — Book of the Holy Trinity, Codex Germanicus 598
occurrences.label: The Rebis — Book of the Holy Trinity, Codex…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Th e Rebis: from "Book of the Holy Trin ity and Description of the Secret of the T ransm utation of M etals" (1420)
body: Plate B3 of CW13: the Rebis from the "Book of the Holy Trinity" (Dreifaltigkeitsbuch) of 1420, Munich Codex Germanicus 598, fol. 105v. Jung notes it "may have served as a model for the hermaphrodite in the Rosarium (pl. B2)."

The same 1420 manuscript was mined again by Reusner's Pandora (1588) for several of its eighteen pictures (¶181 n.52), making this codex a documented hub of the hermaphrodite iconography that Jung reads as "the monstrous, double nature of Mercurius" (¶181) and as the filius's "rounded perfection" (¶157). The picture series of the Rosarium and its kin is the pool from which his rebis instances aggregate.

occurrences.title: The filius as hermaphrodite with bat's wings — Rosarium 1550, fol. X
occurrences.label: The filius as hermaphrodite with bat's wings
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The axiom of M aria is represented by 1 + 3 snakes: the filius, as mediator, unites the one with the three.
body: Plate B2 of CW13: "The filius or rex in the form of a hermaphrodite. The axiom of Maria is represented by 1 + 3 snakes: the filius, as mediator, unites the one with the three. Characteristically, he has bat's wings. To the right is the Pelican, symbol of the distillatio circularia; to the left, the arbor philosophica with golden flowers; underneath, the chthonic triad as a three-headed serpent."

A compressed synthesis of the essay's whole symbolic field: rebis (hermaphroditic Mercurius, ¶268), the quaternity problem of three and four (the axiom of Maria Prophetissa, ¶272-273), the arbor philosophica, the Pelican vessel (¶185), and the chthonic serpent triad.

occurrences.title: Eirenaeus Philalethes — the Queen as the King's sister, mother, or wife (~1645)
occurrences.label: Eirenaeus Philalethes
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "The English alchemist Eirenaeus Philalethes ('lover of truth'), writing about 1645, remarks that the 'Queen' was the King's 'sister, mother, or wife.'" Jung cites this as the alchemical form of the anima's "distinctly 'historical' aspect and her condensation with the figures of the sister, wife, mother, and daughter, plus the associated incest motif" — the same constellation he finds in Goethe ("You were in times gone by my wife or sister") and in the regina / femina alba of Latin alchemy. Published in Ripley Reviv'd (1678), translated into German in 1741 and possibly known to Goethe.

occurrences.title: Ashes turning into a man; dismembered children in glass coffins — Spielrein's patient, Zurich
occurrences.label: Ashes turning into a man
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: The ashes can turn into a man... and she also saw 'dismembered children in glass coffins.
body: The schizophrenic woman in Spielrein's material: fragments of different things and materials "cooked" or "burnt" — "The ashes can turn into a man" — and the vision of "dismembered children in glass coffins."

Jung sets this beside the mythic parallel of Demeter collecting the limbs of the dismembered Dionysus and putting him together again: incineration-dismemberment as the negative face of rebirth, the destroyed body re-collected in the vessel (glass coffin = alchemical vas). One of several loci from this patient recorded in CW5's apparatus (sun-sunbeam-pierces-earth-spielrein-patient-zurich, serpent-gods-animal-spielrein-patient-zurich, arrow-three-wounds-god-spielrein-patient-zurich, water-spermatic-communion-spielrein-patient-zurich).

occurrences.title: 'Cheer up, initiates of the saved god' — the Attis night-liturgy, Rome
occurrences.label: Cheer up, initiates of the saved god
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~4th c. CE (Firmicus Maternus, De errore profanarum religionum)
occurrences.quote: Θαρρεīτε μὑσται τοῡ θεοῡ σεσωσμένου, ἒαται ϒὰρ ήμīν ἐκ πóνων σωτηρíα
body: The nocturnal rite Firmicus reports: an image of the god laid supine on a bier is mourned with measured wailing; then, when the feigned lamentation is sated, a light is brought in, the mouths of all the mourners are anointed by the priest, and he whispers over them the consoling formula — "Cheer up, initiates of the saved god: for salvation from our toils shall come to us."
The movement from lament to light is the ritual kernel of the resurrected-god: grief ritually timed, then answered by illumination and the whispered promise.

occurrences.title: 'Take courage, the god is saved' — Attis lament and light, Firmicus Maternus
occurrences.label: Take courage, the god is saved
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the priest whispers softly: “Take courage, ye initiates, for the god is saved
body: The night-liturgy of Attis: the image laid on its back in a litter, rhythmical laments, then the light brought in and the whispered consolatio — the mystery-formula of dying-and-rising that Jung sets beside the Eleusinian epitaph and Preiswerk's wheat hymn (¶532–535).

occurrences.title: The stone 'daily born anew' yet existing 'from the beginning of the world' — Gloria mundi
occurrences.label: The stone 'daily born anew' yet existing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Et quamvis cottidie denuo nascatur, nihilominus tamen ab initio mundi ille fuit. …
body: The Gloria mundi describes the lapis begotten by sun and moon: born on earth, broken, destroyed, mortified, generated again through vapour, coming with the wind to the sea and from the sea back to the land, vanishing and re-arising. Then the paradox that defines it: "Et quamvis cottidie denuo nascatur, nihilominus tamen ab initio mundi ille fuit. …" — and though it is daily born anew, yet it existed from the beginning of the world. Jung notes the formula of the Fourth Gospel standing behind it (John 1: 1, 14).

This is the alchemical statement of the two time-axes the vault itself insists on: the eternally latent (the self existing from the beginning, cw12 Part I n. 34) and its repeated empirical births — renewal of life through the sea-crossing and return.

occurrences.title: Dead infant in a reed basket laid in an opened nobleman's tomb — Aswan
occurrences.label: Dead infant in a reed basket laid…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Just behind the entrance-door was a little basket made of reeds, containing the withered body of a new-born infant, wrapped in rags.
body: Jung's own field observation (return leg of the 1925-26 East Africa journey): an ancient Egyptian tomb just opened near Aswan held, just behind the entrance door, a little reed basket with the withered body of a new-born infant wrapped in rags — hastily laid there by a workman's wife so that, when the nobleman entered the sun-barge to rise anew, her dead child might "share in his salvation" from within the holy precinct. A living folk-practice piggy-backing on the funerary solar theology Jung cites for the alchemists' transformation: the transformation of the mortal into the immortal "mounts the sun-barge and may take me with it" (¶238).

occurrences.title: 'I approached the very gates of death' — Lucius' initiation, Metamorphoses XI, 23
occurrences.label: I approached the very gates of death
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I approached the very gates of death and set one foot on Proserpine's threshold, yet was permitted to return, rapt through all the elements.
body: Lucius describes his initiation into the Isis mysteries as a willed death: "I approached the very gates of death and set one foot on Proserpine's threshold, yet was permitted to return, rapt through all the elements." The rites "approximate to a voluntary death" from which he was "born again" (p. 284).

Jung generalizes: "This was the real purpose of all the mystery religions. They created symbols of death and rebirth" — with Frazer's primitive initiation mysteries as the lower register of the same pattern. The locus complements the existing note on the initiate elected Helios (the solar apotheosis that follows this night-descent).

occurrences.title: Death enters the world: the old woman who put on her old skin — African myth
occurrences.label: Death enters the world — African myth
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: people renewed themselves by casting their skins like snakes
body: The etiology of death through failed skin-casting — the snake's renewal mechanism withheld from mankind. Pairs with the snake as renewal symbol (¶410) and the snake stealing Gilgamesh's herb of immortality (¶457).

occurrences.title: Osiris as crucified god mourned by Isis and Nephthys — effigy from Philae
occurrences.label: Osiris as crucified god mourned by Isis…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: represents Osiris in the form of a crucified god, mourned by Isis and Nephthys
body: An Osiris effigy in crucified form, flanked by the two mourning sister-wives — the Egyptian dying god on the tree of life, the figure behind Jung's "crucified God" typology of ¶398 and the lamenting-mother motif of ¶415.

occurrences.title: Rex marinus crying from the sea, renewed with the columba spiritus sancti — Splendor Solis
occurrences.label: Rex marinus crying from the sea, renewed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Whosoever will free me from the waters and lead me to dry land, him will I prosper with everlasting riches.
body: Splendor Solis plate: in the background the sea-king cries for help from the water; in the foreground his renewed form stands with the rotundum (golden globe) and the dove of the Holy Spirit.

Jung's reading: the Rex marinus of the Visio Arislei — whose land is sterile because "only like mates with like" — is the projected content in its hidden, latent state; his cry from the deep is the fascination by which the projected content summons the conscious mind. The same MS (fig. 219) shows the "mighty Ethiopian, burned, calcined, altogether dead and lifeless" — the nigredo awaiting the bath of rebirth.

occurrences.title: 'Birds and fishes bring us the lapis … it is in every place' — Ripley
occurrences.label: Birds and fishes bring us the lapis … it is…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The philosophers tell the inquirer that birds and fishes bring us the lapis, every man has it, it is in every place, in you, in me, in everything, in time and space.
body: Sir George Ripley's formula of the stone's ubiquity: birds and fishes bring it, every man has it, it is in you, in me, in everything, in time and space; it "offers itself in lowly form (vili figura)," and from it springs the aqua permanens.

Jung: "The prima materia has the quality of ubiquity: it can be found always and everywhere, which is to say that projection can take place always and everywhere." The passage continues into Ripley's water-hyle, the dark sphere of creation, and the round stone of Empedokles' sphairos, "the most serene God."

occurrences.title: The Risen Christ as filius philosophorum — Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: The Risen Christ as filius philosophorum
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: After my many sufferings and great martyry / I rise again transfigured, of all blemish free.
body: The closing picture of the 1550 Rosarium series: the Risen Christ, with the inscription "After my many sufferings and great martyry / I rise again transfigured, of all blemish free."

Jung cites it as the plainest statement of the lapis-Christ parallel: the filius philosophorum appears in the figure of the resurrected God-man; Ripley's king — "a supreme victor triumphant, a great healer of the sick and a redeemer of all sins" — stands on the same axis (¶501). The stone's passion, death, and glorification re-enact the Christian drama inside matter.

occurrences.title: The River Map (Ho-t'u) — dragon dredges the magical signs from the river (legendary, ~12th c. BCE)
occurrences.label: The River Map — dragon dredges the magical…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: "According to the legend, a dragon dredged the magical signs of the 'River Map' from a river. On it the sages discovered the drawing, and in the drawing the laws of the world-order." The River Map is one of the legendary foundations of the I Ching, whose present form derives partly from the twelfth century BC; in accordance with its extreme age it shows the knotted cords that signify numbers — with the usual primitive character of qualities: all uneven numbers masculine, even numbers feminine. Jung asks whether this primitive conception influenced the much younger Tantric mandala; Wilhelm held no direct connection was assumable — the ideas "arise autochthonously... out of a psychic matrix that seems to be ubiquitous" (¶643).

occurrences.title: The lapis speaks: 'I beget the light, but the darkness too is of my nature' — Hermes quotation in the Rosarium philosophorum (1550)
occurrences.label: The lapis speaks — I beget the light, but…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Two Rosarium speeches of the stone ascribed to Hermes. (1) From a treatise ascribed to Hermes: "And my light conquers every light, and my virtues are more excellent than all virtues.… I beget the light, but the darkness too is of my nature." (cw12 ¶99). (2) "therefore nothing better or more worthy of veneration can come to pass in the world than the conjunction of myself and my son" (¶140).

The same folio gives the killing-and-quickening stone: "For our stone, namely the living western quicksilver which has placed itself above the gold and vanquished it, is that which kills and quickens." Jung: "the transformer is above the transformed."

occurrences.title: Rosarium: the lapis speaks — 'Protege me, protegam te'
occurrences.label: Rosarium — the lapis speaks
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Protege me, protegam te. Largire mihi ius meum, ut te adiuvem
body: "In the Rosarium the lapis says: 'Protege me, protegam te. Largire mihi ius meum, ut te adiuvem' (Protect me and I will protect you. Give me my due that I may help you)" (¶155).

Jung reads the speaking stone as "nothing less than a good friend and helper who helps those that help him, and this points to a compensatory relationship" — the alchemical analogue of dream 13's companion in the depths. The stone that demands its due and promises aid is the self as reciprocal partner, not object.

occurrences.title: Rosarium: 'Out of man and woman make a round circle' — the squaring recipe
occurrences.label: Rosarium — the squaring recipe
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Make a round circle and you will have the philosophers' stone
body: "The Rosarium says: 'Out of man and woman make a round circle and extract the quadrangle from this and from the quadrangle the triangle. Make a round circle and you will have the philosophers' stone'" (¶167, with figs. 59, 60 — Jamsthaler's Viatorium spagyricum 1625 and Maier's Scrutinium chymicum 1687).

Jung introduces it as the medieval counterpart of dream 16's leftward circumambulation of the square: the squaring of the circle as "a stage on the way to the unconscious, a point of transition leading to a goal lying as yet unformulated beyond it… one of those paths to the centre of the non-ego which were also trodden by the medieval investigators when producing the lapis" (¶167). Circle → square → triangle → circle: the coniunctio of man and woman sublimated into the rotundum.

occurrences.title: Rosarium: the secret concealed in the mind ('in ipsa sola')
occurrences.label: Rosarium: the secret concealed in the mind
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the essential secret of the art lies hidden in the human mind—or, to put it in modern terms, in the unconscious
body: "Who therefore knows the salt and its solution knows the hidden secret of the wise men of old. Therefore turn your mind upon the salt and think not of other things; for in it alone [i.e., the mind] is the science concealed and the most excellent and most hidden secret of all the ancient philosophers" (¶359).

Jung's philological move: the Latin reads "in ipsa sola," referring to mens — "One would have to assume a double misprint were the secret after all concealed in the salt. But as a matter of fact 'mind' and 'salt' are close cousins—cum grano salis!" Khunrath's sal sapientiae confirms the pun. Conclusion: "the essential secret of the art lies hidden in the human mind—or, to put it in modern terms, in the unconscious" (¶361).

occurrences.title: The five-petalled rose on Christ's breast — Mechthild of Magdeburg
occurrences.label: The five-petalled rose on Christ's breast
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Lord speaks to Mechthild: "Look at m y heart, an d see! A m ost beau tiful rose with five petals covered his whole breast, an d the Lo rd said: 'Praise m e in m y five senses, which are in d icated by this rose'" (cw13 ¶388; Liber gratiae spiritualis).

Jung reads the rose as m andala and as "a projection of her own fem inine Eros up on C hrist" (cw13 ¶389), and m akes this rose-mysticism the bridge by which "the m ystique of the Rose en tered in to alchem y" (¶387) — surfacing as the rose-coloured blood of the lapis. A sibling locus holds Mechthild's bridal coniunctio (coniumctio-mechthild-flowing-light-magdeburg-13c, cw9i ¶295).
Verbatim: A m ost beau tiful rose with five petals covered his whole breast (cw13 ¶388ocr)

occurrences.title: Rosinus ad Sarratantam — the living stone 'below thee... above thee... from thee... about thee'
occurrences.label: Rosinus ad Sarratantam
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Arabic-style compilation; 'Rosinus' = Zosimos via Arabic transcription

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: The oldest Arabic-style alchemical text: 'This stone is below thee, as to obedience; above thee, as to dominion; therefore from thee, as to knowledge; about thee, as to equals' (¶257) — which Jung says 'fits the paradoxical situation of the self', older than the ego yet needing to be built up by consciousness. The same treatise gives the lapis animalis, the animate stone 'sensible... to the presence and influence of the magnesia and the magnet' (¶243), and the stone 'fixed more in thee... created of God, and thou art its ore... so the end looks to the beginning, and contrariwise' (¶258). Parallels: morienus-thing-extracted-from-thee-7c, dorn-transmutemini-living-stones-16c.

occurrences.title: Zosimos — the cinnabar of the philosophers and the copper man turned to gold
occurrences.label: Zosimos — the cinnabar of the philosophers…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Berthelot (Alch. grecs, III, xxix, 24), quoted by Jung in the cinnabar discussion around Miss X's Picture 2: "(After the preceding process) you will find the gold coloured fiery red like blood. That is the cinnabar of the philosophers and the copper man (chalkanthropos), turned to gold." The kinnabari ton philosophon stood for the rubedo stage of the transforming substance; cinnabar was also supposed identical with the uroboros dragon, and Pliny already calls it sanguis draconis, 'dragon's blood' — a term that lasted all through the Middle Ages. The copper man anticipates the Anthropos-chalkanthropos of later alchemy.

occurrences.title: Rupescissa — the vessel made after the manner of a cherub
occurrences.label: Rupescissa — the vessel made…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'Have a vessel made after the manner of a cherub, which is the figure of God, and have six wings, after the fashion of six arms, turning back on themselves; and above, a round head... and put within this vessel the said burning water' (¶379). Jung reads the cherub as Ezekiel's vision, whose horizontal section 'would produce a mandala divided into four parts... equivalent to the squaring of the circle'; psychologically: 'make the Hermetic vessel out of your psychic wholeness and pour into it the aqua permanens' (¶379). Parallels: pelican-vessel-rhenanus-frankfurt-1613, philalethes-chalybs-royal-child-pole-1667.

occurrences.title: Mysteries of Sabazius: the golden snake let into the lap of the initiated
occurrences.label: Mysteries of Sabazius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: A golden snake is let down into the lap of the initiated and taken away again from the lower parts
body: "It is reported of the mysteries of Sabazius: 'Aureus coluber in sinum demittitur consecratis et eximitur rursus ab inferioribus partibus atque imis' (A golden snake is let down into the lap of the initiated and taken away again from the lower parts)."

Jung cites it in dream 18's commentary as a classical parallel for the ceremonial use of the reptile in transformation: "The idea of transformation and renewal by means of a serpent is a well-substantiated archetype… It is the healing serpent, representing the god" (¶184). The snake passing down into the lap and up from "the lower parts" enacts renewal through the body's depths.

occurrences.title: The pine felled, the youth's effigy tied to its trunk — annual Attis rite
occurrences.label: The pine felled, the youth's effigy tied…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Per annos singulos arbor pinea caeditur, et in media arbore simulacrum iuvenis subligatur
body: "Each year a pine-tree is felled, and an effigy of a youth is tied to the middle of the tree" — the dendritic core of the March Passover of Attis: the sacred tree cut down as the young god dies, his image bound to the trunk he embraces in the myth.
Jung quotes it in the sacrifice chapter as the ritual fixation of the myth (the hanged youth beneath the mother-tree), the cultic twin of the self-castration under the pine recorded in the main text.

occurrences.title: Spring sacrifice to Cinteotl — youth nailed to the cross
occurrences.label: Spring sacrifice to Cinteotl
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: by nailing a youth or maiden to the cross every spring and shooting the victim with arrows
body: Aztec spring rite for the grain-goddess Cinteotl: crucifixion plus arrow-death — the martyr-god complex of the sacrificial father (cf. ¶445, "the martyred and sacrificed god whom we have already met in the Aztec crucifixions and in the sacrifice of Odin"). The cross-name signifies "Tree of our life or flesh" (¶400).

occurrences.title: Hölderlin's Empedocles — pearls dissolved in the krater of rebirth (~1799)
occurrences.label: Hölderlin's Empedocles
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In Hölderlin's Empedocles fragment Jung finds the poet's "secret longing for the maternal depths and for the regenerating womb": "You seek life, and a godly fire / Gushes and gleams for you out of the deeps of earth, / As, with shuddering longing, you / Hurl yourself down to the flames of Etna... / And I would follow the hero into the depths / Did not love hold me" (¶625).

Jung: "He would like to be melted like pearls in wine, to be sacrificed in the chalice, the 'krater' of rebirth. He longs to imitate Empedocles, of whom Horace says: 'Empedocles, eager to be thought a god immortal, coolly leapt into burning Aetna'" (¶626). The leap into the volcano — the same fire that later swallows Chiwantopel — figures self-sacrifice into the maternal container: dissolution in the krater as the price of renewal. The accompanying fig. 40 shows the "womb of the World Mother," a wooden bowl from the Congo.
Verbatim: "to be sacrificed in the chalice, the 'krater' of rebirth" (¶626).

occurrences.title: The eucharist of Huitzilopochtli — Aztec god eaten (Sahagún)
occurrences.label: The eucharist of Huitzilopochtli
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Christ is a divinity who is eaten in the Lord’s Supper. His death transforms him into bread and wine, which we relish as mystical food.
body: The ethnographic anchor of the edible-god complex: the independently attested Aztec ceremonial eating of the god beside the Christian Lord's Supper ("Christ is a divinity who is eaten in the Lord's Supper", ¶526), Agni and soma, Dionysus and wine.

occurrences.title: The Pharaoh devours the gods — the Cannibal Hymn, Pyramid Texts
occurrences.label: The Pharaoh devours the gods
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He devours the great gods for breakfast, the middle gods for dinner, and the little gods for supper … The king devours everything that comes his way.
body: The dead Pharaoh arrives in heaven and overpowers the gods to assimilate their nature: "His servants have caught the gods with lassoes... they have cut them up and cooked them in hot cooking-pots." The king "devours the great gods for breakfast, the middle gods for dinner, and the little gods for supper," consumes the crowns and bracelets, "eats the wisdom of all the gods," and becomes lord of heaven.

Jung reads this "ravenous hunger (boulimia)" as the image of "man's repressive instinctuality at the stage where the parents have a predominantly nutritive significance" — the gods eaten as the primordial parents consumed.

occurrences.title: 'A lamb is a substitute for a man' — Sumerian-Assyrian fragment, library of Assurbanipal
occurrences.label: A lamb is a substitute for a man
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~7th c. BCE (library of Assurbanipal; text far older)
occurrences.quote: A lamb is a substitute for a man. He gives the lamb for his life, he gives the head of a lamb for the head of a man.
body: The substitution formula at the root of sacrificial religion: "To the wise man he said: A lamb is a substitute for a man. He gives the lamb for his life, he gives the head of a lamb for the head of a man." Jung prints it mid-chapter VIII as the baudierte Urform of the sacrifice argument — the surrogate victim standing in the place of the human.
The text gives the logical grammar that Christological and ram/lamb typologies (Melito's ram in the thicket, the Manichaean ram-serpent) elaborate.

occurrences.title: Mithras' tauroctony sequence — Heddernheim Relief
occurrences.label: Mithras' tauroctony sequence
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: First we see the birth of Mithras from the top of the tree; the next picture shows him carrying the conquered bull
body: Four-picture relief series (pl. XL, plate at pdf p285): Mithras born from the top of the tree, carrying the conquered bull, reaching for Sol's nimbus (¶397), Sol kneeling before him (¶398). Jung reads the bull as both father-monster and Mithras' own animal nature: "Mithras has thus sacrificed his animal nature" (¶398) — conquest of instinct no longer by overpowering the mother but by renouncing one's own instinctive desire, the anticipation of the crucified God. The bull is killed by taurokathapsis on its back, itself a life-giving deity (¶421).

occurrences.title: Eating raw the flesh of Zagreus — the Cretan initiates' confession
occurrences.label: Eating raw the flesh of Zagreus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: have eaten raw the flesh of Zagreus, the night-roaming shepherd
body: The initiate's credo in Euripides' Cretans: "Leading a holy life since I have been initiated into the mysteries of Idaean Zeus, and have eaten raw the flesh of Zagreus, the night-roaming shepherd." Through the omophagia the initiates assimilated the essence of the god — the dismembered Dionysus-Zagreus eaten raw, his death made the eater's life.

Jung pairs it with the Mexican rite of Teoqualo, "god-eating," as the trans-cultural theophagy that the Eucharist formalizes; and the sacrifice of Dionysus-Zagreus produced the neos Dionysos, the god's resurrection.

occurrences.title: Sethian light imprisoned as 'the salt of all created things' — Hippolytus
occurrences.label: Sethian light imprisoned as the salt…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus' Sethians: when the wave raised from the water by the wind 'has received within itself the reproductive power of the feminine, it retains the light scattered from on high... It is engendered from the water and commingled and mixed with the bodies as if it were the salt of all created things, and a light of the darkness struggling to be freed from the bodies' (cw14 ¶327). Jung: 'this strangely beautiful passage contains pretty well everything that the alchemists endeavoured to say about salt: it is the spirit, the turning of the body into light (albedo), the spark of the anima mundi, imprisoned in the dark depths of the sea' (¶328). Since the Philosophumena surfaced only in the 19th c., the affinity is not transmission but archetypal kinship (¶328).

occurrences.title: The unicorned scarab, sacred to Mercurius — Horapollo
occurrences.label: The unicorned scarab, sacred to Mercurius
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "An important source of information concerning the unicorn symbolism of Mercurius": Horapollo says "the third genus of the scarab is unicorned (μονόκερως) and, on account of this peculiarity, sacred to Mercurius, like the ibis. Moreover the scarab is a μονογενής (only-begotten, unigena) in so far as it is an [αὐτογενές] (a creature born of itself)" (¶530). Hence the chain: self-born → unicus filius = "the filius philosophorum, i.e., the stone." The scarab shares the dragon's fate of dismemberment ("the sun-beetle … was beheaded and dismembered" — Greek papyrus), and the alchemists' self-name "Children of the Golden Head" points back to the golden head of Osiris.

occurrences.title: Elixir from the scarabs of our water — Consilium coniugii
occurrences.label: Elixir from the scarabs of our water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The rare alchemical scarab, from the Consilium coniugii de massa solis et lunae: "Nulla aqua fit [elixir], nisi illa que fit de scarabaeis aquae nostrae — No water will become the elixir save that which comes from the scarabs of our water" (¶531; "fit quelles" in the chunk is an OCR garble). Jung: "The aqua nostra is nothing other than the aqua divina, i.e., Mercurius."
The scarab thus appears inside the water of the work — the self-born, unicorned beetle swimming in the divine water that is itself the transforming substance.

occurrences.title: 'Secret Inscription' — Great Magic Papyrus of Paris
occurrences.label: Secret Inscription
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O great, greatest, incomprehensible fabric of the world, form ed in a circle!
body: The prayer Jung quotes entire as "the continuation of that religious feeling for nature, so alien to Christianity": "Greetings, entire edifice of the Spirit of the air... greetings, beginning and end of irremovable Nature... O great, greatest, incomprehensible fabric of the world, formed in a circle!... having the form of water, of earth, of fire, of wind, of light, of darkness, star-glittering, damp-fiery-cold Spirit! I praise thee, God of gods, who hast fashioned the world... Destroyer, Begetter of living things, God of the Aeons, great art thou, Lord, God, Ruler of All!"

Jung: just as this prayer survives "embedded in a mass of magical recipes, so does the lumen naturae rise up from a world of kobolds and other creatures of darkness" (¶199). The passage carries his apologia for the symbol as the paradoxical "tertium" that "in reality is the living truth" (¶199).

occurrences.title: 'When thou knowest thyself, thou knowest God' — Zosimos to Theosebeia
occurrences.label: When thou knowest thyself, thou knowest God
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Olympiodorus preserves Zosimos's exhortation to his disciple Theosebeia: "If thou wilt calmly hum ble thyself in relation to thy body... thou wilt sum m on the divine to thyself, and in truth the divine, which is everyw here, will com e to thee. But when thou know est thyself, thou know est also the God who is truly one" (cw13 ¶372).

Jung's footnote draws the theologic: God's attribute is infinity, the daemon's is spatial limit — the ego "separated and split off from God, is likely to becom e daem onic as soon as it accentuates its indep endence of God by its egocentricity" (cw13 ¶372 n5), the dynamism of the self "placed at the service of th e ego" — Burckhardt's "great despoilers".
Verbatim: But when thou know est thyself, thou know est also the God who is truly one. (cw13 ¶372ocr)

occurrences.title: The dirty old man and the stepdaughter — Estonian tale of the moral test
occurrences.label: The dirty old man and the stepdaughter
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Pretty maid, pretty maid, wash me, do, it is hard for me to be so dirty!
body: The obedient stepdaughter jumps into a well after her distaff, meets cow, ram, and apple-tree, then a washhouse where "a dirty old man is sitting who wants her to wash him": fuel of "wooden pegs and crows' dung", bath-water the white mare's piss, a switch of the mare's tail, pumice for soap — she refuses each cruelty and substitutes the humane thing. Rewarded with "a bag full of gold and precious stones"; the jealous real daughter obeys every monstrous instruction and is rewarded accordingly. Jung's point: the old man "even tests the moral qualities of others and makes his gifts dependent on this test" (¶412) — spirit giving only what mercy, not obedience to sadism, draws forth.

occurrences.title: Father-God with 550 membra, shrunk to a five-ton lump — Nelken case
occurrences.label: Father-God with 550 membra, shrunk…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Nelken's patient, a primary-school teacher suffering paranoia, 'developed a theory about a Father-God with immense procreative powers. Originally he had 550 membra virilia, but in the course of time they were reduced to three... His colossal sperm production weakened him in the end, and finally he shrank to a five-ton lump and was found chained up in a ravine' (cw14 ¶378). Jung: 'This psychologem contains the motif of ageing and loss of procreative power. The patient was the rejuvenated Father-God or his avatar'; the embellishment 'is completely original, so that we can safely take it as an autochthonous product' of the collective unconscious (¶378) — the same mythologem Ripley clothed as the 'Ancient of Days'.

occurrences.title: The murder of Philemon and Baucis — Goethe's Faust II
occurrences.label: The murder of Philemon and Baucis
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In his blind urge for superhuman power, Faust brought about the murder of Philemon and Baucis. Who are these two humble old people? When the world had become godless and no longer offered a hospitable retreat to the divine strangers Jupiter and Mercury, it was Philemon and Baucis who received the superhuman guests. And when Baucis was about to sacrifice her last goose for them, the metamorphosis came to pass: the gods made themselves known, the humble cottage was changed into a temple, and the old couple became immortal servitors at the shrine" (¶561).
Goethe's aged couple keep the gods in a godless world — and Faust's development requires their liquidation. (Cf. Jung's own inner figure Philemon, later painted at Bollingen.)

occurrences.title: The little hooded man on the glacier — collective vision after a mountaineering accident
occurrences.label: The little hooded man on the glacier
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: after the catastrophe two of the climbers had the collective vision, in broad daylight, of a little hooded man who scrambled out of an inaccessible crevasse in the ice face and passed across the glacier, creating a regular panic in the two beholders.
body: Jung's strongest evidence that the gnomes and metal-men of fairy-tale are "real": "on the occasion of a serious mountaineering accident... after the catastrophe two of the climbers had the collective vision, in broad daylight, of a little hooded man who scrambled out of an inaccessible crevasse in the ice face and passed across the glacier, creating a regular panic in the two beholders" (¶410). The cucullatus — the hooded, invisible one, genius of the departed (¶298) — crossing the ice in daylight before two witnesses at once. Jung draws no "rational" conclusion beyond noting the uncanny fit of the diminutive to "the world of the infinitesimally small" (¶411).

occurrences.title: Winged senex ithyphallicus reliefs — Padmanabhapura temple
occurrences.label: Winged senex ithyphallicus reliefs
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In the royal tem ple of Padm anabhapura in Travancore (c. fifteenth century) I found two reliefs representing an entirely non-Indian senex ithyphallicus with wings.
body: Two temple reliefs Jung personally inspected: "an entirely non-Indian senex ithyphallicus with wings. In one of them he stands up to his waist in the bowl of the moon." He compares them with the winged ithyphallic old man who pursues the "blue" or "doglike" woman in Hippolytus's Naassene report (Elenchos V), where Kyllenios is "identical on the one hand with the Logos and on the other with the wicked Korybas, the phallus, and the demiurgic principle in general."

The reliefs support his claim of East-West traffic behind the erotic Mercurius: "Mercurius represents the 'continuous cohabitation' which is found in unalloyed form in the Tantric Shiva-Shakti concept"; Indian religious influences were at work in Mesopotamia from the first centuries AD.

occurrences.title: Krates' vision of Hermes as the old man with the book — Book of Krates
occurrences.label: Krates' vision of Hermes as the old man…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Greek original → Arabic transmission (Berthelot, La Chimie au moyen âge III)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~9th c. (Arabic copy); Greek material considerably older
occurrences.quote: Then I saw an old man, the handsomest of men, sitting in a chair. He was dressed in white, and was holding in his hand a board from the chair, on which rested a book.…
body: The oldest extant vision of the Hermetic wise old man. In the Book of Krates — Greek in origin, handed down in Arabic, the present form ~9th century — the narrator sees Hermes enthroned, white-robed, holding a book containing "the explanation of the secret things he has hidden from men."

Jung cites it (Part II ch. 2, n. 7) as the prototype of the vision reported in Senior's Tabula chymica and reused on the frontispiece of Béroalde de Verville's Songe de Poliphile (fig. 4): the senex holding the book of secrets on his knees — the revealer who both hides and gives the arcanum.

occurrences.title: The little grey man as the Lord God — German tale of the soldier and the black princess
occurrences.label: The little grey man as the Lord God
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Suddenly a little man stood before him with along grey beard, but it was none other than the Lord God himself, who could no longer go on looking at all the mischief the devil wrought every night.
body: A princess under curse creeps from her iron coffin nightly and devours the soldier guarding the tomb. One escapes — and "suddenly a little man stood before him with a long grey beard, but it was none other than the Lord God himself, who could no longer go on looking at all the mischief the devil wrought every night. 'Whither away?' said the little grey man, 'may I come with you?'" Good advice follows, as always. Jung: the old man is taken for God "in the same naive way that the English alchemist, Sir George Ripley, describes the 'old king' as 'antiquus dierum' — 'the Ancient of Days'" (¶412, Cantilena, 15th c.). The fairy-tale senex shading directly into the God-image.

occurrences.title: 'The One-sided Old Man' — Siberian tale of the one-legged, one-handed, one-eyed greybeard
occurrences.label: The One-sided Old Man
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: In a Siberian tale, he appears as aone-legged, one-handed, and one-eyed greybeard who awakens a dead man with an iron staff.
body: In a Siberian tale the old man appears "as a one-legged, one-handed, and one-eyed greybeard who awakens a dead man with an iron staff"; the revived man, killed and reawakened several times, finally slays his benefactor by mistake — and with him his good fortune. His missing half appears separately "in the shape of a murderer who seeks the hero's life", and only when both are dead is the identity of victims revealed. Jung: "the old man is his own opposite, a life-bringer as well as a death-dealer — 'ad utrumque peritus' (skilled in both), as is said of Hermes" (¶413-414). The archetype's dark side, split off and walking.

occurrences.title: The old man with the milk-flask — Estonian tale of the runaway orphan
occurrences.label: The old man with the milk-flask
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Estonia (collection, 'How an Orphan Boy Unexpectedly Found His Luck')

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Give me some more to drink,' begged the boy. 'You have had enough for today,' replied the old man.
body: An ill-treated orphan boy lets a cow escape and flees, falls asleep exhausted — and wakes to find "a little old man with a long grey beard... in the act of replacing the stopper in his little milk-flask": "If my path had not chanced to lead me to you, that would assuredly have been your last sleep." He refuses to shelter the boy but gives counsel: go eastward; after seven years he will reach the great mountain that betokens his fortune; he gives his scrip and flask (food and drink each day) and a burdock leaf that becomes a boat. Jung uses the tale to define the archetype: the old man appears when insight "cannot be mustered on one's own resources", compensating spiritual deficiency; he is "purposeful reflection and concentration of moral and physical forces... outside consciousness" (¶401-403). The mountain "often has the psychological meaning of the self" (n14, I Ching hexagram 17).

occurrences.title: Wise old man with the book of secrets — Senior's Tabula chymica (fig. 128)
occurrences.label: Wise old man with the book of secrets
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Arabic author (Mohammed ibn Umail) → Latin print tradition

jung.locator: pdf p660 (Part II ch. 2, n. 7); fig. 128

occurrences.quote: The figure as depicted in the treatise, of a wise old man holding the book of secrets on his knees, was taken over in the frontispiece of Béroalde de Verville, Le Songe de Poliphile (see fig. 4).
body: The frontispiece vision of Senior (Zadith), the Latin name of Mohammed ibn Umail: a wise old man seated, the book of secrets on his knees — the alchemist's personified arcanum as revealer. Jung reproduces it as fig. 128 and reads it alongside the vision of the man on the cathedra in the alchemist's own "seeing in the spirit" (cw12 Part II ch. 2, n. 7).

Jung notes the figure was taken over for the frontispiece of Béroalde de Verville's Le Songe de Poliphile (fig. 4), showing the continuity of the senex-revealer motif from 10th-century Arabic alchemy into Renaissance emblematics. The oldest antecedent he knows is the vision of senex-krates-vision-hermes-white-9c.

occurrences.title: Agathodaimon serpent — antique gem (fig. 37)
occurrences.label: Agathodaimon serpent — antique gem (fig. 37)
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It is both Agathodaimon (fig. 37) and Cacodaimon.
body: Fig. 37 beside the double aspect of the hero-snake: "It is both Agathodaimon (fig. 37) and Cacodaimon. In German legend we are told that the heroes have snake's eyes" (¶593). Tum of Pithum-Heroopolis "was chiefly worshipped as the Agathodaimon serpent, of whom it was said: 'The sacred Agathodaimon serpent goes forth from the city of Nezi'" (¶410).

occurrences.title: Seven-headed snake of Amente, the Egyptian underworld
