occurrences.label: Seven-headed snake of Amente, the Egyptian…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: 'In Amente, the Egyptian underworld, dwells the great seven-headed snake, and in the Christian underworld is the most celebrated snake of all, the devil, "that old serpent"' (cw14 ¶482). Hell's pair of brothers: 'the devil being characterized by the snake and death by worms'; in Old German and Latin 'worm, snake, and dragon coalesce' (vermis, serpens, draco) (¶482). The dragon-slayer 'is therefore always a conqueror of death' (¶482). The seven-headed snake gives the chthonic serpent its maximal, underworld form — counterpart to the Mercurial serpent of the work.

occurrences.title: The Big Snake — twins in the ditch who become dragon-killers (Frobenius)
occurrences.label: The Big Snake — twins in the ditch…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jung's fig-40-adjacent African parallel for the twins-in-the-womb motif: "the Big Snake, which grew out of a little snake in a hollow tree ('stretching forth of the serpent'), and which devoured all human beings (devouring mother = death) until only one pregnant woman remained. She dug a ditch, covered it with a stone, and there gave birth to twins who afterwards became dragon-killers" (¶620).

Jung reads the devouring serpent as the devouring mother = death; the hollow tree as the maternal container; the stone-covered ditch as a substitute womb from which the dragon-killer twins are born — the psyche's compensatory counter-figure to the monster that ate everyone else. It stands beside the Hölderlin material as evidence that "guarded in modest bud" (the fateless gods' eternal infancy) and its violent termination are a universal pattern.
Verbatim: "She dug a ditch, covered it with a stone, and there gave birth to twins who afterwards became dragon-killers" (¶620).

occurrences.title: Snake bites the patient in the genital region — Zürich dream
occurrences.label: Snake bites the patient in the genital region
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: the moment he felt the impulse to go forward he also felt the pull of the bond to the mother.
body: The dream struck "at the moment when the patient was convinced of the truth of the analysis and was beginning to free himself from the bonds of his mother-complex" — the pull of the bond striking precisely as he "felt the impulse to go forward." Jung: "Being bitten in the genital region by a snake … reminds us of Attis, whose self-castration was occasioned by his mother's jealousy" (¶585). Companion reports: the woman filled with an enormous snake, the woman with a snake stuck in her throat.

occurrences.title: Man castrated by a serpent — Rubens' Last Judgment
occurrences.label: Man castrated by a serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "A similar motif can be found in a Rubens' Last Judgment (pl. LXIV), where, in the foreground, a man is being castrated by a serpent. This motif illustrates the meaning of the end of the world" (¶681).

Jung's reading makes the painting's castration-by-serpent the eschatological image of psychological change: "The fantasy of world conflagration, of the cataclysmic end of the world in general, is the projected primordial image of the great transformation, the enantiodromia of life into death, which Rubens represents as emasculation by the serpent" (¶681). The consuming change that dissolves "the phenomenal world of individual psychic existence" originates in the unconscious and announces itself in dreams and premonitions — the more unwilling the ego, the more frightening the symbols. Pair with the Verona Priapus (¶680), the classical twin of the motif.
Verbatim: "a man is being castrated by a serpent. This motif illustrates the meaning of the end of the world" (¶681).

occurrences.title: Cecrops, half snake half man, beneath the Parthenon — Athens
occurrences.label: Cecrops, half snake half man, beneath…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Above his subterranean dwelling rose the Parthenon, the temple of the virgin goddess.
body: "Clear traces of the original identity of hero and snake" (¶594): the buried snake-king under the temple of the virgin goddess; above his subterranean dwelling rose the Parthenon. The flaying of the god (Aztec ceremonies) "is intimately bound up with the snake-like nature of the hero" (¶594).

occurrences.title: Chnuphis / XNOUMIS serpent, seven- and twelve-rayed — Gnostic gems
occurrences.label: Chnuphis / XNOUMIS serpent, seven…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The Agathodaimon serpent on Gnostic gems also has seven or twelve rays about its head (figs 203–5).
body: Gnostic gems and amulets showing the Agathodaimon serpent: fig. 203 the Chnuphis serpent with a seven-rayed crown; fig. 204 a lion-headed, twelve-rayed XNOUMIS serpent over an altar-stone.

Jung adduces them as the antique serpent-photism behind Sapientia's crown of seven (or twelve) stars in the Aurora-Rosarium line: "The Agathodaimon serpent on Gnostic gems also has seven or twelve rays about its head." Seven answers the seven planets/metals and the seven spirits of God; twelve the zodiac and the apostles. The serpent's ray-crown carries the same sidereal numerology the alchemists transferred to the lapis.
Cf. the seven-headed serpent of fate on the seal of St. Servatius, Maastricht (fig. 205) — the seven-starred Sapientia of aurora-consurgens-sapientia-dei-14c.

occurrences.title: 'Thou risest up like the sacred snake' — Hathor temple, Dendereh
occurrences.label: Thou risest up like the sacred snake
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Inscription on the temple of Hathor at Dendereh: 'The sun, who has existed from the beginning, rises up like a falcon out of the midst of his lotus-bud... Thou risest up like the sacred snake as a living spirit, creating the beginnings and shining in thy glorious form in the barge of the sunrise... Coming as one, he multiplies himself a millionfold when the light goes forth from him in the form of a child' (cw14 ¶483). Jung: 'The comparison of the god to a snake reminds us of his chthonic form in the underworld, just as the rejuvenated phoenix (falcon) first takes the form of a worm' (¶483). The snake as the god's renewing form passed into Christian allegory (John 3:14) and 'was readily seized on by the alchemists' (¶483).

occurrences.title: Zosimos' resume: the dragon guarding the round temple of one stone (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' resume — the dragon guarding the round…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The resume (prooimion) Jung places at the end of the visions: "build a temple from a single stone... with neither end nor beginning in its construction... Note carefully on what side is the entrance to the temple... A dragon lies at the entrance, guarding the temple. Lay hold upon him; immolate him first; strip him of his skin, and taking his flesh with the bones, separate the limbs; then... make a step of them, mount thereon, and enter, and you will find what you seek" (cw13 ¶87). The priest within, first brazen, then silver, then golden man.

Jung: the sacrificed is the uroboros serpent, "whose circular form is suggested by the shape of the temple, which has 'neither beginning nor end'"; the temple of a single stone paraphrases the lapis; dismembering = dividing the chaos into four. "The dragon, or serpent, represents the initial state of unconsciousness" whose sacrifice opens the way to the head (¶118).

occurrences.title: Patient who became a snake and crawled into her mother (cw05 ¶676)
occurrences.label: Patient who became a snake and crawled…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: undated patient fantasy (~1911-12 writing period; inferred)
body: Immediately after the Gabricus-Beya legend Jung writes: "Such fantasies are not uncommon among patients. Thus one patient of mine had the fantasy that she was a snake which wound itself round her mother and finally crawled right into her" (¶676).

The clinical twin of the alchemical coniunctio: the patient as serpent (serpens mercurialis in the making) embracing and then entering the mother's body — regression depicted as a voluntary return into the womb, with the snake as the shape of the libido that gets itself swallowed. Jung introduces it to prove that alchemical fantasies of dissolving into the partner's body "are not uncommon among patients," tying the Latin corpus to living psychology. Compare the same chapter's Jonah-and-the-Whale complex (¶54/654): fear of incest turning into fear of being devoured — here turned inside out as desire.
Verbatim: "she was a snake which wound itself round her mother and finally crawled right into her" (¶676).

occurrences.title: The devil as four-horned serpent — Dorn's warlike quaternity
occurrences.label: The devil as four-horned serpent
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn 'saw in the quaternity the absolute opposite of the Trinity, namely the female principle, which seemed to him "of the devil," for which reason he called the devil the "four-horned serpent"' (cw14 ¶238). 'The devil, he thought, was the binarius itself, since it was created on the second day of Creation, on Monday, the day of the moon' (¶238). Later: the battle of copper and quicksilver (Turba Sermo 42) is the vicious quaternity 'which the devil, after his fall from heaven, sought to "infix" in the mind of man'; Dorn 'puts the motif of war on a moral plane and thereby approximates it to the modern concept of psychic dissociation' (cw14 ¶494). Jung: 'This insight must have given him a glimpse into the core of the problem' (¶238).

occurrences.title: Gilgamesh robbed of the magic herb by the demon-serpent
occurrences.label: Gilgamesh robbed of the magic herb…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Old Babylonian version ~1800 BCE (Sumerian tales older)
body: Returning from the Western Land with the herb of immortality (Jung's pl. XIX), Gilgamesh bathes; the demon-serpent robs the treasure and sloughs its skin — mortality stays with man. Jung uses it as the mythological form of a lament of failure: "as once Gilgamesh... was robbed of his treasure by the demonserpent, so Hölderlin's poem dies away in a painful lament, which tells us that his descent to the shadows will be followed by no resurrection in this world" (¶642). The serpent frustrates the hero's rebirth and keeps the renewal for itself — the chthonic power claiming the treasure hard to attain.

In the same chapter the Epic supplies the hero's shadow-brother: the horse that dies first in the Miller drama corresponds to "the early death of the half-bestial Enkidu, friend and brother of Gilgamesh" (¶659); later "Gilgamesh and Enkidu" name the centaur-unit of ego and shadow (¶678).
Verbatim: "robbed of his treasure by the demonserpent" (¶642).

image.title: Tablet XI or the Flood Tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh, currently housed in the British Museum in London

occurrences.title: 'It is God's animal' — the green-blue-white snake of Spielrein's patient (Zurich)
occurrences.label: It is God's animal'
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Spielrein's patient on her snake: "It is God's animal, it has such wonderful colours: green, blue, and white. The rattlesnake is green; it is very dangerous.… The snake can have a human mind, it can have divine judgment; it is a friend of children. It would save the children who are needed to preserve human life" (¶677).

Jung cites it in the chapter's final snake-survey: the snake of the same case had also announced "God pierces the earth with his ray" (¶638, see sun-sunbeam-pierces-earth-spielrein-patient-zurich). Here the serpent is explicitly numinous and rational — "divine judgment" — the regenerative instrument: "The significance of the snake as an instrument of regeneration is unmistakable" (¶677, cf. fig. 37). Green, blue, white: life-colour plus the spirit-colours — the same green Jung assigns to Chiwantopel's fatal viper and to the anima (¶678).
Verbatim: "It is God's animal, it has such wonderful colours: green, blue, and white" (¶677).

occurrences.title: The golden serpent let down into the bosom of the consecrated — Rome / Alexandria
occurrences.label: The golden serpent let down into the bosom…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. CE (Clement) and ~4th c. CE (Firmicus), describing one rite-type
occurrences.quote: aureus coluber in sinum demittitur consecratis et eximitur rursus ab inferioribus partibus atque imis.
body: Two independent testimonies to the same rite-type. Clement, mocking the mysteries, says the god "through the womb" is a dragon, dragged through the womb of the initiated; Firmicus describes the golden serpent let down into the bosom of the consecrated and drawn out again "from the lower parts and from below." The serpent-god passes through the initiate's body as through a birth canal — descent into the body and emergence as second birth.
Jung cites both in the mother-chapter's note on entering the womb as the salvific act, immediately beside the Hermes "as children come into the womb of women" papyrus.

occurrences.title: Coiled granite snake with coin-slit as offering box — Ptolemaïs
occurrences.label: Coiled granite snake with coin-slit…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Fear of the deadly maternal womb has become the guardian of the treasure of life.
body: The Archaeopteryx of the poor-box: the chthonic snake-pit of the Asclepieia (fed with pelanoi, cf. the Cos pit with its square slot) fossilized into a stone serpent guarding a slot for coins. Jung's aphorism over the find: "Here the serpent lies on the treasury as protector of the hoard. Fear of the deadly maternal womb has become the guardian of the treasure of life" (¶578).

occurrences.title: The green snake that wanted to kiss — Jung's patient (cw05 ¶677)
occurrences.label: The green snake that wanted to kiss
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: undated patient report (~1911-12 writing period; inferred)
body: "The snake that killed the hero is green. So was the snake of another patient, who said: 'Then a little green snake came up to my mouth, it had the finest, loveliest feeling—as if it had human reason and wanted to tell me something—just as if it wanted to kiss me'" (¶677).

The exchange with the Chiwantopel viper is exact and unsettling: the same green snake that stings the hero to death here approaches the patient's mouth with "the finest, loveliest feeling" — deadly and tender at once. Jung lets the parallel stand uninterpreted beyond "The significance of the snake as an instrument of regeneration is unmistakable" (¶677): the serpent is the transformative numen, and its affective colour is eros, not only terror. See ¶678 for the identification of the green snake with the anima, "the archetype of life itself."
Verbatim: "as if it had human reason and wanted to tell me something—just as if it wanted to kiss me" (¶677).

occurrences.title: The lizard in the Haoma tree — Bundahishn XVIII
occurrences.label: The lizard in the Haoma tree — Bundahishn XVIII
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Pahlavi cosmology (West, Pahlavi Texts p. 65); Persian
occurrences.quote: The evil spirit has formed therein, among those which enter as opponents, a lizard as an opponent in that deep water, so that it may injure the Hôm
body: In the Zoroastrian Bundahishn, at the crown of the cosmic tree in the deep water grows the Hôm (Haoma), the plant of immortality; the evil spirit "has formed therein, among those which enter as opponents, a lizard as an opponent in that deep water, so that it may injure the Hôm" — the immortalizing tree guarded and gnawed by its built-in serpent-adversary.

Jung's footnote draws the exact alchemical parallel: "In alchemy, the spiritus mercurii that lives in the tree is represented as serpent, salamander, or Melusina," and points to the Ripley Scrowle, where the lizard is half woman celebrating the coniunctio with the filius philosophorum (fig. 257), quoting "The Serpent of Arabia is my name." The lizard/haoma opposition is the mythic template of the alchemical tree with its indwelling, ambivalent Mercurius-serpent.

occurrences.title: Neophyte fondling the serpent of Demeter — Lovatelli urn
occurrences.label: Neophyte fondling the serpent of Demeter
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The fondling or kissing of the “fear-animal” symbolizes the ceremonial conquest of incest.
body: "The fondling or kissing of the 'fear-animal' symbolizes the ceremonial conquest of incest" (¶530) — the neophyte's hand-to-hand truce with the regressive serpent, echoed at Eleusis' Demeter serpent and the Ophite live-snake kiss (¶584).

occurrences.title: Ignatius Loyola's vision of the many-eyed serpent (Spain)
occurrences.label: Ignatius Loyola's vision of the many-eyed…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 4 to Part II, Introduction (pdf p696); index 'Loyola, St., vision, 122n'

body: In the footnote on wind-gods and creator-gods Jung remarks: "the Persian sun-god Mithras is equipped with an immense number of eyes. It is possible that Loyola's vision of the snake with multiple eyes is a variant of this motif" (cf. "On the Nature of the Psyche," par. 395). The index anchors the vision at book p122n, in the discussion of theriomorphic libido — the serpent bristling with eyes as the all-seeing instinct, kin to the Mithraic many-eyed sun-god.
Verbatim (fn 4): "It is possible that Loyola’s vision of the snake with multiple eyes is a variant of this motif."

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 13 — four snakes, 3 + 1 (Aug 1929)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 13 — four snakes, 3 + 1
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The mandala is laced together by four black and golden snakes, the heads of three of them pointing to the centre, while the fourth rears upwards.
body: After the radiation ceased, the mandala is "laced together by four black and golden snakes, the heads of three of them pointing to the centre, while the fourth rears upwards." Jung: "The breaking down of the quaternity into 3 plus 1 is in accord with the archetype" — an instance of the axiom of Maria, alongside Horus' four (or 3+1) sons, Ezekiel's four figures, the four evangelists, and the three synoptic gospels plus John (¶612 n. 169). The full moon outside radiates rainbow-coloured rings; spermatozoon motifs appear between snakes and centre.

occurrences.title: The Naassene serpent and the horn of the one-horned bull — Hippolytus
occurrences.label: The Naassene serpent and the horn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus' report of the Naassenes: the serpent dwells in all things, "all temples were named after her (ναοὺς ἀπὸ τοῦ ναάς)," every shrine, initiation, and mystery is dedicated to her; she is the moist element (as Thales said) without which nothing exists. And decisively for the unicorn chapter: "all things are subject to her … she is good and has something of everything in herself as in the horn of the one-horned bull [ἐν κέρατι ταύρου μονοκέρωτος]. She imparts beauty and ripeness to all things" (¶528).

Jung: "Like the alicorn, therefore, the serpent is an alexipharmic and the principle that brings all things to maturity and perfection" — the same ripening function alchemy assigns to Mercurius, "the salvator and servator" (¶529). The same primal being is named Osiris ("heavenly horn of the moon"), Sophia, Adam, "many-formed Attis."

occurrences.title: The shepherd who bites off the serpent's head — Nietzsche's vision (Zarathustra)
occurrences.label: The shepherd who bites off the serpent's head
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1884 (Zarathustra Part III, 'On the Vision and the Riddle')
occurrences.quote: No longer a shepherd, no longer a man, but a transfigured being with light all about him, who laughed!
body: Jung's reading: the snake is "the unconscious psyche which, like the snake-god in the Sabazios mysteries, crawls into the mouth of the celebrant" — here Nietzsche himself as poimen, "the shepherd of souls and preacher" — to make him entheos; but "fear was swifter and more violent: it bit off the snake's head and spat it out" (¶586). The compensation dished, the wild hysterical laughter, and the insoluble case where "the compensation appears in a form that cannot be accepted" (¶587).

occurrences.title: Snake-shaped chariot gods — black temple of Puri
occurrences.label: Snake-shaped chariot gods — black temple of Puri
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: 'The chariot-driving, snake-shaped gods of southern India, for instance on the immense black temple at Puri, which is itself a chariot of stone' (cw14 ¶266). Jung adduces it as an eastern parallel to the Nous-serpent enthroned on the chariot in the Tractatus Aristotelis, while denying direct influence: 'another model closer to hand' is Ezekiel's Merkabah (¶266). The stone chariot-temple makes the god's vehicle architectural: the serpent-god rides a totality-symbol built in stone.

occurrences.title: Ra stung by Isis' serpent and robbed of his true name — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.label: Ra stung by Isis' serpent and robbed…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The poisonous worm is a deadly instead of an animating form of libido. The “true name” is Ra’s soul and magic power (his libido).
body: Isis kneads the god's spittle into a spear-like worm and lays it on Ra's path; the aging sun is poisoned and only the mother can cure him. Ra surrenders his true name — "Ra's soul and magic power (his libido)" — and is "fulfilled to the letter" in the transference: "the aging god returns to the heavenly cow, the symbol of the mother" (¶455). Jung's master-text for the poisonous mother and the treasure of the secret name.

occurrences.title: Dream of the red worm encircling the leg (patient: girl of six, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Dream of the red worm encircling the leg
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [18], ref. book p245 ≈ pdf p278 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A six-year-old girl dreamed of a red worm encircling her leg. The index files it twice: "worm: red, dream of, 245" and under "entwining, 245" — the worm as serpent-form binding the child's body, in Jung's corpus of child material on the serpent as instinct and the mother's numen.
Verbatim (case-index): "Six-year-old girl who dreamed of red worm encircling leg. — 245"

occurrences.title: The god through the lap — golden snake drawn across the initiates (Sabazius mysteries)
occurrences.label: The god through the lap
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the god entered his devotees as if through the female genitals
body: Arnobius: "A golden snake is let down into the lap of the initiates and is drawn out again from below." Orphic hymn 52 invokes Bacchus as hypokolpie, "lying in the lap" — "which suggests that the god entered his devotees as if through the female genitals" (¶530). The mystery-snake that can degenerate into the orgy (¶584).

occurrences.title: Dream: the Saviour on the way to Golgotha turns into a snake (or crocodile)
occurrences.label: Dream: the Saviour on the way…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: n/a (Jung's clinical material, reported in Aion)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In a footnote to the 7 B.C. conjunction discussion Jung reports: "A characteristic dream of this sort is the following: The dreamer was watching a Passion play in the theatre. On the way to Golgotha, the actor taking the part of the Saviour suddenly changed into a snake or crocodile".

Its frame: "The Cross with a snake on it, instead of the Crucified, is often found in medieval times [Psychology and Alchemy, fig. 217], and also in the dreams and fantasy-images of modern people who know nothing of this tradition" — spontaneous re-emergence of the serpent-for-Redeemer equivalence.

occurrences.title: Fantasy of the snake crawling into the mother (patient: woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Fantasy of the snake crawling into the mother
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [27], ref. book p436 ≈ pdf p469 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A female patient had a fantasy of a snake crawling into her mother (case [27], book p436). With its companion case [28] (snake into the mouth) it belongs to Jung's material on the serpent as "instrument of sacrifice and regeneration, 436f" — the snake entering the mother's body as insemination and return to the womb at once.
Verbatim (case-index): "Female patient who had fantasy of snake crawling into her mother. — 436"

occurrences.title: The snake that crawled into the mouth (patient: woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: The snake that crawled into the mouth
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [28], ref. book p436f ≈ pdf p469-470 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A female patient said a snake had crawled into her mouth (case [28], book p436f). The index ties mouth to re-entry into the mother ("re-entry into mother through, 419") and files "snake in, 378f, 436f" under mouth — the serpent swallowed as ingestion of the numen, kin to the snake-kiss ("snake-kiss, 376, 378").
Verbatim (case-index): "Female patient who said that snake crawled into her mouth. — 436f"

occurrences.title: The snake stuck in the throat (patient: woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: The snake stuck in the throat
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [24], ref. book p378 ≈ pdf p411 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A patient complained of a snake stuck in her throat (case [24], book p378). The index files "throat, snake stuck in, 378" under mouth: the serpent lodged at the organ of speech — the instinctual (snake) blocking the word. It is one of the companion snake-cases Jung reports with the genital snake-bite dream of ¶585.
Verbatim (case-index): "Patient who complained of a snake stuck in her throat. — 378"

occurrences.title: Franz Stuck, 'Sin' (Die Sünde) — Munich, 1893
occurrences.label: Franz Stuck, 'Sin' (Die Sünde) — Munich, 1893
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The famous snake-woman painting, reproduced as Plate X. Jung cites it in his catalogue of the serpent's dream-roles: the snake creeps into the mouth, bites the breast "like Cleopatra's legendary asp," or appears "in the role of the paradisal serpent, or in one of the variations of Franz Stuck, whose snake-pictures bear significant titles like 'Vice,' 'Sin,' or 'Lust'" (¶8).

His reading: "The mixture of anxiety and lust is perfectly expressed in the sultry atmosphere of these pictures" — the serpent as the seductive principle in woman, a coupling Jung finds again in the old painters' feminine Eden-serpent (fig. 8, ¶155) and in the snake-faced maidens of the Mithraic liturgy (¶155). Adjacent in the text: Mörike's "Girl's First Love Song" (eel/snake in the net).

image.title: The Sin label QS:Len,"The Sin" label QS:Lpl,"Grzech" label QS:Lde,"Die Sünde"

occurrences.title: The medicine-woman with a twenty-foot boa familiar — Natal
occurrences.label: The medicine-woman with a twenty-foot boa…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a medicinewoman in Natal who had a twenty-foot boa constrictor as her familiar
body: A medicine-woman in Natal keeps a twenty-foot boa constrictor as her familiar. Jung adduces it to show "how concretely this mythologem is taken on the primitive level" — in the same note complex where the hero must split, bore, or open the earth, and where the wise-woman/serpent union stands at the mythologem's living edge.
The familiar-serpent of the wise woman is the small-scale, social form of the serpent-mother complex the chapter tracks in myth.

occurrences.title: The snake with a woman's head and a bunch of keys — Oselberg, near Dinkelsbühl
occurrences.label: The snake with a woman's head and a bunch…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In Oselberg, near Dinkelsbühl, there is a snake with a woman's head and a bunch of keys round the neck.
body: A local legend-beast: on the Oselberg there dwells a snake with a woman's head and a bunch of keys about its neck. Jung sets it in the row of German legends where "the maiden in distress often appears as a snake or dragon that has to be kissed" — then changes into a beautiful woman; wise women are supposed to have a fish's or serpent's tail; a king's daughter was immured in the Golden Mount as a snake.
His interpretive sentence is the chapter's thesis: "The dragon in the cave is the Terrible Mother" — the serpent-woman as the enchanted, imprisoned, and devouring feminine in one body.

occurrences.title: Sethians — the ray of light mingled with the dark waters; the unmixing
occurrences.label: Sethians — the unmixing
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Sethian theory of 'composition and mixture': the ray of light from above mingles with the dark waters below 'in the form of a minute spark'; at death — or its mystical figure — the two unmix (¶292). The helpful Mercurius appears with the dividing sword ('I came not to send peace, but a sword'), and each substance is drawn 'to its own place... like iron to the magnet'; the spark 'hastens to the Logos' (¶292). Jung deliberately uses the medieval alchemical Latin — divisio, separatio — to mark the identity of Gnostic and alchemical procedure (¶292).

occurrences.title: The Seven Sleepers in the cave — Ephesus (Decius, c. 250)
occurrences.label: The Seven Sleepers in the cave — Ephesus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: c. 250 (sleep begins); woke under Theodosius II (408-450)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The cave is the place of rebirth, that secret cavity in which one is shut up in order to be incubated and renewed.
body: Seven youths flee the persecution of Decius (c. AD 250) into a cave near Ephesus and sleep 309 years, waking under Theodosius II (408-450); the Qur'an recasts them in Sura 18, "The Cave" (eighth companion a dog; versions of 3, 5, or 7 sleepers). Jung reads the cave as the place of rebirth, "that secret cavity in which one is shut up in order to be incubated and renewed", and the "middle" as the centre where the jewel reposes — the same arrangement as Mithraic altarpieces and the alchemical substance between sun and moon (¶240). The sacred number marks them as gods transformed during sleep into eternal youth (¶242); the same seven sleepers reappear in alchemy as "sleepers enchained in Hades" under the seven planetary stars (¶245 n16).

occurrences.title: The seventh day that has no evening — Augustine's Sabbath of rest in God
occurrences.label: The seventh day that has no evening
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~401-415 (De Genesi ad litteram; De Civ. Dei XI)

jung.locator: Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon ¶301 (pdf p281-82)

body: Augustine's week-symbolism, the theological frame with which "Paracelsus as a Spiritual Phenomenon" ends: the cognitio matutina (scientia Creatoris) darkens into the cognitio vespertina (scientia hominis — "Who is it that knows...? Why, it is myself"), and the Sabbath is "the day on which man returns to God and receives anew the light of the cognitio matutina. And this day has no evening" (cw13 ¶301; City of God XI, viii).
Jung reads the pagan day-names symbolically: darkness peaks on Venus-day, turns Lucifer on Saturn's day, full light on Sun-day — "As Mercurius he is juvenis, as Saturn senex" (cw13 ¶301).
Verbatim: And this day has no evening. (cw13 ¶301)

occurrences.title: Shri-Yantra — traditional Tantric figure (reproduced from Avalon, The Serpent Power)
occurrences.label: Shri-Yantra — traditional Tantric figure
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: traditional form (repr. from Avalon, The Serpent Power, 1913)
body: The Shri-Yantra opens Jung's chapter on mandala symbolism: "this word denotes the ritual or magic circle used in Lamaism and also in Tantric yoga as a yantra or aid to contemplation (fig. 39)." (cw12 ¶122).

Ceremonial mandalas are "figures fixed by tradition… drawn or painted or, in certain special ceremonies, even represented plastically" — against which Jung will set the spontaneous, individually formed mandalas of dreams.

occurrences.title: The Shulamite lapis laments in the nigredo — Abraham Eleazar, Uraltes chymisches Werk
occurrences.label: The Shulamite lapis laments in the nigredo
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O! Adam Kadmon, how beautiful art thou!... Like Kedar I am black henceforth
body: The arcane substance speaks in the first person through the Egyptian-Hellenistic and Song of Songs masks: "Through Cham, the Egyptian, I must pass.... Noah must wash me... in the deepest sea, that my blackness may depart.... O! Adam Kadmon, how beautiful art thou!... Like Kedar I am black henceforth, ah! how long! O come, my Mesech, and disrobe me, that mine inner beauty may be revealed.... O Shulamite, afflicted within and without, the watchmen of the great city will find thee and wound thee, and rob thee of thy garments" (¶43).

Jung's conclusion: "the 'hidden' thing, the invisible centre, is Adam Kadmon, the Original Man of Jewish gnosis... personified by the black Shulamite of the Song of Songs. He is the product of the conjunction of sun and moon" — "its father is the sun, and its mother the moon" (¶44). At ¶185 the same lapis "says: 'But I must be like a dove.'"

occurrences.title: Simia Dei: the demon in the shape of a monkey — Speculum humanae salvationis (14th c.)
occurrences.label: Simia Dei — the demon in the shape of a monkey
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the devil is in fact regarded as the 'ape of God
body: Plate 67: "Demon in the shape of a monkey.—'Speculum humanae salvationis' (Cod. Lat. 511, Paris, 14th cent.)." Jung: "Mercurius, however, had several things in common with the devil… and so the ape once more crops up in the vicinity of Mercurius as the simia Dei" (¶173); and later: "the devil is in fact regarded as the 'ape of God'" (¶181).
The medieval ape-of-God completes the triangle Thoth-baboon (divine) / gibbon (archaic) / devil-ape (diabolical): one animal, three valences of the archetypal Other.

occurrences.title: Simon Magus and his Helen, rescued from the Tyrian brothel
occurrences.label: Simon Magus and his Helen, rescued…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Tyre → Samaria? (Simonian legend reported by the Church Fathers)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Helen of Troy, in her reincarnation, lis rescued from aT yrian brothel by the wise Simon M agus
body: Helen of Troy "in her reincarnation" is rescued from a Tyrian brothel by the wise Simon Magus and accompanies him on his travels (¶64). Jung cites her as the anima's hidden-wisdom face: the same figure who was the cause of a war between two worlds now carries, in her Gnostic reincarnation, the "superior knowledge of life's laws".

Jung's reading: behind the anima's cruel sporting with human fate "there lies something like a hidden purpose"; in literature he instances Rider Haggard's She ("Wisdom's Daughter") and Benoit's Queen of Atlantis with her library containing a lost book of Plato — the anima as bearer of secret knowledge, which appears "only to the person who gets to grips with her seriously".

occurrences.title: Sol and Luna united — 'as the cock the hen' — Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: Sol and Luna united — 'as the cock the hen'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: O Luna, folded by my embrace, / Be you as strong as I, as fair of face. / O Sol, brightest of all lights known to men, / And yet you need me, as the cock the hen.
body: The Rosarium woodcut of the embraced solar king and lunar queen (with verses on their mutual need), which Jung calls "the allegory of the psychic union of opposites."

His reading: the brother-sister pair (Thabritius and Beya in the Visio Arislei) "stands allegorically for the whole conception of opposites — dry-moist, hot-cold, male-female, sun-moon, gold-silver, mercury-sulphur, round-square, water-fire, volatile-solid, physical-spiritual." The king's son is the masculine spiritual principle of light and Logos which, like the Gnostic Nous, sinks into the embrace of physical nature.

image.title: Woodcut depicting the king & queen standing atop a sun & moon

occurrences.title: The solar-phallus vision of the paranoid patient (Burgholzli, 1906)
occurrences.label: The solar-phallus vision of the paranoid patient
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
jung.locator: Wandlungen und Symbole der Libido ¶¶149f., 223 — pin tbd

body: About 1906 Jung found a long-interned, incurable paranoid schizophrenic (state-school educated office clerk) standing at the window, wagging his head and blinking into the sun: "Surely you see the sun's penis — when I move my head to and fro, it moves too, and that is where the wind comes from" (¶105). Four years later Dieterich's Eine Mithrasliturgie (1910) disclosed the close parallel; Jung could not have known the book, and the patient had been committed years before even its first (1903) edition.

Jung's reading: the patient played mystic sage to Jung's neophyte, feeling himself "the sun-god himself, creating the wind by wagging his head" — the ritual transformation into the Deity attested by Apuleius as Helios apotheosis; the "ministering wind" is the procreative pneuma (¶107). The case is his showcase that archetypal visions arise autochthonously.

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: the 'Meridian of the Sun' beheaded (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — the 'Meridian…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the fourth-step vision a figure follows the sword-bearer, "one adorned round about with signs, clad in white and comely to see, who was named the Meridian of the Sun," commanded: "Cut off his head, immolate his body, and cut his flesh into pieces" (cw13 ¶86).

Jung's reading: "The decapitation... therefore signifies the obtaining of the arcane substance" (¶95); the initiate has undergone the solificatio, since "the sun's rays are gathered together in the quicksilver" (Aurelia occulta) — the "Meridian of the Sun" himself represents the arcane substance (¶95). The striking-off of the golden head recurs in the Splendor solis manuscripts and the Rorschach printing of 1598; Apuleius' initiate "dressed like the sun" is the mystery-parallel (fn12, M.-L. von Franz).

occurrences.title: Sophia-Achamoth's fall and the outstretched Christ — Irenaeus, Adv. haer. I, 4
occurrences.label: Sophia-Achamoth's fall and the outstretched…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Enthym esis [reflection] of the Sophia who dwells above, com pelled by necessity, departed with suffering from the Pleroma in to the darkness and em pty spaces of the void. Separated from the light of the Pleroma, she was without form or figure, like an untim ely birth... But the Christ dwelling on high, outstretched upon the cross, took pity on her, and by his pow er gave her a form " (cw13 ¶451). From her affects — sadness, fear, bew ilderment, longing, laughing and weeping — "arose the entire created w orld" (cw13 ¶452).

Jung's psychologem: the myth "describes, in the form of acosm ic projection, the separation of the fem inine anim a from am asculine and spiritually oriented consciousness" (cw13 ¶453); the Greek etektathenta "lays particular em phasis on stretching and extension" (cw13 ¶456); neither light nor dark "notices that their suffering is one and the sam e" (¶456).
Verbatim: departed with suffering from the Pleroma in to the darkness and em pty spaces of the void. (cw13 ¶451ocr)

occurrences.title: Irenaeus — Sophia as dove begets Saturn, identical with Yahweh
occurrences.label: Irenaeus — Sophia as dove begets Saturn…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'The Gnostics held that Sophia represents the world of the Ogdoad, which is a double quaternity. In the form of a dove, she descended into the water and begot Saturn, who is identical with Yahweh' (¶307). Saturn is the 'other sun', the sol niger of alchemy, and here the 'primus Anthropos' who created the first man that could only crawl like a worm. Jung's set-piece for the Gnostic dark side of the God-image: the creator-god is the shadowy demiurge (Saturn/Yahweh), set against the Archanthropos (¶307, ¶367). Her equivalent in the Barbelo-gnosis is Prunicos, 'carrying a burden' and 'lewd'.

occurrences.title: The Kore, 'Mother of Wisdom' — hymn from the Acts of Thomas
occurrences.label: The Kore, 'Mother of Wisdom'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: This maiden, according to the Acts of Thomas, is the “Mother of Wisdom.
body: Thomas' song to the maiden who is "the 'Mother of Wisdom'" (¶561) — the feminine agent of the masculine deity, set by Jung beside Brünnhilde, Pallas Athene, the angel of Yahweh, Vohu Manah, Nabu and Hermes as the deity's "split-off" emissary (¶560, ¶563). The Eucharistic feast of the "secret mother" follows the exorcism of an unchaste demon — "the transformation of a sexual obsession into a recognition of the positive qualities of the feminine spirit" (¶562).

occurrences.title: The golden-winged bird from Kaineus' tree-pile — Lapith battle
occurrences.label: The golden-winged bird from Kaineus' tree-pile
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Once again we recognize the typical elements of a libido myth: original bisexuality, immortality (invulnerability) through entry into the mother (splitting the mother with the foot), resurrection as a soul-bird, and production of fertility (rain).
body: Kaineus — born the maiden Kainis, made invulnerable by Poseidon, worshipped his lance, "descended into the depths, splitting the earth with a straight foot", and when the Lapiths buried him under trees a bird flew up. Jung's formula of the libido-myth: "original bisexuality, immortality (invulnerability) through entry into the mother (splitting the mother with the foot), resurrection as a soul-bird, and production of fertility (rain)" (¶441).

occurrences.title: The soul as a spherical glass vessel — Caesarius of Heisterbach
occurrences.label: The soul as a spherical glass vessel
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Caesarius of Heisterbach (thirteenth century) m entions a vision in which the soul appeared as a spherical glass vessel.
body: The Cistercian Caesarius of Heisterbach "mentions a vision in which the soul appeared as a spherical glass vessel." Jung adduces it in his analysis of the fairytale bottle: the vas Hermeticum was sealed "with the sign of Hermes" (cf. Rev 20:3), had to be of glass and as round as possible, "since it was meant to represent the cosmos in which the earth was created." Transparent glass is "something like solidified water or air, both of which are synonyms for spirit"; the retort is "equivalent to the anima mundi, which according to an old alchemical conception surrounds the cosmos."
He adds the parallel of the "ethereal" philosophers' stone as a precious vitrum (sometimes malleabile), equated with the gold glass of the heavenly Jerusalem (Rev 21:21).

occurrences.title: Sphinx-head hypnagogic vision — Miss Miller
occurrences.label: Sphinx-head hypnagogic vision — Miss Miller
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: After the prayer "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth", Miller sees "the head of a sphinx in an Egyptian setting", which vanishes when she is disturbed.

Jung's reading: the Sphinx "propounds riddles, like the Sphinx of Oedipus, and stands on the threshold of man's fate"; "a semi-theriomorphic representation of the mother-imago, or rather of the Terrible Mother" (¶261, 264) — the enigma that precedes the masculine hero-figure (the Aztec) of the next vision.
Verbatim: After the prayer, "the head of a sphinx in an Egyptian setting" appeared, only to disappear again immediately after. (cw05 ¶261).

occurrences.title: 'The Spirit in the Bottle' — Grimm fairytale KHM 99
occurrences.label: The Spirit in the Bottle
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: I am the great and m ighty spirit Mercurius, and now you shall have your reward. Whoso releases me, him I m ust strangle.
body: The fairytale that opens The Spirit Mercurius and carries the whole essay: a student finds a spirit crying "Let me out!" from a glass bottle buried among the roots of a mighty oak. The spirit names himself: "I am the great and mighty spirit Mercurius... Whoso releases me, him I must strangle." The boy tricks him back into the bottle, receives a healing and silver-making rag, and becomes a famous doctor.

Jung's reading: the fairytale "contains the quintessence and deepest meaning of the Hermetic mystery" (¶239); the forest = the unconscious, the oak = "the prototype of the self, a symbol of the source and goal of the individuation process" (¶241); the spirit = the principium individuationis imprisoned by a Master (God) since the principle of individuation "is the source of all evil" (¶244); the boy's release of Mercurius is "alchemically incorrect" (¶251). Mercurius here = the pagan god identical with Wotan (¶246).

occurrences.title: Spitteler's Prometheus: the rejected jewel picked up by Ahasuerus
occurrences.label: Spitteler's Prometheus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: where Ahasuerus picks it up and puts it into his pocket
body: In Spitteler's Prometheus epic the divine jewel is "despised by the stupid… rejected by everyone from the high priest and the academicians down to the very peasants, and 'in viam eiectus,' flung out into the street, where Ahasuerus picks it up and puts it into his pocket. The treasure has sunk down again into the unconscious" (¶160).

Jung uses the episode as a literary double of the dream's cheap "special water": the water of life, "like the lapis, it is 'pretio quoque vilis,' of little price," prized by no one because "every good thing is always outside and somewhere else, and… the source in their own souls is a 'nothing but.'" A continues an existing line of Spitteler material in the corpus (cf. the Imago figure).

occurrences.title: Actaeon devoured by his own hounds — Diana at the bath
occurrences.label: Actaeon devoured by his own hounds
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: his own hounds, not recognizing him, thereupon tore him to pieces
body: Diana's dark half: "she is also a goddess of destruction and death, whose arrows never miss. She changed the hunter Actaeon, when he secretly watched her bathing, into a stag, and his own hounds, not recognizing him, thereupon tore him to pieces" (¶188).

Jung derives from it "the designation of the lapis as the cervus fugitivus (fugitive stag), and then the rabid dog, who is none other than the vindictive and treacherous aspect of Diana as the new moon" — the mythic source of Philaletha's hydrophobic dog and of the "surprise in the bath" motif shared with the De sulphure parable, where Helios finds Diana and the brother-sister incest ends with both drowned.

occurrences.title: Stag and unicorn as soul and spirit — Lambspringk's emblems
occurrences.label: Stag and unicorn as soul and spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Emblem plate III of Lambspringk's Figurae et emblemata (fig. 240), captioned by Jung: "Stag and unicorn, symbolizing soul and spirit." The stag (cervus fugitivus) and the unicorn alternate as fleeting forms of the transforming substance — Mercurius as the soul-principle chased, captured, and united.

The accompanying poem makes the unicorn's indivisibility the central riddle: "I am the right true Unicorn. / What man can cleave me hoof from horn / And join my body up again / So that it no more falls in twain?" — the One that cannot be divided without perishing, i.e. the unicum of the stone.

occurrences.title: The star and moon as witnesses — Epirus love-song (printed 1902)
occurrences.label: The star and moon as witnesses
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 1902 (printed version, Zeitschrift des Vereins für Volkskunde XII, p. 159)

jung.locator: fn 20 to ch. IV, The Hymn of Creation (pdf p682)

body: "O maiden, when we kissed, it was night. Who saw us? — A bright star saw us, and the moon saw us, / And it leaned down to the sea and whispered the tidings, / And the sea told the rudder, and the rudder told the sailor, / The sailor made a song, then the neighbours heard it, / Then the priest heard it too and told it to my mother, / From her my father heard it and was livid with anger." Jung quotes the Epirote song of many variants to show "how collective the elements in such an experience are": the star and moon as watchers whose knowledge travels down a chain of nature and society.

occurrences.title: Queen Maya's dream: six-rayed star and white elephant — Gandhara relief
occurrences.label: Queen Maya's dream — Gandhara relief
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: fertilization by a theriomorphic symbol, the elephant, who, as Bodhisattva, begets the Buddha.
body: The Buddha's miraculous conception by star, wind ("A wind blew with unknown freshness over lands and seas", ¶491), and the theriomorphic Bodhisattva-elephant (pl. XLIXb, plate at pdf p296). Jung: "In Christian picture-language the unicorn, as well as the dove, is a symbol of the spermatic Word or Spirit" (¶492); the four genies of the quarters answer the Wise Men.

occurrences.title: 'I am a star wandering together with you' — Mithraic Liturgy, hieros logos
occurrences.label: I am a star wandering together with you
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The hieros logos of the papyrus Dieterich published as Eine Mithrasliturgie, in which the neophyte, filled with religious ecstasy, declares: "I am a star wandering together with you and shining up from the depths" (¶130).

Jung's reading: the idea of becoming a god is age-old — old belief relegated it to the time after death, "but the mystery cults bring it about in this world" (¶133). The Isis mysteries parallel: the neophyte crowned with palm leaves, set on a pedestal and worshipped as Helios (¶130, pl. VI). Christian echoes: Hippolytus' "You have become God" (¶132), Psalm 82:6. The stars that float down from the opened sun-disc after the second prayer (¶¶135, 143) belong to the same visionary sequence.

occurrences.title: Feeling of relation to the stars as first symptom (patient: male schizophrenic, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Feeling of relation to the stars…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [25], ref. book p402 ≈ pdf p369 (harvested from index, pdf p580)

body: A male schizophrenic's first symptom was "feeling of relation to the stars" (case [25], book p402n). The index clusters the motif: "star: mystic identification with, 402n", "as brothers, 402", "compulsion by, 67, 415" — the psychotic version of the initiate's kinship with the cosmos ("I am a star wandering with you", Mithraic liturgy).
Verbatim (case-index): "Male schizophrenic whose first symptom was feeling of relation to the stars. — 402n"

occurrences.title: Basuto legend: the hero who became a stone and was thrown across the river (transitus)
occurrences.label: Basuto legend — the hero who became a stone…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "In a Basuto legend reported by Frobenius, the hero is left stranded by his pursuers on the bank of a river. He changes himself into a stone, and his pursuers throw him across to the other side. This is the motif of the transitus: the 'other side' is the same as eternity" (cw13 ¶133).

Jung sets it beside the lapis' incorruptibility: "the ancient idea that the body of a saint becomes stone. Thus the Apocalypse of Elijah says of those who escape persecution by the Anti-Messiah: 'The Lord shall take unto him their spirit and their souls, their flesh shall be made stone, no wild beast shall devour them till the last day of the great judgment'" (¶133). Stone = immortality = the crossing.

occurrences.title: The carbuncle under the unicorn's horn — Wolfram von Eschenbach
occurrences.label: The carbuncle under the unicorn's horn
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "According to legend, this stone may be found under the horn of the unicorn, as Wolfram von Eschenbach says: We caught the beast called Unicorn / That knows and loves a maiden best / And falls asleep upon her breast; / We took from underneath his horn / The splendid male carbuncle stone / Sparkling against the white skull-bone" (¶552). "The alchemists attribute the same qualities to their stone, calling it the 'carbuncle'" — the treasure hard to attain hidden at the point of the tamed beast, taken while it sleeps in the virgin's lap.
The white skull-bone under the sparkling male stone: death's field as the ground of the lapis.

occurrences.title: Estsanatlehi, the turquoise goddess ('the woman who rejuvenates herself') — Navaho
occurrences.label: Estsanatlehi, the turquoise goddess — Navaho
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the days of the great darkness the ancestors saw the Sky Father descending and the Earth Mother rising to meet him; "they united, and on the top of the mountain where the union took place the ancestors found a little figure made of turquoise. This turned into (or in another version gave birth to) Estsanatlehi, 'the woman who rejuvenates or transforms herself'" (cw13 ¶130). Mother of the twin gods who slew the primordial monsters; the sun from the turquoise beads of her right breast, the moon from white shell beads of her left; reborn by rolling a piece of skin from under her left breast; so sacred "that no image may be made of her".

Jung: "This matriarchal goddess is obviously an anima figure who at the same time symbolizes the self. Hence her stone-nature, her immortality, her four daughters born from the body, plus one from the spirit, her duality as sun and moon..." (¶131) — and she "contains the secret of the precious stone."

occurrences.title: The Flint Man of the Iroquois twin-brothers tale
occurrences.label: The Flint Man of the Iroquois twin-brothers tale
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Begotten in a miraculous manner in the body of a virgin, a pair of twins were born, one of whom came forth in the normal way, while the other sought an abnormal exit and emerged from the armpit, thereby killing his mother. This twin had a body made of flint. He was wicked and cruel, unlike his normally born brother" (cw13 ¶132).

In the Sioux version "the mother was a tortoise"; among the Wichita "the saviour was the great star in the south, and he performed his work of salvation on earth as the 'flint man.' His son was called the 'young flint.'" Jung: "In this myth, just as in medieval alchemy, the saviour coincides with the stone, the star, the 'son,' who is 'super omnia lumina'" (¶132).

occurrences.title: Mithras born from the rock (petra genetrix)
occurrences.label: Mithras born from the rock (petra genetrix)
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The stone as the birthplace of the gods (e.g., the birth of Mithras from a stone) is attested by primitive legends of stone-births which go back to ideas that are even more ancient" (cw13 ¶128) — Jung's bridge from the earliest Greek alchemy's stone-God-image to pre-alchemical ethnology (Australian child-stones follow immediately).
The rock-born Mithras, wearing the Phrygian cap and grasping torch/dagger, is the standard Mithraic image of the god springing adult from stone — the saviour who coincides with the stone.

occurrences.title: The Stone 'near to the fire' — Pseudo-Aristotle in the Rosarium philosophorum
occurrences.label: The Stone 'near to the fire'
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Choose for your Stone him through whom kings are honoured in their crowns, and through whom physicians heal their sick, for he is near to the fire.
body: A Pseudo-Aristotle quotation printed in the Rosarium philosophorum (1550, fol. q): the alchemist must choose for his Stone one through whom kings are honoured in their crowns and physicians heal their sick — "for he is near to the fire". Jung cites it in "Concerning Rebirth" (¶238) as the alchemical projection of the inner friend of the soul: the "certain other one within" (aliquem alium internum) of the alchemists' meditatio, exteriorized into a substance. The Stone here is a person to be approached in colloquy, not a reagent — the same grammar as the Tractatus aureus speech and the prayer of Astrampsychos.

occurrences.title: Orestes cured by a stone (Laconia, per Pausanias)
occurrences.label: Orestes cured by a stone
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "For example, the madness of Orestes was cured by a stone in Laconia" (cw13 ¶129; footnote to Pausanias, Descriptio Graeciae).

Jung lists it in the magic-stone cluster: "Zeus found respite from the sorrows of love by sitting on a stone in Leukadia. In India, a young man will tread upon a stone in order to obtain firmness of character, and a bride will do the same to ensure her own faithfulness"; the electors of the king stood on stones "in order to give their vote permanence" (Saxo Grammaticus); "the green stone of Arran was used both for healing and for taking oaths on" (¶129).
The stone heals madness, gives permanence and firmness — the psychically stabilizing function Jung later assigns the lapis.

occurrences.title: Quetzalcoatl, 'priest of the precious stone' (Aztec cycle)
occurrences.label: Quetzalcoatl, 'priest of the precious stone'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "For instance, the mother of Quetzalcoatl was made pregnant by a precious green stone. He himself had the cognomen 'priest of the precious stone' and wore a mask made of turquoise. The precious green stone was an animating principle and was placed in the mouth of the dead. Man's original home was the 'bowl of precious stone'" (cw13 ¶132).

The Aztec cycle gives Jung the fullest American stone-body complex: among the Taos Pueblos "a virgin was made pregnant by beautiful stones and bore a hero son, who, owing to Spanish influence, assumed the aspect of the Christ child"; the Natchez culture hero "changed himself into a stone statue, from which the priestly chieftains of the Natchez were descended"; petrifaction legends of Peru and Colombia point to a megalithic stone-cult (¶132).

occurrences.title: The rock of the mosque of Omar that wanted to fly up with Mohammed
occurrences.label: The rock of the mosque of Omar that wanted…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Mohammedan legend of the rock in the mosque of Omar, at Jerusalem, which wanted to fly up with Mohammed when he ascended to heaven.
body: The Mohammedan legend of the sacred rock in the mosque of Omar, which "wanted to fly up with Mohammed when he ascended to heaven" — the stone seized by the same levitation as the ascending prophet, held down (in the fuller legend) only by an iron nail.

Jung cites it (Part II ch. 2, n. 99) beside the alchemists' insistence on meditation and the volatile's longing to rise: the stone that would fly is the folk-religious twin of the volatile alchemical substance and of the "rock" of the philosophers that must be fixed by art. It belongs with the corpus subtile motifs of ascent (Philalethes' pole-star heart of Mercurius, n. 129).

occurrences.title: The seven eyes of the Lord on the corner-stone — Zechariah
occurrences.label: The seven eyes of the Lord on the corner-stone
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Jerusalem (vision); read as scintillae by the Latin alchemists

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: And they shall rejoice and see the tin plummet in the hand of Zorobabel. These are the seven eyes of the Lord that run to and fro through the whole earth.
body: Zechariah's seventh vision (Zech 4:10): "These are the seven eyes of the Lord that run to and fro through the whole earth"; with 3:9, the seven eyes set on the corner-stone of the new temple. Jung cites the passage (¶245 n16) for the alchemical scintillae — the sparks of light appearing in the dark substance at the end of the nigredo and the beginning of the albedo, where the white stone shows on the vessel's edge "like Oriental gems, like fish's eyes" (Hollandus; Lagneus). The seven eyes connect the Stone with the seven planetary gods the alchemists depict in a cave under the earth (Mylius 1622) — "the sleepers enchained in Hades" (Berthelot), alluding to the legend of the seven sleepers.

occurrences.title: The Stone that speaks — 'Protect me and I will protect thee' (Tractatus aureus)
occurrences.label: The Stone that speaks
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Latin West (ed. Ars chemica, 1566; material Hermetic, older)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: Protect me and I will protect thee. Give me what is mine that I may help thee.
body: In the Tractatus aureus the Stone cries out to the sons of the wise: "Protect me and I will protect thee. Give me what is mine that I may help thee." A scholiast adds that the seeker after truth "hears both the Stone and the Philosopher speaking as if out of one mouth" — and the Philosopher is Hermes, the Stone identical with Mercurius, the Latin Hermes (cw09i ¶238). Jung uses the passage to show the alchemists' colloquy: a two-way address in which the projected transformation-substance answers back. The Stone is "like a teacher mediating between the stone and the disciple".

occurrences.title: 'A stone that has a spirit' — Ostanes' saying on the Nile
occurrences.label: A stone that has a spirit
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Go to the stream ings of the Nile, and there you will find a stone that has a spirit.
body: The Ostanes saying Jung calls "of considerable antiquity (possibly pre-Christian)": "Go to the streamings of the Nile, and there you will find a stone that has a spirit." It grounds the whole doctrine of the animated lapis — spirit in matter — that The Spirit Mercurius builds to: "the lapis is none other than the figure of light veiled in matter" (¶299).

Cited twice: among the oldest witnesses that the arcane substance is spirit (¶264, beside the Isis-to-Horus divine water and Zosimos's incorporeal Mercurius), and again at the essay's climax where Mercurius as φωσφόρος brings "the light of nature, the light of the moon and the stars" (¶299 n.10).

occurrences.title: Sulphur the prisoner in the grove of Venus — 'De sulphure' parable
occurrences.label: Sulphur the prisoner in the grove of Venus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Sulphur is not only the 'medicina' but also the 'medicus'—the wounded physician.
body: An alchemist seeking sulphur comes to the grove of Venus and hears Saturn's voice: Sulphur "is held a prisoner at the command of his own mother" — praised as "the 'artificer of a thousand things,' as the heart of all things, as that which endows living things with understanding, as the begetter of every flower and blossom on herb and tree, and finally as the 'painter of all colours'" (¶140). Jung: "This might well be a description of Eros," imprisoned "because... he had shown himself too obliging towards his mother."

The sequel is the allegory's dream-tableau (¶144): Sal wounds Sulphur with an "incurable wound"; the blood flows as "whitest milk," becomes a river; Diana bathes; prince Sol plunges in and both drown; their souls refuse "bodies so polluted"; the adept finds Sulphur's corpse and pieces of it fail in every hand. Conclusion: "Sulphur is not only the 'medicina' but also the 'medicus' — the wounded physician."

occurrences.title: The Aton reform of Amenophis IV — the sun-disc as sole god (Egypt, c. 1350 BCE)
occurrences.label: The Aton reform of Amenophis IV
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The climax of Egyptian solar syncretism. Local gods — "Amon of Thebes, Horus of the East, Horus of Edfu, Khnum of Elephantine, Atum of Heliopolis" — had all been identified with Ra; the composite Amon-Ra-Harmachis-Atum was invoked as "the only god, in truth, the living one." Then "Amenophis IV... replaced all former gods by the 'great living disc of the sun'" (¶147).

Jung's reading, with Erman: "it was not a sun-god who was adored, but the material sun itself, which, by the hands of his beams, bestowed upon living beings that 'eternal life' which was in him" (fig. 5). Psychologically the reform is "a valuable work of interpretation": the bull, ram, crocodile and pile-dwelling gods are united in the sun-disc, their attributes shown compatible with those of the sun (¶148) — the clearest ancient case of libido-symbols being reduced to a common denominator.

occurrences.title: Christ born on the day the sun was created — De Pascha Computus (~243)
occurrences.label: Christ born on the day the sun was created
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 66 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p693)

body: The De Pascha Computus (Migne, P.L. 4, col. 964; Usener, Weihnachtsfest, p. 5) marvels: "O quam praeclara... providentia ut in illo die quo factus est sol, in ipso die nasceretur Christus" — Christ born on the fourth day of creation, the very day the sun was made. Jung adds the Malachi text behind it — "the Sun of righteousness [shall] arise, with healing in his wings" — and notes: "This image recalls the winged sun-disc of ancient Egypt. (Pl. IXa; cf. also pl. VII)." The companion fn 67 cites the December-25 natalis Invicti: "ipse est sol iustitiae."
Verbatim (fn 66, Malachi): "But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise, with healing in his wings."

occurrences.title: Christ bringing the tree of life, 'INTROITUS SOLIS' — Pisa baptistry
occurrences.label: Christ bringing the tree of life, INTROITUS…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Sol mysticus which was before and will be afterwards
body: The crowning witness to pre-existence: the Baptist's "he was before me" and the Johannine Logos prologue introduce "the annunciation of the Light, of the rising sun — the Sol mysticus which was before and will be afterwards" (¶496). The sun-wheel Christ as the reborn god entering again.

occurrences.title: 'The Moth to the Sun' poem — Miss Frank Miller (train to Paris, 1898)
occurrences.label: The Moth to the Sun' poem — Miss Frank Miller
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The second Miller product: a hypnagogic poem at four in the morning in a hot railway compartment, in which the soul-moth begs one rapturous glance of the sun and dies content. Jung: a condensation "of two things that do not really belong together — firstly the moth which flies round the light till it burns its wings; secondly the image of a tiny ephemeral being... which in pathetic contrast to the eternity of the stars longs for the imperishable light" (¶117).

His amplification digs to the sun-hero, "the 'well-beloved'" (¶146, ¶158), and ends: "For him the dreamer longs with her very soul, for him the 'soul-moth' burns her wings" (¶164). Sources Miller herself named: a philosophical article ("the same passionate longing of the moth for the star, of man for God"), the play The Moth and the Flame, and Byron's "Heaven and Earth" with its flood of unleashed passion (¶¶123, 165-167).

occurrences.title: Sun and moon of oiled paper — schizophrenic dream
occurrences.label: Sun and moon of oiled paper
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Sun and moon, as divine equivalents of the parent archetype, possess a tremendous psychic power that has to be weakened apotropaically
body: The apotropaic trick of the psychosis: "Sun and moon, as divine equivalents of the parent archetype, possess a tremendous psychic power that has to be weakened apotropaically, because the patient is already far too much under the power of the unconscious" (¶576). Same mechanism as the mechanical-dragon rationalization ("It's all a fake", ¶576).

occurrences.title: Hölderlin's 'Patmos' — the sun shatters its rayed sceptre (1803)
occurrences.label: Hölderlin's 'Patmos'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The apocalyptic hymn Jung sets at the climax of his Hölderlin series: "Near is God / And hard to apprehend. / But where danger is, there / Arises salvation also" (¶630). The poet identifies with John on Patmos facing the dying Christ: "For now was put out / The day of the sun, the kingly one, / And himself, divinely suffering, / Shattered the straight-rayed sceptre, / For it shall come again / At the proper time" (¶637).

Jung reads the underlying images as "the sacrificial death and resurrection of Christ, conceived as the self-sacrifice of the sun, which voluntarily breaks its rayed sceptre in the certain hope of resurrection" (¶638) — sceptre-breaking = "the sacrifice of power as previously exercised, i.e., of the libido which had been organized in a certain direction." "Wisdom dwells in the depths, the wisdom of the mother" (¶640); the eagle, "the sun-bird, dwells in darkness" (¶633); the vision of Asia blooms as "the mother-city in the land of eternal youth" (¶637). Yet the poem ends in lament — like Gilgamesh, Hölderlin loses the treasure: no resurrection in this world (¶642).
Verbatim: "But where danger is, there Arises salvation also" (¶630).

occurrences.title: Sun = phallus, moon = vessel — late Roman inscription, Verona
occurrences.label: Sun = phallus, moon = vessel
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: An inscription composed of symbols (sun-disc, phallus, moon-vessel); a second monument from the same collection replaces the vessel with a female figure. The Lajard gem (fig. 19) carries the same code: sun-snake/moon-snake around an androgynous deity.
Jung's reading: "The symbolism is plain: sun = phallus, moon = vessel (uterus)" (¶298) — sun and sex as twin symbolic channels of the libido (¶297).
Verbatim: The symbolism is plain: sun = phallus, moon = vessel (uterus). (cw05 ¶298).

occurrences.title: The sun on the back of his mother the sky — Egyptian hymn
occurrences.label: The sun on the back of his mother the sky
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Thy mother, the sky, Stretches forth her arms to thee.
body: The daily solar hieros gamos: Tum/Atum, "the father of his mother," united each night with the sky-mother; the "pupilla" (child-image reflected in the eye) marks the great god becoming a child again, entering the mother's womb for self-renewal (¶408).

occurrences.title: 'God pierces the earth with his ray' — the solid sunbeam of Spielrein's patient (Zurich)
occurrences.label: God pierces the earth with his ray
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Quoted at the climax of the Patmos analysis — Christ as the sun shattering its rayed sceptre: "Spielrein's patient said that 'God pierces the earth with his ray.' For her the earth was a woman; she also regarded the sunbeam in mythological fashion as something solid: 'Jesus Christ has shown me his love by tapping at the window with a sunbeam.' I have come across the same idea of the solid substance of the sunbeam in other insane patients" (¶638).

The ray as penetrative solid makes visible the libido-symbol chain Jung builds here: sceptre, staff, spear, lance, Thor's hammer that "split the earth and penetrated deep into it" and behaves inside the earth "like the treasure, for in the fulness of time it comes to the surface again, i.e., is born again from the earth" (¶638). The sunbeam-phallus motif returns from above instead of from below — same equation, inverted direction.
Verbatim: "God pierces the earth with his ray" (¶638).

occurrences.title: Symeon the New Theologian's inner sun (Constantinople, c. 1000)
occurrences.label: Symeon the New Theologian's inner sun
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Byzantine mystic's account of the invisible light: his spirit searched "through the air... over the heavens... across the abysses" and found nothing created; then "it came as it was wont, and descending like a luminous cloud, seemed to envelop my whole head... I realized suddenly that it was within me, and in the midst of my heart it shone like the light of a spherical sun" (¶141). Earlier: the Invisible "rises in my poor heart like a sun or circular disc of the sun, like light, for it is a light" (¶140).

Jung's reading: "That the thing perceived as an inner light, as the sun of the other world, is an emotional component of the psyche, is clear from Symeon's words" (¶141) — the mystic's sun as direct perception of one's own libido, undiminished when imparted: "you enkindle fire from fire, and you receive the whole fire" (¶140).

occurrences.title: 'You will see hanging down from the disc of the sun a tube' — Mithraic Liturgy passage
occurrences.label: You will see hanging down from the disc…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The Greek papyrus edited by Albrecht Dieterich as Eine Mithrasliturgie: a religious prescription for incantations naming Mithras, from the Alexandrian school of mysticism, with affinities to the Leiden papyri and the Corpus Hermeticum. Quoted passage: "Draw breath from the rays, draw in three times as strongly as you can... The path of the visible gods will appear through the disc of the sun, who is God my father. Likewise the so-called tube, the origin of the ministering wind" (¶106).

Jung's reading: the invoked fire-/sun-god has close historical parallels "for instance with the Christ-figure of the Apocalypse"; the text is a "representation collective" — and the exact match, four years after the fact, for his 1906 patient's sun's-penis/wind vision (¶¶105, 108-109).

occurrences.title: The weeping evening sun — Mathilde von Wesendonck, 'Grief'
occurrences.label: The weeping evening sun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 28 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p690); index 'Wesendonck, Mathilde von, 93n'

body: "The sun, every evening weeping, / Reddens its beautiful eyes for you; / When early death seizes you, / Bathing in the mirror of the sea.... You awaken anew in the morning / Like a proud conqueror." Jung uses the poem (with a parallel by Ricarda Huch: the earth fleeing the sun into winter night, then "warmly embraced with rosy light / Leaning against the lost consort") to gloss "the heavenly wanderings of the soul": "It is an image of the wandering sun (fig. 3), which from its rising to its setting travels over the world." The same footnote sends the motif back to the Harranite Platonis liber quartorum and forward into the alchemical peregrinatio.

occurrences.title: Swastika on the robe of Fossor Diogenes — catacomb of Peter and Marcellinus, Rome
occurrences.label: Swastika on the robe of Fossor Diogenes
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Rome (coemeterium SS. Petri et Marcellini, Via Appia)

jung.locator: fn 70 to ch. V, The Song of the Moth (pdf p693); index 'swastika, 107n, 247'

body: Jung's footnote collects the sun-symbolism of the Roman catacombs: "there is a swastika (sun-wheel) on the robe of Fossor Diogenes in the cemetery of Peter and Marcellinus. The symbols of the rising sun—bull and ram—are found in the Orpheus frescoes in the cemetery of Domitilla; also the ram and peacock (a sun-symbol like the phoenix) on an epitaph in the Callistus catacomb." The gravedigger's own portrait wearing the sun-wheel — Christian art carrying the pagan solar repertory.
Verbatim (fn 70): "there is a swastika (sun-wheel) on the robe of Fossor Diogenes in the cemetery of Peter and Marcellinus."
Parallels (sun-wheel row): tauroctony-osterburken-monument-germany, mithraic-bull-sacrifice-heddernheim-relief-2c, world-wheel-ixion-sun-wheel-negro-dream-usa, sun-patmos-hymn-holderlin-1803.

occurrences.title: Miss X, Picture 6 — right-turning green swastika (Oct 1928)
occurrences.label: Miss X, Picture 6 — right-turning green swastika
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: The most striking thing is the appearance of a swastika, undoubtedly wheeling to the right.
body: Bright red-green-blue mandala whose most striking feature is a swastika "undoubtedly wheeling to the right" — painted in 1928, before swastikas were publicly current. Jung's rule: leftward = toward the unconscious, rightward (clockwise) = toward consciousness; in Tibet the leftward swastika belongs to the Bon religion, and stupas are circled clockwise (¶565). The picture is linked to the tree-in-workroom dream: the philosophical tree, symbol of the opus = individuation (¶570). The upward, rightward movement rescues consciousness from the darkening background the black snake has left behind.

occurrences.title: T'ang bronze mirror: the pearl of Ch'ien amid the four dragons
occurrences.label: T'ang bronze mirror
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: In China it is Ch'ien—heaven—with the four cosmic effluences radiating from it
body: Plate 61: "The pearl as symbol of Ch'ien, surrounded by the four cosmic effluences (dragons).—Chinese bronze mirror of the T'ang Period." Jung uses it in the Holy-of-Holies argument: "in the interior of the Lamaic quadrangle, and again in the Chinese earth-square, there is a Holy of Holies with its magical agent, the cosmic source of energy… In China it is Ch'ien—heaven—with the four cosmic effluences radiating from it" (¶169).
It is the Eastern counterpart of the medieval Western mandalas with the deity enthroned at the centre — and the very centre our dream 16 fills with a gibbon instead of a god (¶169).

image.title: Tang dynasty bronze mirror with dragon and clouds design

occurrences.title: 'When we can no longer help the sun' — Taos pueblo speech
occurrences.label: When we can no longer help the sun
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The religious leader of the Taos pueblo (the Loco Tenente Gobernador) to Jung: the Americans should stop meddling with their religion, "for when it dies and we can no longer help the sun our Father to cross the sky, the Americans and the whole world will learn something in ten years' time, for then the sun won't rise any more" (¶48).

Jung's reading: the primitive barriers — rites and dogmas as "dams and walls to keep back the dangers of the unconscious, the 'perils of the soul'" — whose collapse lets night fall and "the dark sea of the unconscious break in". Ritual helping of Father Sun is the collective work that keeps the cosmos running; the speech is his prime exhibit for symbol-protection in the 1934 essay.

occurrences.title: Head of Mithras Tauroctonos — Ostia
occurrences.label: Head of Mithras Tauroctonos — Ostia
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The head (cw05's frontispiece, attributed by Cumont to Mithras Tauroctonos) shows the god at the moment of the bull-sacrifice: "The face... is that of a young man of almost feminine beauty... the contraction of the brows and lips gives a strange expression of sorrow" (Cumont, ¶666). Benndorf: the ideal features "wear an extremely sickly expression" (¶665).

Jung reads the face as the exact psychic signature of the tauroctony: "He slays it willingly and unwillingly at once" (¶665) — "the disunity and split-mindedness of the sacrificer: he wants to, and yet doesn't want to. This conflict tells us that the hero is both the sacrificer and the sacrificed" (¶668). The expression, "which we know all too well from our patients as one of sentimental resignation," belongs with the sentimentality-brutality pair typical of the first-to-third centuries; only the animal nature, the instinctual libido, is sacrificed, "always in close analogy to the course of the sun" (¶668).
Verbatim: "The head from Ostia... certainly wears an expression which we know all too well from our patients as one of sentimental resignation" (¶667).

occurrences.title: Mithraic monument of Osterburken (Germania superior)
