occurrences.label: Mithraic monument of Osterburken
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The index lists the Osterburken monument at book p197, in the row of Mithraic monuments Jung discusses between Klagenfurt (196f, pl. XXIVa — instance exists) and Heddernheim (238, 246f, 261, 425 — instances exist). The relief of Mithras tauroctonos from the limes fort at Osterburken completes the set of the German mithraea Jung used for the sacrifice chapters.
Verbatim (index): "Osterburken monument, 197"

occurrences.title: Telesphorus, familiaris of Aesculapius — bronze from Roman Gaul
occurrences.label: Telesphorus, familiaris of Aesculapius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: as kinsmen of the unconscious, they protect navigation, i.e., the venture into darkness and uncertainty
body: Plate 77: "Telesphorus, one of the Cabiri, the familiaris of Aesculapius: (a) Bronze figure from Roman Gaul; (b) Marble statuette from Austria." The hooded, cloaked manikin standing beside the healing god.

Jung reads the Cabiri-dwarfs as "hooded and cloaked manikins who are kept hidden in the dark cista, but who also appear on the seashore as little figures about a foot high, where, as kinsmen of the unconscious, they protect navigation, i.e., the venture into darkness and uncertainty. In the form of the Dactyls they are also the gods of invention, small and apparently insignificant like the impulses of the unconscious but endowed with the same mighty power" (¶203). "El gabir is 'the great, the mighty one.'" They surface in the dream-series as the four children carrying the ring (dream 56).

occurrences.title: 'The Son of God is dead, which is worthy of belief because it is absurd' — Tertullian
occurrences.label: The Son of God is dead, which is worthy…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Tertullian's avowal quoted by Jung: "And the Son of God is dead, which is worthy of belief because it is absurd. And when buried He rose again, which is certain because it is impossible." (cw12 ¶18).

Jung sets it as the limit-case of religious paradox: "the paradox is one of our most valuable spiritual possessions, while uniformity of meaning is a sign of weakness… only the paradox comes anywhere near to comprehending the fulness of life." But "the inordinate number of spiritual weaklings makes paradoxes dangerous" — Enlightenment reason cannot endure them (¶19).

occurrences.title: Tetramorph on two wheels — Vatopedi Monastery, Mt. Athos (1213)
occurrences.label: Tetramorph on two wheels
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: from the depths to the heights… to the mystical homo maximus
body: Plate 65: "Tetramorph (Anthropos symbol) standing on two wheels, symbols of the Old and New Testaments.—Mosaic, Vatopedi Monastery, Mt. Athos (1213)."

Byzantine witness to the imago-lapidis chain: the fourfold original-man figure (man, lion, ox, eagle) standing on the two wheels of the Testaments, "from the bestially archaic and infantile to the mystical homo maximus" (¶173) — the tetramorph as the transformed totality the alchemists sought in the stone.

occurrences.title: The theologian's dark-lake dream (wind over the water)
occurrences.label: The theologian's dark-lake dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
jung.locator: ¶33 (pdf p28) — ¶ marker lost in OCR, reconstructed

occurrences.quote: the mysterious water. And now there occurs the miracle of the pool of Bethesda: an angel comes down and touches the water, endowing it with healing power.
body: A Protestant theologian's recurring dream: standing on a mountain slope above a deep valley with a dark lake; something had always prevented his approach, this time he resolves to go down to the water. As he nears the shore "everything grew dark and uncanny, and a gust of wind suddenly rushed over the face of the water" — panic, and he awoke.

Jung's reading: the descent to the water is the descent into one's own depths; the wind is the pneuma which bloweth where it listeth — the miracle of the pool of Bethesda re-enacted: "Man's descent to the water is needed in order to evoke the miracle of its coming to life". The breath of spirit over the dark water is numinous, "a spookish thing" — paralleled with the Elgonyi "maker of fear" and with the old man of Nietzsche's Zarathustra withdrawing into the forest.

occurrences.title: The second theologian's Grail-castle dream (chasm before the mountain)
occurrences.label: The second theologian's Grail-castle dream
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: Another theologian (fn 26 notes clergymen's professional stake in the "ascent" motif) dreamed he saw on a mountain "a kind of Castle of the Grail" and took the road that seemed to lead straight up. Nearer, he found a chasm: "a deep, darksome gorge with underworldly water rushing along the bottom"; a steep path led down and toilsomely up the other side — the prospect looked uninviting, and he woke.

Jung's reading: "the dreamer, thirsting for the shining heights, had first to descend into the dark depths, and this proves to be the indispensable condition for climbing any higher" (¶40). The prudent man avoids the danger lurking in the depths and thereby throws away the good of the venture. Sits inside ¶40's water-symbolism: "Water is the commonest symbol for the unconscious".

occurrences.title: Theotokos proclaimed — Council of Ephesus, 431
occurrences.label: Theotokos proclaimed — Council of Ephesus, 431
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the archetypal numen of feminine deity... imperiously announced her claim to the title of 'Theotokos
body: Jung's framing of the Marian dogma-line: "Behind this stands the archetypal numen of feminine deity, who, at the Council of Ephesus in 431, imperiously announced her claim to the title of 'Theotokos' (God-bearer), as distinct from that of a mere 'Anthropotokos' (man-bearer) accorded to her by the Nestorian rationalists" (¶237).

The claim matured into the 1950 dogma of the Assumption — "motivated chiefly by the religious need of the Catholic masses" — which for Jung converts "the medieval representations of the quaternity" (Trinity + Virgin) into dogma: the fourth, feminine term completing the Trinity, just as alchemy's Sulphur-Mercurius-Sal triad hides a quaternity in its androgynous middle figure (¶¶235-237).

occurrences.title: Thoth as cynocephalus — tomb of Amen-her-khopshef, Luxor (XXth dynasty)
occurrences.label: Thoth as cynocephalus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: near Der el-Medina, Luxor (tomb of Amen-her-khopshef)
occurrences.quote: its godlike affinities make it an equally appropriate symbol for that part of the unconscious which transcends the conscious level
body: Plate 68: "Thoth as cynocephalus" from the tomb of Amen-her-khopshef near Der el-Medina. Jung: "we have seen from the cynocephalus or dog-headed baboon associated with Thoth-Hermes, the highest among the apes known to the Egyptians, that its godlike affinities make it an equally appropriate symbol for that part of the unconscious which transcends the conscious level" (¶175).

The baboon closes the ape argument's other end: if the gibbon is man as archaic fact (below), Thoth's cynocephalus is the divine ape (above) — the archetype spanning layers beneath and beyond consciousness. The idea was "visibly preserved all through the numberless editions of the Book of the Dead" (¶173).

occurrences.title: A man and woman devoured by the Terrible Mother — Tlingit shaman's amulet
occurrences.label: A man and woman devoured by the Terrible Mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pl. XXXVIIIb: walrus-ivory shaman's amulet showing a man and woman disappearing into a fanged mouth — the devouring maw.

Jung's reading: the mother as murderess/eater of flesh (Hansel and Gretel, the lamias) and "the voracious maw, the jaws of death in which men are crunched and ground to pieces" (¶374); Frobenius' monster devouring even "an entire country, which are all delivered by the hero to a glorious rebirth" (¶369).
Verbatim: b. A man and woman devoured by the Terrible Mother Shaman’s amulet, walrus ivory, Tlingit Indians, Alaska, 19th century.

occurrences.title: Nietzsche's toad dream (Basel dinner party)
occurrences.label: Nietzsche's toad dream (Basel dinner party)
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: fn 1 to ch. III, The Miller Fantasies (pdf p679); cf. index 'toad, Nietzsche's dream of, 34n'

body: At a Basel dinner Nietzsche told the young lady beside him a dream: his hand, laid on the table, grew "a skin like glass, shiny and transparent," showing bones, tissues, muscles — and "All at once I saw a fat toad sitting on my hand and I felt at the same time an irresistible compulsion to swallow the creature." The companion felt "an oracle had spoken to her in a parable." Jung (1952 fn) reads the transparent hand and swallowed toad as prophecy of Nietzsche's disease — "a glimpse, as through a narrow crack, into the dark abyss of his inner self" (Bernoulli, Franz Overbeck und Friedrich Nietzsche, I, p. 72).

occurrences.title: Tractatus Aristotelis: the drunken serpent of materia hypostatica
occurrences.label: Tractatus Aristotelis
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Matter is thus formed through illusion
body: "The serpent is more cunning than all the beasts of the earth; under the beauty of her skin she shows a harmless face, and she forms herself in the manner of a materia hypostatica, through illusion, when immersed in water. There she gathers together the virtues from the earth, which is her body. Because she is very thirsty she drinks immoderately and becomes drunken, and she causes the nature wherewith she is united to vanish" (¶354).

Jung: "The serpent is Mercurius, who as the fundamental substance (hypostatica) forms himself in the water and swallows the nature to which he is joined (fig. 130). (Cf. sun drowning in the Fountain of Mercurius, lion devouring the sun, Beya dissolving Gabricus in her own body.) Matter is thus formed through illusion, which is necessarily that of the alchemist. This illusion might well be the vera imaginatio possessed of 'informing' power" (¶355).

occurrences.title: The crowned king chained to his mother — Tractatus aureus, ch. 4
occurrences.label: The crowned king chained to his mother
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Chapter 4 of the Tractatus aureus: "But the king reigns, as is witnessed by his brothers, [and] says: 'I am crowned, and I am adorned with the diadem; I am clothed with the royal garment, and I bring joy to the heart; for, being chained to the arms and breast of my mother, and to her substance, I cause my substance to hold together and rest…'" (cw12 ¶141).

Jung: the "king" is the lapis — "an interesting parallel to the Monogenes who dwells in the bosom of the Mother-City and is identical with the crowned and veiled Monad." The Rosarium adds: "the philosopher is not the master of the stone but rather its minister" (¶142). At ¶144 the heresy breaks open: the Son "was something that man could produce out of his own nature—with God's help."

occurrences.title: 'We marry the crowned king with the red daughter' — Tractatus aureus
occurrences.label: We marry the crowned king with the red daughter
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The king shall come forth from the fire and rejoice in the marriage. The hidden things shall be disclosed, and the virgin's milk be whitened.
body: The Hermetic Tractatus aureus — regarded as of Arabic origin even in the Middle Ages — describes an Easter-drama in other language: the precious stone cast on the dung-heap, altogether vile; the marriage of the crowned king with the red daughter; the son begotten in the gentle fire; death, darkness, and the waters flee away; "our dead son shall live"; the son reigns in the red garment and the purple.

Jung: "We can take this text as a variant of the mythical God-man and his triumph over death, and thus as an analogy of the Christian drama" — with Christian influence probable but undecidable given the text's unknown age.

occurrences.title: The tree with four-coloured blossoms on the sea — Abu 'l-Qasim al-Iraqi
occurrences.label: The tree with four-coloured blossoms on the sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Abu 'l-Qasim's Kitab al-'ilm al-muktasab describes the philosophical tree's four kinds of blossom — "red, m idway between white and black, black, and m idway between white and yellow" — "Th e four colours refer to the four elem ents that are com bined in the opus" (cw13 ¶402). Its habitat: "The philosophical tree usually grows alone and, according to Abu'l Qasim, 'on the sea' in the Western Land, which presum ably m eans on an island" (cw13 ¶406).
Jung connects the sea-habitat to Persian tradition (Vourukasha) and to the Hesperides' island with its dragon and ambrosia fountain (n.1).
Verbatim: Th e four colours refer to the four elem ents that are com bined in the opus. (cw13 ¶402ocr)

occurrences.title: Alexander finds Hermes' tomb: the tree of glorious greenness and the stork
occurrences.label: Alexander finds Hermes' tomb
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: treatise ascribed to Albertus Magnus (Theatr. chem. II p. 527)
occurrences.quote: Alexander invenit sepulcrum Hermetis et quandam arborem sitam ab extra intus tenentem viriditatem gloriosam: super eam ciconia ibi sedebat, quasi se appellans circulum Lunarem: et ibi ipse aedificavit sedes aureas et posuit terminum itineribus suis idoneum.
body: Alexander the Great comes to the tomb of Hermes and finds beside it a tree "green and glorious within"; on it sits a stork "calling itself the circle of the Moon," and there Alexander "built golden seats and put a fitting end to his travels." Jung glosses: the stork is an avis Hermetis, like the goose (fig. 198) and the pelican — the bird as the self-moving, self-renewing aspect of the arcanum.

The locus condenses the alchemical end-goal: the seeker (Alexander = the heroic ego) arrives at the master's grave and the journey ends where the lunar-solar bird sits in the evergreen tree — the arbor philosophica as terminus of the peregrinatio (cw12 Part II, "journeys to the four quarters" ¶452ff).

occurrences.title: The young ash and the two knights — Lower Saxon world-end legend
occurrences.label: The young ash and the two knights
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Each New Year's Eve a white knight riding upon a white horse comes to cut down the young shoot.
body: A young ash grows unnoticed in a wood. Each New Year's Eve a white knight on a white horse comes to cut down the young shoot; each time a black knight arrives and fights him, and after a long battle the white knight wins and fells the tree. "But one day the white knight will be unsuccessful, then the ash will grow, and when it is big enough for a horse to be tethered under it, a mighty king will come and a tremendous battle will begin: i.e., end of the world."
The tree whose fate is the aeon's fate — the apocalyptic growth of the world-tree guarded by an annual duel of light and dark riders.

occurrences.title: The village aswatha (Ficus religiosa), clothed and pierced — Indian tree worship
occurrences.label: The village aswatha, clothed and pierced
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: he is taking a dangerous step, for he is seeking refuge with the mother whose garment is the garment of death.
body: Tree-anthropomorphism: "every village has its sacred tree (pl. LV), which is clothed and treated exactly like a human being"; trees anointed, garlanded, and pierced through the ear "as an apotropaic charm against death" (¶545). Hiawatha's fungus-coated pine is the death-garment of the same mother-tree (¶546).

occurrences.title: Attis — self-castration under the pine and the annual tree rite (Attis-Cybele cult)
occurrences.label: Attis — self-castration under the pine…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: cult attested at Rome from 204 BCE; legend older
body: "Attis was the son-lover of Agdistis-Cybele, the mother of the gods. Driven mad by his mother's insane love for him, he castrated himself under a pine-tree" (¶659). Every year a pine was garlanded, an effigy of Attis hung on it and cut down; Cybele carried the tree into her cave and lamented — the son taken back into the maternal womb. Ovid: Attis "put off his human form and stiffened into a tree-trunk" (¶661); on the Coblenz bas-relief Attis grows out of the tree (¶662). The priests were eunuch Galloi; the archigallos was named Atys; arm-scratching replaced annual castration — "arm as substitute for phallus" (¶662).

Jung disentangles the overlappings: tree = mother and son's phallus at once; felling = castration = mother-sacrifice; "the impulse to sacrifice proceeds from the mater saeva cupidinum" (¶660). The feast moved from lamentation to joy — "(Good Friday and Easter)" — the Terrible Mother as "counterpart and complement of the Pietà" (¶662).
Verbatim: "Driven mad by his mother's insane love for him, he castrated himself under a pine-tree" (¶659).

occurrences.title: Baruch the 'wood of life' and the Naas — the Gnosis of Justin
occurrences.label: Baruch the 'wood of life' and the Naas
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Gnosis of Justin (Hippolytus, Elenchos V, 26): "the trees in the Garden of Eden are angels, while the tree of know ledge of good and evil is the th ird of the m otherly angels, th eN aas" (cw13 ¶420ocr). The angel Baruch, nam ed the "wood of life", is the angel of revelation (cw13 ¶459).

Jung's reading: the Naas is the prim a m ateria of the Naassenes, "a m oist substance" like Thales' water, dividing like Eden's river into four (n.10); the division of the tree-soul into a m asculine (Baruch) and a fem inine figure "c o rre sp on d s to th e alch em ical Me rc u riu s as th e life p rin c ip le of th e tree, fo r as an he rm a p h ro dite he is d up lex" (cw13 ¶420).
Verbatim: the trees in the Garden of Eden are angels, while the tree of know ledge of good and evil is the th ird of the m otherly angels, th eN aas. (cw13 ¶420ocr)

occurrences.title: Bata's soul on the acacia blossom — the Egyptian tale of the two brothers
occurrences.label: Bata's soul on the acacia blossom
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Egyptian tale of Bata (papyrus of the nineteenth dynasty; Flinders Petrie, Egyptian Tales), the hero "placed his soul on the topm ost blossom of an acacia-tree. When the tree was cut dow n with treacherous intent, his soul was found again in the form of a seed. With this the dead Bata was restored to life"; killed again as a bull, two persea trees grow from his blood, and a chip fertilizes the queen, who bears the reborn Bata as Pharaoh (cw13 ¶401).

Jung: "It is evident that the tree here is an instrum ent of transform ation" (¶401); he notes these transformation processes are omitted in Pritchard's recension (n.4) — a parallel to Christ as "tree cut dow n in his passion" (Cassiodorus) and to the pine of Attis (n.13).
Verbatim: his soul was found again in the form of a seed. With this the dead Bata was restored to life. (cw13 ¶401ocr)

occurrences.title: Das Buch der heiligen Dreifaltigkeit — Codex Germanicus 598 (Munich, 1420)
occurrences.label: Das Buch der heiligen Dreifaltigkeit
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: The Spirit Mercurius, fig. B3 — ¶ pin tbd

body: German alchemical picture-manuscript of 1420 whose central image is the Trinity shown as a tree — the "Holy Trinity" growing as the arbor philosophica — with a famous Rebis (double-being) illustration that Jung reproduces as CW13 fig. B3. In the index Jung cites the manuscript at print p144n, in the Melusina/hermaphrodite region of the Paracelsus commentary.

Verbatim: Munich. Staatsbibliothek. Codex Germanicus 598. 1420. "Das Buch der heiligen Dreifaltigkeit und Beschreibung der Heimlichkeit von Veranderung der Metallen." (OCR noise preserved; "Veranderung" = Verwandlung, "transmutation of metals").
The codex fuses the Christian quaternity-of-God motif ("God is four", cf. Barbelo formula, print 13n) with the philosophical tree — a key Latin-Christian instance of tree as quaternity.

occurrences.title: The tree of contemplation, palm with seven birds — Basel MS
occurrences.label: The tree of contemplation, palm with seven birds
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The treatise "De arbore contem plationis" (Basel UB MS AX 128b) shows the tree of contemplation as a palm with seven branches — matching the seven branches of the tree of the m etals — each branch bearing a bird ("pavo, [illegible], cignus, [h]arpia, filom ena, hyrundo, fenix") and a flower ("viola, gladiola, lilium, rosa, crocus, solsequium "), all of m oral significance (cw13 ¶414).

Jung: "Th ese ideas are very m uch like those of the alchem ists. Th ey contem plated th eir tree in the retort, where, according to the Chymical Wedding, it was held in the hand of an angel" (cw13 ¶414).
Verbatim: so also has the tree of contemplation, as a treatise en titled "De arbore contem plationis" show s. (cw13 ¶414)

occurrences.title: The metallic tree whose branches are the veins of the earth — Dorn, De genealogia mineralium
occurrences.label: The metallic tree whose branches are the veins…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn, "De genealogia m ineralium" (Theatr. chem. I, 1659, p. 574): nature plants "the root of the m etallic tree in the m idst of her wom b, viz., the stone which shall bring forth the m etals"; the trunk divides into branches spread "from Germ any even as far as Hungary and beyond... as in the hum an body the veins spread through the different lim bs". The fruits drop, the tree dies and vanishes, "afterwards... another new [tree]" (cw13 ¶375).

Jung: "Th e tree is obviously th o ught of as a system of blood vessels" whose liquid fruit coagulates — and juxtaposes the Persian Gayomart, whose blood became the seven m etals (cw13 ¶376; see gayomart-metals-original-man-persia). The same treatise calls Aristotle, Albertus, Avicenna tares of "that Greek Satan" who "turned the nam e Sophia in to Philosophia" (cw13 ¶377).
Verbatim: After nature has planted the root of the m etallic tree in the m idst of her wom b, viz., the stone which shall bring forth the m etals (cw13 ¶375)

occurrences.title: The tree in the sea Vourukasha / tree of life at Ardvi Sura Anahita — Bundahish
occurrences.label: The tree in the sea Vourukasha / tree…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Persian legend of the tree that grows in the sea nam ed Vourukasha, and of the tree of life at the fountain of Ardvi Sura Anahita (Windischm ann, Zoroastrische Studien, pp. 90, 171) — the Gaokerena com plex Jung invokes to explain why Abu 'l-Qasim's philosophical tree grows "on the sea" (cw13 ¶406).

The same Iranian field gives the world-tree guarded by a lizard (see serpent-lizard-haoma-tree-bundahishn-9c, cw12) and the three-legged ass standing in Vourukasha (ass-three-legged-ass-bundahish-persia-9c). Gaokerena is the good tree against which the com bative powers of Ahrim anic darkness press — the ambrosia-tree guarded, like the Hesperides' tree, by a hostile guardian.
Verbatim: the legend of the tree in the Bundahish that grow s in the sea nam ed Vourukasha, or of the tree of life that grows in the fountain of ArdvI Sura A nahita. (cw13 ¶406ocr)

occurrences.title: From Anthropos and gnosis is born the tree — the Barbeliots
occurrences.label: From Anthropos and gnosis is born the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Barbeliot system (Irenaeus, Adv. haer. I, 29, 3), the Autogenes creates "the m an perfect and true, whom they also called Adam as", and with him perfect know ledge: "From [the perfect] m an and gnosis is born the tree, which they also call gnosis" (cw13 ¶419).

Jung: "Here we find the sam e connection of m an with the tree as in the case of Adam and the Buddha" (¶419) — Adam m ade of "the earth of the tree of life" (¶418), Buddha shaded by the Bodhi tree. Hegem onius's Acta Archelai gives the parallel: "that tree which is in paradise, whereby the good is know n, is Jesus and the know ledge of him " (n.7). The fire-tree of Simon Magus "is a sim ilar conception" (¶459 n8).
Verbatim: From [the perfect] m an and gnosis is born the tree, which they also call gnosis. (cw13 ¶419)

occurrences.title: God hangs the sword of wrath on the tree — Dorn, Speculativa philosophia
occurrences.label: God hangs the sword of wrath on the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Dorn, "Speculativa philosophia" (Theatr. chem. I, 1659, p. 254): "[God] hath determ ined to snatch the sword of his wrath from the hands of the angel, substituting in place thereof a threepronged hook of gold, hanging the sword on a tree: and so God's wrath is turned in to love" (cw13 ¶447).

Jung: "Christ as Logos is the tw oedged sword, which sym bolizes God's wrath" (Rev. 1:16); the golden trident alludes to the Trinity, and 'golden' is "an alchem ical sous-entendu" (cw13 ¶450). The allegory continues: the hook with which God the Father catches the Leviathan is the crucifix (¶450), of Manichaean origin — see anthropos-bait-manichaean-primordial-man-3c; and the sword-on-the-tree "is alm ost certainly an analogy of the serpent hanging on the cross" (cw13 ¶448).
Verbatim: substituting in place thereof a threepronged hook of gold, hanging the sxvord on a tree: and so God’s wrath is turned in to love. (cw13 ¶447ocr)

occurrences.title: The opus as sowing and nurturing the tree — Jodocus Greverus, Secretum (1588)
occurrences.label: The opus as sowing and nurturing the tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Jodocus Greverus's "Secretum nobilissimum et verissimum" depicts the whole opus as the sowing and nurturing of a tree in a walled garden: soil = purified Mercurius; Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus form the trunk; sun and moon supply the seeds — "not the com mon gold, nor the com mon Mercurius... but [the m etals] of the Philosophers" (cw13 ¶355). A wise old man admonishes the adept: "Son, lay aside the snares of worldly appetites" (¶355). The treatise closes with a hymn calling the art "gift of God, containing the secret of the undivided oneness of the Holy Trinity... testim ony to the resurrection of the dead" (¶355).

Jung reads the planetary names as "(astrological) tem peram ents, that is, to psychic factors" (¶355) and the four-trunk union as the coniunctio tetraptiva over the tetrasomia, "a characteristic exam ple of the dilem m a of three and four" (¶357-358).
Verbatim: Th e whole opus is depicted as the sow ing and nurturing of the tree in a well-tended garden (cw13 ¶355ocr)

occurrences.title: The white haoma on lake Vouru-Kasha, guarded by the fish Kar-mahi — Persia
occurrences.label: The white haoma on lake Vouru-Kasha, guarded…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Avestan texts (composition redacted late; material older)
occurrences.quote: the white haoma is a celestial tree growing in the lake Vouru-Kasha, while the fish Kar-mahi circles round it and protects it from the frog of Ahriman.
body: The Persian tree of life standing in the lake of rain, Vouru-Kasha: its seeds, mixed with the waters, maintain the fertility of the earth — "Those plants I, Ahura-Mazda, rain down upon the earth, to bring food to the faithful, and fodder to the beneficent cow" (Vendidad, via Darmesteter). The white haoma in the spring Ardvisura, water of life, gives "eternal life, children to women, husbands to girls, and horses to men"; in the Mainyo-i-Khard it is the "preparer of the corpse." The fish Kar-mahi circles it forever, guarding it from the frog of Ahriman.

Jung uses it as another form of the mother-tree motif opening ch. V's symbolism of rebirth — tree and water as one generative complex, and the ever-vigilant guardian against the devil-frog as the shadow-attack on life's source.

occurrences.title: The old man rejuvenated in the hollow oak — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: The old man rejuvenated in the hollow oak
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: an old man is changed back into a youth by crawling through a hollow oak-tree.
body: Re-entry into the tree-mother as cure of age — the hollow tree as womb, with the snake-guarded cave and the skin-casting myth as siblings of the rejuvenation motif (¶410, ¶538).

occurrences.title: Tree of life growing from the Father-God's breast — Nelken's schizophrenic patient
occurrences.label: Tree of life growing from the Father-God's…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Jan Nelken, "Analytische Beobachtungen uber Phantasien eines Schizophrenen" (p. 541): in his patient's cosmic system the Father-God bore a tree of life growing out of his breast, with red and white fruits or spheres "which were worlds" — red for sun, white for moon, the alchemical colour-pair — and on the tree-top sat a dove and an eagle, recalling the stork on the sun-and-moon tree of the "Scriptum Alberti" (cw13 ¶460).

Jung's use: "Any know ledge of the alchem ical parallels was q u ite out of the question in this case" — a rare modern exception to his rule that cosmic tree symbolism recedes when individuation is no longer projected into the cosmos (cw13 ¶459ocr).
Verbatim: It bore red and white fruits, or spheres, which were worlds. (cw13 ¶460ocr)

occurrences.title: Man as the inverted tree — Alciati's Emblemata
occurrences.label: Man as the inverted tree — Alciati's Emblemata
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Andrea Alciati (d. 1550), Emblem ata cum com m entariis: "It pleased the Physicists to see m an as a tree standing upside dow n, for what in the one is the root, trunk, and leaves, in the other is the head and the rest of the body with the arm s and feet" (cw13 ¶412). The sam e volume supplies the birth-tree: "a tree is planted at the birth of a child, and its and the child's fates are identical. 'Therefore the tree is the im age and m irror of our condition'" (cw13 ¶350 n1).
Jung's arbor inversa chain runs from the Cabala (Vigenere, Knorr von Rosenroth) through this hum anist em blema to the Indian ashvattha (cw13 ¶412-413).
Verbatim: It pleased the Physicists to see m an as a tree standing upside dow n (cw13 ¶412ocr)

occurrences.title: The Nakassa — East Siberian shamans' inverted tree
occurrences.label: The Nakassa — East Siberian shamans' inverted…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: East Siberia; specimen in the Leningrad Museum
body: Kagarow's photograph ("Der umgekehrte Schamanenbaum ", p. 183) of a sham an's tree nam ed Nakassa, preserved in the Leningrad Museum: an inverted tree whose roots signify hairs, with a face carved on the trunk near the roots — "show ing that the tree represents am an. Presum ably this is the sham an him self, or his greater personality" (cw13 ¶462).

Jung's use closes the shamanic row: "Th e sham an clim bs the m agic tree in order to find his true self in the up per world" — shamanism read as "a projection of the individuation process" (cw13 ¶462).
Verbatim: Th e roots signify hairs, and on the trunk, near the roots, aface has been carved, show ing that the tree represents am an. (cw13 ¶462ocr)

occurrences.title: Nebuchadnezzar as the tree in his dream — Daniel 4
occurrences.label: Nebuchadnezzar as the tree in his dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Daniel 4: the king himself is the tree of the dream — "a tree in the m idst of the earth, and the height thereof was great", its heart made beast-like until seven tim es pass over it (cw13 ¶350 n1: "In the drea m of Nebuchadnezzar the king him self is a tree... a tree is planted at the birth of a child, and its and the child's fates are identical").

Jung returns to it for the fruit "not cast in to the fire" (cw13 ¶374) and lists it beside Zarathustra's vision and Bardesanes among "m an's relationship to the philosophical tree" (cw13 ¶458): the tree as "an interm ediate form of m an".
Verbatim: In the drea m of Nebuchadnezzar the king him self is a tree. (cw13 ¶350 n1ocr)

occurrences.title: The old man eats of the white tree and becomes a youth — Turba
occurrences.label: The old man eats of the white tree…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the father is become the son
body: The Turba's rejuvenation recipe in miniature: "Take that white tree and build around it a round dark house covered with dew, and place in it a man of great age, a hundred years old, and close the house upon them and make it fast, so that no wind or dust can get in. Then leave them for one hundred and eighty days in their house.... that old man becomes a youth. O what wondrous natures, which have changed the soul of that old man into a youthful body, and the father is become the son" (¶76).

Sealed vessel as round dark house, dew-covered tree as the white fruit, 180 days of incubation — the senex/puer renewal cycle set inside the opus. Jung cites it between the Trevisan oak-bath and Senior's grave of Sihoka as part of the tree/tomb/womb complex.

occurrences.title: The animus daemon and the gambler — Figs. 29-30 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: The animus daemon and the gambler
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: n/a (Jung's patient, born in the East)
body: A masculine daemon wakes "with an air of triumph: he is the animus, the personification of m asculine thinking in a wom an" (cw13 ¶339). His sentence "I am the Game of the gambler" points to Bhagavadgita X, 36 ("I am the game of dice") — Krishna as self — but Jung warns the animus "has a Janus face" and "is therefore q u ite unfitted to represent totality": Indian theosophy induced "a kin do f p s y ch o lo g ic al sh or t-circuit, to id en ti fy th ea ni mu s at lea st p ro v is io na lly with wholeness" (cw13 ¶342ocr).

Fig. 30 restyles him as a gnomelike monk with outstretched arms — "a un io n of intellect and sexuality, ju st as the alchemical Mercurius duplex... is a q u atern ity composed of the four elements" (cw13 ¶343). In Fig. 31 the animus "no longer usurps the place of the self, bu t has been transcended by it" (¶346).
Verbatim: he is the animus, the personification of m asculine thinking in a wom an (and of her m asculine side in general). (cw13 ¶339ocr)

occurrences.title: Boy in the tree watching two dragons — Fig. 9 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Boy in the tree watching two dragons
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: An old, huge tree on a tangle of roots; two dragons approach from left and right; a tiny boy has climbed up to watch them. Jung recalls the dragons guarding the tree of the Hesperides and the snakes that guard the hoard: "the modicum of security it [consciousness] has just acquired is liable to be devoured again by the unconscious" (cw13 ¶314).

Yet the tree itself is not threatened — its growth is independent of human consciousness, guarded and dangerous, but protective for whoever "summons up courage enough to climb into the tree despite its guardians" (cw13 ¶314).
Verbatim: T wo dragons are approaching from left and right. In the tree there is a boy who has clim bed up to watch the dragons. (cw13 ¶314ocr)

occurrences.title: Pueblo corn-goddess fastened to the tree — Fig. 25 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Pueblo corn-goddess fastened to the tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A later, differentiated stage of the Fig. 24 painter: the female figure, marked as a goddess by corn-cobs at the cardinal points (bird, tortoise, lion, grasshopper), is fastened to the tree by a snake — "an analogy to the crucified Christ, who, as the self, was sacrificed for earthly hum anity, just as Prom etheus was chained to the rock" (cw13 ¶331).

Jung: "M an's efforts to achieve wholeness correspond, as the divine myth show s, to a voluntary sacrifice of the self to the bondage of earthly existence" (cw13 ¶331). The picture's many divine-myth elements let the painter "discrim inate between ego and self" — the protection against inflation stressed in ¶332.
Verbatim: She is fastened to the tree by a snake, and thus form s an analogy to the crucified Christ, who, as the self, was sacrificed for earthly hum anity (cw13 ¶331ocr)

occurrences.title: Fire-tree growing from water — Fig. 5 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Fire-tree growing from water
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Leafless tree with red flowers, branches tipped with flame, fire leaping from the water out of which it grows — "something like the jet of a fountain". Jung names the alchemical fontina (medieval town-fountain pictures) and quotes the saying "Our water is fire" (cw13 ¶310).
Verbatim: Th e branches are tipped with flames, and fire leaps up from the water out of which the tree is growing. (cw13 ¶310ocr)
The union of fire and water here anticipates Jung's later reading of Mercurius as "both water and fire" (cw13 ¶408).

occurrences.title: Tree on the island in the sea — Fig. 1 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Tree on the island in the sea
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A huge solitary tree on an island, upper crown cut off by the picture edge, buds and white blossoms announcing spring. Jung reads its axial position and solitude as world-tree and world-axis, "a symbol that is universal and alien to the personal consciousness" — evidence that the painter's process has "nothing to do with his personal psychology" (cw13 ¶306). One of 32 pictures, 19 drawn before Jung knew alchemy.
Verbatim: The tree stands by itself on an island in the sea. Its great size is indicated by the fact that the upper part of it is cut off by the edge of the picture. (cw13 ¶306)

occurrences.title: Tree of light as candelabrum — Fig. 3 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Tree of light as candelabrum
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: An abstract tree of light that is simultaneously a candelabrum, its branch-tips burning candles in a dark enclosed space — "perhaps a cave or vault". The plate caption describes a seven-branched candelabrum or Christmas tree whose "lights symbolize the illumination and expansion of consciousness".
Jung: "The secret and hidden nature of the process is thus emphasized and its function made clear: the illumination of consciousness" (cw13 ¶308).
Verbatim: Th e picture shows a tree of light that is at the same tim ea candelabrum. (cw13 ¶308ocr)

occurrences.title: Hollow tree with the locked door — Fig. 13 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Hollow tree with the locked door
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A stylized tree of 4+1 branches — sun in the central branch, stars on the four — hollow inside and shut by a door in the trunk. A bird representing the painter weeps "because it has forgotten the key to the door"; it "obviously suspects that there is something valuable inside the tree" (cw13 ¶318).
The middle branch is snakelike and bears a luminous body like a sun — tree and mercurial serpent still distinguishable before their union in Fig. 12's haloed snake.
Verbatim: The stylized tree has in its trunk a locked door leading to a hidden recess. (cw13 ¶318)

occurrences.title: God's birth from the archaic plant — Fig. 27 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: God's birth from the archaic plant
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A thoroughly Western picture in "the archetypal category of the god's birth from the tree or lotus blossom": a human figure grows from an archaic carboniferous plant whose calyx bears four human heads — "in agreement with the alchemical view that the lapis is composed of four elements" (cw13 ¶336). The woman's head rises "like the pistil of aflower", compared by Jung with the Mithras relief from Osterburken (cw13 ¶404).

Its companion Fig. 28 localizes the dark principle: "The black earth... is now in her body as a black ball, in the region of the manipura-chakra... (T he alchemical parallel to this is the “black sun.”)" (cw13 ¶337) — the shadow integrated as a bodily centre.
Verbatim: Th e hum an figure grow ing out of the archaic plant represents the union and quintessence of the four heads at its base (cw13 ¶336ocr)

occurrences.title: Lotus with the gnome and the corona — Fig. 31 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Lotus with the gnome and the corona
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.place: n/a (Jung's patient, born in the East)
body: The tree of the series has "turned into a blossom ing lotus plant, with the gnom elike figure sitting in the flower, rem in din gus that the lotus is the birthplace of the gods" (cw13 ¶345). The figure's head is encircled by a mandala with a flowerlike centre, wreathed by a corona: the alchemists' corona sive diadema cordis tui, "a symbol of perfection" — "the “golden flower” of Chinese and the “sapphirine flower” of Western alchemy" (cw13 ¶346).
Verbatim: Th e animus no longer usurps the place of the self, bu t has been transcended by it. (cw13 ¶346ocr)

occurrences.title: Sapphire treasure and the uroboros — Figs. 16-17 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Sapphire treasure and the uroboros
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: Fig. 16: a leafless tree full of birds guarding a dark blue sapphire hidden in its roots — "the sapphirine flower" of the alchemists, linked by Jung (not the painter) to Ezekiel's sapphire and to Grimm's bottle-elf in the oak's roots, "which contained the spirit Mercurius" (cw13 ¶321). Fig. 17, a later and more differentiated version: a blossoming tree grows from a magic circle enclosing the uroboros with the sapphire at its centre — "Hermaphroditi flos saphyricus", the self-devouring dragon that "begot and gave birth to itself" (cw13 ¶322).
Verbatim: They therefore called the sapphirine flower (i.e., the lapis) “H erm aphroditi flos saphyricus.” (cw13 ¶322ocr)

occurrences.title: Sun-quaternity watered by four rivers — Fig. 24 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: Sun-quaternity watered by four rivers
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The female figure has taken the place of the tree; the sun disk becomes a symbol of individuation "characterized as such by the quaternity fed by four different-coloured rivers flowing down from four mountains, and flanked by four animals. The scene is paradisal". The four "heavenly or metaphysical" mountains already appeared in Fig. 6 and in Psychology and Alchemy figs. 62 and 109 (cw13 ¶329).
Jung's aside on the number four: "there are no t three or, for that matter, five directions, bu t precisely four" (cw13 ¶330).

Verbatim: Th e quaternary elem ents in our picture, as well as accentuating the light-symbol, am plify it in such away that... an acceptance of wholeness by the little female figure, an intuitive apprehension of the self. (cw13 ¶330ocr)

occurrences.title: The tree-born woman emerging — Fig. 22 of the patient picture series
occurrences.label: The tree-born woman emerging
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: The sleeping figure of Figs. 20-21 awakens and half emerges from the tree-trunk, making contact with the animal world: a snake whispers in her ear, and "bird, lion, lam b, and pig com plete the paradisal scene". Jung: the tree-born is "not only as a c h ild of na tu re bu t as an a u to c h th on o us prim o rd ia l be in g" (cw13 ¶327ocr by design).

The tree nymph is "an Eve who, in stead of be in g taken fro mA da m's side, has come in to ex isten ce in de p en d en tly" — the symbol compensates "the bib lic al my th of th e seco n d ary c re a tio nof Eve" (cw13 ¶327). The same motif recurs ethnographically in the Yakut birth-tree (cw13 ¶461).
Verbatim: Th e tree n ym p h is an Eve who, in stead of be in g taken fro mA da m ’s side, has come in to ex isten ce in de p en d en tly. (cw13 ¶327ocr)

occurrences.title: Dream of being poisoned by the fruit of a tree (patient: young woman, Zürich)
occurrences.label: Dream of being poisoned by the fruit of a tree
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.locator: case-index [17], ref. book p221 ≈ pdf p188 (harvested from index, pdf p579)

body: A young woman with sexual marital difficulties dreamed of being poisoned by the fruit of a tree. Jung's case-index (Cases in Summary, [17]) anchors it at book p221, inside the mother-symbolism chapters: the tree as mother — its fruit poisoned, sexuality turning the nourisher deadly. The index glosses the tree entry directly: "dream of being poisoned by fruit of, 221."
Verbatim (case-index): "Young woman with sexual marital difficulty who dreams of being poisoned by fruit of a tree. — 221"

occurrences.title: The tree in the lands of the West growing on the ocean — Abu'l Qasim al-'Iraqi
occurrences.label: The tree in the lands of the West growing…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The Arabic alchemists likewise obtain their prima materia from the tree in the western land. We read in the book of Abu'l Qasim: This prime matter which is proper for the form of the Elixir is taken from a single tree which grows in the lands of the West. … And this tree grows on the surface of the ocean as plants grow on the surface of the earth. This is the tree of which whosoever eats, man and jinn obey him; it is also the tree of which Adam (peace be upon him!) was forbidden to eat … And this tree may be changed into every animal shape" (¶537).

Jung pairs it with the ass in the ocean and the tree Gokard ("both are or have mana," ¶537), and with the verse-shifting power of "Mercurius versipellis" (¶538): tree, beast, and monster are one elixir-substance.

occurrences.title: The Ripley Scrowle — 'Four Rolls Drawn in Lubeck' (BM MS Sloane 5025)
occurrences.label: The Ripley Scrowle
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: drawn in Lübeck, 1588 → London, British Museum (MS Sloane 5025)

jung.locator: The Spirit Mercurius, fig. B5 — ¶ pin tbd

body: Emblematic scroll of the George Ripley tradition: a bird-and-flask picture chain wound around the "tree" of the opus, drawn in Lübeck in 1588 and preserved as British Museum MS Sloane 5025. Jung reproduces it as CW13 fig. B5 and cites it across "The Spirit Mercurius" and "The Philosophical Tree" (index: print 199n, 212, 286n, 303, 306n, 317), reading its beast-and-bird hermaphrodite sequence as a Mercurius transformation series on a tree.

Verbatim: London. British Museum. MS. Sloane 5025. 1588. "Four Rolls Drawn in Lubeck" (The Ripley Scrowle). The verses ("Emblematicall Scrowle") are printed in Ashmole's Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum (1652), ii.

occurrences.title: The tree of the Sefiroth as inverted world-tree — Cabala
occurrences.label: The tree of the Sefiroth as inverted world-tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Sulzbach (Knorr von Rosenroth); via Vigenere, Paris
body: Vigenere quotes "Rabbi, the son of Josephus Carnitolus": "The foundation of every lower structure is affixed above and its sum m it is here below, like an inverted tree" (cw13 ¶411; De igne et sale). "Vigenere had som e know ledge of the Cabala and is here com paring the philosophical tree with the tree of the Sefiroth, which is actually a m ystical w orld-tree. But for him this tree also signifies m an" — im planted in paradise by the roots of his hair (Song of Songs 7:5).

Knorr von Rosenroth (Kabbala denudata): the "great tree" refers to Tifereth, bridegroom of M alchuth; the upper Sefira Binah is nam ed "the root of the tree", the linea m edia through which "it brought life dow n to earth from Binah" (cw13 ¶411).
Verbatim: com paring the philosophical tree with the tree of the Sefiroth, which is actually a m ystical w orld-tree. But for him this tree also signifies m an. (cw13 ¶411ocr)

occurrences.title: Seth at the barkless tree of paradise — the skinless snake and the babe
occurrences.label: Seth at the barkless tree of paradise
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The old English legend of what Seth saw in Eden: a shining fountain with four streams, and over it the tree of the Fall — leafless, without bark, with "a naked snake without a skin" coiled round it; looking again, Seth sees it covered in bark and leaves, and "in its crown lay a little new-born babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, that wailed because of Adam's sin. This was Christ, the second Adam" (cw13 ¶400-401).

Jung's note: "The tree's lack of bark and the snake's lack of skin indicate the identity between them" (n.8) — the dead tree of paradise reviving as the tree of Christ's genealogy, whence the cross-wood legend (cw13 ¶446).
Verbatim: in its crown lay a little new-born babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, that wailed because of Adam's sin. This was Christ, the second Adam. (cw13 ¶401)

occurrences.title: The great tree of supracelestial fire — Simon Magus
occurrences.label: The great tree of supracelestial fire
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus preserves Simon Magus's "great tree" that "consists of 'supracelestial fire.' 'From it all flesh is fed'" (cw13 ¶374; Elenchos VI, 9, 8ff). Jung reads it with the ever-living fire of Heraclitus and with Mercurius as fire and spiritus vegetativus, "both anim ating and destructive" (cw13 ¶374) — and with Nebuchadnezzar's tree, whose fruit ready-formed "is brought in to a barn and not cast in to the fire": the pneum atic m an who has stood the test.
The fire-tree recurs as the fire-tree of the patient's picture (Fig. 15, cw13 ¶320) and in the Barbeliots' tree of gnosis (¶419n, ¶459n8).
Verbatim: In Gnosticism we encounter the “great tree” of Simon Magus, which consists of “supracelestial fire.” “From it all flesh is fed.” (cw13 ¶374)

occurrences.title: The catalapa of the dead hearts — Noel Pierre, 'Soleil Noir' (1952)
occurrences.label: The catalapa of the dead hearts
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Literary close of the picture series: Jung cites verses XXVI-XXVII of "Soleil No ir" by Noel Pierre, "am odern F rench poe t w ho is p erson ally un know n to m e", as "an auth en tic ex p er ie n ce of th e unconscious" (cw13 ¶348). A spiral vortex sucks the crowd down toward a colossal catalapa "Ou pendaient Ies coeurs des morts", a little sage winking at each fork, and below, an island where a cube of grey rock rises — "la Capitale des Mondes".

Jung's feature list: universal midpoint, spiral rotation (often shown as a snake), tree of life and death, heart as centre of vitality joined to the tree, natural wisdom as a dwarf, island as seat of the tree, "Cube = philosophers' stone = treasure guarded by the tree" (cw13 ¶348).
Verbatim: Dans l'axe, un catalpa gigantesque / Oii p endaient Ies coeurs des morts (cw13 ¶348)

occurrences.title: The sun-and-moon tree on the island — Mylius's parable
occurrences.label: The sun-and-moon tree on the island
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Mylius's parable: "the sunand-m oon tree stands on an island in the sea and grows out of the w onderful water that is extracted by the pow er of the m agnet from the rays of the sun and m oon" (cw13 ¶406). In the sam e volume's "Sym posium Saturni" the seven planet-trees grow in "the 'private garden' of the blessed isles" (cw13 ¶407 n11): two outstand — one bearing sun-fruit with gold leaves, one white fruit with quicksilver leaves, "nam ed by Neptune the tree of the sun and th e tree of the m oon."
Jung's use: the tree's special connection with water, salt and sea-water — "thus with the aqua perm anens, the true arcanum of the adepts. This as we know is Mercurius" (cw13 ¶408).
Verbatim: the sunand-m oon tree stands on an island in the sea and grow s out of the w onderful water that is extracted by the pow er of the m agnet (cw13 ¶406ocr)

occurrences.title: Mary's lament against the false tree — Old English lament of the Virgin
occurrences.label: Mary's lament against the false tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Tre unkynde, thou schalt be kud, mi sone step-moder I the calle
body: Mary accuses the cross of being a false tree and step-mother which destroyed "the pure fruit of her body, her gentle birdling"; the Cross answers, calls itself the shining relic that will appear at Doom's-day parliament, and claims its blooming fruit. "Thus the Mother of Death joins the Mother of Life in lamenting the dying god, and, as an outward token of their union, Mary kisses the cross and is reconciled" (¶415) — the dual-mother union of opposite tendencies.

occurrences.title: The wak-wak tree with human fruit — Ta'rikh al-Hind al-Gharbi (11th-c. Munich MS)
occurrences.label: The wak-wak tree with human fruit
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: pl. XXXIX; fn 74 to ch. V (pdf p694); index 'wak-wak tree, pl. XXXIX' (pdf p656)

body: The plate Jung reproduces as XXXIX is the wak-wak tree of the Arabic geography Ta'rikh al-Hind al-Gharbi ("Report on the Happenings in Persia," "from an 11th-cent. MS in Munich: Wirth, ed., Aus orientalischen Chroniken, p. 151"). The index files it among birth-giving trees: "tree(s): birth from, 246f, 248, 425", "with human fruit, pls. XXXIX, XLV", "as birth-giving mother, 246, pl. XXXIX" — the tree that bears human bodies, the vegetable mother of heroes (cf. book p246f, pdf ~279, c02 range).
Verbatim (fn 74): "“Report on the Happenings in Persia,” from an 11th-cent. MS in Munich"

occurrences.title: The tree of wisdom in the Western Land — Ethiopic Book of Enoch
occurrences.label: The tree of wisdom in the Western Land
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: In the Ethiopic Book of Enoch the tree of knowledge of Genesis becomes the tree of wisdom in the Western Land, standing on a mountain: "it is said that the fruits of the tree in the Western Land will be the food of the elect. This is a clear hint of death and renewal" (cw13 ¶403); its fruits are likened to grapes (n.19) — the vine-complex that m edieval alchemy took up in "I am the true vine" (John 15:1).
Jung folds this into the food-of-im m ortality chain: Turba fruits that end the old m an's hunger until "that old m an becom es a youth"; m anna, Host, and panacea (cw13 ¶403).
Verbatim: the fruits of the tree in the Western Land will be the food of the elect. (cw13 ¶403)

occurrences.title: Wotan's self-hanging on the windy tree — Havamal 139
occurrences.label: Wotan's self-hanging on the windy tree
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: I ween that I hung / on the windy tree, Hung there for nights full nine; With the spear I was wounded, and offered I was To Othin, myself to myself
body: Footnote to Jung's analysis of the hunter-God-image: "I ween that I hung / on the windy tree, / Hung there for nights full nine; / With the spear I was wounded, and offered I was / To Othin, myself to myself, / On the tree that none / may ever know / What root beneath it runs." (Havamal 139, trans. H. A. Bellows). Jung cites it as the Germanic deep-structure beneath his fairytale: the swineherd "very nearly made its prisoner, like Wotan" when he climbed the world-tree (¶445); the hunter's suspension in the boughs and the crucified raven are the Christian reflection of this pagan hanged-god. The Wotanic God-image that, "reflected in the ocean of the (Germanic) unconscious", was "the psychological godfather of National Socialism" (¶452).

occurrences.title: The eight-branched birth-tree of the first man — Yakut
occurrences.label: The eight-branched birth-tree of the first man
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Am ong the Yakuts a tree with eight branches is the birthplace of the first m an. He is suckled by a wom an the top part of whose body grow s out of the trunk" (cw13 ¶461; Eliade, Sham anism, p. 272). Jung im m ediately connects it to his own case m aterial: "This m otif is also found am ong m y exam ples (Figure 22)" — the tree-born woman em erging from the trunk (see tree-picture-tree-born-eve-patient-1935).

The eight branches echo the shamanic ogdoad-world-tree planted with the first sham an (cw13 ¶402), and the birth-tree's m aternal num en belongs to the fem inine tree-num en row (Melusina, Isis, the Pandora w oman-trunk).
Verbatim: He is suckled by a wom an the top part of whose body grow s out of the trunk. (cw13 ¶461ocr)

occurrences.title: Zarathustra's dream: the tree with four metallic branches (Iran)
occurrences.label: Zarathustra's dream
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "It is said, for instance, that after Zarathustra had received the drink of omniscience from Ahuramazda, he beheld in a dream a tree with four branches of gold, silver, steel, and mixed iron. This tree corresponds to the metallic tree of alchemy, the arbor philosophica, which, if it has any meaning at all, symbolizes spiritual growth and the highest illumination" (cw13 ¶119).

Jung's point: the inner man's spiritual growth symbolized by metals is "not peculiar to alchemy" — nature exploits man's greed for metals, "and there may be hidden in lead either a deadly demon or the dove of the Holy Ghost" (¶119).

occurrences.title: The transformation as a well-tended tree — Zosimos via Pelagios
occurrences.label: The transformation as a well-tended tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Pelagios's treatise preserves Zosimos's image of the opus: the transformation is "like a well-tended tree, a watered plant, which, beginning to ferment because of the plentiful water, and sprouting in the humidity and warmth of the air, puts forth blossoms and fruits by virtue of the great sweetness and special quality of nature" (cw13 ¶354).

Jung opens the historical half of the essay with this locus: the tree appears in medieval texts "and in general represents the growth of the arcane substance and its transform ation into the philosophical gold" (cw13 ¶354) — and its Greek prototype stands already in Zosimos.
Verbatim: Zosim os had said the transform ation process was like “a well-tended tree, aw atered plant, which, beginning to ferm ent because of the plentiful water” (cw13 ¶354ocr)

occurrences.title: The Feast of the Ass at Beauvais — priest and congregation braying
occurrences.label: The Feast of the Ass at Beauvais
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~11th-12th c. codex; suppressed by the auctoritas supremi Senatus

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: At the end of the mass, instead of the words 'Ite missa est,' the priest shall bray three times (ter hinhamabit), and instead of the words ' Deo gratias,' the congregation shall answer 'Y-a' (hinham) three times,
body: The festum asinorum, "celebrated mainly in France" as a "harmless festival in memory of Mary's flight into Egypt": the ass procession went right into the church at Beauvais, a girl with the ass stationed by the altar, and at each part of the high mass "the whole congregation brayed". An eleventh-century codex prescribes: "At the end of the mass, instead of the words 'Ite missa est,' the priest shall bray three times (ter hinhamabit), and instead of the words 'Deo gratias,' the congregation shall answer 'Y-a' (hinham) three times." Jung notes the hymn Orientis partibus and the danger that the ass be brought "into symbolic relationship with Christ" — "the god of the Jews was vulgarly conceived to be an ass", as the Palatine mock-crucifixion shows. "The more ridiculous this rite seemed, the greater the enthusiasm with which it was celebrated" (Du Cange).

occurrences.title: The Feast of Fools at Notre Dame, Paris (1198; Fools' Pope, 1444)
occurrences.label: The Feast of Fools at Notre Dame, Paris
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: A report from the year I1g8 says that at the Feast of the Circumcision in Notre Dame, Paris, 'so many abominations and shameful deeds' were committed that the holy place was desecrated 'not only by smutty jokes, but even by the shedding of blood.
body: Medieval church carnival as the trickster at the altar's edge: on Innocents' Day an Episcopus puerorum was elected, vested in pontifical robes, and blessed the city from the archbishop's window; the subdeacons' dance degenerated by the late twelfth century into the festum stultorum. A report of 1198: at the Feast of the Circumcision in Notre Dame "so many abominations and shameful deeds" were committed "not only by smutty jokes, but even by the shedding of blood". In 1444 the Theological Faculty still fulminated against the fatuorum papam: masqueraders "sang indecent songs in the choir, ate their greasy food from a corner of the altar..., got out their games of dice, burned a stinking incense made of old shoe leather". For Jung these customs "demonstrate the role of the trickster to perfection" — the remnant of the collective shadow figure inside the Church itself.

occurrences.title: Trimurti picture: tortoise, skull, and lotus-flower as opus allegory (Indian painting)
occurrences.label: Trimurti picture — tortoise, skull…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the tortoise symbolizing the massa confusa, the skull the vas of transformation, and the flower the 'self' or wholeness
body: Plate 75: "The triangle symbolizes the tendency of the universe to converge towards the point of unity. The tortoise represents Vishnu; the lotus growing out of the skull between two flames, Shiva. The shining sun of Brahma forms the background. The whole picture corresponds to the alchemical opus, the tortoise symbolizing the massa confusa, the skull the vas of transformation, and the flower the 'self' or wholeness."

Jung's caption makes the Trimurti a complete Indian allegory of the alchemical opus: chaos (tortoise), container (skull), goal (flower), with the trimurtic triad converging on unity. Paired with fig. 76 (the tortoise as alchemical distilling instrument, Porta 1609) and the "green womb" of Ishvara (¶199).

occurrences.title: The Christian Trinity with the Holy Ghost as a winged man — Master of the Berlin Passion
occurrences.label: The Christian Trinity with the Holy Ghost…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He is often represented as a winged old man, i.e., Mercurius in the form of the god of revelation.
body: Fifteenth-century engraving in which the third person of the Trinity appears as a winged MAN rather than a dove.

Jung's reading: the Holy Ghost is "often represented as a winged old man, i.e., Mercurius in the form of the god of revelation, who is identical with Hermes Trismegistus and, together with the King and the King's Son, forms the alchemical trinity" (fig. 179). The fire extracted from chaos "is the Holy Ghost, who unites father and son" — the model the alchemists copied as Hermes standing between king and son.

occurrences.title: Horus-Hathor-Akori trinity amulet with winged serpent
occurrences.label: Horus-Hathor-Akori trinity amulet…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: A late Egyptian trinity amulet (published by Spiegelberg): 'Horus and Hathor sit facing one another, and between them and over them hovers a winged serpent. The three deities all hold the ankh... "Bait is one, Hathor one, Akori one, one is their power. Greetings, Father of the World, greetings, three-formed God."' (cw14 ¶352). Spiegelberg: despite its Greek form it 'breathes an Egyptian spirit of Hellenistic nature... born of a spirit that made its contribution to the development of the dogma of the Trinity in Christianity.' Jung: 'The illustrations of the coniunctio in the Rosarium, showing King, Queen, and the dove of the Holy Ghost, correspond to the figures on the amulet exactly' (¶352).

occurrences.title: Trinity Vision of Brother Klaus — the Sachseln painting
occurrences.label: Trinity Vision of Brother Klaus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)
The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: It is a mandala divided into six parts, and in the centre is the crowned countenance of God.
body: The central religious experience of the Swiss hermit Nicholas of Flue (Bruder Klaus): a terrifying theophany — Woelflin, the oldest source, reports he "had seen a piercing light resembling a human face" and feared his heart would burst "into little pieces" (¶14). He elaborated it for years with an illustrated devotional booklet, and had it painted on his cell wall: a six-part mandala with the crowned countenance of God at the centre, still preserved at Sachseln (¶12-13).

Jung's reading: the dogmatic symbol assimilated a "fatal incursion of an archetypal image" and saved Klaus from being torn asunder (¶20); the mandala/protective circle is "the traditional antidote for chaotic states of mind" (¶19). In the anima essay he adds the initiation visions where God appeared "once as a majestic father and once as a majestic mother" — the syzygy, "heretical" against Trinitarian dogma (¶¶131-132).

occurrences.title: Turba philosophorum — the punctum solis in the egg-yolk
occurrences.label: Turba philosophorum
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'In the egg therefore are four things: earth, water, air, and fire; but the "punctum solis" is apart from these four, in the midst of the yolk (which) is the chick' (¶345). Ruska reads 'saliens' for 'solis'; Jung is 'not so sure'. In the alchemical tradition the point stands for the arcane substance: Maier's 'purity or homogeneity of the essence', Khunrath's salt-point (Sapientia), the scholiast's circulus exiguus, 'mediator... by persistent rotation changes the angular form of the square into a circular one like itself', Dorn's punctum vix intelligibile, John Dee's monad, Mylius' bird of Hermes (¶345). Parallels: monoimos-monad-iota-2c, egg-rigveda-nasadiya-hidden-one.

occurrences.title: The woman who slays her husbands buried with the dragon — Turba, Sermo LIX
occurrences.label: The woman who slays her husbands buried…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: The coniunctio can therefore take more gruesome forms than the relatively harmless one depicted in the Rosarium.
body: Sermo LIX of the Turba: "the Philosophers have put to death the woman who slays her husbands, for the body of that woman is full of weapons and poison. Let a grave be dug for that dragon, and let that woman be buried with him, he being chained fast to that woman; and the more he winds and coils himself about her, the more will he be cut to pieces by the female weapons which are fashioned in the body of the woman" — until he is "changed wholly into blood," the blood dries in the sun, and "What then appears, is the hidden wind" (¶15).

Jung's comment closes the widow/Isis excursus: "The coniunctio can therefore take more gruesome forms than the relatively harmless one depicted in the Rosarium." The water that "gathers together all my divided and scattered limbs" is "my mother who is my enemy."

occurrences.title: Turukalukundram — the erotic temple sculptures and the Tantrist pundit
occurrences.label: Turukalukundram — the erotic temple sculptures…
occurrences.subject: jung

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Visiting the ancient pagoda, Jung asked a local pundit why the temples are covered 'from top to bottom, with obscene sculptures': to remind ordinary people of their dharma, because Yama 'would instantly carry off' the imperfect who tread the spiritual path unprepared; the two seductresses at the entrance lure visitors to fulfil their dharma before ascending (¶339 n.131). The lingam stands in the garbha griha, the 'house of the womb'. Jung notes the pundit 'was a Tantrist'. A living instance of the same initiation logic as the Eleusinian lower path — the Persephone route before the Brimo-Brimos ascent.

occurrences.title: The two birds on the selfsame tree — Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4, 6ff.
occurrences.label: The two birds on the selfsame tree
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~6th-5th c. BCE (trans. based on Hume, The Thirteen Principal Upanishads)

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

body: The Indian parallel to the Dioscuri motif of the mortal and immortal twin: "Two birds, fast-bound companions, sit /... / Behold, upon the selfsame tree, / This one enjoys the ripened fruit, / The other looks, but does not eat. // On such a tree my spirit crouched, / Deluded by its powerlessness, / Till seeing with joy how great its Lord, It found from sorrow swift release" (Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4, 6ff.).

Jung's reading: the dual motif symbolizing "the hidden immortal within the mortal man" — "Christ himself is the perfect symbol" of it; when the summit of life is reached, "'One becomes Two', and the greater figure, which one always was but which remained invisible, appears to the lesser personality with the force of a revelation" (¶218). Announces the Moses-Khidr analysis (Koran, 18th Sura) as "another notable parallel" (¶219 — treated later in the essay, beyond this chunk).

occurrences.title: The unicorn tied to Noah's ark and Og who escaped the flood — Talmud
occurrences.label: The unicorn tied to Noah's ark and Og…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: Babylonian Talmud redaction (~5th–6th c.); saga older
occurrences.quote: For it is said [Gen. 14: 13]: 'and there came one that had escaped, and told Abram the Hebrew,' and R. Johanan said: 'That was Og who escaped the flood.
body: Rabbinic flood-saga: the re'em (unicorn) could not enter the ark; Noah tied it by its horn to the vessel and it swam behind — but the flood-water was hot, so it was scalded to death (Zebahim 113b, with Goldschmidt's and Jung's comments on the melting pitch of Gen. 6: 14). The same tractate preserves Og: "'and there came one that had escaped' — R. Johanan said: 'That was Og who escaped the flood'" (Nidda 61a), the last of the giants of Gen. 6: 4 riding out the deluge atop the ark.

Jung's apparatus (Part II ch. 6, nn. 62–69) gathers these as the Jewish monstrous counterpart to the unicorn material of the chapter: the too-much-of-the-body that cannot be brought into the vessel of salvation.

occurrences.title: The captive unicorn in the fenced round garden — Verteuil tapestry
occurrences.label: The captive unicorn in the fenced round garden
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "264. Mandala of the unicorn and the tree of life. — Verteuil tapestry (15th cent.), 'The Hunt of the Unicorn'" — the tamed unicorn lying within a circular fence around the tree of life, in a field of flowers. Jung caption-reads the enclosure as a mandala and uses the plate to close his reading of the horn: "The horn as an emblem of vigour and strength has a masculine character, but at the same time it is a cup, which, as a receptacle, is feminine. So we are dealing here with a 'uniting symbol' that expresses the bipolarity of the archetype" (¶553).
The captive unicorn as the rounded, bounded totality — horticus conclusus, temenos, mandala.

image.title: The Unicorn in Captivity (from the Unicorn Tapestries)
image.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art . See the Image and Data Resources Open Access Policy

occurrences.title: The ch'i-lin announcing the birth and death of Confucius
occurrences.label: The ch'i-lin announcing the birth and death…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~551 BCE (birth omen); death omen 481 BCE; reproduced in Sheng Chi-t'u rubbings
body: The Chinese unicorn as herald of the sage. At Confucius' birth: "a ch'i-lin came to the governor's house in Tsou and spat out a jade tablet, bearing the inscription: 'The son of the mountain crystal [lit. water-essence] will perpetuate the fallen kingdom of Chou and be a king without a crown.' His mother … tied an embroidered bow to the unicorn's horn" (fig. 259). Before his death (481 BCE) "a ch'i-lin was caught on a winter hunt"; Confucius wept: "The ch'i-lin, benevolent beast, appears and dies. My Tao is exhausted" (fig. 260).

By the Li Chi the ch'i-lin is chief of the four spiritual animals (unicorn, phoenix, tortoise, dragon) and "shows itself when perfect rulers [chen-jen] appear and the Tao of the king is accomplished"; the male is ch'i, the female lin — "the unicorn is thus endowed with an androgynous quality" (¶548).

occurrences.title: Ctesias' Indian wild ass: the tri-coloured horn that detoxifies
occurrences.label: Ctesias' Indian wild ass
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: India (as reported in Ctesias' Indika, from Persia)
occurrences.quote: There is a horn on the forehead, nearly one and a half cubits in length; the lower part of the horn is white, the upper part purple, but the middle is pitch black.
body: The West's oldest unicorn report. Ctesias (c. 400 BCE, via McCrindle): a wild ass of India, white-bodied, purple-headed, with "a horn on the forehead, nearly one and a half cubits in length; the lower part of the horn is white, the upper part purple, but the middle is pitch black." Princes drink from horn-cups bound with gold rings and are immune to poison and convulsions.

Jung assembles this in the unicorn chapter's zoological apparatus (n. 30) with Aelian's Kartazonon ("the strength of its horn is invincible. It seeks solitude"), Philostratus' fire-walking cup, and Kosmas' unicorn that leaps into an abyss and lands on its unbreakable horn. The antidote-horn — the poison-warding cornu — is for Jung the natural-magic root of the symbol: the one-horned, solitary, fierce animal as bearer of the "alexipharmic," later allegorized as Christ consecrating the baptismal water (Caesarius, n. 21).

occurrences.title: Cardinal Torquemada's unicorn cup at table — Rome
occurrences.label: Cardinal Torquemada's unicorn cup at table
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "Migne says that Cardinal Torquemada always kept a unicorn cup at table: 'La corne de licorne préserve des sortilèges' (fig. 261)" (¶550). The prince of the Inquisition using the alicorn as an anti-sorcery amulet at his own table — the healing cup standing between medicine, sacrament, and mantic use: "The healing cup is not unconnected with the 'cup of salvation,' the Eucharistic Chalice, and with the vessel used in divination" (¶550). Illustrations: the pope with the unicorn as Holy Ghost (Scaliger 1570, fig. 261) and Pisanello's lunar-unicorn medal (fig. 262).

occurrences.title: David rides the re'em to heaven; the lion makes it crouch — Midrash Tehillim
occurrences.label: David rides the re'em to heaven
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "R. Huna bar Idi said: At the time when David was still tending the sheep, he went and found the unicorn [re'em] asleep in the desert, and thinking it was a mountain he climbed to the top and pastured his flock there. Then the unicorn shook himself and stood up. And David rode on his back and reached up to heaven. … He ordained that a lion should come, and when the unicorn saw the lion, he was afraid and crouched down before him, because the lion is his king" (¶545). David, descending, now fears the lion — hence Ps 22:21: "Save me from the lion's mouth, for thou hast heard [freed] me from the horns of the unicorns."
A second midrash (¶546) has unicorn and lion fight: the unicorn's horn sticks fast in a tree "and then the lion comes and kills the unicorn, but sometimes the matter is reversed."

occurrences.title: The unicorn as demon — St. Basil's warning
occurrences.label: The unicorn as demon — St. Basil's warning
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The unicorn's dark side, from the Physiologus tradition — Basil: "it is a swift-running animal, having one horn, and evilly disposed towards man (μνησίκακον … ἐν ἀνθρώποις)," and: "take heed unto thyself, O man, and beware of the unicorn, who is the Demon [fig. 249]. For he plotteth evil against man, and he is cunning in evil-doing" (¶525).

Jung uses these to establish that the one-horned beast "has more than one meaning. It can also mean evil," concluding (¶526): "Originally a monstrous and fabulous beast, it harbours in itself an inner contradiction, a complexio oppositorum, which makes it a singularly appropriate symbol for the monstrum hermaphroditum of alchemy." Illustrated by the wild unicorn of Bock's Kräuterbuch (fig. 249) and the wild man riding the unicorn (fig. 250, Master E.S.).

occurrences.title: Jehovah as unicorn tamed in the virgin's lap — Caussin's compilation
occurrences.label: Jehovah as unicorn tamed in the virgin's lap
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: From Nicolas Caussin, "from whom I have culled these extracts" (Jung): "the unicorn is a fitting symbol for the God of the Old Testament, because in his wrath he reduced the world to confusion like an angry rhinoceros (unicorn) until, made captive by love, he was soothed in the lap of a virgin" (¶522). With Picinelli and Bonaventure: "Christ was tamed and pacified by the most kindly Mary, so that he should not punish the sinner with eternal death."

Jung's point: "This ecclesiastical train of thought has its parallel in the alchemical taming of the lion and the dragon" — the conversion of the wrathful Old-Testament God into the God of Love mirrors the opus' taming of the dangerous beasts of Mercurius (¶522).

occurrences.title: The ch'i-lin — Chinese unicorn of the Confucius legend (figs. 259–260)
occurrences.label: The ch'i-lin — Chinese unicorn…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: China (Tz'u-yuan lexicon; Wilhelm, Kung-Tse, Leben und Werk pp. 189, 60)
occurrences.yearDisplay: Confucius legend (~6th–5th c. BCE); codified in later encyclopedias

jung.locator: pdf p702 (Part II ch. 6, n. 75); figs. 259, 260 (captions trans. E. H. von Tscharner)

occurrences.quote: From the Tz'u-yuan, s.v. 'Ch'i-lin.' The text of the captions for figs. 259 and 260 was specially translated from the Chinese for the Swiss edn. of the present volume by Dr. E. H. von Tscharner.
body: The Chinese unicorn (ch'i-lin, or ki-lin), a hoofed, benevolent chimeric beast that appears only at the birth or death of a sage — in the Confucius legend it heralds the birth of the philosopher and its capture marks his death. Jung closes the unicorn chapter's apparatus with two plates of the ki-lin (figs. 259, 260), their captions specially translated from the Tz'u-yuan for the Swiss edition by E. H. von Tscharner.

Its place in Jung's argument: the unicorn is not a European Christian fantasy but a worldwide image of the singular, wise, gentle-fierce wholeness-beast; the ki-lin ties it to the birth and death of the self-realized man rather than to the virgin's womb.

occurrences.title: The unicorn draws the poison from the water — Physiologus Graecus
occurrences.label: The unicorn draws the poison from the water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The alexipharmic scene at the water-hole: "when a snake has poisoned their drinking water, the animals, noticing the poison, will wait for the unicorn to come down to the water; 'for his horn is a symbol of the cross,' and by drinking he dissipates the virulence of the poison" (¶549). The horn that detects, absorbs, and neutralizes the serpent's venom — the alicorn as antidote, made material in the rhinoceros-horn poison cups of the Africa–China trade ("even today," ¶549) and in the Campion pendant scraped for medicine (fig. 263).
Same text family as the man-hating unicorn of the Physiologus (¶525): the beast that saves the animals from the serpent is the demon that plots against man.

occurrences.title: Priscillian: 'Unicornis est Deus … nobis lapis angularis Jesus'
occurrences.label: Priscillian — Unicornis est Deus … nobis lapis…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Unicornis est Deus, nobis petra Christus, nobis lapis angularis Jesus, nobis hominum homo Christus.
body: The Gnostic-leaning bishop Priscillian compresses the whole unicorn-Christology into one sentence: "Unicornis est Deus, nobis petra Christus, nobis lapis angularis Jesus, nobis hominum homo Christus" — God is the unicorn; Christ the rock; Jesus the corner-stone; Christ the man of men. The unicorn, the stone, and the anthropos fall together into one identity.
