For Jung's argument this is a key patristic witness that the unicorn is a Christ- (hence self-) symbol, not a zoological memory: the horn that crushes all obstacles (Honorius, Speculum; cf. cw12 n. 23) is the same "strong strength of all strength" the alchemists predicate of the lapis. Priscillian is also Jung's source for the wheel of the zodiac-generations (cf. priscillian-wheel-of-generation-385).

occurrences.title: The re'em tied to the outside of the ark — Babylonian Talmud
occurrences.label: The re'em tied to the outside of the ark
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Talmudic legendary zoology of the re'em: too gigantic for the ark, it was tied to the outside — or, per R. Jannai, they took young unicorns in; per Reš Laqiš, "they tied its horns to the ark." Rabba b. Bar Hana "had seen a young unicorn as large as Mount Tabor, which measures forty parasangs, … and that the Jordan was choked with the dirt it voided" (¶540).

Jung links it to Og king of Bashan — also flood-survivor, also gigantic, also mountain-linked — and suggests "an inner connection between Og and the unicorn" (¶545). With Behemoth and Leviathan, "the two manifestations of Jehovah," these beings are "personifications of the daemonic forces of nature. … God is ambivalent so long as man remains bound to nature" (¶547).

occurrences.title: Rishyashringa, the one-horned hermit fetched for the drought — Mahabharata
occurrences.label: Rishyashringa, the one-horned hermit fetched…
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "The virgin and unicorn motif is to be found in the Ramayana and in the Mahabharata": the hermit Rishyashringa ("gazelle's horn"), son of Vibhandaka or Ekasringa ("one-horn"), is fetched from his solitary retreat by the king's daughter Shanta, who marries him — "or, in another version, he is seduced by a courtesan. Only by this means can the terrible drought that is scourging the land be broken" (¶534).

The one-horned ascetic whose only weakness is the feminine: the capture-of-the-unicorn plot in Indian dress, with rain-making (fertility) as the fruit of the taming — the same structure as the Chinese ch'i-lin appearing "when the Tao of the king is accomplished."

occurrences.title: Slaying the unicorn in the Virgin's lap — MS Harley 4751
occurrences.label: Slaying the unicorn in the Virgin's lap
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Slaying the unicorn in the Virgin’s lap. (Note the significance of the “wound in his side.”)
body: Bestiary initial (fig. 242): hunters slay the unicorn as it lies in the Virgin's lap. Jung's caption draws out the Christological point: "Note the significance of the 'wound in his side'" — the killing of the captured unicorn repeats the piercing of Christ's side, and the picture belongs to the same family as the Pieta allusion Jung finds in Ripley's green lion (¶519).

occurrences.title: Christ the unicorn-bull, his horns the ends of the cross — Tertullian
occurrences.label: Christ the unicorn-bull, his horns the ends…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: His glory is that of a bull, his horn is that of a unicorn.
body: Tertullian's exegesis of the blessing of Moses (Deut 33:13–17), the fountainhead of the ecclesiastical unicorn allegory Jung traces through the Psalms (Ps 29:6, 92:10, 22:21):

And: "Christ was named the bull on account of two qualities: the one hard [ferus, 'wild, untamed'] as a judge, the other gentle [mansuetus, 'tame'] as a saviour. His horns are the ends of the cross" (¶521). The wild/tame polarity inside the one beast is exactly the ambivalence Jung later locates in Mercurius and in the God-image itself (¶547). Justin Martyr reads the same verse: "Cornua unicornis cornu eius" — the horns can only be the cross.

occurrences.title: The virgin catches the unicorn — Honorius of Autun
occurrences.label: The virgin catches the unicorn
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The classic scholastic form of the capture allegory: "The very fierce animal with only one horn is called unicorn. In order to catch it, a virgin is put in a field; the animal then comes to her and is caught, because it lies down in her lap. Christ is represented by this animal, and his insuperable strength by its horn. He, who lay down in the womb of the Virgin, has been caught by the hunters; that is to say, he was found in human shape by those who loved him" (¶523). Jung pairs the passage with the Khludov Psalter miniature (fig. 247, Byzantine, 9th c.).
The "wound in his side" of the hunt pictures and the "insuperable strength" of the horn hold together the same polarity Tertullian named: judge-wild, saviour-tame.

occurrences.title: The virgin and the unicorn — Physiologus Graecus
occurrences.label: The virgin and the unicorn — Physiologus Graecus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Alexandria (Physiologus tradition; Pitra, Spicilegium solesmense III p. 355)
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~2nd c. (tradition possibly reaching Didymus of Alexandria, 4th c.)
occurrences.quote: They cast a sacred virgin before it. And it leaps into the lap of the virgin, and the virgin warms the animal with love and bears it to the palace of the kings.
body: The classic Christian unicorn-hunt: "How is it hunted? They cast a sacred virgin before it. And it leaps into the lap of the virgin, and the virgin warms the animal with love and bears it to the palace of the kings." Medieval allegory (Isidore of Seville, Etymologiarum xii, 62, is the transmitting source) reads the virgin as Mary and the captured unicorn as Christ entering the womb.

Jung's unicorn chapter builds on this locus: the fierce, uncatchable one-horned beast that can only be taken through the virgin is the image of the dangerous, autonomic wholeness (or its masculine fierce aspect) that the feminine — the vessel, the virgin as vas (figs. 241, 242, 245, 247) — alone can render incarnate. The wounded unicorn lying in the virgin's lap (Reusner, Pandora) is its alchemical echo (cw12 pdf p693, n. 186).

occurrences.title: Virgin taming a unicorn — pseudo-Aquinas, 'De alchimia'
occurrences.label: Virgin taming a unicorn
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Leiden, Bibliothek der Rijksuniversiteit, Codex Vossianus 29
occurrences.quote: 241. Virgin taming a unicorn.—Thomas Aquinas (pseud.), “De alchimia” (MS., 16th cent.)
body: Alchemical picture (fig. 241) in the 16th-century MS De alchimia attributed to Thomas Aquinas: a virgin holding/taming the unicorn. In Jung's reading the picture carries the Mercurius-Christ identity: because "the symbol of the unicorn as an allegory of Christ and of the Holy Ghost was current all through the Middle Ages," Ripley and his fellows knew exactly what they meant when they let the tamed beast stand for the spiritus mercurialis (¶519).

occurrences.title: Uroboros with 'hen to pan' legend — Codex Marcianus
occurrences.label: Uroboros with 'hen to pan' legend
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: It appears as the ούρο βόρος, the tail-eater, in the Codex Marcianus (fig. 147), which dates from the tenth or eleventh century, together with the legend: νἓ τò πάν (the One, the All).
body: A tail-eating dragon in the Greek alchemical codex Marcianus, tenth or eleventh century, ringed by the legend "hen to pan" (the One, the All). Jung calls the dragon "probably the oldest pictorial symbol in alchemy of which we have documentary evidence."

His reading: the uroboros compresses the whole opus into one figure — "the opus proceeds from the one and leads back to the one, that it is a sort of circle like a dragon biting its own tail." Mercurius as uroboros "devours, fertilizes, begets, slays, and brings itself to life again" (¶460): prima materia, caput corvi, nigredo, and rising lapis in one hermaphroditic body — "a symbol uniting all opposites."

occurrences.title: Harpokrates encircled by the uroboros — gnostic gem
occurrences.label: Harpokrates encircled by the uroboros
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "253. Harpokrates encircled by the Uroboros. — Gnostic gem" (fig. 253): the self-born child-god (Horus the child, finger to lips) ringed by the self-devouring serpent. Jung cites it exactly at the point where alchemy's prima materia is "an increatum … bisexual, capable of self-fertilization and self-parturition" (¶530) — the self-contained circle of generation that needs no other.
The same self-birth the Horapollo scarab carries (unicorned, monogenes, autogenes, sacred to Mercurius).

occurrences.title: Uroboros as symbol of the aeon — Horapollo, Selecta hieroglyphica (1597)
occurrences.label: Uroboros as symbol of the aeon
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Tail-eating serpent as emblem of the aeon, from the Renaissance hieroglyphic manual of Horapollo. Jung places it first in the CW12 illustration sequence, opening the whole volume's uroboros row.
Caption: "7. The Uroboros as symbol of the aeon.—Horapollo, Selecta hieroglyphica (1597)". Jung reads the tail-eater here as a time-symbol of self-contained cyclic totality.

occurrences.title: Kekule's dream of the dancing pairs and the benzol ring
occurrences.label: Kekule's dream of the dancing pairs…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Ghent (Kekule's own account; Jung gives no place/date)
body: "When Kekule had his dream of the dancing pairs and deduced from it the structure of the benzol ring, he accomplished something that Zosimos strove for in vain. His 'composition of the waters' did not fall into as neat a pattern as did the carbon and hydrogen atoms of the benzol ring. Alchemy projected an inner, psychic experience into chemical substances that seemed to hold out mysterious possibilities but nevertheless proved refractory" (cw13 ¶143).

Jung's contrast: the natural-scientific dream worked where the alchemical vision failed — yet both draw on the same archetypal imagery of circling, paired dancers. (The uroboros-family reading is ours: Jung does not name the uroboros here.)

occurrences.title: The tail-eater as prima materia — Reusner, Pandora (1588), p. 257
occurrences.label: The tail-eater as prima materia
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The full plate: "The 'tail-eater' (Uroboros) as the prima materia of the alchemical process, with the red-and-white rose, the flos sapientum. Below, coniunctio solis et lunae, with the lapis philosophorum as the son.". One image compresses Jung's whole reading of alchemy: circular prima materia, rose of wisdom, coniunctio, lapis-son.

Jung uses it at ¶63 to gloss the dreamer's snake-circle vision: "The drawing of a spellbinding circle (fig. 13) is an ancient magical device." The serpens mercurii is "the dragon that creates and destroys itself and represents the prima materia" (¶26).

occurrences.title: Valentinian letter — the Autopator in agnosia
occurrences.label: Valentinian letter — the Autopator in agnosia
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'In the beginning the Autopator contained in himself everything that is, in a state of unconsciousness [agnosia]' (¶298). Hippolytus' parallel: the Father 'deprived of consciousness and substance, neither masculine nor feminine' — nirdvandva, without opposites, therefore unknowable: 'This describes the state of the unconscious' (¶298). Ennoia, consciousness, is present only as 'the latent possibility of consciousness'; the differentiated syzygies and tetrads follow after (¶298). Jung links this to Paul's ignorantia (Acts 17:30) and to Eckhart's Godhead — Gnostic agnosia as the earliest psychology of the unconscious God-image.

occurrences.title: The bedchamber of Venus — Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosencreutz
occurrences.label: The bedchamber of Venus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: they came to the bedcham ber of Venus and found the goddess asleep on a couch.
body: The descent episode of the Chymical Wedding: a boy leads the hero down to an underground chamber whose copper door bears a secret inscription (cuprum — the Cyprian, Aphrodite/Venus); within, a three-cornered tomb on three animals (eagle, ox, lion — "the lower triad, corresponding to the upper Trinity... Reversal of moral values," ¶227 n.18) holds a copper cauldron with an angel and a dripping tree; below lies the bedchamber of the sleeping Venus, whose coverlet the boy twitches away.

Jung cites the episode four times: for the hierosgamos of Venus and Mars (¶227), against Dorn's christianized reading of the "characters of Venus" (¶235), as the central mystery of Mercurius's relation to the goddess of love (¶248), and for Mercurius appearing as Cupid who wounds the adept in the hand with the "dart of passion" (¶278).

occurrences.title: Zosimos' vision: the boiling men in the embalming vessel (Egypt, ~3rd c.)
occurrences.label: Zosimos' vision — the boiling men…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Panopolis / Alexandria, Egypt (Berthelot III i 3 / III vi)
body: Second vision: the same bowl-shaped altar with boiling water and "a numberless multitude of people in it," burning and yet alive. A grey anthroparion ("a barber grown grey with age") explains: "The sight that you see is the entrance, and the exit, and the transformation... This is the place of the operation called embalming. Those who seek to obtain the art enter here, and become spirits by escaping from the body" (cw13 ¶86).

A brazen man with a leaden tablet commands the punished to write their inspirations with eyes upraised and mouths open — Jung: "might be compared with the technique of active imagination". The brazen man "is the priest who sacrifices and is sacrificed, and spews forth his own flesh". The vessel is the krater/vas Hermetis.

occurrences.title: Cista and serpent on Ephesian silver coin
occurrences.label: Cista and serpent on Ephesian silver coin
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: there are in fact representations of the magic basket with a phallus lying in it surrounded by fruits.
body: The synthema (confession) of the Eleusinian neophyte, handed down by Clement, beside the Ephesian cista coin (pl. at pdf p304). Dieterich reads the "working" as phallic activity; the basket with phallus surrounded by fruits is attested; Clement reports a snake in the mystical basket — "the danger that comes from the regressive movement of libido" (¶530).

image.title: Thyateira - 133-132 BC - silver cistophoric tetradrachm - cista mystica with serpent - quiver with two serpents - Berlin MK AM 18204059

occurrences.title: Krater with snake and lion — Mithraic monuments
occurrences.label: Krater with snake and lion — Mithraic monuments
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: "On the Mithraic monuments we often come across a strange symbol: a krater (mixing-bowl) with a snake coiled round it, and a lion facing the snake like an antagonist. It looks as if they were fighting for the krater" (¶671). Jung's decoding: "The krater symbolizes the maternal vessel of rebirth, the snake fear and resistance, and the lion raging desire" — a scene in which the opposing instinctual forces contend for the maternal container of transformation.

The same chapter reads the snake at the tauroctony: it glides to the blood flowing from the bull's wound — "the bull's life—its blood—is offered to the snake... a sacrificial offering to the powers of the underworld, like the blood drunk by the shades in the nekyia of Odysseus" (¶671). Bull's blood + snake = "a union of opposites," the cause "of the miraculous fertility that results from the sacrifice of the bull."
Verbatim: "The krater symbolizes the maternal vessel of rebirth, the snake fear and resistance, and the lion raging desire" (¶671).

occurrences.title: The liknon (winnowing-basket), cradle of Iacchus — Eleusinian procession
occurrences.label: The liknon, cradle of Iacchus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the cradle of Iacchus (λíκνον, mystica vannus Iacchi)
body: In the Orphic legend Iacchus was reared by Persephone in the underworld and, "after slumbering for three years, he awoke in the λíκνον" — the winnowing-basket as cradle of the buried-and-risen boy (¶528); cf. the Farnese stucco relief where Silenus holds the covered liknon before the veiled neophyte (¶536).

occurrences.title: The Lovatelli urn (Rome, ~1st c. CE)
occurrences.label: The Lovatelli urn (Rome, ~1st c. CE)
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The index files the Lovatelli urn at book p342, inside the Eleusinian-mysteries discussion (339–44): the famous Roman marble urn (Torlonia collection) carved with the ritual scenes — the maiden in the liknon/cista, the phallic pastries of the Haloa ("pastries, phallus-shaped, 342", index p613). It stands for the mystery vessel: womb, basket, and initiation box in one (cf. "vessel: symbol of uterus, 203", index p654).
Verbatim (index): "Lovatelli urn, 342"

occurrences.title: Christ in the Virgin's womb — Upper Rhenish Master (Germany, c. 1400)
occurrences.label: Christ in the Virgin's womb
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The unusual late-medieval iconography showing the Christ-child within the Virgin's belly, reproduced as Plate III (from Wachlmayr, Das Christgeburtsbild der frühen Sakralkunst). Jung invokes it at the point where Miss Miller's adolescent problem — "How am I to be creative?" — meets the mythological consolations: "Did not the Word become flesh? And did not the divine pneuma enter into the Virgin's womb?" (¶70).

His reading of the image's enduring power: "Why do we cherish the image of the Immaculate Mother even to this day? Because it is still comforting and speaks without words or noisy sermons to the comfortless, saying, 'I too have become a mother' — through the 'Idea spontaneously creating its own object'" (¶70). Reappears when the tube/hose of the Holy Ghost-dove fecundation paintings is discussed (¶150).

occurrences.title: Korion festival at Alexandria: the virgin Kore gives birth to the Aeon
occurrences.label: Korion festival at Alexandria
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: Epiphanius describes the pagan festival at the Korion in Alexandria: all-night songs and flutes, then, after cock-crow, torches carried down to a subterranean sanctuary to fetch up a naked carved wooden image marked with five golden crosses — forehead, both hands, both knees — carried seven times round the precinct and returned to the crypt. Asked the meaning, the worshippers answer: "Today, at this hour, the Kore, that is to say the virgin, has given birth to the Aeon".
Jung: the mother-goddess — like the star-crowned woman of Rev. 12 — is "usually thought of as a virgin"; the Christmas message "the virgin has brought forth, the light increases" is pagan.

occurrences.title: The Virgin as vas of the divine child — Venetian Rosario (1524)
occurrences.label: The Virgin as vas of the divine child
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the Virgin as the vas of the divine child
body: Plate 87: "The Virgin as the vas of the divine child," from a Venetian Rosario della gloriosa vergine Maria (1524). It follows the dream-31 commentary on the birth of the centre from the amorphous mass: "That this birth can issue from an amorphous mass has its parallel in the alchemical idea of the prima materia as a chaotic massa informis impregnated by the seeds of life" (¶244).

The Marian parallel confirms the vessel-family's Christian branch: the Mother as container in which the divine child takes form — the same structure as the alchemical vas bearing the filius philosophorum (¶338) and the dreamer's "uterus" point (dream 32).

occurrences.title: Virgil's Fourth Eclogue — the return of the Virgin (Rome, ~40 BCE)
occurrences.label: Virgil's Fourth Eclogue
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The messianic eclogue: "Now has come the last age foretold in the song of the Cumaean Sibyl; the great cycle of centuries begins anew. Now the Virgin returns, and the reign of Saturn is restored... Only do thou, chaste Lucina, favour the birth of the child, through whom the iron brood shall cease to be, and a golden race arise throughout the world" (¶119).

Jung's reading: proof that "even before the spread of Christianity, mankind was seized by wild, eschatological hopes of redemption" — the pagan expectation into which the Christian redeemer-figure was born, and the classical counterweight to Faust's opposite road (¶¶119-121).

occurrences.title: The beautiful woman standing in the dragon — gospel miniature, Bruges
occurrences.label: The beautiful woman standing in the dragon
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: there is a miniature which shows the 'woman,' beautiful as the mother of God, standing with the lower half of her body in a dragon.
body: In a 14th-century gospel copy at Bruges, a miniature shows the "woman" — beautiful as the Mother of God — standing with the lower half of her body in a dragon.

The footnote is one line, but the image is the Rev. 12 woman caught mid-metamorphosis: the radiant virgin and the devouring beast share a single body, the Terrible Mother and the benevolent mother not yet split.

occurrences.title: The Visio Arislei: the king's glass house, Thabritius and Beya
occurrences.label: The Visio Arislei — the king's glass house…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Arisleus is in danger of succumbing to the fate of Theseus and Peirithous … a repetition of the cosmic embrace of Nous and Physis.
body: One of the oldest allegories of the opus: Arisleus flees to the kingdom of the Rex marinus, where nothing is begotten because "only like mates with like." On the philosophers' advice the king unites his two children — Thabritius and Beya, hatched in his brain — in incestuous marriage; the son dies in the embrace; the party is imprisoned in a triple glass house (Beya's womb) for eighty days of heat; Pythagoras, seen in a dream, sends Harforetus with the food of life; the fruit of the immortal tree ripens and Thabritius lives again.

Jung: "its whole character relates it very closely to those visions known to us from the psychology of the unconscious" (¶392); he reads it as the descent of consciousness into the unconscious, mortificatio, and renewal (¶436-441), with the Ruska-discovered Codex Berolinensis preface naming the tree whose fruit ends all hunger (¶449).

occurrences.title: Vision 20: the unknown woman on the globe, worshipping the sun
occurrences.label: Vision 20 — the unknown woman…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A globe. The unknown woman is standing on it and worshipping the sun." (cw12 ¶110).

The anima is distinct from the sun: "the latter is a personification of the unconscious, while the sun is a symbol of the source of life and the ultimate wholeness of man" (¶112). "The dreamer's anima still seems to be a sun-worshipper, that is to say, she belongs to the ancient world" — scholastic intellect drove her to regress, as the Renaissance's Hypnerotomachia shows with Polia at the court of Venus. Early Christians themselves "had some difficulty in distinguishing the ἣλιος ἀνατολῆς (the rising sun) from Christ."

occurrences.title: Vision 22: the ape-man in the primeval forest and the Dionysian danger
occurrences.label: Vision 22 — the ape-man…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "In a primeval forest. An elephant looms up menacingly. Then a large ape-man, bear, or cave-man threatens to attack the dreamer with a club… Suddenly the 'man with a pointed beard' appears and stares at the aggressor, so that he is spellbound… The voice says, 'Everything must be ruled by the light.'" (cw12 ¶117).

Behind the nymphs "there lurks the Dionysian mystery of antiquity, the satyr play with its tragic implications: the bloody dismemberment of the god who has become an animal" (¶118) — Nietzsche, who knew "that the dismal fate of Zagreus was reserved for him." The pointed-beard intellect exorcizes: "the devil is the 'strange son of chaos' who can most readily be trusted to deal effectively with his mother" (¶119).

occurrences.title: Vision: the bear with four-coloured eyes, the tunnel, the treasure in the east (visual impression 39)
occurrences.label: Vision — the bear…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: In alchemy the bear corresponds to the nigredo of the prima materia
body: A waking dream: falling into the abyss, the dreamer lands before a bear whose eyes gleam alternately "in four colours: red, yellow, green, and blue. Actually it has four eyes that change into four lights." The bear vanishes; a long dark tunnel leads to shimmering light, a treasure, and on top of it the ring with the diamond — "this ring will lead him on a long journey to the east."

Jung: the bear "stands for the chthonic element that might seize him," but proves only "leading up to the four colours… which in their turn lead to the lapis, i.e., the diamond whose prism contains all the hues of the rainbow. The way to the east probably points to the unconscious as an antipode. According to the legend the Grail-stone comes from the east and must return there again. In alchemy the bear corresponds to the nigredo of the prima materia (fig. 90), whence comes the colourful cauda pavonis" (¶263).

occurrences.title: Vision 19: death's-head changing into a red ball, then a woman's head emitting light
occurrences.label: Vision 19 — death's-head changing…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A death's-head. The dreamer wants to kick it away, but cannot. The skull gradually changes into a red ball, then into a woman's head which emits light." (cw12 ¶107).

Faust and Hamlet skull-soliloquies stand behind it. "Evidently an enantiodromia, a play of opposites, has occurred: after being rejected the unconscious insists on itself all the more strongly. First it produces the classical symbol for the unity and divinity of the self, the sun; then it passes to the motif of the unknown woman who personifies the unconscious." (¶108).

occurrences.title: Vision: the black eagle seizes the golden ring; the ship follows (visual impression 58)
occurrences.label: Vision — the black eagle seizes the golden ring
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: Out of the egg… will rise the eagle or phoenix, the liberated soul
body: "The dark ring, with an egg in the middle." Then: "A black eagle comes out of the egg and seizes in its beak the ring, now turned to gold. Then the dreamer is on a ship and the bird flies ahead." Jung: "The eagle signifies height. (Previously the stress was on depth…) It seizes the whole mandala and, with it, control of the dreamer." Birds are thoughts and the flight of thought; the ship is the methodical vehicle over "the sea and the depths of the unconscious" (like Hinayana/Mahayana); "Man cannot walk the rainbow bridge like a god but must go underneath" (¶305).

The egg is "the chaos apprehended by the artifex, the prima materia containing the captive world-soul"; from it rises "the eagle or phoenix, the liberated soul, which is ultimately identical with the Anthropos who was imprisoned in the embrace of Physis" (¶306).

occurrences.title: Hildegard of Bingen's vision of the light (Bingen, 12th c.)
occurrences.label: Hildegard of Bingen's vision of the light
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.yearDisplay: 12th c. (Scivias period; Acta S. Hildegardis, Migne PL 197, col. 18)
body: Quoted by Jung for the light-vision phenomenon: "Since my childhood I have always seen a light in my soul, but not with the outer eyes, nor through the thoughts of my heart; neither do the five outer senses take part in this vision... The light I perceive is not of a local kind, but is much brighter than the cloud which supports the sun... While I am enjoying the spectacle of this light, all sadness and sorrow vanish from my memory" (cw13 ¶42).

Jung: the vision of light "proves to be something unconditioned and absolute, a combination of supreme power and profound meaning" at all times and places (¶42); such states bring in "a solution of psychic complications" and liberation (¶43).

occurrences.title: Vision: mother's hand with haloed fingers; the golden pheasant
occurrences.label: Vision — mother's hand with haloed fingers
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: A patient in hypnagogic condition sees his mother painted like a Byzantine church mural, one hand wide open, fingers swollen into knobs each surrounded by a small halo; associations: frog-suckers, phallus; then a skyrocket rises from her hand and turns out to be "a shining bird with golden wings—a golden pheasant".
Jung's reading: "Fire is bored with the hand; therefore fire comes from the hand; and Agni, fire, was worshipped as a golden-winged bird" (¶271) — the hand's spermatic-creative significance.
Verbatim: he saw what looked like a skyrocket going up from his mother’s hand, which on closer inspection proved to be a shining bird with golden wings—a golden pheasant (cw05 ¶271).

occurrences.title: Vision 21: surrounded by nymphs — 'We were always there, only you did not notice us'
occurrences.label: Vision 21 — surrounded by nymphs
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The dreamer is surrounded by nymphs. A voice says, 'We were always there, only you did not notice us.'" (cw12 ¶114, pdf 112).

Regression to an unmistakably classical image; the voice in dreams carries final, indisputable authority. The splitting of the anima into many figures equals dissolution into the unconscious — parallel: "the Paracelsan regio nymphididica, mentioned in the treatise De vita longa as the initial stage of the individuation process" (¶116). Jung adds the alchemical corollary: the vessel must be round like the head, and "the work is crowned by the production of the rotundum."

occurrences.title: Vision 5: the snake describes a circle round the dreamer
occurrences.label: Vision 5 — the snake describes a circle round…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "A snake describes a circle round the dreamer, who stands rooted to the ground like a tree." (cw12 ¶62).

Jung: "The drawing of a spellbinding circle (fig. 13) is an ancient magical device… He thereby protects himself from the 'perils of the soul'" — the same act that sets a place apart as holy, like the Roman sulcus primigenius at a city's founding. The dreamer has "succeeded in establishing a protected temenos, a taboo area where he will be able to meet the unconscious" (¶63). The snake is anticipatory: the circular movement will later grip the dreamer himself (¶129).

occurrences.title: Vision — the spark that became a star in the fathomless dark (Wickes)
occurrences.label: Vision — the spark that became a star…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: 'On the shaft there hung a human figure that held within itself all the loneliness of the world... Alone, and hoping for nothing, the One hung and gazed down into the void... Then deep in the fathomless dark was born an infinitesimal spark. Slowly it rose from the bottomless depth, and as it rose it grew until it became a star. And the star hung in space just opposite the figure, and the white light streamed upon the Lonely One' (¶344 n.47). Jung: 'a typical piece of individuation symbolism' — the Gnostic spinther, Eckhart's scintilla vitae. Cf. Zoroaster, who drew down sparks from a star and was scorched.

occurrences.title: Vision 7: the veiled woman uncovers her face and it shines like the sun
occurrences.label: Vision 7 — the veiled woman uncovers her face…
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The veiled woman uncovers her face. It shines like the sun." (cw12 ¶67).

"The solificatio is consummated on the person of the anima. The process would seem to correspond to the illuminatio, or enlightenment" (¶68) — against the rational 'elucidation' of the conscious mind, which "only satisfies the little tip of personality that is contemporaneous with ourselves, not the collective psyche that reaches back into the grey mists of antiquity."

occurrences.title: Symeon the New Theologian's vision of the inner light (Constantinople)
occurrences.label: Symeon the New Theologian's vision…
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.locator: index 'Symeon, "the New Theologian," mystic experience of light, 91f' (pdf p645); c01 mention at ¶141 (pdf p101)

body: The mystic experience of light of Symeon "the New Theologian" (index, book p91f). Jung quotes the vision at ¶141: "I realized suddenly that it was within me, and in the midst of my heart it shone" — the divine light as inner fire-substance, the same lumen Jung sets beside Hildegard's vision ("mystic perception of light, 91, pl. XXXa", index p565) and the pneuma-doctrines of late antiquity.
Verbatim (index): "Symeon, “the New Theologian,” mystic experience of light, 91f"

occurrences.title: Living stones streaming into the tower — Shepherd of Hermas
occurrences.label: Living stones streaming into the tower
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: human beings, streaming from the four quarters, inserted themselves as living stones, melting into it 'without seam
body: The vision behind the lapis angularis: "the temple built upon the foundation of the saints inspired in the Shepherd of Hermas a vision of the great building into which human beings, streaming from the four quarters, inserted themselves as living stones, melting into it 'without seam'" (¶11). "The Church is built upon the rock that gave Peter his name (Matthew 16:18)."

Jung sets it against the alchemists' cornerstone-Christology: "the lapis is frequently compared to Christ as the lapis angularis," and Mercurius as the peace-maker of Ephesians 2:13ff. who "might create in himself one new man in place of two, so making peace" (¶10). The tower of self-inserting living stones is the ecclesiastical twin of the lapis' "one homogeneous substance."

occurrences.title: Vision 6: the veiled woman on the stair — first appearance of the anima
occurrences.label: Vision 6 — the veiled woman on the stair
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
body: "The veiled figure of a woman seated on a stair." (cw12 ¶64).

"The motif of the unknown woman—whose technical name is the 'anima'—appears here for the first time" (¶65). Personification signals autonomous unconscious activity with an anticipatory character; the stair indicates ascent or descent. Jung then opens the initiatory row: the Stairway of the Seven Planets in Apuleius, the ladder as burial gift for the ka in Egypt, Zosimos' visions, and the solificatio in which "the initiand was crowned as Helios" (¶66).

occurrences.title: The 'Great Vision': the World Clock (second dream series, vision 59)
occurrences.label: The 'Great Vision': the World Clock
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.quote: It is a three-dimensional mandala—a mandala in bodily form signifying realization.
body: A vertical blue disc with white border, divided into 4×8 = 32 partitions with a rotating pointer; a horizontal circle of four colours bearing four little men with pendulums, encircled by the ring once dark, now golden; three rhythms — small, middle, and great pulse. The dreamer carries away "an impression of 'the most sublime harmony.'"

Jung calls it "a three-dimensional mandala—a mandala in bodily form signifying realization… Whatever a man does in reality he himself becomes" (¶308). The self is "the centre and the circumference of the conscious and unconscious systems"; two heterogeneous systems intersect in it (¶310). The figure may even be "a small-scale model or perhaps even a source of spacetime" (¶312). The 32 partitions lead to the Sepher Yetsirah's thirty-two paths of wisdom (¶313); Guillaume de Digulleville's rotating siècles supply the historical parallel (¶315ff.).

occurrences.title: Wachandi rite of spring — hole in the earth as woman
occurrences.label: Wachandi rite of spring
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Spring fertility-magic: a hole shaped and bushed to look like a woman's genitals; men dance all night with spears thrust into it, shouting "Pulli nira, pulli nira, wataka!"; during the whole ceremony they may not look at a woman (¶221).

Jung's reading: "a sacramental mating, with the hole in the earth representing the woman, and the spear the man" (¶214); the hole is "an analogy of the mother's genitals... a kind of mother-substitute" by which incestuous energy is desexualized and canalized (¶226).
Verbatim: In this rite of spring there is enacted a sacramental mating, with the hole in the earth representing the woman, and the spear the man. (cw05 ¶214).

occurrences.title: Wasserstein der Weysen (1619): the stone as 'Prototype of the heavenly Stone Jesu Christ'
occurrences.label: Wasserstein der Weysen
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: How that the terrestrial Philosophical Stone is a veritable Harmonia, Contrafactur, and Prototype of the true spiritual and heavenly Stone Jesu Christ.
body: An alchemical book of devotions of 1619: on page 67 the anonymous author promises to show how the rejected cornerstone (lapis angularis = Christ) "accords and is in exceeding subtle and artful agreement with the terrestrial and corporeal Philosophical Stone" — a demonstration occupying nearly fifty pages and concluding that the terrestrial stone is "a veritable Harmonia, Contrafactur, and Prototype of the true spiritual and heavenly Stone Jesu Christ."

The book "made a great stir, and even Jakob Böhme is to be counted among its admirers"; the historian Kopp was scandalized by "the blasphemous mixture of alchemical ideas … and religion." Jung: "We should not judge medieval naïveté too severely, but must try to understand what such an unwieldy language was intended to convey."

occurrences.title: Divine water gestated in sea-water — treatise of Ostanes
occurrences.label: Divine water gestated in sea-water
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The treatise of Ostanes directs that, in preparing the divine water, 'the vessel with the ingredients should be immersed in sea-water, and then the divine water will be perfected... gestated in the womb of the sea-water' (cw14 ¶317). Its self-description: 'This [divine] water makes the dead living and the living dead, it lights the darkness and darkens the light, concentrates the sea-water and quenches fire.' Because such water occurs in the oldest texts, Jung takes it as 'of pagan rather than of Christian origin' (¶317), kin to the Chinese 'flowing pearl' of the 142 CE treatise and to Komarios' 'blessed water' that brings the spring.

occurrences.title: The 'union of irreconcilables': marriage of water and fire (Indian painting)
occurrences.label: The 'union of irreconcilables'
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: a circumspect and farsighted synthetic procedure… the paradoxical union of irreconcilables
body: Plate 72: "The 'union of irreconcilables': marriage of water and fire. The two figures each have four hands to symbolize their many different capabilities.—After an Indian painting."

Jung sets it at the climax of the dream-18 commentary: "If reason is not to be outraged on the one hand and the creative play of images not violently suppressed on the other, a circumspect and farsighted synthetic procedure is required in order to accomplish the paradoxical union of irreconcilables (fig. 72). Hence the alchemical parallels in our dreams" (¶186). The four-armed deities — water and fire married — carry the quaternary completeness of the coniunctio.

occurrences.title: Isis the Prophetess to Horus: the angel Amnael and the shining vessel (Egypt, ~1st c. A.D.)
occurrences.label: Isis the Prophetess to Horus
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hormanuthi, Egypt (Berthelot, Alch. grecs I xiii)
body: In the Isis treatise Jung cites: retiring to Hormanuthi, "Egypt's [city] of the sacred art," Isis is desired by an angel of the first firmament; refusing him, she demands the preparation of gold and silver. A greater angel, Amnael, comes the next day "as the sun was crossing the midpoint of its course," bears the sign on his head and shows "a small, unpitched vessel filled with a translucent water," revealing the secret she may pass only to Horus (cw13 ¶99).

Jung: the angel is winged spirit, like Mercurius the pneuma; the shining water is the divine water of the art, the arcanum after prima materia (¶96 fn24). Amnael's meridian relation makes him "a kind of solar genius or messenger of the sun who brings 'illumination'" (¶105); his indecorous behaviour — angels and the daughters of men, Genesis 6:2 (¶105).

occurrences.title: Peratic crossing of the Red Sea — 'genesis outside of generation'
occurrences.label: Peratic crossing of the Red Sea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Hippolytus' Peratae read the exodus from Egypt as 'the exodus from the body, which is Egypt in miniature'; the crossing of the Red Sea is 'the crossing of the water of corruption, which is Kronos', and the arrival in the desert 'a genesis outside of generation' (cw14 ¶257). There 'the gods of destruction and the god of salvation are all together' (¶258). Jung reads the Red Sea as a death-water for the 'unconscious' and a baptismal water of rebirth for the 'conscious', making it the Gnostic twin of the alchemical aqua pontica and a figure of the transcendent function (¶257).

occurrences.title: The divine water that is 'the whole' — Zosimos, Peri tou Aeiou Hydatos
occurrences.label: The divine water that is 'the whole'
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Zosimos's fragment on the divine water (ὕδωρ θεῖον), the aqua permanens: "This is the great and divine mystery which is sought, for it is the whole [hen to pan]. And from it is the whole and through the sam e is the whole. Two natures, one substance [ousia]... This is the silver water, m ale and fem ale, which forever flees... It is the whole in all things. And it has life and spirit and is destructive" (cw13 ¶370).

Jung: "the water is wholeness" — a totality image already in 3rd-c. Greek alchemy; the quicksilver is a pneuma (¶371); the 'whole' is a m icrocosm whose attraction of the m acrocosm works "a kind of apocatastasis" (¶372).
Verbatim: Two natures, one substance [ούσία]. But the one [substance] attracts the one, and the one rules the one. (cw13 ¶370)

occurrences.title: Coins cast into the sacred well of the Amphiaraion — Oropos
occurrences.label: Coins cast into the sacred well…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: There were any number of entrances to Hades in antiquity
body: The healing-well as katabasis spot — "Presumably this Oropian well was also the scene of his katabasis" (¶572) — where incubation-healed patients pay the earth with metal. Jung follows the whole chasm-series: Aidoneus' gorge near Eleusis, the Hermione chasm of Heracles and Cerberus, the Areopagus fissure (¶572).

occurrences.title: Fount of the Saviour in secret Judaea — Gloria mundi
occurrences.label: Fount of the Saviour in secret Judaea
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The Gloria mundi invokes the aqua permanens as 'a very limpid water, so bitter as to be quite undrinkable... O water of bitter taste, that preservest the elements!' and locates its origin in 'that "fount in Judaea" which is named the "Fount of the Saviour or of Blessedness"' (cw14 ¶341). Jung insists the spring lies in a 'secret place' — accessible to no creed: it 'springs from the lumen naturae' (¶341), a 'secret Judaea' in man's inner life where 'the aqua solvens et coagulans, the medicina catholica or panacea, the spark of the light of nature, are to be found' (¶344). Alchemy as knowledge parallel to revelation (¶346).

occurrences.title: The temenos of Gaia Olympia and its fissure — Athens (Pausanias)
occurrences.label: The temenos of Gaia Olympia and its fissure
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the deadly flood flowed off into the fissure, back into the mother again
body: The fissure as one of "the doors of life and death" (¶578): the Deluge flowed off "back into the mother again, for it was from the mother that death came into the world in the first place"; honey-cakes are offered "that she may spare one from death" (¶571).

occurrences.title: Money-offerings into the lacus Curtius — Rome
occurrences.label: Money-offerings into the lacus Curtius — Rome
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: He was the hero who went down to the underworld in order to conquer the danger that threatened the Roman state after the opening of the chasm.
body: Curtius "was the hero who went down to the underworld in order to conquer the danger that threatened the Roman state after the opening of the chasm" — the yearly coin thereafter substituting for the human sacrifice (¶571); cf. the obolus to Charon, "the second Cerberus" (¶577).

occurrences.title: Synesius hymn: 'Fountain of fountains... monad of monads'
occurrences.label: Synesius hymn — Fountain…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Cyrene/Egypt (cited via Wirth, Aus orientalischen Chroniken)

jung.workTitle: Aion: Researches into the Phenomenology of the Self (CW9ii)

body: In a hymn Synesius addresses the divine as "Fountain of fountains, source of sources, root of roots, monad of monads art thou". The context is the Sassanid court debate (5th c.): the fountain of the Babylonian Hera was said to contain "the one fish... that is caught by the 'hook of divinity' and 'feeds the whole world with its flesh.'"
In Christian language pege ("fountain") means Mary — so invoked in orthodox and Gnostic circles (Acts of Thomas) — while in Christian symbology the crucifix is the hook that catches Leviathan.

occurrences.title: The wheel picture shown by Brother Klaus (Pilgrim's Tract)
occurrences.label: The wheel picture shown by Brother Klaus
occurrences.subject: n/a

jung.workTitle: The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious (CW9i)

occurrences.quote: We know from experience that the protective circle, the mandala, is the traditional antidote for chaotic states of mind.
body: The "Pilgrim's Tract" (Ein nutzlicher und loblicher Tractat von Bruder Claus und einem Bilger, 1488) records that Brother Klaus showed a visiting pilgrim a picture of a wheel that had long preoccupied him. Tradition connected the wheel with the great vision and the Trinity picture at Sachseln; Blanke doubted the connection.

Jung's reading: against Blanke's scepticism, the connection is "very probable on psychological grounds" — visions like Klaus's cause disintegration (the heart bursting into little pieces), and "the protective circle, the mandala, is the traditional antidote for chaotic states of mind", which is "only too clear why Brother Klaus was fascinated by the symbol of the wheel" (¶19).

occurrences.title: The wheel with twelve buckets that fishes souls from the deep — Acta Archelai
occurrences.label: The wheel with twelve buckets…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: scooped up the souls from the deep and deposited them on the moon-ship
body: The strange apparatus of the "son of the living Father" in the Acta Archelai: "He constructed a great wheel with twelve buckets which, as they revolved, scooped up the souls from the deep and deposited them on the moon-ship" (¶34).

Jung juxtaposes it with the alchemical rota as "the symbol of the opus circulatorium" and with the Manichaean angels who, alternating male and female form, excite the archons' sweat — "rain" for the Manichaeans, "dew" for the alchemists (¶34). The bucket-wheel of salvation and the circulating vessel are one archetype of rescue-by-rotation; cf. the twelve urceos of the Manichaean world-wheel already harvested from Aion.

occurrences.title: The Great Whore of Babylon — Burgkmair engraving, Augsburg 1523
occurrences.label: The Great Whore of Babylon
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: Engraving (fig. 22) of Revelation 17: the woman arrayed in purple and scarlet on the scarlet seven-headed beast, golden cup in hand — "Mystery, Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots".

Jung's reading: the seven mountains = Rome, the mother-city whose "sons" the kings commit fornication with; "In this primordial image of the woman on the dragon we recognize Echidna... Babylon is the symbol of the Terrible Mother" (¶315); her wine is a libido-symbol. She is cast out so that the heavenly mother-bride, New Jerusalem, may be attained (¶316-318).
Verbatim: Babylon is the symbol of the Terrible Mother, who leads the peoples into whoredom with her devilish temptations and makes them drunk with her wine (cw05 ¶315).

occurrences.title: The widow marries her son: Beya and Gabritius — Delphinas via Maier
occurrences.label: The widow marries her son — Beya and Gabritius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: she is identified with Beya—'the widow marries her son.
body: Maier reports the treatise of the anonymous "Delphinas," who "insisted particularly on the mother-son incest," and constructs the genealogical tree of the seven metals: the lapis at the top, whose father is "Gabritius," born of Isis and Osiris; after Osiris' death "Isis married their son Gabritius; she is identified with Beya — 'the widow marries her son'" (¶14). Maier adds an "Epithalamium in Honour of the Nuptials of the Mother Beya and Her Son Gabritius," which "was begun with the expression of great joyfulness, ended in the bitterness of mourning": "when the son sleeps with the mother, she kills him with the stroke of a viper (viperino conatu)" (¶14).

Jung links the murderous bride to Isis "who laid the 'noble worm' in the path of the heavenly Father, Ra" (cross-link isis-serpent-wounds-ra-egypt.md) and to Kerényi's Medea combination — "love, trickery, cruelty, motherliness, murder of relatives and children, magic, rejuvenation, and — gold" (¶16) — the core of the drama "instigated by the mother-world, without which no union seems possible."

occurrences.title: Wenonah conceives Hiawatha from the West Wind — Song of Hiawatha
occurrences.label: Wenonah conceives Hiawatha from the West Wind
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: from “wind and water” man shall be born anew.
body: Mudjekeewis, having slain the bear and become "the West Wind, the fertilizing breath, the father of the winds" — the Zosimos parallel: the entrant of the womb becomes pneuma (¶484) — begets the hero on Wenonah by breath alone. "From 'wind and water' man shall be born anew" (¶485).

occurrences.title: Winged and wingless birds/dragons — De Chemia Senioris
occurrences.label: Winged and wingless birds/dragons
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Another favourite theriomorphic image is that of the two birds or two dragons, one of them winged, the other wingless.
body: Two birds or two dragons, "one of them winged, the other wingless," from the ancient text De Chemia Senioris antiquissimi philosophi libellus (Muhammad ibn Umail). "The wingless bird or dragon prevents the other from flying. They stand for Sol and Luna, brother and sister, who are united by means of the art" (¶3).

Jung cites it as the archetypal form of the spirit/soul polarity in theriomorphic dress, alongside Lambspringk's reversed fishes (mare nostrum = the body) and his stag (soul) and unicorn (spirit) in the forest (body) — the latter already harvested from cw13. The winged/wingless motif returns in ¶141, where the winged dragon (quicksilver) becomes a poison-breathing monster only through union with the wingless dragon (sulphur).

occurrences.title: The tormos witches that eat darkness out of burning stones — Senior
occurrences.label: The tormos witches that eat darkness out…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: they conceive in the baths and give birth in the air
body: Marchos' parable in Senior: "There is an earth near us, which is called 'tormos,' where there are serpents [or witches] that eat the darkness out of the burning stones, and on these stones they drink the blood of black goats. While they remain in the darkness, they conceive in the baths and give birth in the air, and they stride on the sea, and they inhabit vaults and sepulchres, and the serpent fights with the male, and the male continues forty nights in the grave, and forty nights in the little house" (¶77).

Jung notes the Latin "serpent" renders Arabic jinn — female desert demons — under "the widespread primitive idea that the spirits of the dead are snakes," with goat sacrifice to chthonic numina. Continuation: the male's seed cast "upon the marble into the image [or spirit that dwells in the marble]," gathered by ravens who fly to unclimbable mountain tops and "become white, and multiply" (¶80) — resurrection as coniunctio of white dove and black raven, the ravens as "dark messengers of heaven, who at this point themselves become white" (¶81).

occurrences.title: Ixion on the sun-wheel — dream of an American Negro patient (~1900s)
occurrences.label: Ixion on the sun-wheel
occurrences.subject: patient-anon
occurrences.yearDisplay: ~1900s (Jung's US research on mentally deranged Negroes)
body: The clinical datum that forced the archetype concept: Jung "was able to convince myself that the well-known motif of Ixion on the sun-wheel (cf. pl. XLVIb) did in fact occur in the dream of an uneducated Negro" (¶154), found during researches on mentally deranged Negroes prompted by the sun-phallus hallucination of his Zurich schizophrenic.

His conclusion is the hinge of the volume: "These and other experiences like them were sufficient to give me a clue: it is not a question of a specifically racial heredity, but of a universally human characteristic. Nor is it a question of inherited ideas, but of a functional disposition to produce the same, or very similar, ideas. This disposition I later called the archetype" (¶154).

occurrences.title: Manichean wheel with twelve buckets that raises the souls of the dying
occurrences.label: Manichean wheel with twelve buckets…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.place: Hegemonius, Acta Archelai pp. 12f. (also Epiphanius, Panarium LXVI); Syro-Mesopotamian Manicheism
occurrences.quote: set up a wheel with twelve buckets, which is turned by the rotation of the sphere and raises the souls of the dying; these are caught by the rays of the greater light, which is the sun, and purified and passed on to the moon
body: The Living Father, seeing the soul tormented in the body, sends his beloved Son, who "made a device for the redemption of souls, and set up a wheel with twelve buckets, which is turned by the rotation of the sphere and raises the souls of the dying; these are caught by the rays of the greater light, which is the sun, and purified and passed on to the moon, and thus is the disc of the moon filled."

Jung quotes this (Part II ch. 5, n. 110) as a direct Gnostic-Mythological parallel to the alchemical opus circulatorium — the wheel/rota that elevates the divine soul out of matter — and immediately adds: "There are secret connections, or at least striking parallels, between alchemy and Manicheism which still need investigating" (n. 111).

occurrences.title: Tibetan World Wheel (sidpe-korlo) — painted banner, private collection
occurrences.label: Tibetan World Wheel
occurrences.subject: n/a
body: The sidpe-korlo or World Wheel, "which represents the course of human existence in its various forms as conceived by the Buddhists" (cw12 ¶123).

Jung keeps it strictly distinct from the khilkor (mandala): "the World Wheel is based on a ternary system in that the three world-principles are to be found in its centre: the cock, equalling concupiscence; the serpent, hatred or envy; and the pig, ignorance or unconsciousness (avidya)." — "Here we come upon the dilemma of three and four, which also crops up in Buddhism."

occurrences.title: Dionysius Zacharius: the Easter transmutation witnessed (1550)
occurrences.label: Dionysius Zacharius
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: Vidi perfectionem… conversum in purum aurum prae meis oculis
body: "After a fit of despair he revived with the help of the Holy Spirit and, applying himself to a serious study of the literature, read diligently, and meditated day and night until his finances were exhausted. Then he worked in his laboratory, saw the three colours appear, and on Easter Day of the following year the wonder happened: 'Vidi perfectionem'—'I saw the perfect fulfilment': the quicksilver was 'conversum in purum aurum prae meis oculis'" (¶365).

Jung's point is not the chemistry but the sequence: despair → Holy Spirit → study and meditation → the three colours → completion at Easter. "There is an unmistakable hint here that the work and its goal depended very largely on a mental condition" — the rubedo arriving as psychically conditioned event, dated like a resurrection.

occurrences.title: Zosimos to Theosebeia: be baptized in the krater
occurrences.label: Zosimos to Theosebeia: be baptized in the krater
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: she should, he says, hasten to the Poimandres in order to be baptized in the krater.
body: In his letter to Theosebeia, Zosimos — "a Gnostic who was influenced by Hermes" — recommends the krater as vessel of transformation and urges her to hasten to the Poimandres to be baptized in it.

The image comes from the Hermetic treatise "ho krater": after creating the world, God filled the vessel with nous and sent it to earth as a baptismal font, so that whoever wished to rise from the state of anoia (insufficient consciousness) could dip himself and partake of ennoia — enlightenment. The nous is a dyestuff, a tincture; its equivalent is the stone-extract, "which is also a pneuma and, as Mercurius, possesses the Hermetic dual significance of redeeming psychopomp and quicksilver" (¶409).

occurrences.title: Zosimos' Man of Light, Thoyth-Adam, and the daemon Antimimos
occurrences.label: Zosimos' Man of Light, Thoyth-Adam…
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: For our mind says: 'The Son of God, having power in all things and becoming all things when he wills, appears as he wills to each.
body: Jung's literal translation of the Anthropos doctrine in the Zosimos texts: the Son of God becomes all things to draw souls out of the dominion of Heimarmene. The first man is Thoyth (Thoth) to the Egyptians, Adam to Chaldeans, Parthians, Medes, and Hebrews — "virgin earth, blood-red earth, fiery or carnal earth" — his name spelled by the four quarters (Anatole-Dysis-Arktos-Mesembria), the cross-structured Anthropos. The Man of Light (phos) in Paradise is persuaded to put on the earthly Adam; Hesiod knew him as Prometheus, bound, with Pandora — Eve — sent after. Jesus Christ "made himself one with Adam and bore him up." Against him stands Antimimos, the jealous imitator who falsely claims to be the Son of God and whose Persian forerunner's name has nine letters. Nikotheos alone knows the Man of Light's secret name.

Jung: this Son of God is "a Gnostic Christ who has more affinity with the Iranian conception of Gayomart than with the Jesus of the Gospels" (¶457); Antimimos is the dark twin whose chemical parallel is Mercurius duplex in the Uroboros (¶460).

occurrences.title: Zwiefalten Abbey breviary: rectangular mandala with the Lamb
occurrences.label: Zwiefalten Abbey breviary
occurrences.subject: n/a
occurrences.quote: the deity is enthroned at the centre
body: Plate 62: "Rectangular mandala with cross, the Lamb in the centre, surrounded by the four evangelists and the four rivers of Paradise. In the medallions, the four cardinal virtues." Jung: "equally in the Western mandalas of medieval Christendom the deity is enthroned at the centre, often in the form of the triumphant Redeemer together with the four symbolical figures of the evangelists" (¶169).

The dream's square-with-gibbon "presents the most violent contrast to these highly metaphysical ideas" (¶169) — the Lamb replaced by the reconstructed ape. The plate anchors the Western squared-mandala family: centre + cross + tetramorph + four rivers.
